5929-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Wonders claimed and doubted fill chapters twenty-three through twenty-five of this second-volume Don Quixote portion. Chapter twenty-three treats the wonderful things Quixote said he saw in the profound cave of Montesinos, whose impossibility and magnitude cause the adventure to be deemed apocryphal. It was about four in the afternoon, sun veiled in clouds, when the cave adventure began, in subdued light.

Chapter twenty-four relates a thousand trifling matters, as trivial as they are, and chapter twenty-five sets down the braying adventure and a droll companion piece. Readers get Cervantes at his most playful, as Quixote's vision meets Sancho's skepticism and village humor. The part suits readers following volume two, since the cave tale tests belief, storytelling, and friendship at once.
a-lecture-on-phrenology-as-illustrative-:
A Lecture on Phrenology, delivered and published in 1826 by Disney Alexander, presents phrenology as illustrative of the moral and intellectual capacities of man. That claim was the young science's great promise: if faculties have organs, then moral and mental powers can be mapped, measured, and perhaps improved. A single lecture was the usual vehicle, given to a local audience curious about the new doctrine from Vienna and Edinburgh.

The copy preserved here rests in the University of Leeds Library. The lecture belongs to phrenology's first British decade, when itinerant lecturers and printed talks spread the system town by town. It shows the doctrine in its hopeful early form, offered as a key to human nature rather than a parlor entertainment.
arcandam-or-alcandrin-1626:
Richard Roussat's Most Excellent Booke of Arcandam, or Alcandrin, appeared in English in 1626. Arcandam was said to be an old wise man whose rules could reveal a person's destiny from his birth. The book belonged to a popular line of fortune texts sold across Europe.

Rules and tables let a reader work out character, health, and likely fortune from birth signs and numbers. Added material on physiognomy taught how faces and features could be read for the same ends. Such books were cheap, much used, and often condemned by clergy. This one shows the kind of everyday fate lore that ordinary readers bought long before modern horoscopes.
arxiv-2509-00026:
Abu Shad Ahammed, Sayeri Mukherjee, and Roman Obermaisser ask in 2025 whether machine models can help spot psychiatric illness in emergency care. Mental disorders shape conduct and can impair work, social, and family life. They are often misread, since signs are less visible than in many body illnesses. In a crisis, fast and sound spotting can save lives.

Data came from emergency psychiatric patients at a rescue station in Germany. The team tested classic machine models and large language models, including Llama 3.1, on conduct records. The goal was to judge if model forecasts can serve as a useful aid for staff. Such aids must support, not replace, trained clinical judgment in urgent cases.
arxiv-2509-00126:
Ionel-Dumitrel Ghiba, Robert Martin, Marius Apetrii, and Patrizio Neff gather facts about elastic energy models for solid materials in 2025 as a service to their field. In nonlinear elasticity, an energy function sums up how a solid stores work as it stretches. Two traits matter for sound use: whether stress can be mapped back to strain, and whether that map is monotone, which means it never reverses trend.

The team tests a collective list of isotropic energies, which behave the same in all directions, for compressible solids. Their own algorithm checks each stress-strain pair by computation. Results land in a yes-or-no table, the first such overview. The table will grow on arXiv as new energies are added over time.
arxiv-2509-00326:
Renat Sergazinov and Shao-An Yin present Chunked TabPFN in 2025, a way to run a strong tabular model on long data sets with no training and no pre-processing. TabPFN v2 beats tree-based models on many table benchmarks, which is notable since trees usually lead on tables. Its limit is ten thousand context tokens, set by the quadratic cost of transformer attention.

Instead of compressing context by picking sample rows, their tiled-block strategy computes attention in chunks inside the TabPFN frame. The design fits standard GPU setups. Tests on the TabArena benchmark show the method works. Long tables in medicine and finance could now use in-context learning as-is.
arxiv-2509-00426:
Yong Yang, working alone, studies restricted Heisenberg Lie superalgebras in 2025 over a field of prime characteristic greater than two, with the field closed under taking roots. A Lie superalgebra is a graded algebra where some parts commute and others anticommute, with signs set by the grade. The restricted form adds a power rule that prime characteristic makes possible. The Heisenberg type is a basic, low-step form of such an algebra.

Extensions that add one central element are the focus. A central element is one that commutes with all others, so such extensions grow the algebra in the mildest way. Yang uses plain first and second cohomology spaces, with trivial coefficients, to compute their restricted counterparts. Cohomology here is a tool that sorts extensions by algebraic data. As a use of that result, all restricted central extensions of dimension one are set out in full.
arxiv-2509-00626:
Maggie Chen leads six authors in total, with Hala Lamdouar, Luca Marini, Laura Martinez-Ferrer, Chris Bridges, and Giacomo Acciarini, on detecting methane from satellites. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas, and running machine learning onboard a satellite can speed detection while cutting the cost of sending data down.

Chen and her co-authors skip standard preprocessing by training on unorthorectified data, images not yet corrected for geometric distortion. Models trained this way match those trained on corrected data, and models on corrected data beat a matched filter baseline, a classic signal-enhancing method. They release model checkpoints and two ready datasets of hyperspectral images from the EMIT sensor, plus code, for faster plume response.
arxiv-2509-00926:
Wijdane El Hadri and Maryem Jemri studied charged black holes in a noncommutative version of anti-de Sitter space in a 2025 paper. Noncommutative geometry blurs points at tiny scales, an idea inspired by string theory. Their black holes carry electric charge and a smeared, bell-shaped matter distribution rather than a sharp center.

The authors first expand the mass and charge formulas for large black holes. They then work in extended phase space, where pressure and volume join the usual thermodynamic variables. Stability is checked, and the pressure-volume critical behavior comes out resembling a Van der Waals fluid, the classic model of a liquid-gas transition. A final section on Joule-Thomson expansion, cooling under expansion at fixed enthalpy, reports tidy universal results shared with other charged black holes of this family.
arxiv-2509-01026:
Kotomi Taniguchi leads a team of fifteen authors on aromatic infrared bands around WR140. WR140 is a Wolf-Rayet binary star system. Its colliding winds produce episodic dust shells. The team analyzes bands in the six to eleven micron range. Data come from the James Webb Space Telescope and its MIRI instrument.

Bands from carbon-carbon stretching modes are detected in both dust shells. They also appear in off-shell regions in the coverage. A carbon-hydrogen bending band is tentatively detected in the second shell. The features do not agree with established AIB classes A through D. Their peaks and widths match R Coronae Borealis stars instead. Those stars have hydrogen-poor conditions. The team proposes carbon compounds form from the carbon-rich WR wind. Hydrogen from the companion O star may then enrich them.
arxiv-2509-01126:
Cooperation can fail when selfish players exploit those who give, yet movement may offer an escape. Dhaker Kroumi studies how migration driven by local conditions shapes cooperation in groups placed on a structured population. Players take part in public goods games, where all share the gains from what members put in.

In Kroumi's model, cooperators move more often when surrounded by defectors, while defectors spread at a steady rate. This lets cooperators flee bad settings and cluster with each other. Cooperation grew when baseline movement, group size, and sensitivity to neighbors fell in the right ranges, even where it would normally struggle. The results show how flexible movement and local structure can jointly support shared behavior.
arxiv-2509-01626:
Scientific simulations produce data too vast to store or move easily, so error-bounded lossy compression, which shrinks data within a set error limit, is a leading remedy. Daoce Wang, with eleven co-authors, presents STZ, a streaming compression framework that keeps quality and speed high while adding flexible access. Progressive decompression, which refines data gradually, and random access, which reads any part on demand, usually degrade both.

The framework is described as the first to support both features at once. A hierarchical partitioning strategy enables streaming, and a matching prediction scheme offsets the quality cost of splitting the data, reaching quality comparable to a leading non-streaming compressor. Wang and the team also report high compression and decompression speeds, aiming at analysis workflows that need data on demand.
arxiv-2509-02126:
Ronggang Li and Shaoqing Wang stretch a classic theorem on curved spaces with a bound on bend. The Bonnet-Myers theorem says a space with bend that stays at or past zero must be closed and small. Their new forms give tests for closed form in a wider set of bend cases. Ways to bound the width of such a space come with each new test.

Uses cover spaces whose bend fades with range at a power law or fast drop rate. Even with fade, closed form can still hold under their terms in the proof. The work widens a base stone of the study of curved spaces. It also sharpens how fade in bend links to the whole shape of a space. More work may push the fade bounds yet more.
arxiv-2509-02226:
Borut Bajc and Katarina Trailović wrote a 2025 physics paper. It studies a thing called the holographic thermal propagator. The term names how signals spread in a hot system that has a gravity dual. Their work links that propagator, in four spacetime dimensions, to a special limit of a supersymmetric gauge theory. That theory also holds extra matter fields.

The authors work at zero energy to keep the math simple. They split the problem into two expansions. One covers low heat. The other counts instantons, which are brief field events. They show the second one gives quasi-modular forms. Those forms are near-symmetric functions, and they can be rebuilt from Eisenstein series. The low-heat series looks asymptotic. It helps at first but cannot be summed for good. That is a useful warning for later work.
arxiv-2509-02926:
Youngwoo Kim and 3 co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on uncovering the hidden rules that Reddit moderators actually enforce. Each community posts some rules, yet much day-to-day removal of posts follows unspoken standards. Those standards differ from one community to the next.

The authors turn past moderation records into score tables that link word patterns with removal. Their readable approach matched the accuracy of opaque neural models while showing its reasoning in plain form. Comparing many communities exposed quirks that shared rule books hide. Some places tolerated language that others removed, and some banned topics without saying so. Such maps could help moderators write fairer, clearer standards.
arxiv-2509-03126:
Christian Doh Dinga and 3 co-authors studied how to schedule flexibility in combined energy systems in a 2025 paper. Such systems link electricity, heat, and gas, and flexibility assets can shift when they draw or supply energy. Coordinating them well helps absorb variable wind and solar power at lower cost.

Growing numbers of assets that answer demand signals make coordination tangled. The authors propose a coupling method modeled on market auctions. It aims to keep providers autonomous and their data private while still scaling to large systems. Benchmarks against joint optimization and a price-response loop showed good scaling and schedules close to optimal in cost. Their open-source software lets providers and grid operators link models without exposing private details.
arxiv-2509-03526:
Yansong Liu and one co-author propose a 2025 method for improving speech large language models, systems that answer spoken requests directly. Such models still follow instructions and reason worse than text-based models do. The same request can trigger different behaviour depending on speaker, accent, noise, or hesitant speech.

Their framework, called VIRBA, groups several spoken versions of one instruction together during reinforcement learning. Responses earn rewards for correct meaning, checkable answers, stable behaviour across voices, and sound reasoning. A new optimisation method compares answers within each spoken group. Tests span spoken questions, distorted speech, and translation tasks. The largest gains appear on reasoning-heavy prompts and on speech distorted by noise or pauses.
arxiv-2509-03726:
Niclas Dern and five co-authors focus on sampling from Boltzmann distributions using continuous normalising flows in a 2025 research paper. A Boltzmann distribution weights each state by its energy, and drawing fair samples from one is central to molecular science. Complex energy landscapes make that sampling hard.

Generative models can help, but earlier energy-only training could not use advanced architectures well, while other routes needed ready-made samples from the target. Their Energy-Weighted Flow Matching objective trains flows using only energy evaluations. Importance sampling lets training samples come from any proposal distribution. Two algorithms follow: an iterative version refining its own proposals round by round, and an annealed version lowering temperature gradually for rough landscapes. On benchmarks, including a 55-particle Lennard-Jones cluster, sample quality matches established energy-only methods. The new methods need up to a thousand times fewer energy evaluations to get there.
arxiv-2509-03826:
A 2025 research paper by Tony Wells and ten co-authors measures spin-orbit alignment in two short-period eclipsing binary star systems. In an eclipsing binary, one star passes in front of the other. Alignment asks whether the primary star's spin axis matches the orbital axis, and misaligned systems challenge standard formation stories.

Photometry from the TESS space telescope joins radial velocity measurements from Minerva-Australis. One system pairs an F-type star with a small M-dwarf, the other a hotter F star with a late K-class companion. Both companions circle in two to three days on nearly circular orbits. Two analyses of the eclipse-time velocity wobble, classical and Reloaded Rossiter-McLaughlin, agree on a minor misalignment for both systems. The reloaded method gives smaller tilts but confirms the classical result. Even modest tilts on circular orbits are notable, suggesting gaps in current formation models.
arxiv-2509-04026:
In a 2025 mathematics paper, Mujin Choi and one co-author examine graphs excluding a ladder as an induced minor and containing no induced star. A ladder joins two equal paths with rungs between matching vertices. Excluding such configurations defines well-behaved classes.

The main theorem: for every ladder size and star size, graphs avoiding both have bounded tree-independence number, a width measure combining tree decompositions with independence. Boundedness matters: many hard problems become tractable on such classes. The method sharpens several known results along the way. It improves an existing bound for graphs excluding wheels as induced minors. Graphs excluding thetas or prisms with long paths also get bounded tree-independence number, improving a result of Chudnovsky, Hajebi, and Trotignon. Finally, an induced Erdős-Pósa type result extends from long induced cycles to all subdivided-ladder minors. Graph theorists gain one argument covering several separate cases.
arxiv-2509-04326:
Silvio Chito and two co-authors slim down a model for spotting the odd object out in a scene in a 2025 research paper. The task sounds simple: several similar items appear, and one looks different. Solving it demands comparing objects across views and layouts, which strains modern deep learning. Their model builds on DINO, a self-taught vision system, and trims one third of the parameters while cutting training time threefold compared with the best existing system.

Performance stayed competitive despite the diet. The authors also tested a large multimodal language model on the same task as a baseline. Its struggles reveal current limits in structured visual reasoning. Efficient odd-one-out detection could serve quality inspection and surveillance.
arxiv-2509-04626:
Under extremely strong magnetic fields, hot and dense quark matter behaves in ways simpler settings cannot show. Eduardo S. Fraga, lead author with two co-authors, compute key quantities for that setting in a 2025 paper on perturbative quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons.

Working to two-loop order at finite temperature, they calculate pressure, the chiral condensate, and strange quark number susceptibility, using physical quark masses. They also discuss cold, dense quark matter in a very strong field. Their discussion includes constraints relevant to quark magnetars, hypothetical stars with exceptionally strong magnetism.
arxiv-2509-05026:
Nickel-zinc batteries could serve stationary storage with safety and resource advantages over lithium, but their internal processes are poorly understood. The team set out to close that gap.. Felix K. Schwab, lead author with six co-authors, model and simulate an alkaline nickel-zinc cell in a 2025 paper. One cell serves as the test case throughout.. Their goal is deeper insight into cycling behaviour and zinc-specific effects such as shape change.

The runs rest on a thermodynamically consistent, volume-averaged continuum model. A prototype cell provides the reference for parameter estimation. It also allows direct comparison between simulated and measured behaviour. The authors aim to use that validated basis to improve cyclability and performance. The battery type itself has been known for a long time.
arxiv-2509-05126:
Reading out a superconducting qubit with strong microwave power can knock it into unwanted states. Cyril Mori, lead author with fourteen co-authors, study a readout scheme designed to suppress those transitions in a 2025 quantum computing paper. The scheme uses a nonlinear cos-phi coupling from a transmon molecule circuit, whose symmetry blocks parity-breaking transitions.

The team perform multi-state single-shot readout reaching the fifth excited state, revealing leakage paths from the computational space. Measurements show no measurement-induced transitions even at high photon numbers in the readout mode. Breaking the symmetry with flux tuning switches the transitions back on, confirming the mechanism.
arxiv-2509-05226:
Teaching math models to think only as long as a problem needs is the aim of Abdul Waheed and four co-authors in a 2025 paper on language model reasoning. Long chains of step-by-step thought help hard problems, but they waste time and tokens on easy ones.

Their framework trains models on worked examples whose length matches problem difficulty, with no change to the model itself. Fine-tuning mainly teaches length and format, while a preference method protects accuracy, and the two together shorten output while keeping or improving scores. Models can learn to think in proportion, using brief reasoning for simple questions and full depth for hard ones.
arxiv-2509-05326:
Proving a computation was done right, without revealing its secrets, usually needs memory that grows with the computation. Logan Nye claims a way around that limit in a solo 2025 cryptography paper. Large jobs and small devices have both been shut out by that memory cost.

Nye's system processes work in blocks with a space-saving tree method, cutting memory growth from linear to roughly square-root scale while keeping proof time similar. For common polynomial commitment schemes the proofs and checks come out identical to before. Hash-based systems gain the same memory savings with slightly different proof shapes. Smaller memory demands could bring private, verifiable computing to everyday devices and very large calculations.
arxiv-2509-05426:
Insurance companies can estimate unpaid claims better by learning from each other, Pengfei Cai, Anas Abdallah, and Pratheepa Jeganathan propose in a 2025 actuarial paper. Loss reserving uses past claim triangles, tables of payments over time, and each firm's data alone can be thin in the late tail.

Their model mixes company-level random effects with copulas, tools that describe how different business lines move together, allowed to differ by company. A penalty steadies estimates where observations are scarce, and a modified bootstrap gives full reserve distributions. On regulatory data from United States insurers, the model gave more stable splits of unpaid losses and lower risk capital than simpler benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-05526:
Special cycles on moduli spaces of bundles over curves are linked to derivatives of L-functions by Zeyu Wang in a solo 2025 paper in the Langlands area of number theory. Shtukas are the function-field objects that carry these cycles, and a Hecke eigensheaf is a special sheaf picked out by symmetry operators.

Wang relates certain classes built from that eigensheaf in earlier work to the part of the special cycles of matching type. As an application, the self-intersection number of those cycles, arising from the Rankin-Selberg period method, connects to higher derivatives of Rankin-Selberg L-functions. Such bridges between geometry and L-functions are a central theme of the relative Langlands programme.
arxiv-2509-05626:
Carbon dioxide struck by electrons can rearrange into molecular oxygen, Qibo Ma and seven co-authors demonstrate in a 2025 chemical physics paper. Double ionisation strips two electrons from the molecule, after which it may fragment in unexpected ways.

By imaging fragment ions and electrons together and measuring the incoming electron's energy loss, the team pins down the mechanism behind the carbon ion plus oxygen ion channel. Calculations of energy surfaces and trajectories reveal a path through a triangular intermediate shape. A second, roaming path appears when a carbon-oxygen bond almost breaks: the stranded oxygen wanders over flat energy regions before joining the other oxygen. Free electrons are common in interstellar space, so the process may matter there.
arxiv-2509-06126:
Game-like digital tools changed how a biomedical engineering course runs, report Gonzalo R. Ríos-Muñoz and two co-authors in a 2025 study. Their project-based course in biomedical image processing layered experiment tracking, real-time collaboration, and peer assessment over two years in a row of master's students. The aim was better collaboration, transparency, and fairness in grading.

Project outcomes, peer rubrics, and surveys tell a consistent story: the platforms supported accountability, improved group work, and made evaluation feel more equitable. Students reported stronger engagement and clearer performance criteria, while faculty monitored progress and gave feedback with less effort. Adoption hurdles and the need for instructor guidance remain, but the authors offer the setup as a replicable model for science and technology teaching.
arxiv-2509-06326:
Proving that the model running on your phone is the authorized one is the problem AttestLLM solves, in a 2025 paper led by Ruisi Zhang with four co-authors. On-device language models protect privacy and cut network dependence, but vendors need to verify legitimacy and guard their hardware-level intellectual property. Existing attestation was not built for billion-parameter models.

AttestLLM co-designs algorithm, software, and hardware: watermark signatures are embedded in the activation distributions of model building blocks, and the checking protocol runs inside a trusted execution environment without slowing inference. Tests across the Llama, Qwen, and Phi families show reliable, faithful attestation. The framework also resists model replacement and forgery attacks, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-06426:
A fruit fly's leg, rebuilt muscle by muscle inside a computer, is presented in a 2025 paper led by Pembe Gizem Özdil with seven co-authors. Near-complete maps of the fly's nervous system, muscles, and exoskeleton exist, yet no anatomically grounded leg muscle model bridged motor neurons to joint motion. The team builds the first three-dimensional, data-driven musculoskeletal model of Drosophila legs, in two simulation platforms.

Hill-type muscles are fitted from high-resolution X-ray scans of several specimens, with a pipeline that optimizes unknown fly-specific parameters. Combined with pose estimates from behaving flies, the model replays walking and grooming with muscle actuation and predicts testable muscle synergies. Imitation learning tests show joint damping and stiffness speed policy learning.
arxiv-2509-06626:
Censoring files on a supposedly decentralized storage network is shown to be practical by Jan Matter and one co-author in a 2025 security paper. The InterPlanetary File System, or IPFS, is the standard for decentralized storage in Web3. In practice, many nodes and content providers sit in large public clouds, which reintroduces central points.

Cloud concentration exposes IPFS to routing attacks on BGP, the system that directs internet traffic, including hijacking and passive interception. The authors gathered three thousand content identifiers and simulated such attacks against them. One malicious network operator could censor most content for more than half of all requesting nodes, and hijacking a small set of address blocks already achieves most of that effect. Countermeasures based on worldwide cooperative copying and hardened backup providers are proposed and validated.
arxiv-2509-06726:
Certifying how entanglement is structured across many particles, using a guessing game, is proposed by Carles Roch I Carceller in a solo 2025 quantum physics paper. Knowing the pattern of entanglement matters for building large quantum networks. The parties involved are distant and their devices uncharacterized, which limits ordinary tests.

Players receive quantum states with limited energy and play a discrimination game, trying to identify which state they hold. The best possible success rate forms a strict hierarchy set by how many ways each state splits and how large its entangled subsets are. One fixed measurement setting, shared by everyone, wins the game optimally whatever the structure is. Performance and noise robustness improve steeply as parties are added. Whole classes of entanglement structure can therefore be ruled out, certifying what a network actually holds.
arxiv-2509-06826:
Predicting a movie's age rating from its video is automated by Dipta Neogi and three co-authors in a 2025 multimedia paper. Streaming platforms face a flood of content needing MPAA ratings, from G to R. Older automated methods demand large labeled sets, generalize poorly, and learn features inefficiently.

Three contrastive learning frameworks are explored: instance discrimination, contextual contrastive learning, and multi-view contrastive learning. The best design pairs a convolutional-plus-recurrent backbone, which reads frames and their order, with an attention mechanism that prioritizes important frames. In the contextual framework it reached the top accuracy and a strong F1 score, and it handled the fine line between PG-13 and R content well. Several contrastive losses were compared. The finished model runs as a web application for real-time rating classification.
arxiv-2509-07126:
Kateryna Melnyk, Lee Friedman, and Oleg Komogortsev study gaze prediction as time-series forecasting for virtual reality in a 2025 paper. Gaze prediction is needed for addressing motion-to-photon latency and ensuring seamless foveated rendering, which renders detail only where the eye looks. Reliability is highly sensitive to single differences and to the eye movements being predicted.

The authors evaluate recurrent, transformer-based, and sorting-guided architectures for generalization across oculomotor events, using two data sets from VR headsets. Analyzing median and high-percentile error profiles across subjects reveals notable results variability: subjects with low median errors do not always exhibit the lowest extreme-case errors. Low median errors therefore do not guarantee robustness. The results find a gap in standardized scoring, arguing for high-percentile, subject-certain metrics.
arxiv-2509-07226:
Yann Alibert and 2 co-authors built a transformer-based generator in 2025 that invents realistic planetary systems. Full physics simulations of planet formation are slow and costly, yet they reveal links between planets in the same system. A fast generator that learns those links could help observers decide where to look for Earth-like worlds.

The model uses the transformer architecture, the sequence-learning design behind modern language models, trained on systems from the Bern formation model. Visual checks, statistical tests, and machine learning tests all show its fake systems closely match the simulated ones. As a trial, the team used known traits of one planet in the TOI-469 system to predict traits of two others. Cheap, believable synthetic systems could let astronomers test survey plans long before spending telescope time.
arxiv-2509-07726:
Abolfazl Ahmadirahmat returns with 3 co-authors in 2025 on glass formation in a colloidal monolayer steered by light. Colloids are tiny particles suspended in fluid. A dense layer of them, nearly two-dimensional, can freeze into a glass. Interfering laser beams impose a one-dimensional periodic potential on the layer. The particles sit caged in light-made grooves, whose strength can be tuned.

The team uses a mode-coupling approach for the study. They map the non-equilibrium state diagram for hard disks. The axes are density and the period of the modulation, at several potential strengths. Local packing competes with cage distortion from the potential. That contest produces a strikingly nonmonotonic glass-transition line. In places, a moderate modulation stabilizes the liquid state. A glass can then be melted merely by changing the external field. Light-controlled freezing could become a lab dial for glass physics itself.
arxiv-2509-07826:
Paulo Forni and 4 co-authors compute how electrons respond to magnetic probing inside a puzzling state of matter, in a 2025 condensed matter paper. The setting is the pseudogap regime of the two-dimensional Hubbard model, a standard model for materials like high-temperature superconductors. Magnetic order there fluctuates in spiral patterns instead of settling down.

Electrons are split, on paper, into chargons carrying charge and spinons carrying spin, within a gauge theory framework. Chargons settle into Néel or spiral order across a wide range below a transition temperature, while spinons handle the wobbling of the spin direction. The resulting spin susceptibility can be compared with experiments on real materials, helping physicists judge which picture of the pseudogap state is correct.
arxiv-2509-07926:
Benjamin Liber constructs number sets that avoid arithmetic patterns around a circle, in a solo 2025 combinatorics paper. Building on earlier work by Berglund, he gives a method for choosing subsets of a cyclic group with no k-term arithmetic progression wrapping around the modulus. Such constructions set concrete lower bounds on how large a pattern-free set can be.

The same constructions tightly bound certain chromatic numbers and raise lower bounds for cyclic Van der Waerden numbers. Those numbers, introduced by Burkert and Johnson, themselves bound the classical Van der Waerden numbers from below, quantities famous for growing extremely fast. Every improved construction narrows the gap between what mathematicians can build and what theory says must exist.
arxiv-2509-08426:
John Southworth and Dominic Bowman review stars that both pulsate and orbit a partner in a 2025 astronomy paper. Space telescopes now give long, precise light curves for most of the sky. The count of pulsating stars in eclipsing pairs has grown fast. That pairing is a gift. Eclipses pin down the stage on which the pulsations play.

Spectra taken over time add the rest. Masses and radii come out with no need for models. On top of that, pulsations read the star's deep interior, like a scan. Pairs caught before and after they swap mass show how such swaps rewrite a star's insides. Single stars cannot show that story. Silent pairs cannot either. Pulsating pairs can.
arxiv-2509-08626:
The CMS Collaboration reports the first measurement of D-zero meson photoproduction in ultraperipheral heavy ion collisions in a 2025 paper. In such collisions, lead nuclei pass close without a direct hit, and one acts as a source of photons. Data were taken at very high energy.

Photonuclear events are picked out by neutron signals and a quiet region with no particles. The mesons are rebuilt from their decay into a kaon and a pion. Cross sections are measured against momentum and direction. Results are compared with quantum chromodynamics calculations and a color glass model, probing how partons sit inside lead nuclei.
arxiv-2509-08726:
Luo Luo and 3 co-authors propose a new method for decentralized optimization in a 2025 paper. Many agents on a network each hold part of a shared problem, and the goal may be nonconvex, meaning it has many uneven valleys. Noise enters through random samples.

Their normalized gradient method aims to reach a near stationary point at each agent. A new analysis uses a Lyapunov function, a measure that tracks error and disagreement together. Bounds on samples and messages match known limits in the standard smooth case. Numerical tests show the method beating rivals in practice.
arxiv-2509-08926:
Waqar Ahmad and 2 co-authors tackle label noise in object re-identification in a 2025 paper. Re-identification matches images of the same person or vehicle across cameras. Wrong labels in training can sharply degrade performance.

The task is reframed as judging image similarity with a Siamese network, which compares pairs. A new outlier detector, Beta-SOD, models similarity scores with a mixture of two Beta distributions. A proof shows that mixture can be identified uniquely. Training mixes several losses for feature learning. Tests on person and vehicle datasets beat prior methods across noise levels from ten to thirty percent.
arxiv-2509-09426:
Dwarf galaxies were long studied as loners, but hydrogen surveys keep finding them in pairs and groups. B. Šiljeg and 10 co-authors quantify those multiples in a 2025 research paper. Dwarf encounters can ignite or suppress star formation and end in mergers. Optical studies undercount them because faint dwarfs fall below surface-brightness limits.

The team used an untargeted interferometric hydrogen survey covering thousands of gas-rich dwarfs. Companions were identified by sky separation and velocity difference, under both fixed and mass-dependent thresholds. Roughly one dwarf in eight has a companion under the stricter definition. In one mass range, the companion frequency was three times the optical estimate. Close pairs of similar-mass dwarfs show boosted star formation. The results demonstrate hydrogen's power for finding the small multiples that optical light misses.
arxiv-2509-09526:
A microphone array hears a whole room, but a smart system often needs to know what is happening in just one corner of it. Jinzheng Zhao and 8 co-authors define region-specific audio tagging in a 2025 research paper. The task labels sound events inside a chosen region, specified by angle or by distance from the microphone. Ordinary audio tagging labels the entire recording.

The team first studied which feature combinations carry the needed information: spectral, spatial, and position features. They then extended two leading tagging systems to the regional task. Tests on simulated and real datasets showed the task is feasible and their method effective. Directional features also improved ordinary omnidirectional tagging as a side benefit. Region-aware listening fits hearing assistance, smart homes, and surveillance, wherever the question is not just what sounded, but where.
arxiv-2509-09726:
Seiji Hattori and 2 co-authors present a method in 2025 for turning machine-checked formal proofs into readable plain language. Formal steps are precise but hard for a person to follow, so their pipeline first verbalises each step informally, then summarises recursively along the proof's own structure. Language models supply both the wording skill and the summarising skill inside that design.

For testing, the method ran on formal proofs written to mirror an undergraduate textbook's natural arguments, and its output was compared with the original human text. The team also applied it to the Lean proof assistant's existing library. Results are described as highly readable and accurate, suggesting formal libraries could gain a friendlier face without losing the checked proof underneath.
arxiv-2509-09826:
Kayla Duskin and 4 co-authors measure how Twitter's recommender and a user's own follow network jointly shaped election feeds in a 2025 study of the 2022 United States midterms. Automated accounts recorded both the algorithmic timeline and the plain reverse-chronological one throughout the campaign. That pairing lets the team separate what the ranking system did from what the chosen social circle already supplied.

The curated feed measurably shifted topic mix, partisan lean, and how much low-quality material and rumour surfaced. Personal networks often mattered more than the algorithm itself. Left-leaning accounts saw a smaller share of election items under curation, feeds tilted toward right-leaning sources overall, and rumour exposure rose for right-leaning accounts, with mixed effects on source quality.
arxiv-2509-09926:
Zhiyuan Huang and 2 co-authors bring foundation models to a lopsided learning problem in a 2025 paper on long-tailed semi-supervised training. Rare classes offer few labelled examples, while unlabelled data arrives with shaky machine-made labels that can mislead. Older methods train from scratch and grow overconfident on the common classes, starving the tail further.

The authors first prove that starting from a foundation model shrinks the hypothesis space, tightening the error guarantee and cutting a balanced error measure. Its compact features also squeeze the region where outliers can sneak in. Their LoFT framework then fine-tunes such a model cheaply, and a second version, LoFT-OW, faces open-world data that may contain wholly foreign samples mixed into the unlabelled pool.
arxiv-2509-10126:
Sumant Pandey and 1 co-author park a glowing liquid crystal droplet onto a cluster of gold particles with light itself in a 2025 optics paper. Dye-filled nematic droplets ring with whispering gallery modes, light trapped circling inside the sphere, and those resonances shift with size, shape, and surroundings. Optical tweezers grip the droplet and set it down on the gold cluster, where near fields flare up and feed the droplet's fluorescence.

Contact strengthens the circling modes and moves their colour detectably toward the red, a signature of true photonic-plasmonic coupling. Tuning reached seven nanometres while the resonance stayed sharp, and larger gold clusters tuned further. Pulling the droplet away reverses the shift, so the pairing works as a reusable, adjustable micro-resonator for sensing and light control experiments.
arxiv-2509-10226:
Speeding up finite element work on lumpy three-dimensional meshes is the goal here. Dominik Still and three co-authors present their method in this 2025 engineering paper. Their setting is tetrahedral grids. Their method avoids building the full system matrix. Instead, it works cell by cell, using numerical quadrature. Workers call this a matrix-free approach.

Turning the per-cell work into dense matrix-matrix products pays off. The code passes sixty percent of the hardware's peak rate, at least for low and moderate polynomial degrees. A mesh reordering step keeps nearby data close together. The payoff reaches a sixfold speedup over a standard sparse-matrix version. Tests use the Poisson and Navier-Stokes equations. Scaling runs on the Helmholtz problem show the method can handle large real-world cases.
arxiv-2509-10326:
Dmitry Lesnik and Tobias Schäfer present State Algebra, a framework for handling propositional logic with algebra, in this 2025 paper. Logic formulas are usually manipulated as symbol strings or truth tables. State Algebra instead organizes them in a three-level hierarchy, moving between sets, coordinates, and row decompositions, with each level tied to familiar meanings.

The design trades one guarantee for flexibility. Reducing a state vector by the default route does not always land on a unique canonical form, though fixing a variable order restores uniqueness. Giving up automatic canonicity can buy more compact representations for some problem families. The authors show how the framework expresses both search-based methods and knowledge compilation, and they sketch a natural path toward probabilistic logic and weighted model counting.
arxiv-2509-11026:
Ziang Li and 5 co-authors rethink how the explanations of language models should be graded in this 2025 paper. Models often give free-form reasons for their answers, which helps users trust them. Judging those reasons by a simple preference, mine versus yours, hides why one explanation beats another and gives model builders little to act on.

The team first listed the attributes that make a rationale good, drawing on earlier literature, then measured those attributes with automatic tools, model judges, and human labels. On two large preference data sets they found which attributes best explain human choices. Grading models attribute by attribute, with separate scores per trait, gave sharper comparisons than winner-take-all voting, and the authors argue for that finer practice.
arxiv-2509-11226:
Xi He wrote this 2025 computer science paper with no co-authors. It is part one of a two-part series. The topic is optimal decision trees. Such trees are now built by rough rules of thumb. He first wants a precise sense of what an optimal tree even is.

He gives four new definitions of the problem. Three bound trees by size. One bounds them by depth. Each reads as a clear recursive program, fit to run. He then derives matching algorithms from the definitions. The math builds the algorithms so they are correct by design. Known depth-bound axis-parallel methods fall out as a special case. The frame can stretch to even freer tree shapes.
arxiv-2509-11526:
Wenhao Tang and five co-authors teach a model to learn from hard tissue patches. This 2025 medical imaging paper treats digitized pathology slides. Such slides are gigapixel images. Cancerous tissue may fill a tiny share. Multiple instance learning scores small patches and pools the verdicts.

Standard attention pooling favors easy, obvious patches. Borderline patches get neglected. Yet those define good decision edges. The team's framework pairs a teacher with a student. A momentum teacher masks the salient patches. The student must then mine the hard ones. A consistency rule ties the pair. A global recycle network guards key features from the masking. On diagnosis, subtyping, and survival tasks across a dozen test sets, the method beat recent rivals.
arxiv-2509-11726:
Grzegorz Wiktorowicz and five co-authors use self-lensing binaries to probe supernova physics. This 2025 astrophysics paper treats pairs where one star passes before its compact mate. The mate's gravity briefly magnifies the star's light. Such systems may reveal the Galaxy's neutron stars and black holes.

Two population synthesis codes ran across the disk and bulge. Three supernova remnant models were tested. They differ in how fast convection grows in the exploding star. Distinct groupings of systems emerged. Lens mass and crossing time separate neutron stars from black holes. Close orbits split from wide ones. One delayed model gives up to ten times more lenses in the two-to-five solar mass gap. Realistic detection cuts slash the rates. ZTF and LSST should still catch a few dozen good systems.
arxiv-2509-12026:
Copying an expert well means copying the expert's attitude toward risk, not just the average score, argue Filippo Lazzati and one co-author in 2025. Their setting is imitation learning, where an agent learns from demonstrations instead of a reward signal. They ask the learner to match the full spread of the expert's returns, measured with the Wasserstein distance.

Ordinary memory-free policies turn out to be too weak for that matching job. The authors define a richer class of policies that can look back at history, then give two algorithms with proofs of efficiency, one for known dynamics and one for unknown dynamics. Simulations back the theory.
arxiv-2509-12126:
Why some wounds stall for months is the question a system of differential equations from Alinafe Maenje and one co-author models in 2025. The equations track pathogens, inflammatory cells, fibroblast cells, and collagen, together with the starting wound size, split between local and body-wide influences.

The authors first show solutions stay positive, as biology demands, then define a threshold quantity that decides when a wound-free equilibrium can exist. Sensitivity analysis weighs which parameters drive fibroblast behavior and that threshold most. In simulations, oxygen levels, pathogen and inflammatory activity, age, smoking, alcohol, and stress all shift the dynamics, and the wrong combination pushes the model toward delayed healing and chronic wounds.
arxiv-2509-12326:
A classic theorem says any continuous function can be rebuilt by a shallow network whose inner functions are wild and jagged. Michael H. Freedman and one co-author ask in 2025 whether ordinary training stumbles into that same wild geometry on its own, without anyone designing it.

Watching the Jacobian of the inner map across the data, they measure its texture through row patterns and minor statistics. The distinctive Kolmogorov-Arnold geometry does often emerge in vanilla single-hidden-layer networks. The authors sketch where in the space of model settings and task difficulty it appears, hoping timely tweaks to training could coax it out faster.
arxiv-2509-12526:
Chengjia Chen, Qiyuan Pan, and Jiliang Jing study polarized images near a rotating black hole in a 2025 paper. Recent work showed that the electric vector position angle of polarization vectors in near-horizon images is governed solely by spacetime geometry, regardless of plasma flows. That property makes polarization a clean probe of gravity.

The authors generalize the study to a rotating hairy black hole in Horndeski gravity, a modified theory where an extra setting, called hair, alters the spacetime. For a fixed viewing angle, the hair raised the observed angle for slow rotation but decreased it for rapid rotation. Its influence also depended on observer inclination and on the azimuthal angle of the polarization vector. The effect was strongest at low inclination within a certain angle range.
arxiv-2509-12626:
Tao Long and 4 co-authors present DoubleAgents in a 2025 paper on aligning AI agents with human intent in coordination tasks. Preferences for socially embedded work are often implicit, evolving, and hard to specify upfront. Delegating such tasks safely needs a system that can learn what the user actually wants over time.

DoubleAgents has three parts grounded in distributed cognition. A coordination agent maintains state and proposes plans. A dashboard visualization makes its thinking legible for user evaluation. A policy module turns user edits into reusable alignment artifacts such as policies, email templates, and stop hooks. Evaluation included a two-day lab study, three real-world deployments, and technical tests. Comfort with offloading tasks and reliance on the system both increased over time.
arxiv-2509-12726:
Shuzhen Lv and Sergey Kitaev count special pairings in 2025 that grow from knot theory and are named for Stoimenow. These pairings link to counts known as Fishburn numbers, and a recent question asked which groups of them are counted by the Catalan numbers.

Earlier work found five groups, each set by avoiding one shape. Lv and Kitaev now count all cases where sets of shapes are avoided at once. The full sweep is broader than the single-shape work and turns up links to nine known number lists. The results give a complete map for this corner of pairing counts.
arxiv-2509-13026:
Adriana Balan and Silviu-George Pantelimon argue in 2025 that being costrong is a trait a functor may hold, like being strong. Strong types are standard in computing science. The dual trait had passed with scant note.

Costrength proves to be a graded split law in disguise. The known link for plain monads thus lifts to graded ones. That link ties split laws to extensions into the Kleisli class. Cases are given for varied graded monads, with stress on the plain product case. Uses for optics and coalgebras close the work. The shift reframes old results cleanly.
arxiv-2509-13126:
Miquel Oller, An Dang and Nima Fazeli model soft touch sensors for robot grasping in 2025 with path-aware fluid-like contact. Touch sensors reveal the hidden face between hand and object. Their softness drives rich forces, yet that softness is rarely modeled well.

Their Hydrosoft model tracks how contact force spreads and how patch size shifts with path. The object state grows to hold spread forces from the sensor. Smooth math lets planners tune paths by slopes. Tests in fake and real grasps back the model. Path history proves key to true sensor dynamics.
arxiv-2509-13226:
Wenjie Deng, Song Jiang, Minling Li, and Zhaonan Luo study the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. These equations describe ideal fluid motion, and a central mystery is how violent behavior can develop. The team examines a non-implosion mechanism, a route where the flow avoids collapsing inward.

They prove that vorticity, the local spinning of the fluid, blows up in finite time while a time-integrated measure of the velocity itself stays bounded. Under an extra assumption on the scaling index, even the strongest version of that bound holds. The proof builds a refined framework around the null structure of the transport term and checks the stability of a self-similar model.
arxiv-2509-13426:
M. Elliott and B. Jones compute in 2025 elastic and spin-changing cross sections for spin-polarized atomic tritium across fields and temperatures. Rates govern cold trapped tritium vapor traits and trap life. Next spectrometers for neutrino mass need those inputs to set supply and cooling.

Elastic scatter rules total rates and sets cooling efficiency plus fluid traits. Exchange and dipolar spin flips set hyperfine trap lifetimes. New values span zero to high field and zero to warm gas ranges for tritium and hydrogen channels. Past hydrogen marks benchmark the work. Ranges extend far past prior coverage.
arxiv-2509-13626:
Amanda Chan and three co-authors address mental health information search in a 2025 paper. People seeking help early need reliable material. But knowledge bases grow slowly. They often miss the topics users actually ask about, or the informal words users choose. Retrieval systems then return weak results.

Their gap-informed framework overlays real user data, such as forum posts, on the knowledge base. This exposes underrepresented topics, and new content targets those gaps first. In a case study across four retrieval-augmented pipelines, targeted additions reached near-optimal performance. They needed far smaller expansions than random additions. Random growth needed impractically large expansions for the same quality. The authors present the method as a scalable way to build trusted health collections.
arxiv-2509-14126:
Viktor Lorentz and four co-authors present CrazyMARL in a 2025 robotics paper. It is a decentralized reinforcement learning framework for the job. Several small drones carry one cable-suspended load together. Cooperative aerial transport promises bigger payloads and adaptable shapes. Coordinating many aircraft through bent load dynamics has defeated earlier approaches. Cables switch between slack and taut, and earlier work assumed rigid links.

CrazyMARL learns direct motor control policies for each drone without a central coordinator. It explicitly faces the slack-taut transitions. In simulation, the learned policies beat classical local controllers on disturbance rejection and tracking precision. They recovered from harsh conditions far more often. The policies transferred to real hardware with no further training. They stayed robust under wind, random pushes, and cable mode changes.
arxiv-2509-14226:
Morris Brooks and David Mitrouskas study the renormalized Nelson model in 2025, a model of a quantum particle coupled to a field. They work in a regime where the field turns classical while the particle stays quantum. A small parameter measures how classical the field is.

Particle and field move on very different time scales in that regime. The coupled Schrödinger and Klein-Gordon system makes the split explicit. Applying the adiabatic principle, which assumes slow change for the field, yields a new field equation with no small parameter left. The field is driven by the particle ground state at each instant. Their main result shows the new equation closely approximates the full Nelson dynamics in norm.
arxiv-2509-14326:
Philippa S. Cole and Jacopo Fumagalli present pbhstat in 2025, a public Python package for primordial black holes. Such black holes may have formed in the early universe from dense patches. Given a starting power spectrum, researchers need their mass spread and total share.

The package computes both outputs in a modular framework that offers several statistical routes. Options include Press-Schechter theory, peaks theory and methods based on the nonlinear compaction function. Users can compare routes within one tool rather than rebuilding code for each. The current version is limited to cases with nearly Gaussian starting conditions. Even with that limit, a shared package should make abundance claims easier to check and reproduce across studies.
arxiv-2509-14626:
Feiran Qin and four co-authors test coverage guided fuzzing in 2025 for deep learning library interfaces such as PyTorch. Fuzzing feeds random inputs to find bugs, and coverage guidance steers inputs toward unexplored code. Library application interfaces are vast, so guidance could matter greatly.

Prior deep learning testing used interface level or model level fuzzing without coverage guidance. The study asks whether LibFuzzer style guidance improves coverage, bug finding and scalability in this setting. A key hurdle is bridging a native fuzzer with Python library code. Results give the first in depth answer for this combination. Library bugs sit beneath major AI applications, so better automated hunting has wide downstream value.
arxiv-2509-14926:
Amirhossein Yousefiramandi and Ciaran Cooney pre-train language models specifically for patent text in a 2025 paper. Patents are long, technical, and legally structured, and general models lose accuracy on them. Earlier patent systems mostly fine-tuned general models or adapted them on limited data.

The authors pre-train three masked language models on a curated corpus of more than sixty million patent records, using the ModernBERT architecture. Speed and memory features include FlashAttention, rotary embeddings, and gated feed-forward layers. On four patent classification tasks, their base model beats the general ModernBERT baseline on three and rivals a dedicated PatentBERT system. Further runs with variant and larger models examine how scale and tokenizer choices affect patent performance.
arxiv-2509-15126:
Pierre Marchand and five co-authors follow complex organic molecules from collapsing cloud to young disk in a 2025 astrochemistry paper. Such molecules, built from carbon chains and rings of atoms, are thought to seed prebiotic chemistry. They are observed around many young stars, but where each species forms along the way is unsettled.

An analytical star formation code supplies the physical history, while a chemical network code evolves abundances through collapse and into the disk's midplane up to the end of the Class I stage. Most species form mainly during collapse or inside the disk. The lightest ones, including methanol and several nitriles, are substantially inherited from the prestellar phase instead. Over the disk's first phase, some abundances barely move while others swing by a factor of ten.
arxiv-2509-15226:
Abhishek Basu and four co-authors tune the trust levels of medical image-text models in a 2025 paper. Such models pair scans with text and do well on many clinic tasks. Yet how much trust their stated confidence deserves is barely studied. Bold, wrong calls can mislead care and break trust in the tools.

Their frame, CalibPrompt, is the first to tune that trust while the prompts of the model are learned. Labeled data are scarce in this setting, so the method learns just a small prompt set. One rule pulls stated confidence toward smoothed hit rates. A second rule spreads text features by angle so confidence reads more truly. Broad tests check whether trust can rise without giving up the hit rates that made the models prized.
arxiv-2509-15326:
Daniel Pérez-Troncoso presents DCEtool, an R package for building choice tests, in a solo 2025 paper. Choice tests ask people to pick among goods set out by their traits. The picks reveal how much each trait is worth. The worth of the answers rests on the test design: which mixes of traits get shown to whom.

Early designs chased orthogonality, a straight-line rule later shown to misfit choice models, which are nonlinear by nature. Sharp designs that cut the spread of the gauges became the norm, but they lived in paid software. DCEtool pairs that sharp design math with a Shiny screen-based front end. New and seasoned users alike can build sound designs for free, for use in health, transport, and market studies.
arxiv-2509-15726:
Marco Mordacci and Michele Amoretti train quantum circuits with a swarm method instead of slopes. Quantum classifiers have settings that must be tuned. Slope based tuning can stall on flat regions called barren plateaus, where the signal fades. A swarm search, modeled on flocking birds, needs no slopes at all.

Their swarm tunes the whole circuit: which gates to use, which qubits they hit, and the turn angles. Only four gate types are on offer. They test the method on medical image sets built for classification. Against slope tuning of a fixed circuit, the swarm matches or beats accuracy. It does so with fewer quantum gates.
arxiv-2509-15826:
Leon Hannig leads a team that compares a university's own chatbot with a commercial one. Many campuses now adapt a rented language model service into a house chatbot. Most past study covers the tech side, not how users feel about the changes. The team ask whether visible tweaks, like the interface, shape trust and use.

In a field study at a German university, over five hundred students and staff took part. Those who used both systems trusted the campus bot more. They also felt it guarded privacy better and saw fewer made up answers from it. The team draw lessons for tuned trust: users should trust a system as much as it deserves, no more. They give design advice for campus bots.
arxiv-2509-16026:
Systems that obey energy rules, like planets or swinging arms, are often traced with computer steps of fixed size. Konrad Janik and Peter Benner study neural tools that learn such steppers when data arrive at uneven time gaps. They extend a known network type to handle systems whose rules also change with time.

The pair prove that their networks can match any smooth stepper for a broad class of separable systems. They also show the same promise cannot hold for systems outside that class. Tests with varied step sizes back the theory. They also fix an error in a prior proof about matching such maps.
arxiv-2509-16226:
Learning a hidden rule from a few examples is a core skill of science, and one that language models still find hard. Brian S. Lin and ten co-authors frame this skill as a test task drawn from real scientific discovery, where rules cannot be written as plain equations. Their new benchmark checks whether models can infer such rules in fresh settings and apply them well.

Tests show current models struggle with the task. The gap marks how far models remain from human-like induction in novel worlds. The benchmark gives researchers a shared yardstick for tracking progress on this front.
arxiv-2509-16326:
Judging AI-written tissue reports is hard, since standard text scores miss whether the clinical facts are right. Yunsoo Kim and four co-authors build HARE, a grading frame that compares the key entities and their links in a draft report against a reference. They hand-labeled more than fourteen hundred real reports to build the test set and train the extraction models.

Their models scored best among those tried at pulling out entities and links. The HARE score also tracked expert judgments better than word-overlap scores and a radiology grader. The full set of data and models is released for others to use.
arxiv-2509-16426:
Sea ice resists simple flow laws: the classic continuum model works for packed ice but fails at the loose edges, while floe-by-floe simulation is too slow for whole oceans. Gonzalo G. de Diego and Georg Stadler learn a flow law straight from floe simulation data, using a neural network for the ice's effective thickness response. The physics equations are built into the training itself.

The learned law captures complex ice motion across a wide range of ice cover. Viscosity swings by orders of magnitude with tiny changes in cover, and the law transfers to new forcing and time-varying cases. That opens a path to fast, faithful polar forecasts.
arxiv-2509-16726:
Kaixing Cao, in a second solo paper in this set, compares two cohomology theories in a 2025 study. Both theories attach algebraic data to geometric objects over a special number field. One is named for Hyodo and Kato. The other refines crystal-like data on a curve named for Fargues and Fontaine.

Cao proves the two give the same bundles on that curve. The proof respects the full structure of the objects. Adding symmetry actions makes the match canonical, with no arbitrary choices. A payoff is a graded chain for a key cohomology of smooth spaces. The work ties two deep toolkits into one.
arxiv-2509-16926:
Ragib Amin Nihal, Benjamin Yen, Takeshi Ashizawa, and Kazuhiro Nakadai align multi-channel audio with a confidence score in a 2025 paper. Recorders in the field drift apart over time, and the drift is rarely linear. Alignment tools must fix the drift and say how sure they are. Their cross-attention method does both.

Tests come from bioacoustic monitoring, where many recorders track wildlife. The method should transfer to spatial audio and sound localization tasks. Code is shared in public. Confidence scores let researchers drop shaky alignments before they skew counts of animal calls or maps of sound sources in a habitat.
arxiv-2509-17026:
W. Desrat and co-authors grow a rare form of boron nitride crystal in a 2025 materials paper. Boron nitride usually forms a hexagonal layered phase. A rhombohedral phase, with a shifted stacking, is harder to grow well. The team use an iron flux at normal pressure to grow it.

The shell they grew holds many small triangular crystals, mostly in the rare phase. X-ray checks found only weak traces of the common phase. Laser spectra match calculations for the rare phase's symmetry. Good crystals of this phase could serve deep-ultraviolet optics and quantum light sources, where boron nitride is already prized.
arxiv-2509-17126:
Stefanos Chaliasos and co-authors attack the pricing of blockchain rollups in a 2025 paper. Rollups scale Ethereum by running transactions on a second layer and settling on the main chain. They secure tens of billions in assets. Fees inside rollups, though, can misprice the true cost of a transaction, and that gap invites attack.

One attack, dubbed a prover killer, slowed finalization by a huge factor in their tests. The team propose broad mitigations for the pricing flaws. They also suggest practical fee designs that fix the mis-pricing. Rollup builders can use the findings to harden systems that now guard very large sums.
arxiv-2509-17326:
Efrén Morales-Amaya, writing alone, proves a shape theorem in a 2025 arXiv paper on convex geometry. A convex body is a solid with no dents. Fix a point inside it, slice the body by every flat plane through that point, and ask when each slice carries a symmetry plane of its own. Points with that property are called Larman points, with a stricter cousin called a revolution point.

The paper studies a body that has a Larman point which is not a revolution point. It adds that every slice's symmetry plane runs parallel to one fixed hyperplane. Under those terms, Morales-Amaya proves the body must be an ellipsoid of revolution. Its axis stands at a right angle to the fixed hyperplane. The result ties a weak local symmetry clue to a very rigid global shape.
arxiv-2509-17426:
Fernanda M. Baêta and Monika Ludwig study when functionals on function spaces vary in a controlled way. Their 2025 arXiv paper proves results on upper and lower semicontinuity for functionals built on convex functions and more general ones. Semicontinuity is the one-sided form of continuity that optimization theory leans on when exact limits fail.

The headline result handles a functional formed by integrating a concave weight of a measure density tied to the function. Under two growth conditions on the weight, the functional depends upper semicontinuously on the function. The measure in play is the absolutely continuous part of a Radon measure linked to each input function. Examples include functional affine surface areas for convex functions, a topic in modern convex geometry. The proofs give analysts a firmer grip on how such surface-like quantities behave under limits of functions.
arxiv-2509-17626:
Jan Moser, writing alone, presents new results in analytic number theory in a 2025 arXiv paper. The work grows from asymptotic formulae he derived in 1981 for the derivative of Hardy's Z function, a real-valued form of the Riemann zeta function on its critical line. Those formulae now serve as the base for fresh constructions.

Moser builds new functionals from them and states corresponding zeta-equivalents of the Fermat-Wiles theorem, recasting that famous result in zeta terms. He also argues that the Lindelöf hypothesis exerts an essential influence on where the odd-order roots of a key equation lie. The paper is brief and dense, aimed at specialists in zeta function theory. Its claims rest on the author's long-running Jacob's ladder framework, which readers will need from his earlier work.
arxiv-2509-18026:
Brian Harvie and Ye-Kai Wang pin down the shape of static black holes in a curved space with a twist. Their 2025 paper works in three dims, for spaces that look locally like a hyperbolic world far out. A horizon, the edge past which light cannot flee, bounds each such space.

For one class, they show the space must match a known Kottler form. For round far fields, they bound the horizon's surface pull from below, with one known case as the sole match. For hyperbolic far fields, a mass rule holds in reverse. Those facts yield sole-form results for a class of fillings.
arxiv-2509-18326:
Medical AI systems must flag scans that look unlike anything they were trained on. That flagging step is called out-of-distribution detection, and it matters for safe use in clinics. Chun Kit Wong and five co-authors study it for fetal ultrasound, where scan quality and clinic settings vary a lot. Their 2025 paper asks a fresh question: does the sorting task itself change how well the flagging works?

The team tested eight ways of measuring model uncertainty across four sorting tasks. Flagging skill changed a lot with the task, and the best task depended on the kind of shift. A shift could come from image traits or from a change in body parts shown. They also found that strong flagging did not ensure the best held-back predictions. Task choice and uncertainty method must fit the real clinic use.
arxiv-2509-18426:
Test gear for radio circuits must be calibrated before it can measure well. Ziad Hatab, Michael Ernst Gadringer, Arash Arsanjani, and Wolfgang Boesch improve one calibration route in this 2025 paper. The route is the symmetric-reciprocal-match method for vector network analyzers. It normally assumes one standard part, the match, is known in full.

The team shows the match can instead be modeled with any curve that varies with frequency. A global search procedure finds that model on its own. In number tests, the method recovered the true match model down to software precision. On real microstrip line measurements, results matched a trusted multi-line calibration. So the new route reaches the same accuracy without a pre-defined match. That frees labs from keeping a perfectly known standard on hand.
arxiv-2509-18626:
Self-driving systems learn mostly from safe, uneventful driving, so they get little guidance near the edge of danger. Jay Patrikar and five co-authors argue for learning from negative data in this 2025 paper. Crash reports hold exactly the contrast that safe logs lack. But reports are messy: third-person stories, loosely tied to what the car's sensors saw.

The team rewrites crash stories into the car's own point of view. Logs and crashes alike become a shared scene-and-action format that can be searched. At decision time, the system pulls matching precedents to judge a proposed action. A counterfactual step drafts other actions, pulls their precedents too, and weighs all outcomes. On a standard benchmark, recall of the context-preferred action more than doubled. The added step also sharpened choices near risk. The authors frame crash data as a usable teacher.
arxiv-2509-18826:
Grouping data into clusters is easier when the similarity graph is clean, and many methods secretly relax the same ideal problem. Wenlong Lyu, Yuheng Jia, Hui Liu, and Junhui Hou revisit graph clustering from that angle in this 2025 paper. Spectral methods and factorization methods all trace back to kernel k-means, they note. Each relaxes several hard constraints to stay computable.

The team argues those stacked relaxations cost accuracy. Their model, LoRD, relaxes only the orthonormal constraint and keeps the rest, yielding probabilistic clusters. A block-diagonal booster, B-LoRD, sharpens the result further. A reworked constraint keeps the problem solvable, and a projected gradient method provably converges. Wide experiments validate both models. Code is public. The message: relax less, and clustering improves.
arxiv-2509-19026:
Dou Wang and fifteen co-authors settle a timing question for the CEPC, a planned circular collider in China about 100 kilometers around. The machine's radio-frequency systems and its detectors must share one clock, or signals get sampled at the wrong moment. The accelerator team and detector team restudied the timing plan together.

They set the bunch pattern so that gaps between neighboring bunches are whole multiples of a fixed spacing, about 23 nanoseconds. A master clock of about 43 megahertz, locked to the beam, will feed the detector systems. The team also found that a small change to the ring's circumference, bringing it closer to exactly 100 kilometers, would help detector operation over the first ten years.
arxiv-2509-19426: Daniel Grumiller and two co-authors sum up the key facts about Carroll spinors. Carroll spinors sit at the edge of math and physics. The note is short and crisp by design. It is also a tribute. It honors Dharam Ahluwalia, a strong voice for ELKO spinors. The source claims no more than that. Readers get a brief guide to the topic, plus the dedication.
arxiv-2509-19526:
Neural models of moving systems often leak or gain energy, so long forecasts drift into nonsense. Ali Baheri and Lars Lindemann build a learning method that respects energy rules by design. Their method splits motion into a part that keeps energy and a part that spends it, following a classic physics frame. Training matches short moves only, which avoids costly long simulations.

At run time, a two-step sampler keeps energy from creeping up. An optional check can force strict energy decay when a trusted energy value is known. On a controlled mechanics test, forecasts matched the true paths more closely than a free-form rival. False energy gains were far rarer. The work targets systems such as machines and fluids, where energy honesty is not optional.
arxiv-2509-19926:
Detecting Alzheimer's disease from speech transcripts can be as simple as prompting a large language model, with no training at all. Jana Sweidan, Mounim A. El-Yacoubi, and Nasredine Semmar sharpen that trick on the ADReSS benchmark. Few-shot prompts use balanced examples, up to twenty per class, under a strict answer schema. Two variants push further.

One anchors each example's probability to bands of the Mini-Mental State Examination, a standard cognitive score. The other adds reasoning traces drafted by a multimodal model that saw the test picture and transcript. Both reach accuracy near the top reported for prompting methods. Transcript-only testing keeps the setup realistic for clinics. Cheap, training-free screening could flag patients for fuller workups earlier.
arxiv-2509-20126:
Hannah Clercx and Rudie Kunnen wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on fluid experiments. They study convection in a rotating cylinder of water. Heat drives the flow while steady rotation shapes it, a setup that mimics flows at planetary scale. The authors focus on how heat transfer depends on a property called the Prandtl number.

The Prandtl number compares how fast momentum and heat spread through a fluid. By changing the water temperature, the team covered a modest range of its values. They measured the Nusselt number, which gauges how well convection carries heat. Doubling the Prandtl number cut heat transfer by about a quarter. The authors link the drop to changes in the thin boundary layers near the plates. Sidewall temperature readings also let them gauge heat carried by a wall-bound flow mode.
arxiv-2509-20526:
Molecules that assemble themselves could in principle compute, and Erin Crawley, Qian-Ze Zhu, and Michael Brenner find the equilibrium limits of that idea in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their benchmark is the directed Hamiltonian path problem, a classic hard problem. Particles with directional lock-and-key patches encode it, and assembled chains spell out candidate paths. Off-target binding and runaway competing structures have blocked practical versions.

The authors derive the energy gap needed between correct and incorrect binding for the encoding to work. They also ask whether components with that gap can actually be designed. Combining both answers gives a phase diagram of where problem instances are both encodable and solvable. The diagram sets fundamental upper bounds on equilibrium molecular computing. Scalable designs, the authors conclude, will need non-equilibrium machinery.
arxiv-2509-20626:
How strongly a material's electrons magnetize as a whole is hard to write down once they interact. Jian Kang, Minxuan Wang, and Oskar Vafek derive the needed formulas in a 2025 arXiv paper. They work in the Hartree-Fock scheme, where each electron feels the mean field of the rest. Their orbital magnetization comes out in full, built only from zero-field states and energies.

The magnetization formula keeps the same shape as the free-electron one, with Hartree-Fock parts in place of free ones. The response to a field, the susceptibility, is less kind: it picks up an extra term born of the interaction, which no plain swap can give. Tests on an interacting Rashba model matched direct runs at a small applied field. The formulas give modelers a cheaper way to get magnetic response in correlated systems.
arxiv-2509-20826:
Flows on a surface can sometimes be straightened by a clever change of variables. David Marin and Marcel Nicolau study the flows where this works in a 2025 paper in algebraic geometry. The setting is smooth complex projective surfaces, and the flows come from rational vector fields that generate one-parameter groups of maps.

A vector field is called birationally integrable when its flow forms such a group of birational maps of the surface. The authors prove every such field can be moved, by a birational change, to a holomorphic one. They extend this to whole Lie algebras of such fields, placing them inside algebraic subgroups of the birational group. They also classify the two-dimensional and semisimple cases in full, organizing a field where dynamics meets group theory.
arxiv-2509-21126:
Vision-language models know a lot about the world but are clumsy at low-level control; reinforcement learners are the opposite. Xiefeng Wu and three co-authors pair them in VARL, a 2025 framework for online reinforcement learning. The vision-language model acts as an action advisor to the learning agent.

Online learning is slow because agents need enormous numbers of interaction steps to shape their value estimates. Vision-and-language action policies help in principle, but usually demand task-specific expert demonstrations for fine-tuning. VARL instead has the big model suggest actions, which the agent can follow or override while it learns. The advice injects domain knowledge into exploration without freezing the policy. The authors aim for faster learning on complex tasks without costly demonstration datasets.
arxiv-2509-21326:
MACD, a staple trading indicator, turns out to be a smoothed derivative in disguise. The 2025 paper is by Yuelong Li. MACD compares two moving averages of a price series. Traders use it to spot trends and turning points. The paper builds a rigorous operator framework for this classic tool. It asks what MACD computes in exact signal terms.

Li shows that MACD acts as a smoothed derivative with a phase correction. Nested and recursive averages are analysed in detail. The indicator is shown to work as a band pass filter, keeping a middle range of frequencies. Exact formulas write it as a finite difference of delayed, twice averaged signals. The results link MACD to harmonic analysis and give a firm basis for its use in signal detection.
arxiv-2509-21526:
