The result rests only on a few broad assumptions, such as Galilean invariance and weak coupling between the gas and the reservoir.
arxiv-2512-10126:
S. Shajidul Haque, Ghadir Jafari, and Bret Underwood ask what is truly quantum about the seeds of cosmic structure. Perturbations from inflation, the universe's early expansion, carry striking quantum features: entanglement and enormous circuit complexity. Yet every observation so far matches what classic random variables would produce. The authors measure the gap using quantum magic, a resource measure tied to Wigner negativity. Magic is what a quantum state needs to be hard to mimic with classical machines and useful for universal quantum computation.

They show inflationary perturbations are continuous variable stabilizer states with no magic. Despite their quantum origin, they can be run fast by classic algorithms. Any magic from primordial non Gaussianity is suppressed twice: by the small nonlinearity of the early universe and by the extreme squeezing of the perturbations themselves. The picture that emerges is a high complexity, low magic regime.
arxiv-2512-10226:
Shuhan Tan leads a team teaching self driving cars to reason in a latent language instead of English. Vision language action models often explain themselves in words before acting, but text is a clumsy medium for driving futures. Their model, LCDrive, reasons by interleaving two kinds of tokens. Action proposal tokens use the same vocabulary as the driving commands themselves. World model tokens, grounded in a learned latent world model, express what would happen if an action were taken. Thinking and deciding thus share one action aligned space.

Training starts cold, supervised by real future rollouts of each scene, so proposals and predicted outcomes learn from ground truth. Closed loop reinforcement learning then strengthens the reasoning interactively. On a large end to end driving benchmark, the latent reasoner inferred faster, drove better trajectories, and gained more from reinforcement learning than both silent and text reasoning baselines.
arxiv-2512-10426:
N Mangala and co-authors design a privacy-protecting layout for healthcare systems that mix bedside devices, edge computers, and the cloud. Wearables and connected medical devices now feed remote monitoring and emergency care, but the data is deeply personal. And fast response in a crisis cannot come at the cost of leaking it.

Their design spreads tasks across device, edge, and cloud layers by how urgent and lasting each job is. Differential privacy noise is added inside several learning models, and a hybrid noise scheme with an adaptive budget gave the best balance between accuracy and protection. While blockchain records keep the traffic traceable and tamper-proof. Edge handling cut emergency delays sharply, and inference and rebuilding attacks became measurably harder.
arxiv-2512-10526:
Nils Siemonsen and William East follow an instability that strikes spinning objects with an ergoregion but no horizon. Such spacetimes are known to be linearly unstable, yet what happens once the growth turns nonlinear was largely unexplored. The authors evolve a massless vector field on a rapidly spinning boson star in full general relativity to find out.

The instability feeds on itself: backreaction makes the star more tightly bound, which speeds the growth, until a black hole forms. Along the way, fine features develop and nonlinear gravity drives a direct turbulent cascade in both the unstable mode and the emitted radiation. The gravitational wave signal comes in bursts of rising strength, resembling the echoes discussed in other contexts, right up to the collapse. The study gives the first full picture of how this instability ends.
arxiv-2512-10726:
Jonah Nagura, Mykyta Onizhuk, and Giulia Galli explain why diamond quantum sensors go deaf near the surface. Nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond are superb nanoscale sensors, but the closer one sits to the surface, the faster surface noise, both magnetic and electric, scrambles its quantum state. Where that noise comes from, and exactly how it bites, had stayed murky.

The team combined atomistic surface models built with density functional theory and decoherence calculations by cluster correlation expansion. They mapped how the echo lifetime depends on crystal orientation, surface treatment, and the density of unpaired surface electrons, and found the depth where surface effects stop mattering. A key ratio, sensor depth against the spacing of surface electrons, governs whether the noise flickers fast or sits quasi-static. Only when surface spins were allowed to hop along the surface did the calculations match measured lifetimes.
arxiv-2512-11426:
Shuowei Cai, Yansong Ning, and Hao Liu design multi agent language model systems that respect real budgets for cost and response time. Such systems now power web search, social analytics, and customer support, where expense decides whether deployment is practical. Prior work shaped communication patterns or picked models in isolation, rarely optimising under explicit token and latency limits, and often designed the wiring before choosing the models.

Their AgentBalance framework reverses that order: backbones first, topology second. It builds a pool of candidate models, selects from it, and matches roles to suitable backbones, creating a deliberately mixed team. Then it learns agent representations and synthesises a communication topology that accounts for latency. Across benchmarks with fourteen candidate backbones, the method gained clear performance under matched budgets and produced strong trade off curves. It also plugs into existing systems and generalises to models it never saw during design.
arxiv-2512-11526:
Joel Ekstrand, Zahra Taghiyarrenani, and Slawomir Nowaczyk teach forecasting models to treat anomalies with care: some shocks change the future and must be heeded, while others are blips to ignore. Standard forecasters cannot tell the difference, so they either chase noise or sleep through real shifts. Their setup, Co-TSFA, learns the distinction through contrastive training.

Two kinds of added data manufacture cases: changes confined to the input, modelling irrelevant shocks, and changes carried into the output, modelling relevant ones. A latent alignment loss ties how much the internal picture moves to how much the forecast moves, enforcing calm under irrelevant disturbance, and a readiness to react to real change. Tests on traffic and electricity benchmarks plus a real cash demand data set bettered forecasting under anomalous settings without sacrificing scores on normal data. Code is provided for release.
arxiv-2512-11626:
Leonardo García-Heveling studies a fresh way to tell time in cosmology. The cosmic volume function marks time by the volume of space up to each event, as a swap for the older cosmic time function. A useful time label must vary smoothly, or the math built on it breaks.

García-Heveling proves that in many cases of interest the volume function is smooth in the needed sense, with a steady first derivative. That fact splits the space time metric into clean space and time parts. It also yields a matched Riemannian metric by a Wick rotation trick. Extra results and cases round out the picture for both the time and volume functions.
arxiv-2512-11826:
Weihong Xu and co-authors built FSL-HDnn, a silicon chip that learns new classes from a few examples right on the device. Edge gadgets often cannot phone home for training, and normal learning chips burn too much power. Their chip, made in a 40 nanometer process, joins feature extraction and few shot learning in one pipeline.

A weight clustering trick shrinks the feature extractor. The classifier uses hyperdimensional computing, which learns in a single pass with no gradient steps. Early exit and batched training boost speed further. On a 10 way, 5 shot task the chip used 6 millijoules per image and trained at 28 images per second. Training lag fell by 2 to 20.9 times versus rival chips.
arxiv-2512-12326:
J Alexander Curtis and Nasir U Eisty review how AI is changing penetration testing in a 2025 paper. Penetration testing probes a system's defenses by acting like an attacker, and the work is slow and manual. The authors survey 58 peer-reviewed studies from major academic databases.

Reinforcement learning led the field, as the focus of 77 percent of the works. Most studies target finding and exploiting flaws, where AI can automate repeat tasks and sharpen attack plans. Real tools include the European Space Agency's PenBox. Gaps remain in recon and post-exploitation phases, and large language model uses are still little studied, marking a clear path for future work.
arxiv-2512-12826:
Matei Drilea and co-authors study beams made by 3D printing with continuous carbon fiber inside them. Carbon fiber is strong, and it also changes its electrical response when bent. That dual role lets a beam act as both a structure and its own strain sensor.

The team shows that a large bending load applied first can raise the sensor response for good. They link the gain to small local breaks in the fibers. They also print a conductive filament around the fibers, which cuts noise and improves the contact. Together, the two steps point to printed parts that can sense load with high sensitivity.
arxiv-2512-13026:
I. A. Seit-Dzhelil and A. Yu. Shvets study a non-ideal system that couples a tank of liquid with an electric motor. Non-ideal here means the motor's power limits feed back on the motion, so the liquid and the drive shape each other. Delays in that feedback are their focus.

They consider two models that approximate the delay and ask how it changes the system's limit sets, the patterns motion settles into. They compute the main traits of steady regimes, both regular and chaotic. They also trace how orderly motion gives way to chaos. A route called generalized intermittency, driven by the delay, is shown to occur in this system.
arxiv-2512-13526:
Asa Cooper Stickland and co-authors stress-test delayed monitoring for AI coding agents. Such agents work on real code, at times with access to private data or security-critical files. A delayed monitor reviews acts after the fact, adding no runtime lag, but must still catch sabotage before harm is fixed in place.

The team frames monitor design as a game between a blue team that builds monitors and a red team that builds sabotaging agents. They built five software settings based on work inside an AI firm. Their combined monitor reached a 6% false negative rate at a 1% false positive rate on a held-out test setting. They then model how that rate maps to risk at deployment.
arxiv-2512-13626:
Dev Prakash Jha and Raju K. George study control of heat-like equations that carry memory of the past. To stop such a system for good, both the state and the stored memory must reach zero at the end time. If memory remains, the motion can restart after control stops.

They assume the memory kernel is a finite sum of exponentials, which lets them rewrite the problem as a coupled parabolic and ordinary system. They define a Memory Geometric Control Condition: the moving control region must visit every point in space. Under that term, they prove an observability bound and gain null controllability. They also note why a full necessity proof stays out of reach with memory effects.
arxiv-2512-13826:
Dylan Bissuel and a large team present a reproducible container solution for materials science codes and workflows. Computational materials work needs software environments that others can rebuild exactly. Their approach pairs the GNU Guix package manager with the Apptainer container system for fully declarative, reproducible setups.

The system can host complete frameworks with workflow managers such as AiiDA and Ewoks, deployed on clusters. Examples include AiiDA workflows for making data sets and path-integral molecular dynamics from ab initio runs. Other cases cover training machine-learning interatomic potentials and Ewoks analysis of X-ray diffraction data at synchrotrons. The authors present the environment as a reliable base for data-driven materials research.
arxiv-2512-14026:
Yibing Fu and co-authors present CITab, a self-supervised framework that learns from medical images and tabular data across different cohorts. Combining scans with tables has helped clinical decision-making, and self-supervised pretraining can use large unlabeled data sets. Past methods were often limited to one cohort because their tabular modeling was too rigid for varied table structures.

CITab uses column headers as semantic cues, so knowledge can transfer across tables with different columns. A prototype-guided mixture-of-linear module specializes tabular features and handles that variety. Tests on Alzheimer's disease diagnosis covered three public cohorts with 4,461 subjects in total. CITab beat state-of-the-art approaches, supporting scalable cross-tabular multimodal learning for medicine.
arxiv-2512-14526:
Debendra Meher, Nikhil Avula, and Sundaram Balasubramanian chase a long-missing computer model of boron oxide glass. Experiments say much of the glass is built from six-membered boroxol rings, yet ordinary simulations rarely form enough of them. The team trained a machine-learned atomic potential to near quantum accuracy and cooled the virtual melt unusually slowly.

Slow cooling pushed more than thirty percent of boron atoms into rings. One technical choice proved decisive: the network describing each atom's surroundings needed a wide enough view, or pressure and ring counts went wrong. The lowest-energy glasses sat near seventy-five percent rings, close to what experiments suggest for the real material.
arxiv-2512-14726:
Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from pre-collected data, with no live interaction with the environment. Decision transformers brought sequence modeling to that task, but they struggle with long-horizon credit assignment and complex links between states and actions.

The quantum decision transformer, QDT, answers with an architecture that adds quantum-inspired mechanisms, drawing on entanglement and interference as computational motifs. The synergy is meant to represent long-range dependencies more richly than a plain transformer can. If it performs as hoped, offline agents could learn better policies from fixed logs in settings like robotics, games, and operations.
arxiv-2512-14826:
Stephan Foldes and Russ Woodroofe prove a neat result about lattices, the ordered grids of math where elements can be joined and met. They work with lattices that carry a rank graded by a bounded span of real numbers. An antichain cutset is a set of pairwise unranked elements that every path from bottom to top must cross.

Their theorem says any such cutset is a level set, a slice at one height, for a grading built to fit it. The result holds in the rank supersolvable case they study. It then applies to three classic settings: the measurable Boolean lattice, the continuous partition lattice, and continuous projective geometry. In each, a fresh grading can be chosen so the cutset sits exactly on one level.
arxiv-2512-14926:
George-Andrei Dima and two coauthors work to close a language gap in AI that can see and talk. Their focus is Romanian, a language with few multimodal training resources. Progress in such languages is a step toward making generative AI useful to more of the world.

The team translated the Flickr30K image dataset into Romanian and extended it for visual question answering with help from open language models. They then fine tuned vision language models from three families, LLaMA 3.2, LLaVA 1.6, and Qwen2, using the efficient LoRA method. The tuned models answered Romanian questions about images better and even improved at tasks they were not trained on, like writing Romanian captions. The best, a seven billion parameter Qwen2 model, gained 2.29 percent on question answering and 4.45 percent on captioning, and made far fewer grammar errors.
arxiv-2512-15126:
Yupeng Zhu and three coauthors animate a single still image into controllable 3D motion, without a full 3D production pipeline. Classic 3D animation is slow, expert, and costly. Recent AI tools either keep those costs or switch to video synthesis, which gives up true 3D control and interaction.

Their system, 3DProxyImg, splits the job in two. A coarse 3D estimate acts as a structural carrier that handles geometry and motion control. Learned image space priors then supply fine appearance and new views. This 2D-3D aligned proxy gives control close to classical pipelines, with no need for exact geometry or heavy optimization, and it extends to background animation. In tests it ran on low power platforms and beat video based methods on identity preservation, consistency, and precise interactive control.
arxiv-2512-15426:
Cecilia Cavaterra and co authors prove solutions exist for a relaxed tumor growth model in a 2025 math paper. The model pairs a Cahn Hilliard equation, which tracks how tumor and healthy phases separate, with a nutrient equation. Its mobility degenerates and its potential is singular, which makes the math delicate.

The system also includes terms for cell growth, nutrient use, and chemotaxis, the pull of cells toward chemical signals. The authors add an elliptic regularization set by a parameter delta and prove a weak solution exists for the relaxed system. Letting delta go to zero then gives a weak solution for the original tumor model.
arxiv-2512-16026:
L C Gonzalez-Morales, I Perez Castillo, and J I Jimenez-Aquino study heat and disorder in a physics paper posted on arXiv during 2025. Their system is a charged particle jittering in a fluid, held by a spring-like trap, and pushed by crossing electric and magnetic fields. The fluid has memory, so friction arrives with a delay, described by a generalized Langevin equation.

Solving the motion exactly, the authors compute how the particle's position and velocity spread over time. From that they derive the entropy produced along each random path. For two driving setups, a direct time-varying force and a dragged trap center, they prove the entropy obeys a detailed fluctuation theorem. Such theorems link tiny random events to the second law of thermodynamics.
arxiv-2512-16426:
Andrey I Bondarev recalculates atomic fingerprints in an arXiv paper posted in 2025. The hyperfine structure of an atom's spectrum, tiny splittings from the nucleus's magnetism, is summarized by constants called A. For singly ionized thulium, early measurements clashed with theory, and newer experiments showed two of the old measured values were simply wrong.

Bondarev computes the A constants for several low-lying levels of Tm II using the configuration interaction method, with random-phase corrections included. His results agree well with the corrected experimental data. He also predicts values for states that have never been measured, giving spectroscopists targets to test. Reliable hyperfine data for thulium matter for atomic physics and for reading the element's lines in stellar spectra.
arxiv-2512-16726:
Alexandru Ciobanu and coauthors find a way to lower the interaction order in hard search problems such as 3-SAT, where each rule links three choices at once. In physics terms the task is to find the lowest energy state of a spin system with three-way links.

Past fixes cut the order by adding extra units, but those units slow the search badly at scale. The new route uses renormalization ideas to build a two-way system that keeps the same free energy. The extra units act freely once the main ones are fixed, so they can be traced out step by step. The team shows the ground state hunt then costs the same as in the raw form.
arxiv-2512-16826:
Arslan Amin and coauthors test YOLOv8 models for reading license plates, a core task for traffic systems and vehicle watch tools. Past methods often miss real-time accuracy when scenes vary in light, angle, and plate style.

Two data sets covered plate finding and character reading. YOLOv8 Nano hit 0.964 precision and 0.918 mAP50 on plate finding, while YOLOv8 Small hit 0.92 precision and 0.91 mAP50 on characters. A custom step orders found characters by their sideways position to form the plate string. The paired pipeline, Nano for plates and Small for characters, keeps compute low, suiting edge devices in smart traffic setups.
arxiv-2512-16926:
Oren Bell and coauthors address scheduling for ROS 2, the robot software frame, on a single processor. Real robot apps form branching task graphs, not simple chains, and past scheduling work leaned on chain models with ad hoc timing math.

The team shows ROS 2 apps can be viewed as forests of trees, mapping them to classic real-time DAG task models. Using the events executor with a custom queue and LIFO message delivery, they run fixed-priority and EDF schedulers for full graphs. The setup yields the same schedules as a standard DAG scheduler, even without direct access to precedence data. That match closes a gap between scheduling theory and ROS 2 practice.
arxiv-2512-17026:
Óscar Carrión-González, Sylvestre Lacour, and Mathias Nowak propose adding a fifth 8-meter telescope, UT5, to the Very Large Telescope Interferometer in Chile. The white paper targets exoplanets seen in reflected starlight, a hard direct-imaging prize.

UT5 would add four new baselines of about 200 meters aimed northwest. Longer baselines shrink the inner working angle and sharpen contrast, the two traits that decide whether a mature planet can be split from its star glare. The authors frame the upgrade as an optimization of the whole array for planet hunting, offered to the ESO Expanding Horizons call for 2040s astronomy.
arxiv-2512-17626:
Tijn De Wringer and three co-authors cut the wait for peering inside an exoplanet from days to minutes. Guessing a planet's core and mantle from its mass and size means running a slow physics model thousands of times inside a Bayesian search. That cost has kept interior studies one planet at a time.

Their stand-in model, a blend called polynomial chaos-Kriging, learns the physics model's behavior from just a few hundred runs, then answers in its place inside the search loop. The swap speeds inference about 320-fold, and the stand-in tracks the true model with R-squared above 0.99 in most cases. A check on 1,000 fake planets confirmed the error bars stay honest. Population-wide interior surveys are now within reach.
arxiv-2512-18526:
Leonardo Bohac studies what can be learned from a quantum memory you may read but never touch directly. The interface is U-QRAM, a fixed interaction that performs coherent random-access reads against a truth-table basis. The memory may sit in any state, even one entangled with a hidden reference. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, proves a sharp limit on such read-only access.

For any protocol with finitely many reads, however clever the steps between them, the accessible output depends on the memory only through its diagonal in the truth-table basis. Coherences between truth tables are simply invisible. Every test of memory hypotheses thus reduces to standard state discrimination, governed by Helstrom theory. Three examples illustrate the result, including one with best possible success of three quarters.
arxiv-2512-19026:
Connor Kilrain and five co-authors propose a sharper test for image generators that personalize output to one subject, such as a pet. Most scores reward overall likeness and miss small identity marks, like a spot on the head. Their protocol, Finer-Personalization Rank, scores identity as a retrieval task instead.

Each generated image is used as a query against a gallery of similar real photos labeled by identity. Strong scores mean the fine details survived generation. Tests span bird species, car models, and animal re-identification sets. The protocol caught identity drift in popular methods that looser scores missed, giving builders a stricter check.
arxiv-2512-19226:
Shubham Dey and Sean Raymond test whether the seven planets of TRAPPIST-1 could keep moons. The system packs its planets tightly, so each planet's gravity well is squeezed by its neighbors. N-body simulations follow test moons around each planet, from the Roche limit outward toward the prograde stability edge.

Moons stayed stable out to about forty to forty-five percent of the Hill radius for every planet. Neighbor pulls were weak alone but shrank the stable zone together, most for the innermost and middle planets they name. Simple tidal decay math then caps the largest moon that could survive for billions of years at a tiny fraction of Earth's mass.
arxiv-2512-19326:
Philipp Schneider and Julian Werthmann compare two distributed computing models that shard a graph across many machines. In massively parallel computation, machines hold pieces of the input with small memory each. In the node-capacitated clique, every graph node is a machine that knows its neighbors but may trade only a few words per round.

The strongly sublinear memory regime had no known simulation results between the models. The authors give techniques that simulate one in the other with only constant round overhead, under set restrictions. They also prove impossibility results for other settings, showing the limits are real, not a lack of cleverness. Parameter ranges, problem families, and graph classes all matter.
arxiv-2512-19526:
Li Puyin, Tiange Xiang, Ella Mao, and Shirley Wei built QuantiPhy, a benchmark that asks vision-language models for numbers, not adjectives. A general agent must judge size, speed, and acceleration from video, yet most tests grade only wordy plausibility. More than three thousand video-text cases carry exact numerical ground truth.

Each task hands the model one true property as a prior and asks it to estimate another at a set moment, under standard prompts and scoring. Leading models were tested across the set. A steady gap opened between answers that sound right and numbers that are right. Side analyses probe background noise, false priors, and other failure drivers.
arxiv-2512-19726:
Carlos Purves tackles a deployment problem for reinforcement learning: smart visual policies usually live on a server, so every decision waits on a network round trip. His MiniConv approach splits the policy in two. A tiny on-device encoder, written as OpenGL fragment-shader passes so it runs on almost any embedded graphics chip, compresses each camera observation into a compact feature tensor for transmission.

Only that small tensor crosses the network to the remote policy head, cutting bandwidth, decision latency, and server load per request. Benchmarks span a Jetson Nano, a Raspberry Pi 4B, and a Pi Zero 2 W, measuring learning quality, behavior under sustained load, and latency under shaped bandwidth. Final learning performance stayed broadly comparable to unsplit policies, with modest trade-offs in average return, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2512-20326:
Felix Huber works on Quantum Max Cut, a quantum analogue of the classic Max Cut problem tied to the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model. He asks how well the optimum can be bounded from below using a famous graph invariant. The invariant is the Lovász theta function, applied to the complement of the graph.

Huber proves a lower bound in which a graph with many edges gains a correction term that shrinks as the theta value grows. A simple product state achieves the bound. A relaxed version replaces theta with the maximum degree, making it handy for quantum many-body systems. He also strengthens earlier results for triangle-free graphs using ideas of Carlson and Shearer.
arxiv-2512-20426:
Junjie Chen and co-authors expose a structural clash inside quantum sensing. Quantum metrology gains precision by letting a signal imprint coherently on a probe. Error correction protects that probe from noise, but correction works by distinguishing errors, while sensing needs signal and noise responses to stay indistinguishable along the signal direction.

The authors quantify the clash with trade-offs between code distance and quantum Fisher information for several code families. Their escape is asymmetric error correction: relax protection along the signal direction, keep it elsewhere. Codes built this way for local sensing restore Heisenberg-limited precision while distance still grows. Sparse, tunable versions based on quantum LDPC codes and concatenation make the approach scalable, with shallow adaptive circuits preparing the probes.
arxiv-2512-20526:
Xiao-Peng Wang, Yi-Jie Li, Guang-Zhi Xu, and Kui-Yong Liu compute a rare particle-making process with unusual care about relativity. Electron-positron annihilation can create two Bc mesons, bound states of bottom and charm quarks. The authors work inside nonrelativistic QCD factorization, then add the relativistic corrections that the name seems to contradict.

The calculation spans energies from the production threshold up to twice the Z boson mass, covering both photon and Z channels. Those corrections prove large, with K factors around six tenths, meaning naive predictions overshoot substantially. Angular shapes, sideways patterns, and momentum spectra are also presented. Future electron-positron colliders hunting heavy-flavour states will need exactly these fixed rates.
arxiv-2512-20726:
Davide Breoni, Emanuele Locatelli, and Luca Tubiana simulate star polymers whose arms tie themselves into rings. A star polymer has many arms grafted onto one core; circularizing the arms links them in patterns that depend on the solvent the rings close in. Bad solvent, where the polymer crumples, turns out to matter long after the fact.

Stars circularized in bad solvent end up more interlinked, and once moved to good solvent they stay smaller than stars circularized there directly. With few arms, bad solvent clumps every arm to one side of the core so all can interact. With enough arms, the core is fully wetted, the distribution turns radially symmetric, and linking fades. A critical grafting density and arm length govern the clumping transition.
arxiv-2512-20826:
Simon Foucart extends a classic result about best possible estimates. When the quantity of interest is a simple linear summary of an object in a convex set, the best worst-case estimator is itself linear in the observations. Many real targets, though, are not linear: a maximum, for example, or the third largest of several readings.

Foucart proves the same neat structure survives for those nonlinear targets. The best estimator of a maximum is a maximum of matching form. One case needs an unusual sharpening of the Hahn-Banach theorem, a cornerstone of functional analysis. He also gives practical recipes, based on convex optimization, that actually build these optimal estimators.
arxiv-2512-21126:
YuK-Kwan Wong, Sai-Kit Yeung, and three co-authors ask whether vision-language models know anything about the ocean. Marine questions demand specialist knowledge and carry their own visual quirks, from murky survey footage to species identification. MarineEval is the first large-scale benchmark of its kind. It assembles two thousand image-based question-answer pairs spanning seven task dimensions and twenty capacity dimensions. Marine experts verified that domain requirements are genuinely baked in.

Seventeen current models were benchmarked, and the verdict is sobering: none answers domain-specific marine questions effectively, leaving wide headroom for improvement. The failure patterns map where general visual competence ends and marine expertise begins. For researchers building scientific assistants, the benchmark supplies both a yardstick and a to-do list, and its construction method transfers to other underserved domains.
arxiv-2512-21326:
Sida Wang performs an audit of the yardsticks the AI field argues about. Leaderboard scores for language models wobble for two distinct reasons: prediction noise, because a model sampled twice answers the same question differently, and data noise, because a benchmark samples finitely many questions. Wang defines both, plus their total under the law of total variance. He proposes all-pairs comparison, pitting every model against every other on identical questions. That measures the components across millions of question-level predictions.

Two regularities emerge. Total noise per evaluation turns out characteristic and highly predictable across model pairs. Paired prediction noise usually exceeds paired data noise. So something as cheap as averaging repeated generations buys real statistical power. Evaluation designers gain a diagnostic habit: report the noises with the scores, and many breathless leaderboard reversals become measurable non-events.
arxiv-2512-21426:
Mohammed Sayagh studies a practical question for software teams that now assign work to AI coding agents: what makes a GitHub issue good enough for an agent like Copilot to carry out? An issue is the written ticket describing a feature or bug. If the ticket is unclear or badly scoped, the agent's work often fails and its pull request is never merged.

Sayagh builds thirty-two detailed criteria for judging issue quality, then compares issues that led to merged pull requests with those closed unmerged. Merged work tends to come from issues that are shorter, well scoped, and clear about which files matter and how to proceed. Issues that lean on external references, setup details, or outside services merge less often. He also trains an interpretable machine learning model that predicts an issue's chance of merging, so writers can improve a ticket before handing it to an agent.
arxiv-2512-21526:
Shanglin Yang and Zhan Shi propose a careful way to let large language models help train recommendation systems. Language models carry rich semantic knowledge, but using one directly as the recommender is costly and unreliable over much of the user-item space. Global distillation, the common alternative, forces the smaller model to copy the language model everywhere, even where the guidance is wrong.

Their method, Selective LLM-Guided Regularization, switches the language model's ranking supervision on only where it is likely to help. A trainable gate decides from the user's history length, the item's popularity, and the recommender's uncertainty. All language model scoring happens offline, so the deployed recommender costs nothing extra to run. Across several datasets the selective strategy improves accuracy overall, with the largest gains for cold-start users and long-tail items. The framework works with any base recommendation model.
arxiv-2512-21626:
Hong Xie, Haoran Gu, Yanying Huang, Tao Tan, and Defu Lian study a variant of the multi-armed bandit problem motivated by shared computing resources. In each round, several plays compete for the capacity of several arms, as when language model requests contend for servers. Each arm offers a random amount of capacity, each unit yields a random reward, and each play carries a priority weight.

When plays compete, capacity goes to the higher-priority play first. The authors prove lower bounds on regret, the loss compared with knowing the best allocation in advance, in two forms. They then design an offline algorithm that finds the optimal allocation when the model parameters are known. Built on top of it, an upper-confidence-bound learning algorithm achieves regret matching the lower bounds up to modest factors. The technical difficulty is the nonlinear, combinatorial payoff created by prioritized sharing.
arxiv-2512-21726:
Dennis Gaitsgory, Nick Rozenblyum, and Yakov Varshavsky record a formalism for algebro-geometric derived categories, called AGCat, following a suggestion of Vladimir Drinfeld. Derived categories are the working language of modern algebraic geometry, organizing sheaves and their higher structure. Care matters because later work builds entire theories on these foundations.

The paper is deliberately foundational: it sets out the definitions of AGCat rather than proving uses, which the authors reserve for two announced sequel papers. Papers like this one function as shared infrastructure: they fix notation and the rules of the game so later work can be stated precisely. Readers should expect a technical reference for specialists in the field, not a self-contained research result.
arxiv-2512-23126:
Yu Li, Tian Lan, and Zhengling Qi propose InSPO, a refinement of the preference optimization methods used to align large language models with human judgments. The popular direct preference optimization approach has two flaws the authors target. Its optimal policy depends on free choices, like the scalarization function and reference policy, so behavior can reflect those choices rather than true preferences. And it scores each response alone, ignoring the comparison sitting in the data.

InSPO derives an optimal policy that conditions on both the context and the other response, unlocking, in the authors' phrase, the model's self-reflection. They prove the method beats the older objectives while staying invariant to scalarization and reference choices. It drops into existing pipelines with no design changes and no inference overhead. Experiments show gains in win rates and length-controlled metrics, supporting the claim that comparison-aware training aligns models better.
arxiv-2512-23426:
Dohyun Kim, Seungwoo Lyu, Seung Wook Kim, and Paul Hongsuck Seo tackle a weakness of text-to-image diffusion models. Their outputs often miss fine points of user intent and vary in visual quality. Earlier preference training methods helped, but they rely on costly human-labeled data and on targets drawn from the forward noising process. This does not match how the model actually removes noise.

Their method, called DDSPO, sets preference supervision directly on the backward denoising steps, using a contrastive pair of policies as the guide. The pair can be built by training separate winning and losing models, or without extra training by comparing a prompt with a weakened version of itself. Tests show stronger text-image alignment and better aesthetic quality than forward-process supervision.
arxiv-2512-23526:
Maryam Mirzaei, Farzaneh Shayegh, and Hamed Narimani work on recognizing emotions from brain signals recorded with electroencephalography, or EEG. EEG reflects neural activity directly and with fine time resolution, which suits emotion recognition for human-machine interaction. The obstacle is that recordings shift between sessions, so a model trained on one day often performs poorly on another.

Their framework, EGDA, adapts between sessions by aligning both the overall distribution of signals and the distribution within each emotion class. Graph regularization preserves the natural structure of the EEG data during this alignment. On the SEED-IV data set, EGDA scored above eighty percent accuracy on all three cross-session tasks and beat several baselines. Gamma-band activity, and regions at the center-back and front of the scalp, mattered most.
arxiv-2512-23626:
Federico Baldo and Charles Assaad tackle causal discovery when the data live in separate hands. Hospitals and other institutions cannot pool their records, yet each wants the causal structure behind them. Federated causal discovery handles the privacy problem, but usually assumes every client shares the same causal model, an assumption real policies and protocols break through client-specific interventions.

Their algorithm, I-PERI, first recovers the causal graph class shared across clients, then exploits structural differences created by the unknown interventions to orient extra edges. The result is a tighter equivalence class than standard methods return, with its own graphical representation. The authors prove convergence and privacy guarantees for the method, and synthetic experiments support its effectiveness. The work is slated for ICML 2026.
arxiv-2512-23826:
Vladimir Karas surveys, in a conference write-up, what happens to a smaller companion orbiting inside the accretion disk of a supermassive black hole. In a nuclear star cluster, a secondary orbiter's path is shaped by competing influences: gravitational relaxation from countless star-star encounters, outright physical collisions between stars. Then there is the drag of plowing repeatedly through the disk's gas.

The self-gravity of the accretion disk itself further modulates the long-term evolution. Using simple arguments rather than heavy computing, Karas outlines how these processes compete with one another. Together they govern the feeding of the central black hole and what telescopes can see from the cluster. The piece was prepared for the RAGtime workshop proceedings on black holes and neutron stars, held at the Silesian University in Opava. The tone is that of a field guide, not a proof.
arxiv-2512-23926:
Charles Orioma and six co-authors improve how eye-tracking software separates the two basic events of vision: fixations, when the gaze rests, and saccades, the jumps between them. Their statistics proxy for cognition in many experiments, yet most detection algorithms use hand-picked thresholds that ignore how eye dynamics vary between tasks and people, biasing results.

Their method adapts the threshold from the data, using a Markov-style model of gaze dynamics in which the best threshold minimizes switching between the two states. Applied to velocity, angular velocity, and dispersion algorithms, adaptation was judged against a multi-threshold benchmark. Velocity thresholds were most accurate in clean data, reaching the low nineties percent, but collapsed under noise if left fixed. Adaptive dispersion thresholds proved the most robust, staying above eighty percent accuracy even at extreme noise, at some cost in saccade recall.
arxiv-2512-24026:
Mustafa Munir and four colleagues tackle a hard problem in computer vision. Editing long videos with diffusion models grows very costly as footage gets longer. The cost comes from joint editing and inversion steps run across extended sequences. Their method, called PipeFlow, is built to scale.

PipeFlow works in three ways at once. First, it measures motion between frames. Frames with little motion are skipped rather than edited. Second, it splits a video into segments. Several graphics processors then edit the segments in parallel. Third, a neural step smooths the joins between segments. It also fills in the skipped frames. Editing time then grows only in step with video length. The team reports speedups of roughly ten times over one rival method. Against another method, the gain is more than thirty times.
arxiv-2512-24226:
M C Araújo, J Furtado, J G Lima, and T Mariz compute vacuum polarization in an unusual setting. The base model is the Rarita-Schwinger model. It describes spin three-halves fields. The framework is Very Special Relativity. That framework keeps only a subgroup of the usual Lorentz symmetry. Both massive and massless fields are examined. Each couples to the Maxwell field.

The calculation is a one-loop computation. The Mandelstam-Leibbrandt prescription handles the loop integrals. Work proceeds within the SIM(2) limit of the framework. Vacuum polarization tells how the vacuum itself responds to the field. In a symmetry-reduced theory, that response can differ from the standard case. The paper adds one more data point to the study of spin three-halves fields. It also tests how robust loop results are when Lorentz symmetry is trimmed.
arxiv-2512-24326:
Camron Alexander Hirst, Chris Reale, and Eric Frew guide a small fixed-wing aircraft along three-dimensional paths. Their method is nonlinear model predictive control. It plans control moves over a horizon while respecting the aircraft's dynamics. Two guidance algorithms are presented. Both were implemented and flight-tested on the RAAVEN uncrewed aircraft.

Control-augmented modeling and system identification come first. The first controller schedules a fixed reference path rate. That choice rewards constant inertial speed. The second controller optimizes the path rate as it flies. It trades path progress against distance from the path. Both work on general smooth curves parameterized by arc length. Flights covered several high-curvature test paths. A baseline lookahead law served as the comparison. The predictive controllers proved feasible and superior. Ground speeds reached thirty-six meters per second.
arxiv-2512-24426:
Zhenghao Peng and five colleagues make a driving model question its own plans. Vision-language-action models steer cars end to end. Reasoning versions narrate what they see and intend. They rarely ask whether the plan is safe. The team's model, CF-VLA, adds that self-check before acting.

CF-VLA first drafts time-segmented meta-actions that summarize intent. It then runs counterfactual reasoning over those actions and the visual scene. Simulated outcomes expose unsafe behavior. Corrected meta-actions guide the final trajectory. A rollout-filter-label pipeline supplies the training data. It mines valuable scenes from a base model's rollouts and labels the reasoning traces. On large driving datasets, trajectory accuracy and safety metrics both improved by wide margins. The model also thinks adaptively. It switches on the extra reasoning only in hard scenarios.
arxiv-2512-24826:
Jason Armitage and Rico Sennrich help two-dimensional vision-language systems work inside three-dimensional multi-object scenes by steering an in-scene camera. Models trained on flat images face a dimensional shift in 3D, and the camera must be learned as a control module. Their method improves multivariate mutual information estimates through regret minimization with derivative-free optimization.

Off-the-shelf cross-modal systems then adapt online to occlusions and tell features apart, learning from noisy vision-language outputs. Readers in embodied AI get a control scheme that needs no gradients through the perception model. Active viewpoint choice becomes a way to make flat-trained models useful in spatial scenes.
arxiv-2512-25026:
Nasim Borazjanizadeh and James McClelland propose modeling language as a sequence of thoughts rather than a sequence of tokens. Token models rely on surface co-occurrence and fail to build globally consistent representations of entities and events, causing poor relational generalization, the reversal curse, and data inefficiency. Cognitive science shows humans convert language into compact event-like representations that persist while wording fades.

Motivated by that contrast, they introduce an approach built around thought-like units. AI and cognitive science readers get a framework aiming at consistent world representations from text. If language models thought in events, many familiar failures might soften.
arxiv-2601-00126:
Utkarsh A Mishra, David He, Yongxin Chen, and Danfei Xu tackle a failure mode in planning with composed generative models. Their 2026 method addresses long-horizon tasks by stitching together local models, an approach used for robot manipulation, panoramic images, and long video. When each local model allows several distinct modes, older composition methods average incompatible modes together, yielding plans that are neither locally workable nor globally coherent.

Their system embeds search directly inside the diffusion process. It samples diverse combinations of local modes, prunes unworkable candidates by likelihood, and enforces global consistency by resampling across overlapping segments. On seven robot manipulation tasks it matches oracle performance and beats baselines lacking composition or needing long-horizon training data. The same machinery produces coherent text-guided panoramas and long videos. The broader lesson is that choosing among modes must happen during generation, not by blending them away.
arxiv-2601-00426:
Md Zesun Ahmed Mia, Malyaban Bal, and Abhronil Sengupta borrow ideas from astrocytes, the glial cells that support memory in the brain, to make Transformer models handle longer texts. Standard attention grows in cost very fast as sequences lengthen. Their design, RMAAT, processes text in segments and carries context forward in special memory tokens.

A retention factor modeled on long-term changes in astrocytes controls how those memory tokens are compressed. Inside each segment, a cheaper attention step mimics short-term astrocyte effects. A new training method replays stored memories to save memory during learning. Tests on long-context benchmarks are used to judge whether the brain-inspired design keeps accuracy while cutting the cost of long sequences.
arxiv-2601-00726:
Onur Ata and three co-authors present, in 2026, a new way to run fluid flow on a computer. The flows are near the slow, dense kind, like air at low speed. Fine swirls in such flows are too small to track one by one. Large eddy methods track the big swirls and let small ones blur out. The team's method builds that blur into the maths itself, with no add-on model.

Their maths splits the flow into blocks, each solved with a high-grade method based on the Boltzmann equations. Those equations track how bits of gas spread and hit. The block method wastes little energy, so it blurs only the finest swirls. The team tested it on a swirl box test with rich structure. They also ran flow past a ball at a set speed. The method is a sound new route to hard flow runs.
arxiv-2601-01126:
Andrew Borthwick and Stephen Ash present RoboPhD, a system in which AI agents improve themselves at turning plain questions into database queries. Two agents work in a loop. One writes the query code and its instructions. The other studies the results and designs the next version, with a rating system picking the winners in a survival-of-the-fittest cycle.

Starting from a naive seventy-line seed, the system grew its best agent to fifteen hundred lines over eighteen rounds, with no outside hints about the task. It found tricks on its own, such as adjusting how deeply it studies a database based on that database's size. Gains were largest on cheaper models, letting a small tuned model beat a bigger untuned one. The best agent scored about seventy-four percent on the BIRD test set. The work suggests AI can build strong agent systems from a trivial starting point.
arxiv-2601-01326:
Avik Mahata tackles a materials design puzzle: ruthenium-based compounds could strengthen heat-proof superalloys, but the best chemistry on paper often fails in practice. These ordered compounds form as tiny precipitates inside an alloy. If their spacing mismatches the host crystal, strain builds up and the useful temperature range shrinks.

Mahata combines high-throughput quantum calculations with a random forest screen and symbolic regression to search the design space. The symbolic step yields a plain physical law: each percent of lattice mismatch cuts the top operating temperature by roughly two hundred degrees. That explains why some pure compounds fall short of their predicted limits. The fix is multi-element alloying. Additions such as aluminum and titanium tune the spacing and cancel the strain penalty. The work sets out a constraint-first protocol for designing stable, strain-free microstructures in refractory alloys.
arxiv-2601-02226:
Before any analysis, a registry dataset deserves a careful first look. Lukas Klein and six co-authors perform an initial data analysis of Germany's national transplantation registry. The focus is first-time kidney-only transplants in adults. Organs came from deceased donors between 2006 and 2016. Nearly fifteen thousand recipients and ten thousand donors spread across twenty-five tables.

Missing data varies wildly. Some tables are nearly complete. Others miss over half their values. Decision trees expose the missingness patterns. Flow analysis shows which variables can support imputation. One hundred sixty-eight variables are reported by multiple providers. That creates discrepancies, but also imputation opportunities. The authors warn that event-time results hinge on variable selection. They close with concrete preprocessing recommendations for future registry research.
arxiv-2601-02426:
Cong Li studies collinear factorization, the method that splits a hard particle process into simpler parts, when the process sits inside a strong electromagnetic background. The background is allowed to change only the numerator part of the photon propagator, leaving its pole structure and prescription untouched.

Li shows the set of Landau pinch surfaces and the leading momentum regions does not change, so the leading power factorized form survives. The leading cusp kernel feels the background only through one specific contraction in the soft region, and when that contraction vanishes the soft kernel reduces to the vacuum case. An occupancy based example shows genuine background effects then start only beyond leading power.
arxiv-2601-02926:
Owen J. Scutt and eight co-authors present PITCHFORK, a neural network that quickly mimics the outputs of detailed stellar models for Sun-like stars that ring with oscillations. Asteroseismology reads those oscillations to pin down a star's age and inner structure, but standard grid interpolation is slow and handles random errors poorly. PITCHFORK is a multilayer perceptron with a branching design, built to predict both classical observables and individual oscillation frequencies.

The network predicts surface temperature, luminosity, and iron content with high precision, plus thirty-five radial mode frequencies to within a small fraction of a percent. Paired with a fast Bayesian inference pipeline, it returns full posterior distributions. The authors validate their treatment of random uncertainties, which opens the door to studying systematic errors in stellar models.
arxiv-2601-03226:
Raphael Appenzeller constructs generalized affine buildings for semisimple algebraic groups defined over real closed fields. Buildings are geometric spaces that encode a group's structure through apartments and chambers, and the affine version with a general value group, here called a Lambda-building, extends the classical theory. Appenzeller builds the space using real algebraic geometry, starting from the rational points of the group over a valued real closed field.

He then characterizes the spherical building at infinity, which captures the group's asymptotic directions, and the local building at a base point. Stabilizers of various subsets of the building are computed along the way. Those computations yield group decompositions, the factorizations that let algebraic group theorists break elements and subgroups into standard pieces.
arxiv-2601-03626:
Parampreet Singh and three co-authors reduce the labeling burden in Indian art music analysis by letting a few labels spread through a graph. Expert annotation of recordings is slow and costly, so large labeled sets are rare in music research. Label propagation is a semi-supervised method that links similar recordings and passes labels from the few known examples to the many unknown ones.

The team applied it to two tasks: identifying the raga, the melodic framework of a piece, and classifying instruments. They merged several public datasets with extra recordings from the Prasar Bharati Archives. Experiments showed propagation cut labeling effort while producing better labels than the small set alone could support. The approach could open large unlabelled archives of Indian music to systematic study.
arxiv-2601-03826:
Sheikh Moonsun Pervez and Saptarshi Mandal study a tiny quantum heat engine built from a cluster of interacting spins. The working medium follows the Kitaev-Heisenberg model, which mixes two kinds of magnetic coupling, and an external field varying linearly in time drives the Otto cycle. Engine efficiency turns out to depend strongly on the relative size and signs of the two couplings.

Intriguingly, swapping both signs while keeping relative size leaves efficiency about the same, which the authors trace to frustration, quantum fluctuations, and a duality in the energy spectrum. Peak efficiency appears when energy levels form narrow bands where total spin is well defined, a regime of weakly interacting magnons, the spin system's wave-like excitations. The work maps how exotic magnetism could help or hinder nanoscale engines.
arxiv-2601-03926:
Haeun Jang, Hwan Chang, and Hwanhee Lee introduce Doc-PP, a benchmark testing whether vision-language models obey user-set disclosure policies when answering questions about documents. Real deployments face dynamic rules about what may be revealed in which context. Safety research has mostly studied implicit social norms or text-only settings, leaving multimodal documents, with their mix of images and text, unexamined.

The benchmark is built from real-world reports requiring reasoning across visual and textual elements under strict non-disclosure policies. Evaluation exposed a systemic reasoning-induced safety gap: models often leak information when the answer must be inferred by combining pieces across modalities. Supplying extracted text improved perception yet made leakage easier. For companies deploying document assistants over sensitive files, the benchmark names a failure mode that standard safety tests miss entirely.
arxiv-2601-04026:
David González Méndez and Vicente Garzó derive flow equations for a confined mix of small hard spheres that lose energy when they collide. The mix is nearly flat, held in a shallow layer, and can have several kinds of grains at moderate density. Such grains appear in powders and industrial handling.

Using a revised Enskog theory for inelastic collisions, the pair obtain balance laws for mass, motion, and energy. A Chapman-Enskog expansion then gives formulas for the fluxes. They solve the linked integral equations approximately with steady-state and Sonine polynomial methods. The resulting transport values depend on bounce loss, mix shares, grain sizes and masses, and density. As a use case, they study how a temperature gradient plus gravity can sort larger grains toward the hotter or colder side.
arxiv-2601-04226:
Thijs Snelleman, Peter Lundestad Lawrence, Holger H. Hoos, and Odd Erik Gundersen argue that automated reproducibility work lacks a clear problem statement. Reproduction is vital to science yet slow by hand, and automatic attempts use shifting definitions of what counts as success. The team sets out to state the problem in a general form.

Their idea is to represent any empirical study through the structure of the scientific method: hypotheses, experiments, and interpretations. They extract that structure automatically from twenty studies and ask the original authors to judge the result. Most feedback is positive across all parts, though some study elements and fine result details are missed. The four authors conclude the formulation captures reproducibility across many AI subfields and could guide finer structured output later.
arxiv-2601-04626:
Therese Biedl and Prashant Gokhale find a smallest set of guards for a special class of graphs without ever listing the edges, in a 2026 arXiv paper. RDV graphs arise as the intersection graphs of downward paths in a rooted tree, sitting between interval graphs and chordal graphs. Earlier work showed their adjacency questions reduce to whether horizontal and vertical segments cross, which yielded a fast maximum matching.

Adding a ray shooting data structure to that geometric kit, the authors compute a minimum dominating set. A smallest set of vertices such that every vertex is in it or next to one — in near-linear time, still without examining all edges. As a by-product, the same idea gives a new proof that interval graphs admit a minimum dominating set in strictly linear time. The results extend a programme of fast algorithms for graph problems whose inputs have compact geometric representations.
arxiv-2601-04726:
Yuyang Hu and four co-authors give language model agents a memory organized like a map of events instead of a pile of notes, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents working over long horizons must retain and retrieve experience. But most memory systems store it flat and fetch by shallow similarity, missing the logical relations between episodes that real reasoning needs.

CompassMem, inspired by event segmentation theory, slices experience into events as it arrives and links them into an event graph with explicit logical relations. The graph acts as a logic map: instead of grabbing whichever memory looks similar. The agent navigates the structure step by step, gathering the memories a goal actually requires. On the LoCoMo and NarrativeQA benchmarks, the approach consistently improves both retrieval accuracy and downstream reasoning across several backbone models.
arxiv-2601-05026:
Pierre Lairez, Rafael Mohr, and Théo Ternier coin a data form for a key tool of algebra in a 2026 paper. Their tool tracks sets built from plain power terms, the bread and butter of algebra software. Such software must test, again and again, if a term sits in a set, and must add new terms to the set as work goes on. Their form grows from a tree that is shared as much as it can be, so it stays small.

The team prove bounds on how fast a test or an add runs in the new form. They also check its size in real runs. Then they plug it into a known code base, where fast tests flag terms that shrink to zero. Swift bookkeeping of this kind speeds the deep algebra jobs used in shape, code, and proof work.
arxiv-2601-05126:
E.-O. Eljaouhari and 8 co-authors use sound waves to catch swift shifts in the electron sea of a rare stuff in a 2026 paper. Their stuff is a crystal of rare earth atoms, nickel, and phosphorus. They chill it and run a magnet field down one axis of the crystal. Past work had shown a run of shifts in the shape of its sea of free electrons as the field climbs.

Their sound tests show a run of sharp dips in the speed of sound. The dips line up well with that run of shifts. Sound modes of a set twist pick the shifts out with more clear marks than the rest. One mark shows a small loop of the sea's edge fade away as the field grows. Sound proves a fine probe here, and the match firms the case for odd states in this stuff.
arxiv-2601-05226:
In a 2026 paper, Giorgio Facelli, Hamza Fawzi, and Omar Fawzi prove a plain trick for fermion play runs fast when the fermions pull on each other weakly. To run the play of a watched trait as time runs on is a top hope for quantum machines. Plain machines are not thought to do it fast in the main. The trick here, Majorana Propagation, strings short steps with cuts that keep just the plain parts.

The team show the trick finds a low-grade gloss fast. It works as soon as such a gloss is there to be found. That is the first proof of its kind for this trick in time play. To know just when a cheap plain trick works is to map the line where quantum machines start to be a true need.
arxiv-2601-05726:
Lassaad Mandhour and Frederic Piechon investigate, in a 2026 paper, how a massless Dirac particle scatters from a domain wall where Berry curvature changes. Berry curvature is a geometric property of quantum states that affects how particles move. The two regions share identical energy spectra but carry different Berry curvature dipoles.

Despite identical incoming and outgoing momenta, the geometric mismatch causes partial reflection and partial transmission at the wall. In other words, geometry alone can act like a barrier. The authors present engineered quantum geometric interfaces as a new control tool for Dirac particle scattering. Such control could matter for future electronic devices built from materials where quantum geometry dominates transport.
arxiv-2601-05826:
Íris Damião and 5 co-authors map in 2026 how news outlets across five European countries covered political families during the 2024 European Parliament elections. Visibility in news is a central campaign resource. Their dataset covers close to twenty-one thousand five hundred articles from leading outlets in Austria, Germany, Ireland, Poland, and Portugal.

Parties and leaders were identified from article titles and links, mixing computational and human classification, then grouped by European Parliament family and leaning. Mainstream and radical right groups were mentioned most. The radical right received attention disproportionate to its election results and projections, especially in Austria, Germany, and Ireland, and the imbalance grew in the final campaign weeks. Right-leaning coverage dominated high-traffic outlets too, suggesting a structural pattern rather than isolated editorial choices.
arxiv-2601-05926:
Ernest Ma and 2 co-authors explore in 2026 how neutrinos could be Dirac particles with naturally small masses, while also supplying dark matter, inside a gauged B-L extension of the Standard Model. In the conventional version, a scalar's charge choice lets right-handed neutrinos gain heavy Majorana masses, powering the seesaw mechanism.

Choosing a different charge for that scalar removes the Majorana option, leaving neutrinos Dirac fermions. A new vector-like fermion then becomes a dark matter candidate, Dirac or Majorana depending on the scalar's charge. Symmetry breaking in this setup can be strongly first-order, producing gravitational waves testable by future experiments. Light right-handed neutrinos also shift the effective number of relativistic species, adding cosmological constraints.
arxiv-2601-06226:
Toxic outputs persist inside language models even after output-level fixes. Zenghao Duan and 10 co-authors propose removing the problem at its source in a 2026 paper on detoxification. Alignment changes what a model prefers to say, but the underlying toxic regions in its parameters remain, leaving it open to adversarial prompts.

Their analysis shows removed toxic vectors can be rebuilt from combinations of harmless ones, so the whole toxic subspace must go. Sampling noise also corrupts layer-by-layer extraction. Their GLOSS method identifies a global toxic subspace in the feed-forward parameters and suppresses it. On models such as Qwen3, GLOSS achieved top detoxification while preserving general abilities, without large-scale retraining.
arxiv-2601-06426:
Tests grade what a model says. They miss if the model acts right in a chat. Robert J. Moore and 3 co-authors built NC-Bench to close that gap in a 2026 paper. It grades chat skill: the right move, like a fix, a close, or a no, at the right point in the talk.

The test rests on a frame from the science of talk. It has three sets. One set checks base moves: give a reply, fix a slip, close a pair. The next set adds fact hunts through search. The third set takes on hard asks that need deft move work. Seven models faced twice seven talk forms, and the gaps in skill could be counted. The tool is light, can grow, and rests on sound talk rules. It names the exact moves a model lacks.
arxiv-2601-06526:
Claudio Afeltra sets out a new kind of shape space in a 2026 math paper. The spark is an old curve task on groups of Heisenberg type. Those groups move like a car: they can roll and turn, but not slide to the side. The task lacked a shape-based read on such groups.

His new form is a contact form of Heisenberg type. On spaces built like the group, it plays the role that contact forms play in the plain case. He gives a link rule for the form, a way to join slopes from place to place. He also works out how the bend of the space shifts when the scale is stretched by a smooth factor. Then he states the Yamabe task for these spaces: find a stretch that makes the bend the same at each point. The work gives this branch a firm base.
arxiv-2601-06726:
Mohammad Khateri and three co-authors give tools for fetal brain scans in a 2026 paper. Sound-wave scans are safe, cheap, and at hand in most clinics. They suit day-to-day care of unborn babes well, the team notes.

Yet such scans bear flaws that shift with the probe's angle of use. Skill gaps between staff and a small field of view add to the flaws. Sense and counts from the scans thus get hard to make with trust. Their tools merge views from many angles into one full brain view. Merged views could make counts hold up across staff and clinics alike. The work gives real tools, not just a plan on a page. It aims at a scan done vast counts of times each year round the world.
arxiv-2601-06926:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Illia Ovtsynov and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers structure of morse flows and co-dimension one gradient flows on the sphere. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. We describe all possible topological structures of typical one-parameter bifurcations of gradient flows on the 2-sphere with holes.

In the case that the number of singular point of flows is at most six. To describe structures, we separatrix diagrams of flows. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07226:
Seongyun Lee and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with lost in the noise. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Recent advances in reasoning models and agentic AI systems have led to an increased reliance on diverse external information. However, this shift introduces input contexts that are inherently noisy, a reality that current sanitized benchmarks fail to capture.

The authors introduce NoisyBench , a comprehensive benchmark that systematically evaluates model robustness across 11 datasets in RAG, reasoning. Alignment, and tool-use tasks against diverse noise types, including random documents, irrelevant chat histories, and hard negative distractors. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07326: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Huan Li and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers convergence rate analysis of the AdamW-Style shampoo. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The work studies the AdamW-style Shampoo optimizer. An effective implementation of classical Shampoo that notably won the external tuning track of the AlgoPerf neural network training algorithm competition. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07426:
Andrea Colesanti, Lei Qin, and Paolo Salani wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how a curved shape holds as heat spreads. The shape in view is log-concave, which means the log of its height bends down at all points. The flow comes from a parabolic equation. That equation is tied to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, a tool for random drift back to a mean.

The team studies the kernel of that operator, the core that sets the flow. The work is set in a bounded, convex domain. They show that the kernel is log-concave. As a result, a start shape that is log-concave stays log-concave as the flow goes on. The team then gives a new proof of a Brunn-Minkowski type rule. That rule bounds the first eigenvalue of the operator. Past work proved these facts by other means.
arxiv-2601-08026:
Jifeng Song and colleagues present FigEx2, a system that finds and captions each panel of a scientific compound figure. Compound figures pack several labeled panels into one image. In real pipelines, captions are often missing or only summarize the whole figure. Panel-level understanding is therefore difficult. FigEx2 localizes panels and generates a caption for each one, directly from the figure image. Their 2026 preprint describes the visual-conditioned framework.

Panel captions unlock the content of published figures for search and reading tools. Accessibility also gains, since screen readers need panel-level descriptions. Conditioning on the visual layout keeps captions tied to the right panel. The work targets the messy figures found in real journals. The paper serves scholars in document AI and scientific publishing tools. It treats figures as structured content, not decoration.
arxiv-2601-08126: M. Auer and S. Liu study trimmed ergodic sums for systems with exponential mixing. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from the Birkhoff ergodic theorem, which gives pointwise convergence for integrable observables. For heavier-tailed observables, no normalization yields almost sure convergence in the usual sense. The authors instead remove the largest observations and study the trimmed sums. The observables have polynomial tails, with a stated power-law form. Distributional limits for trimmed sums extend ergodic theory to data with extreme outliers, common in finance and climate records.
arxiv-2601-08526: Gouri Lakshmi S and co-authors introduce supervised spike agreement dependent plasticity for spiking networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on spike-timing-dependent plasticity, a biologically grounded learning rule. That rule relies on precise spike timing and pairwise updates, which limit fast weight learning. The new supervised extension swaps pairwise timing checks for population-level agreement metrics such as Cohen's kappa. Agreement across a population can signal a correct response more robustly. Faster local learning could help neuromorphic hardware train on chip with little energy.
arxiv-2601-08926:
Amy Secunda and three co-authors use AI to weigh the height of disks round huge black holes. Light from such a disk rings back with a lag. The lag by hue tells us the span of the disk. The team wants the height as well, which is far more hard to read from lags. A new huge sky survey will soon give rich lag data for many disks.

They train a transformer model, a net that weighs which past points count, on sim lag data. The model learns to read height signs in the lag shape. A reader in space work gets a tool set for the new survey. It may turn lag lists into full disk shapes for a vast set of black holes.
arxiv-2601-09126:
Pratim Guha Niyogi and four co-authors link wrist move data to loss of skill in multiple sclerosis. MS is a nerve ill that can slow walk and hand use. Wrist sensors can track move all day. Past work shows the full spread of move counts beats a plain mean as a health sign. The tail of that spread, rare bursts or long rests, oft holds the key sign.

The team gives one frame for such spreads, called generalized odds. It reads a spread by the odds of move in any zone of counts. Old signs, such as risk and life curves, fall out as cases. A reader in health data gets a joint frame for rich sensor spreads.
arxiv-2601-09326:
Tomoya Takahashi and three co-authors read how a quantum spin chain waves at low heat with grid net tools. Heat states of such chains are hard to hold in a net. Bonds grow fast, and low heat is the worst zone. Past tools use a clean up trick or a few sample states. Both lose truth or scale poor at low heat.

The team grows a state space by parts, with a matrix form for each state. That growth keeps key wave traits while it caps bond size. From the held state they read the wave spread by force and time. A reader in quantum stuffs gets a path to low heat wave facts that past tools could not reach clean.
arxiv-2601-09526:
Zhen-Zhen Zhang, Hua-Lei Wang, Kui Xiao, and Min-Liang Liu probe a long-lived excited state in a nucleus at the edge of stability. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies osmium-160, which sits at the two-proton drip line. The state of interest is a two-quasiparticle isomer with spin-parity 8+.

Recent experiments reported signs that the isomer lasts longer than expected. The authors use configuration-constrained potential-energy-surface calculations to test the claim. The state's structure is tied to neutron orbitals h9/2 and f7/2. Isomers at the drip line reveal how nuclei hold together when protons barely stay bound at all. They are rare probes of nuclear structure under extreme strain.
arxiv-2601-09726:
Hien Tran, Quinten Steenhuis, Alexandros Christoforos, and Chadbourne Davis defend a flaw of language models as a feature. Their 2026 arXiv paper argues that forgetting past evidence mirrors human cognition. Models are often judged against perfect Bayesian inference, which never discounts old evidence.

In practice, the authors note, model updates in context behave like discounted filters that let old evidence fade. That fading resembles how people weigh recent information more. Reframing forgetting as cognitive alignment changes what builders should fix. A model that forgets like a person may interact more naturally than one with perfect recall.
arxiv-2601-09926:
Kirandeep Kaur, Vinayak Gupta, Aditya Gupta, and Chirag Shah study help that comes before a user asks. Most aids wait for a clear request. They work in a ask and reply loop. Needs that users do not state can then be missed.

Some new agents try to act first. One path asks more prompts, which keeps the load on the user. A second path guesses needs from context. That guess can fire at a bad time or add noise. The paper sets tests for this skill. It calls the core task gap finding: spot what the user lacks, and help at the right time.
arxiv-2601-10126:
Chong-long Xie, Guo-yun Shao, Ming-zheng-xuan Wu, and Wei-bo He work out how quark soup resists a squeeze. Quark soup is the hot dense form of matter from the early world. Its flow traits shift as it cools and turns to plain matter. Bulk drag is one such trait.

The team use a move based math with a set rest time. Mass terms come from a model with a loop field for the phase shift. They track bulk drag across the shift range. They also track its ratio to shear drag. Those traits shape how the soup flows in star cores and in lab hits.
arxiv-2601-10426:
Zeping Hao and Meng Fai Lim prove swap rules for big Galois forms over many p power towers. A Galois form tracks how roots of a law link. Big forms hold a whole tower of fields at once. Selmer groups sort the key facts in such a tower.

The team give a broad path to such swap rules. The rules hold in two frames: Selmer groups and Selmer complexes. They span a wide set of Iwasawa type cases. Iwasawa work studies towers that grow by a prime power at each step. Firm swap rules tie the two sides of such a tower.
arxiv-2601-10526:
Adway Girish, Robinson Cung, and Emre Telatar show that plain codes fall short for a shared test task. Two agents see linked bit rows. Each sends a short sum to a core judge. The judge must call which of two world states holds. The agents send at the same rate.

Linear codes are a plain pick for the sums. The team show a plain cut beats all such codes in two cases. One case tests sign of the link. One tests if a link is there at all. The result marks a bound on what linear sums can do.
arxiv-2601-10626:
Getoar Sopa, Marco Avella Medina, and Cynthia Rush work on private statistics for data collected over time. Differential privacy gives a strict way to release results while shielding each person's data. Much work on private linear regression assumes each user gives one data point. Real health and social studies follow the same people for years.

Longitudinal data, with repeated measures per person, break that one-point setup. The authors develop private inference methods for this case. The goal is valid estimates of trends without leaking any one person's record. Their work extends privacy tools to the repeated-measures data that clinics and surveys actually hold.
arxiv-2601-11226:
Bernhard Heim and Markus Neuhauser take up a conjecture of Sun in this work. Their 2026 preprint deals with partitions of whole numbers. A partition splits a number into a sum of smaller parts. The count of such splits is written p of n.
