As n grows, the nth root of p of n tends to 1. That fact links to the Cauchy-Hadamard test for power series. Andrews found a basic proof of the key limit as well. The new work turns Sun's claim into polynomial form. That shift is what the title calls polynomization of the claim. Polynomial forms can make growth facts much easier to test.
arxiv-2601-11626:
Maksym Shamrai studies shrinking large sets of matrices by SVD. The 2026 preprint covers joined-matrix SVD in depth. Big matrix sets arise across machine learning and computing. Signal work and science computing add their own sets.

The standard trick concatenates the matrices into one. A truncated SVD then compresses the joined matrix. That enables parameter sharing and efficient reconstruction. Shamrai derives size bounds for the strategy. A step-wise method updates the shrinkage as data arrive. Error-constrained clustering groups matrices under a set error cap. The results serve multi-view learning and network compression. Users gain theory for a widely adopted practice.
arxiv-2601-11926: Ananya Halgatti, Shaunak Biswas, Hiya Bhatt, and their co-authors present a test case for steady machine learning work in the field. Models in use meet shifts in their world over time. With no watch, those shifts can harm output, raise cost, and cut value. Their system, named in the work with a styled title, acts as a self-adaptation exemplar. It is built for the MLOps task of keeping models sound as data drift. A shared exemplar lets teams test their own watch and fix tools.
arxiv-2601-12026:
Muhammad Bayu Saputra, Handhika Satrio Ramadhan, Ibnu Nurul Huda, and Leonardus Brahmantyo Putra study balance points for a third body in a three-body system. Two big bodies move on an elliptic path, and a small third body moves in their field. Extra forces bend that field.

They add radiation pressure, the non-round shape of the main bodies, their stretch, and disk-like forms. Each force can shift where the small body can rest in balance. The team check when those points stay stable. Such maps aid craft paths in real, messy systems.
arxiv-2601-12426:
Mohammadhossein Homaei and four co authors work on safety for water distribution systems. These networks face growing cyber physical risks, from faults to attacks. Spotting anomalies fast is key to limiting harm. Many data driven tools ignore the shape of the network, though. Others that use physics lean hard on exact parameter values.

The team propose a graph attention network that knows the hydraulics. Its features come from breaches of conservation laws, put in normalized form. In plain terms, water that fails to balance flags a problem spot. Graph attention lets the model weigh links between nodes in the network. The work aims for detection that is both sharp and easy to interpret.
arxiv-2601-12626:
Raphi Kang, Hongqiao Chen, Georgia Gkioxari, and Pietro Perona, at Caltech, probe how vision language models reason about space and time. These models can answer questions about where things are and how scenes change. The mechanisms behind that skill remain largely opaque, though. The team start from a simple postulate about how the skill must work.

At some point in the computation, visual and textual views of space must be combined. Geometry from images and words about layout have to meet. The team look for linear mechanisms that do that joining. Finding simple linear structure inside a huge model would be a strong clue. It would suggest that spatial reasoning rests on readable, low level features.
arxiv-2601-13726:
Michael Björklund, Reynold Fregoli, and Alexander Gorodnik study how whole-number solutions spread out in 2026. Their problem sits in multiplicative Diophantine approximation, a field on how well numbers can be matched by fractions. They count the integer solutions to a set form of the problem. The key question is the shape of that count over many cases.

The team shows the counting function tends to a normal law in distribution. In plain terms, its spread acts like a bell curve in the limit. Their proof uses correlations of measures on homogeneous spaces. It also uses bounds for Siegel transforms cut down to subspaces.
arxiv-2601-14226:
Leonardo Placidi and co-authors use deep learning to clean noisy quantum circuit outputs in 2026. Quantum error mitigation corrects noisy output probability distributions from measured circuits. The team presents a systematic investigation of deep learning methods for this task. They compare architectures from fully connected networks to transformers.

They also test different design and training modalities. Sequence-to-sequence, attention-based models were the most effective on their datasets. Learned mitigation could extend the reach of today's noisy quantum machines. It offers a data-driven complement to analytic error correction. The test bed spans many circuit types and noise forms. Wins that hold across that range are more likely to hold on real rigs.
arxiv-2601-14426:
Maximilian Vovk, Peter G. Brown, Denis Vida, and their co-authors weigh tiny space rocks in this 2026 paper. Accurate estimates of meteoroid bulk density matter for a practical reason. Sub-millimeter to millimeter meteoroids form the bulk of the impact hazard to spacecraft. Density tells engineers how much damage a hit can do.

Past studies fit ablation and fragmentation models to optical meteor data by hand or by optimization. The team uses dynamic nested sampling instead, a Bayesian method that explores model space in depth. They apply it to Orionid and Capricornid shower meteors as a case study. Readers get a more rigorous way to infer what shower meteors are made of.
arxiv-2601-14526:
Mengmeng Long and a team of nine co-authors measure magnetic order in a metal in this 2026 paper. Electronic phases of matter, such as magnetism and superconductivity, are defined by their order parameters. An order parameter quantifies the spontaneous symmetry breaking under each phase. The simplest cases are the uniform magnetisation of ferromagnets and the isotropic gap of conventional superconductors.

The team's material is the metallic altermagnet CrSb. Altermagnets are a newly recognized class of magnetic order. The authors determine its bulk-resolved order parameter symmetry in three dimensions. Their title names it g-wave magnetic order. The read is threefold. It checks the bulk, not just the face of the slab, so the call is firm. Readers get a direct read on the symmetry of a phase that textbooks are still absorbing.
arxiv-2601-14726:
Ragheed Alhyder, Rishabh Sahu, Johannes M. Fink, Mikhail Lemeshko, and Georgios M. Koutentakis study light mixing in a microresonator in this 2026 paper. Integrated optical microresonators that exploit second-order or third-order nonlinearities are key platforms. They serve frequency conversion, low-noise microwave photonics, and quantum entanglement generation. The team presents an analytic theory of Kerr-enhanced three-wave mixing amplification.

Their device is an electro-optic microresonator with both second-order and third-order nonlinearities present. Kerr effects come from the third-order response. The title also names emergent masing regimes, states where the device emits coherent microwaves like a laser. The tool is tiny. It sits on a chip, yet it can mix tones in ways that used to need a bench of gear. Readers get theory for a small device with rich mixing behavior.
arxiv-2601-15526:
J. Hermenegildo R. González, Gustavo O. Carvalho, and Fábio P. Machado study the frog model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The frog model is a classic setup in probability. Particles sit on the integer line, each with its own lifetime. Here each particle draws a random survival parameter. Given that parameter, its lifetime follows a discrete Weibull law.

The Weibull form adds a shape parameter that bends the lifetime curve. Particle lifetimes are independent but not identical in this design. The authors study how the model behaves under these rules. Frog models mimic spread, like infection or rumor passing. Changing the lifetime law changes how far and fast the spread runs. Probabilists use such models to test ideas about growth and survival in random media.
arxiv-2601-15726:
Poonam Sharma and Suman Banerjee maximize marketing spread in social networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Firms now use online social networks heavily for viral marketing. The key problem is choosing seed users. A limited set of influential users gets the brand first. If chosen well, their adoption spreads influence widely. If chosen poorly, the campaign dies early. The budget for seeds is limited, so each pick counts.

The authors propose a two-phase diffusion approach, per the title. Splitting diffusion into phases can balance reach with cost. Profit maximization is the stated goal, not spread alone. A wide spread that costs more than it earns is a failure. For marketing science, the paper adds one more method to the seed-selection toolbox.
arxiv-2601-15926:
Aryiadna Yesmanchyk and five co-authors validate a solar physics model outside its training data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning is spreading through nearly every field, solar physics included. Their model, MagNet, was built for a hard data-mining task. It generates transverse magnetic fields of solar active regions. Those fields are hard to measure directly. A model that fills them in aids many studies.

Out-of-sample validation is the paper's focus. A model can look strong on data like its training set yet fail elsewhere. Testing on truly new data gives the honest score. Solar observations shift with instruments and solar cycles, so robustness matters. The validation tells users where MagNet can be trusted and where it should be doubted.
arxiv-2601-16026:
Dong-Sheng Liu and a large team simplify quantum measurement in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum metrology beats classical limits with exotic probe states. Entangled or squeezed states are the usual tools. Preparing them needs careful calibration of system parameters. It also needs finely optimized quantum controls. Those demands limit scalability and robustness in real labs. The authors propose echoed random quantum metrology, per the title.

The name suggests randomness replaces fine tuning. Echoes imply a sequence that undoes errors while keeping the signal. If random probes work, precision measurement gets much easier to run. Sensors for fields, time, and gravity all chase quantum gains. A method that drops the delicate preparation step could move those gains from hero experiments toward routine instruments.
arxiv-2601-16226:
Ixandra Achitouv and David Chavalarias draw a live maths model of view shifts from real feed data. Their 2026 preprint is the first of its kind in this field. They track user views on a yes or no climate topic through time. From the tracks they infer how each view drifts and spreads. Drift and spread are the two parts that drive the model.

The drawn model runs in smooth time, not step time. It can then show how views move and clump. A model drawn from data beats one built from guesses. It can test which feeds push views to poles. The work gives a data based tool for view studies.
arxiv-2601-17026:
Shridharan Chandramouli splits a hard cut task for fast work on many cores. The task finds the least cut twixt two points in a graph. Such cuts drive cuts of 3D scans in care work. Big 3D graphs make lone-core cuts crawl. His 2026 preprint builds a fast path for a clean class of 3D graphs.

Those graphs stack in a set, rank-kept form. The fast path splits the cut hunt across cores. Each core takes a slice of the graph grid. Fast true cuts could speed scan work in clinics. They may also aid chip and net layout tasks.
arxiv-2601-17126:
Ting-Hsiang Hsu and a team of ten co-authors build a base model for collider event data. Deep learn tools now aid work at big colliders. Yet compute caps curb what those tools can do. Their 2026 preprint shares EveNet, a base model for whole events. It pre-trains on half a billion fake events. Two aim types guide that train in one mix.

One aim is self-taught, from the events' own forms. The next aim bakes physics facts in the marks. A shared base can then tune to many tasks. That saves each team a from-scratch train run. Collider labs gain speed on rare-event hunts.
arxiv-2601-17426:
Zhengqing Zang and seven co-authors probe logic in large language models with syllogisms. A syllogism is a short formal argument with two premises and a claim. The probe centers on existential import. That is the old question of whether a general term implies that things of that kind exist. Traditional and modern logic answer it in unlike ways.

Human logic moved from gut feel to formal systems over time. The team asks if models show a like shift. Their tests trace how model answers change across setups. The probe gives a clean lens on machine reasoning. It can show if models hold one logic or mix two. That matters for law and science aids.
arxiv-2601-17526:
Mohammad Atif and co-authors help teams pick GPU portability layers. Graphics processors now supply most high-end compute power. High energy physics uses them for a fast-growing share of tasks. NVIDIA leads the market, but AMD and Intel are gaining. Code must run well on all three. Portability layers promise that reach.

The team evaluates app traits that should drive the choice. Kernel shape, memory use, and team skill all matter. A wrong layer can lock a lab into poor speed. Their guide turns vendor claims into test-based picks. Big science codes live for decades. The layer choice shapes cost for years. This work makes that choice a studied one.
arxiv-2601-17626:
Somphong Jitman and Wannarut Rungrottheera find explicit determinants for polynomial evaluation matrices. The matrices come from homogeneous bivariate polynomials. Each polynomial is a weighted sum of x and y powers. It is evaluated at pairs of vectors to fill the matrix. The authors derive a clean factorization of the determinant.

Explicit forms turn costly numeric work into direct reads. They also expose when the matrix is singular at a glance. Such matrices arise in codes, designs, and interpolation. A factorization can speed all those uses. The work is a tidy result in matrix theory. It gives users a formula where iteration stood before.
arxiv-2601-17726:
Zhe Wei, Zhenzhen Lou, and Changxiang He set spectral conditions for embedding graphs. The signless Laplacian spectral radius, or Q-index, is a key network measure. It has grown central in spectral graph theory. The authors prove new extremal results tied to it. They study graphs that forbid a 4-cycle. They also study star embeddings under the same lens.

Forbidden subgraph rules shape what networks can form. Spectral conditions give fast tests for those shapes. A dedication marks the paper for Professor Eddie Cheng's 60th birthday. Extremal results tell builders the best a network can do. They also mark where phase shifts in structure occur. The Q-index is their chosen gauge.
arxiv-2601-18026:
Pedro Ortiz Suarez and co-authors re-test how well machines can tell one language from another. Their 2026 preprint presents CommonLID, a benchmark for language identification. Telling languages apart is a first step in building multilingual corpora. Yet models still do poorly for many languages, above all on noisy web text. Web text is exactly what trains today's multilingual models, so errors flow downstream.

CommonLID is community-driven and labeled by people. It covers 109 languages in the web domain. A shared, honest benchmark shows where models fail and for whom. It also gives builders a target to improve against. Better language ID means cleaner training data for low-resource languages.
arxiv-2601-18226:
Haotian Li and co-authors present the Yunjue Agent, a system that improves itself while it works. Their 2026 preprint is a technical report. Conventional agents struggle in open-ended settings where tasks keep drifting and supervision is scarce. Static toolsets and offline training fall behind such change. The result is a system whose limits stay rigid and unknown even to itself. The authors propose an in-situ self-evolving paradigm to break that pattern.

The system is billed as fully reproducible and built from a zero start. It evolves in place, in the very setting where it runs. Agents that can grow with their tasks are a major goal of the field. The report lays out the design for others to test.
arxiv-2601-18426:
Mingyao Cui, Qunsong Zeng, and Kaibin Huang set out a theory for a new kind of radio sensor built from excited atoms. Such atoms can sense faint waves with great care and across a wide band. Past work treats each sensor as a plain point that takes waves the same from all sides. That view skips how the state of the atoms shifts from place to place in the gas cell.

The pair of authors and their colleague map how the wave take shifts across the cell. From that map they build the idea of beam forming with a lone sensor. A beam can be steered to one side, so the sensor hears more from that side and less from the rest. A true map of that skill could guide new kit for weak signal work and for fine maps of wave fields.
arxiv-2601-18526:
Yen-An Chen and Ching-Jui Lai study a weak but deep kind of firmness for a class of shapes in maths. The shapes, called Fano shapes, have a twist that makes them key in the maths of form. A firm shape holds its form when its lines are pushed a bit. A strong form of that trait has seen fast gains in the past few years.

The weak form rests on the slopes of lines that lie on the shape. It is more a thing of pure maths, and it is far less known. One old guess says the line set of a key class of such shapes should be firm in the weak sense too. The pair probe that guess and the shapes that may break it. Their work maps where weak firmness holds and where it fails.
arxiv-2601-18926:
Cassie Sevilla, Anna Y. Q. Ho, and many co-authors study six bright, fast, blue flashes in the sky. These events, called fast blue optical transients, rise and fade fast and glow blue at their peak. The team found them in survey data from the Zwicky Transient Facility and tracked them in many colors of light.

Their light curves fall by half in under two weeks, which marks them as an extreme class. Data from radio to X-ray help test what powers such brief, bright blasts. Each new well watched case sharpens the debate on whether stars, black holes, or both drive them.
arxiv-2601-19026:
Andrea Fasoli and six co-authors ask how far tiny number formats can shrink language models. Microscaling formats store blocks of numbers with a shared scale, which lets models compress hard while losing little accuracy. Real gains need hardware that can multiply in the native format and clean up the errors that arise.

The team probes where the finer formats stop helping, as their title asks. Past a point, smaller blocks cost more than they save, or errors grow too fast. Their map of the limits helps chip and model designers pick formats that save memory without giving up quality.
arxiv-2601-19126:
Xi Wang, Parastoo Sadeghi, and Guodong Shi study how entanglement reshapes privacy in quantum systems. Quantum differential privacy gives a strict way to state how much a process hides about its inputs. Classically, correlations between parties are usually seen as a threat to privacy.

Entanglement is the quantum kind of correlation, and its role was not well understood. The team examines how it shapes the local form of quantum privacy. Their findings could cut either way, and knowing which matters for quantum networks where linked particles are shared on purpose, not by accident.
arxiv-2601-19326:
Georg Engelhardt, Dahai He, and JunYan Luo find a limit on measuring chemicals with light that comes from chemistry itself. Spectrophotometry infers how much of a substance is present from how it absorbs light. Photon noise is the known floor on its precision, set by the grain of light itself.

The team shows that chemical reactions add their own floor on top of that. Using a new photon resolved theory, they study a model molecule whose light response depends on its chemical state. Flicker between states blurs the reading. Labs chasing ultra precise measures will have to budget for this chemical noise as well.
arxiv-2601-19526:
Fouad Boutaleb and five colleagues work on a hard problem in mental health care. Major depressive disorder is often judged from what patients say and how doctors rate them. One core sign, called psychomotor retardation, is a slowing of movement and reaction. Doctors still rate this sign mostly by eye, so scores can vary from one clinician to the next.

The team builds a framework that reads walking patterns in three dimensions. It needs no sensors on the body and no contact with the patient. From the gait data it pulls out clear, objective features that describe how the person moves. Such features could give doctors a steadier way to track the slowing over time. The work joins computer vision with everyday clinical care.
arxiv-2601-19826:
Fan Yang, Renkai Ma, Yaxin Hu, and Lingyao Li study how people react when robots are mistreated. As robots enter homes and public spaces, scenes of robot abuse are increasingly witnessed. Whether bystanders care, and how they reason about it, has ethical and design implications. The authors run a mixed-methods study with just over two hundred participants.

They vary how human-like the robot appears and measure participants' moral foundations. Both factors shape reactions to abuse, in what the authors call a dual role. People may condemn the act yet differ in why they care. Findings like these inform how robots should be designed and presented. They also speak to wider debates about kindness toward machines.
arxiv-2601-19926:
Nora Graichen, Iria de-Dios-Flores, and Gemma Boleda review what is known about grammar inside language models. Transformer models handle syntax well in practice, but how they represent it is debated. Interpretability research has attacked the question from many angles. A systematic map of that literature was missing.

Their review covers several hundred articles evaluating the syntactic abilities of transformer models. It organises over a thousand model results across syntactic phenomena and interpretability methods. Patterns emerge about which methods agree and which phenomena are robustly captured. Such stock-taking helps researchers avoid repeating settled experiments. It also highlights where claims about machine grammar rest on thin evidence. The stock take is broad and fair.
arxiv-2601-20126:
Abha Jha, Akanksha Mahajan, and Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan tackle a known flaw of large language models. These models often state false or unchecked claims as if they were facts. The authors ask whether training can teach a model to hold back. Their method rewards the model both for right answers and for saying it does not know.

The team fine-tunes and tests a Granite model under this reward scheme. The training style is called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The goal is a model with more intellectual humility, one that stays silent when an answer would be a guess. Such care matters most in factual fields where a wrong answer can do real harm.
arxiv-2601-20626:
D. Tozzi summarizes machine learning approaches for the CYGNO experiment, which hunts dark matter with an optical-readout time projection chamber. The chamber records rare, low-energy interactions as finely resolved scintillation images. Optical readout gives rich shape information, but the images are large, sparse, and megapixel-sized, which challenges real-time triggering and background rejection.

Two complementary learning approaches are described: one for triggering and data reduction, one for telling signal from background. Rare-event searches live or die on this sorting, since the data stream is vast and the true events are few. Most of the stream is noise, and it must be cut fast.
arxiv-2601-20826:
The Euclid Collaboration prepares to read the cosmos with care in this 2026 paper. Euclid is a space telescope built to survey galaxies. Its spectroscopic data will map how galaxies cluster in space. To read that map, scientists must model redshift-space distortions. These distortions arise because galaxy motions stretch the map along the line of sight.

Accurate models are essential to squeeze full value from the data. The team tests three approaches to modeling the effect. They apply them to the power spectrum multipoles of mock galaxies. The mock galaxies emit the H-alpha line, a standard marker. The study is groundwork for the real survey analysis. It helps ensure that Euclid's map of the universe is read without bias.
arxiv-2601-21026:
Louis Grenioux and Maxence Noble explore generators that sample matter at thermal balance. Their 2026 paper studies diffusion-based annealed Boltzmann generators. Sampling such states is a central challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators pair a generative model with a Monte Carlo fix-up step. The fix-up yields unbiased samples from an unnormalized target. Most such generators use classic fix-ups, such as importance sampling.

Those fix-ups carry two burdens. They need tractable likelihoods from the base model. And they scale poorly in high-dimensional, multi-modal targets. The authors weigh the benefits and pitfalls of a diffusion-based design. Annealing eases the path from noise to target in steps. The paper is candid about hopes and limits. It guides physicists who simulate molecules and materials.
arxiv-2601-21526:
Alireza Nadafian, Alireza Mohammadshahi, and Majid Yazdani present a framework that writes and improves programs on its own. Given a goal in plain words and a way to score results, the system cycles through stages. It drafts ideas, writes code, runs it, scores it, and learns from the outcome.

Each loop aims to push a working artifact closer to the stated goals. Grounding the loop in outside knowledge keeps the search from wandering. A modular build lets teams swap parts for their own tasks. The framework targets research and engineering chores where the target is clear enough to measure.
arxiv-2601-21626:
Jinhao Zhang, Yunquan Zhang, Zicheng Yan, Boyang Zhang, Jun Sun, and Daning Cheng fix a paradox in compressing language models. Post-training quantization shrinks models by rounding their numbers. It often shows low rounding error yet high loss, which seems contradictory.

The cause lies in the shape of the loss landscape. A few high-curvature directions are extremely sensitive to small nudges. Errors there cost far more than errors elsewhere. Their method conditions the problem using that curvature map, so rounding avoids the fragile directions. Steadier compression keeps small models accurate enough for real use on modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-21926:
Jinhao Zhang and co-authors try to slim down the networks that teach robots to move. Diffusion-based visuomotor policies learn complex skills from three-dimensional visual input, and they perform strongly. But most designs use an oversized denoising decoder, the part that turns noise into action.

The authors note that more capacity can help denoising, yet evidence suggests it also adds redundancy and noise in the middle feature blocks. Their 2026 preprint uses information filtering, guided by variational regularization, to strip out what the policy does not need. Leaner policies would run faster on robot hardware and react quicker, which matters when a robot arm must correct itself mid-motion.
arxiv-2601-22026:
Constantin Kleinbeck and co-authors render medical volumes fast enough for immersive use. Three-dimensional scans hold rich information about disease, but flat slices force clinicians to rebuild anatomy mentally. Direct volumetric path tracing in virtual reality gives true spatial understanding, yet it is computationally expensive.

The team's 2026 preprint mixes two techniques. Sharp path tracing covers the fovea, the center of vision where detail matters, while smooth Gaussian representations fill the periphery, where the eye notices less. That hybrid foveated approach targets immersive anatomy viewers that stay fluid on real hardware. Better spatial views could help surgeons plan operations and students learn anatomy from real patient data.
arxiv-2601-22226:
Edoardo Latini, Fausto Rossi, and Fabrizio Dolcini set out a new way to build a qubit, the basic unit of a quantum computer. Their 2026 preprint uses the edge states of a thin material that acts as a topological insulator. A Josephson junction and added magnetic atoms complete the setup.

The team shows that spin states in this setup can form a working qubit. They also show that pulses of microwave light can steer the qubit through shifts in its spin states. The plan gives labs a fresh route to test. It may aid work on small, stable quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-22826:
Dart-yin A. Soh builds a model for how photons can create vector mesons, heavy particles of light-matter interaction. The model rests on Regge theory and a soft dipole Pomeron, a tool for describing high-energy scattering. It handles photons with any kind of polarization, round or linear.

The model fits three kinds of data at once: total rates, momentum patterns, and spin patterns for one key meson. Fitting all three pins down its twenty free settings with care. Good models of this process help plan and read particle physics experiments.
arxiv-2601-23026:
Hendrik Suhr, David Kaltenpoth, and Jilles Vreeken separate two kinds of anomaly that are usually lumped together. A value may look wrong because it was recorded badly, while the real process ran fine. Or the process itself may have changed, shifting how data are generated.

Root cause methods that ignore this split can blame the wrong features. Their causal characterization distinguishes measurement errors from mechanism shifts. The distinction matters in factories and hospitals, where a sensor fault and a real failure demand opposite responses. Measurement anomalies and mechanism shifts demand different remedies, which is why telling them apart is operationally valuable.
arxiv-2601-23126:
Pascal Lenzner and Paraskevi Machaira study routing games where each sender sees only its local network. Modern networks mix many autonomous entities, from smart devices to parts of AI systems. Each has a local view and must rely on a local protocol to forward packets.

The authors analyze when greedy routing, always forwarding toward the target, can reach its destination. Selfish local choices can loop or stall in the worst case. Understanding reachability helps design protocols that work without central control. Local views are the realistic constraint, since no device in a vast network can hold the whole map.
arxiv-2602-02426:
Simon-Olivier Duguay and 5 co-authors attack the problem of outlining individual tree crowns in dense tropical forests, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Tropical forests hold most of the planet's tree diversity, and canopy trees store a disproportionate share of carbon. Mapping them at scale needs accurate crown outlines from high-resolution aerial images, a task where current models still perform poorly in the tropics.

The team releases SelvaMask, a dataset of over eighty-eight hundred hand-drawn crowns from sites in Panama, Brazil, and Ecuador, with inter-annotator agreement measured. Their modular pipeline pairs detection with segmentation and adapts vision foundation models using a domain-specific prompter. It beat both zero-shot generalist models and fully supervised end-to-end systems. Gains held on external tropical and temperate datasets, making the benchmark a tool for wider forest monitoring.
arxiv-2602-02726:
Xuemin Yu and 3 co-authors replace clustering with a learned codebook to discover the latent concepts inside language model hidden states, in work posted to arXiv in 2026. Clustering-based concept discovery faces a trade-off: hierarchical clustering gives coherent concepts but scales quadratically, while k-means scales yet yields muddier concepts.

Vector quantized latent concepts learn a discrete codebook directly on frozen hidden states, borrowing the machinery of vector quantization from compression. Across twelve dataset-model settings the method stays near k-means in cost, scales better than hierarchical clustering, and remains competitive on faithfulness, with clearest gains on decoder-only models. Language-model-based evaluation, qualitative reading, and a comparison against sparse autoencoders all indicate the learned concepts are interpretable and task-relevant. The approach offers concept discovery that survives contact with large hidden-state datasets.
arxiv-2602-02926:
Lisa Orloff Clark and 2 co-authors study abstract structures called étale groupoids in a 2026 mathematics paper. Groupoids generalize groups by allowing partial symmetries. The paper examines three conditions that control isotropy, the internal symmetry at a point, especially when the space may be non-Hausdorff, meaning points can fail to separate cleanly.

Examples show the three conditions are genuinely distinct. The authors also revisit a characterization of topological freeness due to Anantharaman-Delaroche. They work without the axiom of choice, using only Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory. Finally, they prove that a groupoid theorem is equivalent to the Baire Category Theorem. Similar equivalences hold for other weakenings of the axiom of choice.
arxiv-2602-03026:
Weilin Ruan and 1 co-author build a multi-agent system for time series in a 2026 paper. Time series analysis supports many real applications, but existing methods integrate visual reasoning poorly. They also generalize weakly across tasks and use tools inflexibly when a new kind of series or question appears in practice.

Their system, MAS4TS, follows an analyzer-reasoner-executor design. A vision-language model first reads plots of the series, using structured priors to extract temporal patterns. Predictive trajectories are then reconstructed in latent space. Three specialized agents coordinate through shared memory and gated communication. A router picks task-specific tool chains. Experiments across benchmarks reached state-of-the-art results with strong generalization and efficient inference.
arxiv-2602-03226:
Long documents lose key details in the middle, and Xuancheng Li, leading 4 other authors, builds a compressor that adapts to the task. Context shrinking shrinks long inputs for language models, but earlier methods balance preservation against speed poorly. Their ATACompressor instead adjusts shrinking dynamically based on what the given task actually requires from the full context provided to the model.

A selective encoder compresses only task-relevant portions, keeping essential information while cutting the rest. An changing allocation controller senses how much relevant content exists and sets the shrinking rate accordingly. Review uses three question answering datasets, including HotpotQA and SQuAD. The method outperformed earlier methods on both shrinking speed and task results. Ablation studies examine which parts drive those gains.
arxiv-2602-03526:
Indoor light-based wireless networks steer laser beams at receivers whose height changes as people move around. Hossein Safi and 3 co-authors use reinforcement learning to control that steering in a 2026 paper. The systems use VCSELs, small vertical-cavity lasers. Fixed beam widths fail: widening a beam spreads power thinner, while narrowing it misses the receiver.

Their Q-learning agent interacts with the environment and learns, on its own, which beam divergence suits each receiver height. No analytical model or exhaustive search is needed. Simulations show coverage up to 92 percent at low receiver heights and robust performance under harder conditions. The approach promises scalable, real-time, energy-efficient beam control for dense laser arrays.
arxiv-2602-03926:
Francesco Bedogna and 1 co-author construct exotic defects in topological field theories tied to two lattice models, the XY-plaquette and XYZ-cube. Their 2026 paper works within symmetry topological field theory, a framework describing exotic symmetries that break the usual rules of Lorentz invariance.

By gauging a non-compact symmetry with a twist, they build condensation defects of codimension one. These defects turn out to realize self-duality symmetries that cannot be inverted, at any coupling value. In the plaquette model the symmetry is continuous, extending earlier results. Such non-invertible symmetries are reshaping how physicists classify phases of matter.
arxiv-2602-04226:
Coding agents submit pull requests that humans reject for agent-specific reasons. Sota Nakashima and 4 co-authors inspected six hundred fifty-four rejected agentic pull requests from five coding agents, plus a human baseline, in a 2026 study. Earlier work covered one agent's rejections only.

Seven rejection modes appeared only in agentic submissions, including outright distrust of AI-generated code. Patterns differed by agent, such as one agent automatically withdrawing its own inactive requests. Agents are chosen for different purposes, so their failure fingerprints differ. Maintainers and agent builders alike get a map of where trust in automated code breaks down.
arxiv-2602-04326:
Embodied agents guess constantly; the trick is pricing those guesses. SeungWon Seo and 4 co-authors convert language model reasoning traces into structured decision trees in a 2026 paper. Their PCE framework targets multi-agent settings where objects hide and partners' intentions are unclear.

Internal tree nodes hold environment assumptions; leaves hold actions. Each path is scored by scenario likelihood, goal-directed gain, and execution cost, guiding choice without heavy communication. Frequent messaging is the usual uncertainty cure, but it burns tokens and disrupts human partners. On two multi-agent benchmarks, structured assumption pricing offered a cheaper route to rational action under uncertainty.
arxiv-2602-04626:
Fabio Deelan Cunden and 3 co-authors study how to pick the most spread-out subset from random points in a 2026 probability paper. Each point carries several traits, and a dispersion measure rewards sets whose members sit far apart from one another.

The authors compute the full statistics of the best achievable dispersion, including rare-event tails. Two methods agree: a mean-field theory for order statistics and the replica method from disordered systems theory. For large populations with symmetric distributions, the optimal subset is simply all points outside a ball of a self-determined radius. The single-trait case also yields finite-size formulas. Simulations and heuristic algorithms supported the results.
arxiv-2602-04826:
Alexei Naianzin defines a new distance between metric spaces in a 2026 geometry paper. The classic Gromov-Hausdorff distance compares spaces that are nearly isometric, meaning nearly distance-preserving in a strict sense. Naianzin's analogue instead compares arbitrary quasi-isometric spaces. Such spaces may stretch distances, but only within bounded multiplicative and additive limits.

He also studies which traits survive when spaces converge under this new distance. A further topic is the shape of the whole class of metric spaces once it carries this distance. For the proofs, he defines quasi-isometric distortion for correspondences between spaces. With that tool, he proves the class is path-connected. In fact, any two metric spaces can be joined by a curve of finite length.
arxiv-2602-04926:
Retrieval-augmented generation is a standard approach for knowledge-intensive questions, and the hard ones require composing evidence through several dependent reasoning steps. It is the work of Ning Wang and 6 co-authors. Most systems start from scratch for every query, fetching the same evidence and rebuilding the same reasoning again and again.

Their system, AutoPrunedRetriever, stores facts and past reasoning in a shared symbolic codebook that serves as both index and memory. New queries retrieve ready-made reasoning paths instead of raw text, and a pruning step keeps the growing memory compact. A lighter add-on applies the same trick on top of existing retrievers. Across five reasoning benchmarks, accuracy rose by about 2 to 11 points over the best rivals while using up to 96 percent fewer input tokens.
arxiv-2602-05026:
Inkee Jung and Siu Cheong Lau propose basic laws for how learning itself unfolds in this 2026 machine learning paper. Their framework states a conservation law and a law that total entropy decreases during learning. From those laws they build a method for ensembles that keep learning over a lifetime, rather than training once and freezing.

The test bed is defense against transfer-based adversarial attacks on the CIFAR-10 image dataset. Such attacks craft misleading inputs on one model and reuse them against another. The authors' entropy-based ensemble, nicknamed a logifold, immunizes a model by combining versions trained on clean and attacked samples. Compared with simply averaging those models, the logifold scored higher accuracy in most test cases, with especially large gains when the attacks were strong.
arxiv-2602-05126:
Whether a tumor carries human papillomavirus changes prognosis and treatment for head, neck, and cervical cancers. Weiyi Qin and 3 co-authors built an interpretable predictor for HPV status from whole-slide tissue images in this 2026 computer vision paper. Standard attention-based methods predict well at the slide level but cannot show pathologists what tissue patterns drive the call.

Their framework, CLEAR-HPV, restructures the model's internal space around attention so that meaningful concepts surface without concept labels during training. It discovered keratinizing, basaloid, and stromal patterns on its own, drew spatial maps of each, and summarized every slide as a short vector of ten concept fractions instead of a 1,536-number embedding. Predictive power survived the compression. Results held across three cancer datasets, and the framework works with any attention-based backbone.
arxiv-2602-05226:
Central banks read expert forecasters' inflation distributions to judge risk, but the panel keeps changing: forecasters skip rounds, leave, and return. Matthew C Johnson and 3 co-authors tackle that sporadic turnout in this 2026 applied statistics paper, using the European Central Bank's Survey of Professional Forecasters. Naive fixes, like reweighting whoever showed up, inject jumps that reflect presence rather than economics.

Their solution keeps a latent predictive state for each forecaster, updated coherently even in rounds where that forecaster is silent. The mix then follows the panel's given structure instead of rescaling or filling in. Mechanical turnout effects split cleanly from real skill gaps, and each forecaster's sway evolves clearly over time. On the ECB survey the method beat equal-weight benchmarks on accuracy and gave smoother, better-tuned inflation density forecasts, with the largest gains in high-turnover periods.
arxiv-2602-05526:
Quantum key distribution lets two parties share a secret key with security backed by physics, but the raw keys must first be reconciled. Rávilla Leite, Juliana de Assis, Micael Dias, and Francisco de Assis study arithmetic reconciliation, a newer protocol for the continuous-variable form of the method. The protocol is known for low complexity and for working better as signal noise grows.

The authors estimate mutual information to obtain reconciliation efficiencies under realistic conditions, rather than ideal ones. They also report match rates for the secret key sequences held by the two parties, Alice and Bob. Results indicate the technique is feasible and promising for real continuous-variable systems. The paper is a journal submission under review, aimed at researchers who build quantum communication links. It helps fill a gap, since this protocol's behavior outside theory has been little studied.
arxiv-2602-05926:
Counting events, from photons to neutrinos, is basic scientific work, and predicting those counts well takes models that respect their integer nature. Anushka Saha, Abhijith Gandrakota, and Alexandre Morozov propose the Poisson Log Normal process, a framework that uses Gaussian processes to model Poisson log rates. Gaussian process regression handles continuous data elegantly but cannot emit integers, which is where their construction steps in.

Correlations between data points, captured by the kernel, drive predictions instead of an explicit functional form. The predictive distribution is shown to be Poisson Log Normal, and an algorithm optimizes the kernel hyperparameters. The team also adapts the method to hunt weak localized signals on a smooth background, predicting a signal strength, location, and width. Tests use synthetic data and real data, including the open CERN data set from the Higgs boson discovery. The paper targets scientists who model count data.
arxiv-2602-06626:
Hadiseh Rezaei, Rahim Taheri, and Mohammad Shojafar work on radio tag systems where many readers sit close together to cover an area. Crowding causes collisions, when readers and tags interfere with each other and slow the network down. Centralized control schemes have shown promise for cutting these clashes.

Their protocol, IE-RAP, mixes time slots and separate frequencies so nearby readers take turns and stay out of each other's way. It also tracks distances between readers, avoids re-reading tags, and frees channels on time. In simulations it raised throughput by about a quarter, cut average waiting time by about three quarters, and halved energy use compared with earlier approaches. It also supports readers that move through the network.
arxiv-2602-06926:
Hannah T. Rüdisser and eight co-authors offer a hands-off pipeline for short-term forecasts of solar storm magnetic fields at L1. The pipeline starts when a new entry lands in the CCMC DONKI catalog. First, a drag-based model called ELEvo judges if Earth will be hit and when. That arrival guess sets the time window for hunting storm signs in live L1 solar wind data.

A deep learning model called ARCANE then spots the magnetic obstacle on its own. Once it starts, a semi-empirical flux rope model called 3DCORE rebuilds the field again and again, using Monte Carlo fitting, to forecast the rest of the profile as data arrives. Tests on 3,870 archived entries show early forecasts for 61 clear events match full-event rebuilds. Timing errors run near five hours, and field strength errors near ten nanotesla, with extremes often underplayed.
arxiv-2602-07126:
Synthetic tables are shared as a privacy-safe stand-in for real data, but most real data lives in linked tables, where one person's records span several tables at once.  Joshua Ward and two co-authors show that privacy audits built for single tables miss leakage that travels through those links between tables.

The paper sets up a membership inference attack aimed at the whole user entity across tables, rather than at single rows. Row-level audits understate how much leaks.  For anyone releasing synthetic relational data, the lesson is direct: audit privacy at the level of the person, not the row, or the safety claim will be weaker than it looks.
arxiv-2602-07226:
When a company buys a model as a service, it needs to estimate results cheaply by labeling only a few cases.  Zihan Zhu and two co-authors show that standard testing tools misfire exactly when variance is low: error measures hide persistent bias. Significance tests reject good estimators over trivial gaps.

Their fault-tolerant method combines bias and variance considerations in an adjusted testing, so estimators are judged fairly in low-variance settings.  The work matters as model marketplaces grow, because buyers need trustworthy, cheap validation before deployment.  Users get an testing method that stays honest when the usual ones turn brittle.
arxiv-2602-07426:
Evolutionary trees branch over time, and some tree shapes admit far more labeled histories than others.  Emily H.  Dickey and Noah A.  Rosenberg identify the maximally probable topologies for trees where each branching splits into r descendants, using a connection with Huffman trees from information theory.

Their characterization of the unique maximally probable r-furcating topology generalizes the classic bifurcating result and supplies a new proof of it. It also offers a claim for the case where simultaneous branchings across nodes are counted.  Phylogenetics and combinatorics readers get a clean answer to which tree shape history favors most, and a claim for the next case.
arxiv-2602-07726:
The partition function counts the ways to split a whole number into parts, and its first digits raise a natural question: how far must one look before a chosen digit string appears? Siddharth Iyer takes up a problem posed by Douglass and Ono about the smallest such number in a given base.

Using a basic discrepancy framework, he proves new upper bounds that improve substantially on earlier work by Luca. The argument stays elementary while delivering stronger guarantees about where a prescribed opening string first shows up. Readers interested in partitions, digit patterns, or elementary analytic number theory will find a short, sharp improvement on a concrete open question.
arxiv-2602-08026:
Ensemble sampling explores uncertain choices by perturbing estimates with random noise, but its theory lagged behind the Thompson sampling benchmark it resembles. David Janz and two co-authors give a sharp analysis for linear bandits with standard Gaussian perturbations.

With an ensemble size scaling like dimension times log horizon, ensemble sampling attains regret of order dimension to the three-halves times root horizon, closing the gap to Thompson sampling at comparable compute. The proof reduces the analysis to a time-uniform exceedance problem for independent Brownian motions, a continuous-time viewpoint the authors call strikingly natural. Bandit theorists gain both a tight bound and a proof technique worth reusing.
arxiv-2602-08126:
Self-driving cars must spot objects in 3D by combining cameras, which see rich detail but poor depth, with LiDAR, which measures shape precisely but sparsely. Venkatraman Narayanan and five co-authors propose MambaFusion, a unified method that fuses the two sensors adaptively.

Selective state-space models interleaved with windowed transformers carry global context in linear time while keeping local geometry. A token-alignment module and reliability-aware gates re-weight camera and LiDAR traits by spatial confidence and calibration consistency, and a structure-conditioned diffusion head adds graph thought under uncertainty. Autonomous-driving teams gain a fusion design that adapts to each sensor's strengths scene by scene.
arxiv-2602-08226:
Modern firms need fast, multi-sense, cost-effective data work, but ByteDance's live systems hit from wasteful multi-sense storage, rigid query tuning, and nearness loss under resource split-up. Yuxing Han and fifteen co-authors offer ByteHouse, a cloud-native data store built for real-time multi-sense data work.

Its storage layer unifies tables through a two-tier logical layer with a really steady layout. It adds a cluster-scale SSD cache shared across compute nodes, and a virtual file setup letting lean local access. The compute layer supports analytical, batch, and incremental execution. Data engineers gain a live-tested architecture for data work where text, images, and tables must be queried together at speed, not bolted on afterward.
arxiv-2602-08426:
Block-sparse attention speeds up long-context pre-filling, but picking the right blocks cheaply is the bottleneck. Xinghao Wang and six co-authors trace a flaw in the usual shortcut: mean pooling plus rotary position embeddings creates a blind spot for local position signals. Their arXiv paper proves that pooling acts as a low-pass filter, wiping out high-frequency cues.

Their fix, Prism, splits block selection into high- and low-frequency branches and recalibrates the pooled signals with an energy-based temperature. Block importance then comes from block-level operations alone, with no token-level search. Tests show accuracy matching full attention with speedups up to 5.1 times. Readers get a training-free repair for a subtle but costly approximation.
arxiv-2602-08526:
Building large entangled states that tolerate noise is a central challenge for quantum tech, and hand-designed gate sequences scale poorly. Duc-Kha Vu and three co-authors propose an automated control frame for making symmetric Dicke states in collision-model setups. Their arXiv paper treats prep as a closed-loop design problem rather than a handcrafted recipe.

Partial-SWAP collisions that preserve excitation counts run between two qubit groups, mediated by shuttle qubits, and two collision angles are tuned under practical bounds. The method needs no projective checks and extends beyond single-excitation states to any excitation count. Under dropouts and decoherence, fidelity stays high while only the required rounds grow a bit. Readers get a reproducible controller for deterministic multipartite entanglement.
arxiv-2602-09126:
Since 2004, the Keck Observatory Archive has served all data from the twin 10-meter Keck telescopes on Mauna Kea. G. Bruce Berriman and one co-author describe a new interactive metrics dashboard. It is built on the archive's modern Python infrastructure, which ingests fresh data within about a minute and answers queries twenty times faster using Plotly-Dash and R-tree indices.

The dashboard reports live metrics on archive health and growth, guiding plans for future hardware and software upgrades. It arrives as new instruments and the Vera Rubin Observatory's alert deluge promise far larger, more complex data flows. For archive operators, one screen now tracks ingestion, holdings, and performance in real time.
arxiv-2602-09226:
Daniele Artico's thesis expands weak-coupling techniques in quantum field theory, from loop integrals to defect correlators. The first part derives linear relations among Feynman-parameterized integrals from their properties as projective forms, tests them on one- and multi-loop examples, and uncovers links to polynomial ideal algebra. Those relations shrink the set of integrals any calculation must handle.

The second part studies the defect conformal field theory of N equals 4 super Yang-Mills theory with a Maldacena-Wilson line defect, through bulk-defect-defect and multipoint correlators up to next-to-next-to-leading order. The perturbative information condenses into classes of integrals that evaluate to rational functions or Goncharov polylogarithms, a tidy result for a complex theory.
arxiv-2602-09326:
Shapley values credit data points or features for a model's behavior, but they assume every contributor can be swapped for any other. A 2026 paper led by Kiljae Lee, with three co-authors, points out that this fails when contributions depend on each other. Reused data, causal feature orderings, and settings where trust and risk should shift credit are cases in point. The authors propose a priority-aware version that handles both concerns.

Their method, called PASV, combines hard precedence rules about what must come first with soft weights that favor some contributors over others. It recovers the precedence-only and weight-only variants as special cases, and natural axioms pin it down. A sampling method based on adjacent swaps makes estimation feasible at scale. Trials on data valuation and income-data attribution show structure-faithful allocations, plus a sweeping tool for probing sensitivity to priority choices.
arxiv-2602-09426: Perrine Jouteur and Hoel Queffelec study the role of q-rationals in the study of link invariants in their 2026 paper. That work leads them to introduce and study web categories that q-deform Deligne's categories. The paper thus ties a q-deformed notion of rational numbers to the invariants used to study links, building its account through a new framework.
arxiv-2602-09526:
Moiré layer stacks in two tungsten-based bilayers trap band-edge carriers in repeating wells, making flat bands and stronger links. Yet the well's origin stayed unclear. Youwen Wang and two co-authors study both stacking patterns in their 2026 paper, showing two causes jointly build the well: lattice rework and between-layer charge transfer.

Rework strains the lattice uneven, shifting band-edge levels by tens to hundreds of tiny energy units, and adds a strain voltage whose size varies with stacking and carrier type. Charge transfer builds an internal field, shifting levels apart for the two stacking patterns. Both effects explain well buildup for both patterns. The trapping pins moving-charge and valence waves at the same site for one pattern, but at apart sites for the other.
arxiv-2602-09726:
Deep reinforcement learning solves varied tasks well, yet tuning stays hard due to policy gradient construction and training dynamics. Hanyong Wang and Menglong Yang note that proximal policy optimization clips the policy gradient within careful on-policy updates, giving reliable stable gains but possibly wasting samples. Off-policy methods reuse samples more fully, at the cost of higher estimation variance and bias. Their 2026 paper offers ExO-PPO, joining the stability promise of careful on-policy iteration with efficient off-policy data use.

The method derives an extended off-policy gain from the generalized policy improvement lower bound. Clipping is then extended with segmented exponential functions for a suitable surrogate objective. Paths from past policies sit in a replay buffer for off-policy training. Against proximal policy optimization and other variants, ExO-PPO shows better performance with balanced sample efficiency and stability across varied tasks.
arxiv-2602-09826:
Arabic language models are pretrained predominantly on Modern Standard Arabic and expected to transfer to its dialects. Abdulmuizz Khalak and two co-authors note that the standard written variety serves formal settings. People speak and write online in various dialects spread across the Arab region, and dialects vary in similarity to the standard. Their 2026 paper studies cross-lingual transfer of Arabic models using probing on three natural language processing tasks plus representational similarity.

Results show transfer is possible but disproportionate across dialects, partially explained by geographic proximity. Evidence also emerges for negative interference in models trained to support all Arabic dialects. The findings question the degree of similarity among dialects and raise concerns for cross-lingual transfer in Arabic models, where closeness to the standard varies by region.
arxiv-2602-09926:
In ride-hailing, a car that takes a rider vanishes from its spot and a fresh car appears somewhere random. A 2026 paper led by Andrés Fielbaum, with two co-authors, studies that loop in a general spatial matching model. When a server is taken, a gap opens, and the gap itself draws the next users, widening further. The authors call the loop Increasing Gap Dynamics.

On a one-dimensional circle the system settles into an inefficient balance, worse than even spacing or random placement. The authors prove that even an optimal assignment, always choosing a neighboring server, lets long gaps widen, so the effect is not mere greed. Simulations in two dimensions and on real Manhattan ride data confirm the pattern and link it to the Wild Goose Chase, where drivers chase distant riders.
arxiv-2602-10126:
Wind farms draw momentum from the air through advection, pressure gradients, Coriolis forces, turbulence, and unsteadiness, and a key parameter tracks that supply. A 2026 paper led by Mads Baungaard, with two co-authors, validates an analytic momentum availability model against large-eddy simulation data. It covers six wind farm cases, three varying boundary-layer heights and three varying turbine layouts.

The full model performs well throughout, but its linearized version increasingly overpredicts momentum supply as boundary layers grow taller. The authors trace that drift to the boundary-layer Rossby number and propose an extension of the linear model. The extension improves accuracy for the cases studied and generalizes better to tall boundary layers and strong Coriolis forcing.
arxiv-2602-10226:
Tuning large recommendation models means searching a huge hyperparameter space and designing optimizers, architectures, and reward functions by hand, iteration after iteration. A 2026 paper led by Haochen Wang, with four co-authors, proposes a self-evolving system that hands that loop to large language models from Google's Gemini family. It generates, trains, and deploys complex model changes end to end.

Two agents split the work. An Offline Agent runs a fast loop of high-throughput hypothesis generation against proxy metrics, while an Online Agent runs a slow loop validating candidates against delayed business metrics in live production. Acting as specialized machine learning engineers, the agents discover new optimization and architecture improvements and craft reward functions aimed at long-term engagement. Several launches at YouTube show the autonomous approach beating traditional workflows on both speed and model quality.
arxiv-2602-10426:
Hidetsugu Sakaguchi proposes a compact model for particles that cluster under forced swing in a 2026 paper. The key idea borrows from the Einstein viscosity law: neighboring particles raise the strong viscosity around them. That local feedback is enough, the paper argues, to sort an initially uniform spread into patterns.

Linear steadiness analysis and number simulations agree on the outcome. The uniform spread proves unstable, and regular patterns emerge instead. In one size the particles form cyclic stripes of spacing, while in two sizes the pattern becomes striped in space. The model offers a simple real process for cyclic clustering in driven particle systems.
arxiv-2602-10626:
Ruisheng Shi and five co-authors show that anonymized tracking data can still expose users in a 2026 paper. Tracking companies sell data they claim to anonymize, but the authors show that identity alignment attacks can link tracker records to accounts on other sites. Anonymization alone, they argue, does not protect privacy.

The paper builds a data collector and an alignment recipe, then constructs two de-anonymization attacks. A passive attack analyzes tracker data to align identities, while an active attack induces users to interact online for higher success rates. The authors also present an testing system for online tracking risks. The work is a warning to data markets: stripped identifiers do not strip identity.
arxiv-2602-10926:
Philipp J. di Dio presents extended lecture notes on linear rules and positivity preservers in a 2026 document. The notes cover linear rules for many-term math, K-positivity preservers, and their generators. The material comes from a lecture given at the University of Konstanz in the winter semester of 2025-26.

As lecture notes rather than a research article, the document organizes theory for learners and teams entering the area. It covers how rules preserve positivity with respect to a set, and how generators of such rules can be set out. The extended format allows proofs and context that a short paper would compress. That makes the notes a useful reference for the interplay between rule theory and positivity.
arxiv-2602-11026:
Cars now watch their drivers with cameras, lidar, and GPS, yet drivers rarely protest. Yehuda Perry and Tawfiq Ammari interviewed sixteen self-driving car users and read their accounts through grounded theory. They find few car-specific privacy worries; drivers treat car monitoring as normal by comparing it with phones and platforms.

The authors frame the car as one more node in a wider surveillance ecology. It is a mobile extension of the leaky home, whose connected gear keeps sending conduct data outward. They note that limited driver access to logs, now mainly in California, blocks informed debate, and that data-hungry machine learning pushes firms toward more collection. Their fixes include universal log access, binding transparency, and data minimization rules.
arxiv-2602-11326:
Entangling distant trapped ions usually needs one carefully addressed motional mode. Modesto Orozco-Ruiz and Florian Mintert propose a scheme where all axial motional modes help, driven by a time-dependent magnet-field gradient. As ion strings grow, single-mode gates slow down, and addressing many modes demands complex drives.

Their nonperturbative construction implements multi-qubit gates and two-qubit gates between any pair in a straight string. Explicit examples show advantages over current magnet-gradient schemes, including simultaneous gates on multiple ion pairs. The work offers a faster, simpler route to large-scale trapped-ion linkage, where mode crowding otherwise caps gate speed and fidelity.
arxiv-2602-11726:
Fine-tuning usually rewrites model weights, but weight changes are hard to interpret. They hide which internal steps a new task reuses or skips. Shervin Ghasemlou explores a brain-inspired alternative: adaptation as a change in mode. Instead of rewriting weights, the method selects and rescales existing steps. Base weights stay frozen; only per-neuron thresholds and gains are learned.

During training a smooth gate decides whether each activation takes part. At inference the gate can be hardened to give explicit conditional computation and neuron-level attributions, showing which neurons fire. As proof of concept, a small network trained on plain and rotated handwritten digits is specialized to the rotated mode. Rotated-digit scores improve over the frozen baseline using only a few hundred trainable values per layer. It trades some score against the standard low-rank method for far fewer trainable values and clearer interpretation.
arxiv-2602-11826:
Perpetual scheduling asks for a timetable that repeats: at every step an independent set is chosen so each element appears often enough. Mirabel Mendoza-Cadena and three co-authors study combinatorial variants, focusing on bamboo garden trimming. There, elements grow at set rates and reset to zero when scheduled, and the goal is to minimize the maximum height any element reaches.

Assuming growth rates form a convex combination of set vectors, matroid structure yields guarantees. When the system is a matroid, a maximum height of at most two can be guaranteed, and that bound is optimal. Efficient algorithms achieve height two for uniform and partition matroids and height four for graphic and laminar matroids. For general systems the optimal guaranteed height grows like the log of the element count. Pinwheel scheduling, where each element must recur within a number of steps, inherits bounds on the density needed to schedule.
arxiv-2602-12126:
Temporal graphs model networks whose edges appear only at specific moments, as in logistics, information spreading, and wireless networks. Daniele Carnevale and one co-author introduce the multi-broadcast scheduling problem: choose when edges are available so chosen sources reach every vertex while optimizing the worst-case temporal distance.

They characterize complexity across six notions of time-based distance. For a single source, earliest-arrival and latest-departure versions admit polynomial-time solutions, while the others are NP-hard and hard to approximate. Approximation algorithms are given for fastest-time and minimum-waiting distances, and for multiple sources without assumed feasibility, the problem is inapproximable in general, though structural conditions restore tractability for two distance notions.
arxiv-2602-12226:
Knot diagrams carry hidden numeric traits, and one new trait comes from electrical ideas. Michal Jablonowski works alone here, defining a Laplacian trace invariant for special, reduced, alternating diagrams of oriented knots and links. The value is fixed by two neighbouring coefficients at one extreme of the Alexander polynomial.

It also reads as half the sum of directed resistances from a normalised, balanced Tait-graph Laplacian, giving the invariant a concrete circuit meaning. Explicit examples linked by flype moves show a subtle point: the full Laplacian characteristic polynomial can change even while this invariant stays put. Readers get a small, sturdy number that survives a move that breaks larger data.
arxiv-2602-12426:
Decentralised optimisation over wireless links can use over-the-air computation, where signals add in the air to form averages without scheduling or channel knowledge. Nicolò Michelusi works alone here, addressing a flaw in non-coherent over-the-air computation. Outside interference biases shared estimates and harms settling of the underlying optimisation.

The proposed robust scheme rotates the frame of reference in a coordinated random way across all nodes, and sends a pseudo-random pilot signal. Interference then becomes even in all directions with zero mean in the rotated frame, leaving shared estimates unbiased and keeping settling proofs intact. Numerical tests on a task where items are put into classes show the robust scheme beating the baseline scheme when interference is present.
arxiv-2602-12826:
On the light front, the consistency of interacting theories hinges on closing the Poincaré algebra, and the quartic order poses the hardest test. Mattia Serrani studies massless spinning fields in flat space, focusing on a non-holomorphic constraint mixing two kinds of vertices. He recovers known results first: Yang-Mills theory and gravity survive, while interacting multi-graviton theories fail.

Building explicit lower-derivative and lower-spin quartic vertices, he then turns to higher-spin fields. Most cubic interactions die under the quartic constraint, as no-go results suggest, yet higher-derivative cubic vertices open a path to non-trivial solutions. From those solutions he conjectures the full set of quartic vertices, classifies allowed unitary local higher-spin theories, and finds new quasi-chiral families.
arxiv-2602-12926:
Flipping a graph means complementing edges inside a chosen vertex set, a move often used to push vertices apart. Karolina Drabik and four co-authors study flips in graphs with no large complete bipartite subgraph. They show that any short flip sequence can be mimicked by a short deletion sequence. That sequence separates vertices almost as well, with distances at least a third as large.

That simulation explains a pattern across structural graph theory and finite model theory: dense tameness notions often match sparse ones once large bipartite subgraphs are banned. The authors recover equivalences between bounded shrub-depth and tree-depth, clique-width and tree-width, flip-width and expansion, and monadic dependence and nowhere-denseness. They also reprove a merge-width result with explicit bounds, and introduce separation-width, a new parameter family sitting between strong and weak colouring numbers.
arxiv-2602-13326:
Animating a still image of a character is now routine for one person, but scenes with several humanoid figures add tangled interactions, varied body forms, and frequent occlusions. MotionWeaver tackles the multi-figure case with two ideas. First, unified motion codes strip identity from movement and bind each motion to its character. Second, a shared 4D space fuses motion with video latents under layered 4D supervision.

To support the task, the authors curated 46 hours of multi-person video and built a 300-video benchmark with paired humanoid characters. MotionWeaver led the field on that benchmark and carried over to varied forms and hard multi-figure scenes. Xirui Hu leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13426:
In homological algebra, a differential graded algebra is formal when it can be linked to its cohomology algebra by a chain of quasi-isomorphisms, maps that preserve multiplication and induce isomorphisms on cohomology. Formality is a strong rigidity property, and this paper pins it down for complex nilmanifolds, a class of compact complex manifolds built from nilpotent groups.

The Dolbeault algebra of a complex nilmanifold is formal only when the manifold is a torus, the simplest case. For forms of type (0,p), formality holds exactly when the complex structure is abelian, a clean algebraic test for a geometric property. Tommaso Sferruzza leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13526:
Ising models on planar graphs describe magnets through interacting spins, and their spectral curves encode much of their behavior. This paper gives a complete classification of two-dimensional Ising models on isoradial graphs, frustrated or not, whose spectral curve has genus one. Baxter's Z-invariant Ising model falls out as a special case, now extended to real coupling constants.

Two further families appear, both with non-Harnack spectral curves, and in every case the spectral curve is maximal. Each family passes through an algebraic phase transition where the genus drops from one to zero, explaining differing behaviors seen in physics. As an application, the frustrated Ising model on the triangular lattice is fully classified. Béatrice de Tilière leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-14626:
Concept bottleneck models try to make AI choices readable by routing them through human concepts. Karim Galliamov, with three co-authors, adds an information bottleneck to that concept layer. The aim is a lean set of concepts that still carries what the task needs.

Two forms are derived: a variational objective and an entropy-based stand-in. Both slot into standard training with no new architecture or labels. Across six model families and three benchmarks, the regularized models beat their plain versions. The work also makes concept-level fixes more reliable, since the concepts leak less.
arxiv-2602-14726:
Kohio Deflesselle and colleagues present ManeuverNet, a soft actor-critic framework for precise manoeuvring of double-Ackermann-steering robots, built for farm work in tight spaces. Classical planners like the timed elastic band need constant retuning when robot shape or surroundings change, while end-to-end deep reinforcement learning often fails on non-holonomic constraints for want of a fitting reward.

ManeuverNet answers with optimised reward functions tailored to double-Ackermann motion, letting learned control handle complex turns without endless recalibration. The framework targets agricultural robots that must move exactly in narrow rows and yards. Precise, adaptable steering is its prize.
arxiv-2602-14826:
Junyan Cao surveys recent work extending Hodge theory to twisted log-differential forms, differential forms valued in bundles with singular metrics. The survey rests on joint work with Ya Deng, Christopher D. Hacon, and Mihai Paun, tracing how classical Hodge ideas adapt when metrics develop singularities.

Logarithmic poles and twisted coefficients complicate the picture, yet the extended theory keeps much of its power, opening new routes in algebraic geometry. Cao's review gathers scattered advances into one readable map. Singular Hodge theory gains a clear, current survey. The review keeps its focus on forms with singular metrics, where old tools need care.
arxiv-2602-14926:
Gen Zhou and colleagues present MAC-AMP, a closed-loop multi-agent collaboration system for multi-objective antimicrobial peptide design, against the global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Antimicrobial peptides promise potency against resistant pathogens, yet most AI design models struggle to balance activity, toxicity, and novelty under rigid or opaque scoring.

Multi-agent language models, rising fast in complex design settings, run the closed loop here, letting agents collaborate, score transparently, and iterate toward peptides that satisfy several goals at once. Drug design gains a team of agents that argue, test, and refine together. Peptides for resistant infections get a collaborative designer.
arxiv-2602-15626:
Regazzi and Leonetti work out how a soft capsule deforms and tilts in linear flows. Their capsule starts spherical, with radius R, a viscosity contrast against the surrounding fluid, surface tension, and bending rigidity. The membrane response follows one of three elastic laws, Hookean, neo-Hookean, or Skalak, giving a surface shear modulus and a Poisson ratio or their analogues.

At leading order, deformation scales with the elastic capillary number. That number is the ratio of viscous stress to membrane response, measured by the Taylor parameter, and it does not hinge on which elastic law is chosen. With no tension or bending, the work recovers Barthes-Biesel and Rallison 1981 results, including the striking fact that deformation ignores viscosity contrast, unlike droplets. At higher order, deformation gains dependence on tension and bending ratios, and the tilt angle follows a droplet-like equation in each case, matching boundary integral simulations well.
arxiv-2602-15726:
Asashiba and Patel set out a stability theory covering minimal projective resolutions of modules over a finite metric poset P. Their tools are the Gülen-McCleary distance for P-modules and a fresh complex matching distance that works on bounded complexes built from finitely generated projective P-modules. That fresh distance yields an extended metric covering homotopy classes of these complexes, and it narrows down to minimal projective resolutions.

Their main theorem bounds the induced distance on minimal resolutions above by the Gülen-McCleary distance. Passing to the interval poset and kernel construction, persistence diagrams appear as the homotopy class of minimal resolutions of kernel modules. The stability theorem recovers bottleneck stability in the one-parameter case and covers signed diagrams in the multiparameter case.
arxiv-2602-15826:
Arranz Regidor and colleagues present QwaveMPS, an open-source Python library that models one-dimensional waveguide systems holding many quantum bodies. It uses matrix product states. It gives users a friendly way to build, evolve, and analyse quantum states and operators, opening studies in quantum physics and quantum information on waveguide QED systems. The approach runs efficient, scalable simulations by putting compute where the quantum system matters most.

Users can explore many complex dynamical interactions, among them time-delayed feedback in the non-Markovian regime, plus deeply non-linear systems. Cost is highly reduced compared with full Hilbert space approaches. That makes modelling varied open waveguide-QED systems practical and convenient, across Markovian and non-Markovian regimes, with quantised atoms and quantised photons treated on an equal footing.
arxiv-2602-16026:
Eduardo Ochs writes about a hard problem in calculus teaching: students who can run memorized steps yet lack the basic sense behind them. He pictures one extreme case, a Calculus 2 student called E. E solves a simple equation by moving a number across the equal sign. Yet E cannot check the answer by putting it back in. Such a student tests a result only by repeating the same method and getting the same answer again.

Ochs argues that classes full of students like E need fresh strategies and tools. Teachers can no longer treat steps like taking a particular case as obvious.
