He shows how the computer algebra system Maxima can make those operations easy to see. That gives learners a visible way to follow what a step does. The piece offers teachers a concrete route toward stronger foundations rather than faster memorization.
arxiv-2602-16126:
Hongyi Chen studies long-run steady states of a class of random heat equations with multiplicative noise, in the weak disorder regime. Under a natural second-moment condition, he shows that positive steady measures match one to one with bounded positive harmonic functions of the space at hand. That match gives the set of steady measures the shape of the Martin boundary, a classic tool that sorts such functions at infinity.

Chen also links the random flow to its deterministic twin. When the deterministic flow settles to a bounded harmonic function, the random flow settles to the steady measure that matches it. The results hold in many settings where the Martin boundary is nontrivial, such as negatively curved manifolds and trees. For those who study random partial differential equations, the paper turns hard questions about long-run random states into cleaner questions about deterministic functions and their limits.
arxiv-2602-16226:
Seyyed Mohammad Sadegh Nabavi Sales introduces a new class of mappings called cyclic p-phi-contraction mappings. The paper investigates existence and uniqueness of fixed points for such mappings defined on metric spaces, uniformly convex Banach spaces, or reflexive Banach spaces. That scope covers three distinct settings where fixed-point theory is often applied, from general metric structure to spaces with strong convexity and reflexivity properties.

For readers in nonlinear analysis, the contribution is a new contraction class with existence and uniqueness results across those settings. Cyclic mappings alternate in a structured way, and the p-phi-contraction condition constrains how distances shrink under iteration. By establishing fixed points in metric, uniformly convex, and reflexive Banach settings alike, the paper gives analysts a single framework to invoke when cyclic contraction behavior appears. The abstract is brief, but the class and its fixed-point results are stated plainly.
arxiv-2602-16626:
SungJun Cho and co-authors test sample-level token schemes for MEG brain models in a head-to-head way. Brain models must chop smooth neural time series into tokens, but the effect of that chop is poorly known. The study pits learned choppers against fixed ones on magnetoencephalography data, checking rebuild faith, token forecasts, lifelike generated data, subject info kept, and later tasks.

A new autoencoder-based learned chopper is brought in. Tests span three public MEG sets from varied sites, scanners, and tasks. Both learned and fixed schemes rebuild well and score much the same on most checks. The upshot is that plain fixed sample-level token plans can serve brain models, sparing builders needless fuss.
arxiv-2602-16726:
Hua Yan, Heng Tan, and Yu Yang present COMPASS, a system that bridges individual and collective realism in language-model-based human mobility simulation. Geospatial uses such as city planning, epidemic forecasting, and transport modeling need individual mobility data, but such data are costly, patchy, and privacy-sensitive. Language models simulated as agents can mimic individual cognition, yet agents run in isolation lack population coordination, so collective patterns fail to emerge.

COMPASS turns empirical mobility scaling laws into a feedback signal that guides prompt building. It starts from coarse population-level tweaks driven by those laws and refines them into individual prompts, jointly meeting several aggregate goals while keeping single trajectories realistic. Across two public datasets, COMPASS beats state-of-the-art language-model-based simulators, giving planners a more faithful synthetic population.
arxiv-2602-16826:
Nigel Doering and co-authors present HiVAE, a hierarchical latent variable architecture that scales theory of mind reasoning to realistic spatiotemporal domains. Theory of mind lets AI infer hidden goals and mental states, but prior work centers on small, human-readable gridworlds. Inspired by the belief-desire-intention structure of human cognition, a three-level variational hierarchy is built.

On a campus navigation task with over three thousand nodes, the hierarchy yields substantial performance gains. Yet the authors flag a critical limit: learned latent codes lack explicit grounding to actual mental states, even as prediction improves. Self-supervised alignment strategies are proposed, and the work is offered to solicit community feedback on grounding routes. AI researchers get both a scaling advance and an honest account of what remains ungrounded.
arxiv-2602-17126:
Satoshi Higashino led a six-author team measuring a quantity that direction-sensitive dark matter searches depend on: the ionization yield of low-energy ions in low-pressure gas. Theory and measurement still disagree at low energies for charged particles in matter, and gaseous detectors with ionization readout need solid recoil-nucleus yields. The team used a low-energy ion beam facility at Kanagawa University with a dedicated proportional wire chamber.

Fluorine ions across a low-energy band were fired into tetrafluoromethane gas at low pressure, establishing a scheme for injecting slow ions into a gaseous detector. The measured yield for fluorine ions sat below one at the reference energy, with moderate dependence on ion energy. The result gives dark matter hunters a firmer calibration for the faint nuclear recoils their detectors aim to catch.
arxiv-2602-17426:
Marco Autili led a four-author team on ethics at runtime in self-adaptive systems. Such systems now work close to people, sharing physical or virtual spaces and making choices with ethical weight while they run. Current methods hard-code ethics as fixed rules or as one ethical theory chosen at design time. That misses how ethical preferences vary across people, shift with context, and clash, while staying inside a hard envelope of safety and compliance rules.

The paper argues for moving from static rules to runtime ethical reasoning. Preferences then count as runtime requirements, gathered, represented, and revised as stakeholders and situations change. Meeting those requirements calls for ethics-based negotiation. It must handle trade-offs among the people who use, are represented by, or are affected by a system. The authors name challenges, including ethical uncertainty, value clashes, and multi-party negotiation, and sketch research directions.
arxiv-2602-17526:
Peter Balogh is the sole author of a 2026 arXiv paper that treats some transformer attention heads as membership testers. The question such a head seems to answer is plain: has this token shown up before in the context. Balogh hunts for those heads across four language models, including three sizes of GPT-2 and a Pythia model, and finds a spread of styles.

Two early heads in the small GPT-2 act as sharp filters, with false positive rates in a low single-digit range even at a large count of distinct context tokens. A third head follows the classic Bloom filter capacity curve, saturating early, while a fourth candidate fails confound checks and is reclassified as a general prefix attention head. The three survivors sit in the earliest layers, form a multi-resolution system, and generalize to any repeated token type.
arxiv-2603-01526:
Adapting one large model to many tasks at once often works at small scale, then collapses as tasks pile up. Zichen Tian, Antoine Ledent, and Qianru Sun diagnose that collapse in this 2026 study of low-rank adaptation. They trace it to clashes between task updates and to blurred traits that routing needs.

The team finds that shared knowledge sits in strong components, while uniform rules force those parts apart. Working at block level, rather than on small pieces, cuts gradient clashes a lot with fewer settings. Their fix, mtLoRA, guards strong parts, adapts by blocks, and routes with fine per-dimension weights. Across vision and language suites with many tasks, it beat top rivals while using fewer settings and less training time.
arxiv-2603-01626:
Xinxun Zhang, Pengfei Jiao, Mengzhou Gao, and colleagues help graph models cope when data patterns shift over time. Their 2026 work studies dynamic graphs, where nodes and links evolve, in fields from social feeds to traffic. Most models assume test data matches training data, yet real streams drift in ways that break that match.

Their model, DyCIL, hunts for steady causal patterns inside the changing graph. A generator first pulls out dynamic subgraphs that carry the causal core of each change. An attention module then reads how those core patterns evolve through space and time. A third part invents varied shift settings, so training sees more kinds of drift. Tests on real and synthetic dynamic graphs beat top baselines under distribution shift.
arxiv-2603-02226:
Bojian Yin, Shurong Wang, Haoyu Tan, and colleagues rethink how recurrent networks handle long signals in this 2026 paper. Audio and video hold brief key moments inside long stretches of quiet or noise. Standard recurrent networks update their memory at every step, even when nothing changes. That habit erases old memory and blocks learning from distant events.

Their network, the suRNN, gives each neuron a switch that opens only for useful input. During dull stretches, memory stays exactly as it was, untouched. Learning signals can then flow straight back across long gaps. On long-range tests and text data, suRNNs matched or beat far larger models. They did so while staying much cheaper for long-term storage of past events.
arxiv-2603-02426:
Leo Muxing Wang, Pengkun Yang, and Lili Su study cooperative learning across agents in this 2026 paper. Each agent faces its own environment and learns its own value function. A shared linear representation links them, with personal weights lying in one unknown subspace. Borrowing from personalized federated learning, agents jointly estimate that subspace and their local parts.

The single-timescale method runs all updates together, without nested loops. Splitting shared and personal parts filters out conflicting signals between agents. Misaligned signals otherwise drag learning in wrong directions. The analysis proves a linear speedup from cooperation. Challenges include agent differences, Markovian sampling, and tightly coupled error dynamics. Experiments on a broader control problem confirm the shared-structure gains.
arxiv-2603-02526:
Yi Zhang, Yichao Wang, Wei Xiao, and colleagues protect automated vehicles from data attacks in this 2026 paper. Connected automated vehicles share roads with human drivers whose behavior is uncertain. False data attacks can corrupt acceleration inputs with growing, unbounded fakes. Safety methods assume honest data, while resilient methods often ignore crash risk.

Their event-driven framework fuses both concerns into one controller. Barrier functions enforce safety and Lyapunov functions enforce stability, both checked at events, not constantly. Adaptive control absorbs attack effects, and human driver behavior is estimated from data. The test case is lane changing amid unpredictable human drivers. Simulations show crash-free maneuvers and stable speed under attack. The method beat conventional safety-only controllers in their comparisons.
arxiv-2603-02926:
Qiming He, Jing Li, Tian Guan, and colleagues train a foundation model devoted to the kidney's tiny filtering units. GloPath, presented in 2026, learned from over a million glomeruli drawn from more than fourteen thousand biopsy samples. These structures vary widely, and their fine lesion patterns drive diagnosis and prognosis in kidney disease.

Across three separate cohorts and dozens of tasks, from lesion grading to few-shot sorting, GloPath beat leading methods in most head-to-head tests. A large real-world study confirmed strong accuracy for lesion recognition in routine practice. The model also linked measurable tissue traits to clinical indicators across hundreds of trait pairs. The authors present it as a scalable, readable platform for kidney pathology and discovery.
arxiv-2603-03126:
Jonas Wilinski assembles nearly three hundred million papers into one searchable lake. Scholarly records sit scattered across siloed databases with clashing metadata and missing links. His 2026 Science Data Lake unifies eight open sources, from Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex to Retraction Watch and Crossref, on a single local setup.

Records join through normalized DOIs while each source keeps its own schema, stored as plain files a single drive can hold. An embedding-based alignment maps thousands of topics onto thirteen scientific ontologies with strong measured accuracy, beating classic text-matching baselines. Ten automated checks and cross-source citation comparisons validate the merge. Four showcase analyses demonstrate questions no single database could answer alone.
arxiv-2603-03226:
Enea Monzio Compagnoni and four colleagues compare training methods that protect privacy in the data they learn from. Differential privacy adds noise so no single example can be picked out, but that noise interacts with the optimizer, the rule that updates the model. Their 2026 paper gives the first analysis of private optimizers using stochastic differential equations, a tool for tracking noisy change over time.

Two methods face off: standard private gradient descent and an adaptive sign-based variant. With fixed settings the adaptive method wins clearly in high-privacy regimes, and its best learning rate barely changes as privacy tightens, so settings transfer without retuning. Experiments back the theory and extend the advantage to a private form of the popular Adam optimizer.
arxiv-2603-03326:
Florian Hoppe and three colleagues give language models personality sliders that users can adjust directly. Setting a persona today usually means costly fine-tuning, with a separate trained model for every personality profile. Steering the model's internal activations at run time is cheaper, but pushing several traits at once makes the steering signals interfere and garble the result.

Their 2026 method, Sequential Adaptive Steering, fixes the interference. Each new steering direction is trained on the model's internal state after earlier adjustments, so the directions stay compatible and reusable. Users then blend traits by turning coefficients up or down, with no change to the model's weights. Tested on the Big Five personality traits, the approach beat naive steering on both hitting the target personality and keeping replies coherent.
arxiv-2605-00026:
Hikaru Wakaura and Taiki Tanimae map where a particular quantum denoising heuristic helps most. The procedure works on states damaged by a uniform dephasing and depolarizing channel, pulling the noisy state's off-diagonal entries toward those of a known target, aided by a purification catalyst. The authors are explicit that this is a benchmark procedure, not blind error correction, since target access is a classical resource.

Their main tool is a covariant purification map giving an exact closed form for one purification round, which reduces the catalyst to a scalar iteration. With it they derive where the fidelity gain peaks as dimension grows, and large numerical sweeps agree with the predicted limit. The peak moves with the protocol's resources and rounds. All results can be reproduced from their open-source benchmark package.
arxiv-2605-00126:
Arnaud Zinflou presents SPLICE, a method for filling long gaps in time series data, with a focus on electric power load records. Missing load values shape dispatch and planning choices, so a filled value needs a reliability bound, not just a best guess. SPLICE pairs a JEPA encoder with a latent bridge, an hourly decoder, and adaptive conformal inference.

Tests on thirteen load datasets with gaps of ninety-one days gave SPLICE the lowest average error among seven established baselines. Its uncertainty bands held their target coverage where fixed calibration fell short. The same ranking held on twelve river catchment datasets. A shared encoder also moved to four new datasets with only light retraining, which points to a practical route for dependable gap filling.
arxiv-2605-00526:
Weichen Liu and 3 co-authors make suspect faces for crime work with a diffusion system built to keep the person identifiable. Sketch workflows are slow and uneven in quality. Text-to-image diffusion struggles here for two reasons: words alone leave a face underdetermined, and a single sampling pass varies too much to pin down identity. Their system, IdentiFace, attacks both problems.

Multi-modal inputs strengthen the control beyond text alone, and a step-by-step loop lets defining features be adjusted rather than taken or dropped whole. The team adds a facial identity loss and builds two task datasets. In tests on fake data and in real-world cases, IdentiFace beat prior methods, especially on tests of whether the made face can pick out the right person. The authors see strong promise for use in real casework.
arxiv-2605-00826:
Maria-Eirini Pegia and six co-authors investigate why progress in text-to-video retrieval has plateaued. Retrieval systems find video from a written query, and many methods have appeared in six years, from dual encoders to attention and fusion models. The team evaluates fourteen leading methods on three widely used datasets under one shared preprocessing and evaluation setup.

They link performance to caption traits such as length, clarity, and whether a caption stresses action or scene. Short, clear, single-action captions score highest, while complex events and fine scene detail challenge every model. Attention models handle time-dependent queries better, and larger diverse caption sets aid transfer across datasets. Generative captions do not reliably help.
arxiv-2605-01026:
Ioannis Diamantis constructs a HOMFLYPT-type polynomial invariant for pseudo links, which generalize classical links by allowing crossings where over and under information is missing. Those pre-crossings block standard Hecke algebra constructions, mainly because of the pseudo Reidemeister move. Diamantis works through the pseudo Hecke algebra of type A and builds a resolution map for the problem.

The map sends each pseudo generator to a combination of a braid generator and its inverse, treating a pre-crossing as a superposition of classical crossings. Composing with the Ocneanu trace and normalizing yields an invariant satisfying a natural pseudo skein relation. It also admits a state-sum form as a weighted sum over all classical resolutions of the pseudo crossings.
arxiv-2605-01126:
Amy McGovern and eight co-authors introduce Extreme Weather Bench, an open community benchmark for evaluating forecasts of high-impact weather. Forecasting such events is hard for both AI and numerical weather models, and verification before deployment is critical. Current AI evaluation often uses global scores or a handful of hand-picked cases, which cannot support fair comparison across models or hazards.

The suite provides standard case studies across scales and parts of the weather spectrum, observational data, impact-based metrics, and open-source evaluation code. Users can test models on specific high-impact phenomena that matter to the public. The free system is designed to evolve with the worldwide forecast verification community, adding phenomena, cases, and metrics over time.
arxiv-2605-01226:
Keyan Chen and four co-authors present ARCH, a model for events spread across space and time, such as crimes, quakes, or disease cases. Standard point process models lean on strong assumptions and usually predict one event at a time, in order. That limits them on broader tasks, like working backward from effects to causes, rebuilding a full path, or filling in missing event locations.

ARCH uses a hierarchical flow matching design with a history encoder and a generative decoder. A hybrid masking scheme lets the model condition on any chosen set of observed events, not just the past. It stays expressive while still giving exact, accurate values for conditional intensities, the measure of how likely an event is at each place and moment. One model thus covers forecasting, inverse inference, and partial path recovery. Tests on synthetic and real data beat prior methods on both prediction and inference tasks.
arxiv-2605-01726:
Zenan Dai and five co-authors listen for rhythm in shopping behavior to predict clicks. A user's clicks over time hide periodic interests, weekly, seasonal, payday-driven, but time-domain records are noisy, and earlier frequency methods read each user's sequence alone, ignoring the item now being judged.

The team first report a telling observation: when the target item truly matches the user, attention scores bunch into tight, low-entropy spectral patterns; for mismatches they smear into high-entropy noise. Their network, FEDIN, builds a frequency branch with a target-aware filter that isolates those periodic interest signals before they steer the prediction. On three public data sets it beats the strongest sequential recommendation baselines across the board and holds up better under noise. Code is public.
arxiv-2605-02326:
Yangzhou Chen, Shuaida He, and Xin Chen select assets for large portfolios using high-frequency information that standard rules discard. Portfolio choice is sensitive to estimation error, so a preliminary selection step matters in practice. Past rules use scalar returns or low-dimensional intraday summaries, losing within-day risk dynamics that affect risk-adjusted allocation.

Their Metric Dependence Screening represents each asset-day as a point-curve object: the daily return plus an intraday risk state curve, under a weighted product metric. Assets are ranked by a Fréchet variation dependence score, measuring how much a risk-adjusted target explains the spread of those objects. Screening then shrinks the investable universe before a standard mean-variance step, in a simple two-stage procedure.
arxiv-2605-02526:
Miriam Kranzlmüller and three co-authors change how neural barrier certificates are trained for proving a system safe. A barrier certificate is a function that separates all unsafe states from all reachable ones; if it exists, safety is formally verified. Prior work trained a network, then checked it, looping until the check passed.

The new method folds the check into training itself. A set-based loss encodes every required property of the certificate in a sound way, so a loss of zero is itself a proof of validity. Training and verification merge into one procedure. Experiments show the approach scales well as system dimension grows and handles complex nonlinear dynamics naturally. For safety work on robots and other controlled systems, that merger removes a costly loop.
arxiv-2605-02626:
Inoussa Mouiche and Abderaouf Bahi diagnose a failure mode in direct preference optimization, a popular way to train language models from ranked answers. Training widens the gap between chosen and rejected answers, but the objective does not say where the freed probability should go. Probability can collapse away from both the good answer and unrelated ones, a squeezing effect.

The fault, they show, is local: once a rejected answer falls into a low-probability valley, further suppression harms the whole distribution through the softmax link. Their fix, Gate-DPO, scales down each rejected answer's update based on its current probability, slowing excess suppression. Across four architectures, two datasets, and several objectives, gating reduced squeezing and raised the likelihood of chosen answers, without tying the method to one objective.
arxiv-2605-02826:
E. M. Tursunov, D. S. Toshova, and S. A. Turakulov study the structure of two light mirror nuclei, boron-8 and lithium-8, inside a three-body cluster model. Each nucleus is treated as an alpha particle, a helium-3 or tritium core, and a proton or neutron, with realistic pair potentials from prior work. The method solves the three-body problem on a hyperspherical mesh.

Ground and excited bound states are computed, with converged values for binding energy and matter radius. Normalization constants for the key virtual transitions are extracted by matching wave functions to their outer form, in both spin channels for each nucleus. Comparing the pair shows mirror symmetry of the strong force is broken by roughly a quarter, an effect of electric repulsion and three-body dynamics. An astrophysical capture factor is also estimated.
arxiv-2605-03026:
Yue Yu develops a theory for creating odd-parity spin splitting inside collinear altermagnets, materials prized for spin currents without net magnetism. Momentum-linked spin splitting depends on inversion and time-reversal symmetry, and the odd-parity form is rare in the more common collinear case.

Yu shows two routes: driving with a two-color polarized light field, or coupling to an odd-parity loop-current order. Either route can produce a mixed-parity spin texture that light or current could control. Applied to a different symmetric magnet, the same idea yields a dissipation-free anomalous spin Hall response.
arxiv-2605-03326:
Gordon J. Ross develops Bayesian monitoring for processes that can recover or drift, where the key question is whether the process is acceptable right now. Standard Phase II control often asks whether a change ever happened, which misfits settings where monitoring continues after an alarm or a fix restores control.

For recoverable processes, Ross derives recursions for the current in-control probability as states alternate. For drifting latent parameters, the methods track the chance the parameter sits inside an acceptable region. Calibrated failure-time experiments, Gaussian and binomial tracking cases, and a wine quality example test the approach.
arxiv-2605-03926:
Nikolay A. Emelyanov and five co-authors compute how electrons diffuse and conduct in a collisionless plasma. The plasma carries Weibel-generated turbulence plus a uniform external field. The Weibel instability makes slowly varying turbulent fields, and those fields strongly affect transport. The team uses an original code based on the Boris algorithm. With it, they find the diffusion coefficients. They also find the mobility factors along, across, and in the Hall direction.

The values they find depend strongly on electron temperature. They also depend on the external field, and on the level and spectrum of the turbulence. The authors indicate the origin of those links, and their expected limits. They discuss uses in coronal plasma, where anomalous resistivity prevails over collisional resistivity. There, it can move large-scale currents in loops. It can also move small-scale currents where field lines reconnect.
arxiv-2605-04426:
Mikhail L. Arbuzov and four co-authors introduce a protocol for compressing prompts to language models by rewriting them in a compact, symbol-rich dialect. Unlike methods that simply delete low-value tokens, their rewrite breaks the text into single-fact lines and swaps verbose phrases for logical symbols.

Because each output line is one addressable fact, the compressed text doubles as a semantic index. On thousands of question-answer pairs from a long-context benchmark, tested across five models, the method halved the token count while preserving almost all accuracy on key facts. It beat a leading deletion method at matched compression, with the largest gains on smaller models.
arxiv-2605-04526:
Rishad Shahmurov studies a source-driven transition in a swirling flow. The flow looks the same around an axis, and the Euler equations for an ideal fluid describe it. For one explicit, smooth, compactly supported starting state, he proves a set of exact equalities. They cover sources, moments, and how labelled fluid parcels are transported.

Computer-assisted interval bounds then enclose key rate values at a final time. Under further global matching assumptions, those estimates would force two material labels together. They would also produce an outward level set of finite radius. Shahmurov lists the open steps on their own. He is explicit that the work as it stands claims no whole-space Euler singularity.
arxiv-2605-04626:
Julia Hörmayer and Florian Schreier-Aigner present determinant formulas for a family of polynomials built by summing over totally symmetric plane partitions, three-dimensional stacks of cubes with full symmetry. The family connects to alternating sign matrices and to symmetric tilings of a hexagon with a triangular hole.

Their formulas express these polynomials as determinants, which in turn produce new lattice path models for them and a novel family of tableaux. The tableau picture shows the polynomials generalise three classical dual Littlewood identities from representation theory. The work, following earlier joint work by the second author with Ilse Fischer, deepens the enumerative theory of these symmetric objects.
arxiv-2605-04826:
Panagiotis Charalampopoulos and four co-authors speed up two classic string problems: finding a shortest substring that occurs only once, and a shortest substring that never occurs at all. Both have long had linear-time solutions using suffix trees. For small alphabets, though, a string can be stored and read faster than its raw length suggests.

Their new algorithm beats the linear bound in that compact setting by splitting the problem by substring length and period. Tools such as synchronising sets, runs analysis, and wavelet trees reduce the search to a simple geometric question. An adaptation using de Bruijn sequences then handles the absent-substring problem at the same improved speed.
arxiv-2605-04926:
Bingkun Zhao, Chenwei Zhang, and Hao Peng study how promotional language affects the evaluation of patent applications in the United States. Hype words are increasingly used to sell new ideas in science, but their role for inventions was unclear. The team built a checked list of one hundred thirty-five promotional words for this study.

Across millions of patent applications, more promotional wording was linked to lower chances of approval, ownership transfer, and successful appeal. Yet such language was not hiding weak inventions, since it tracked real novelty and later citation impact. Tolerance also varied by examiner, with men and experienced examiners accepting promotional framing more readily.
arxiv-2605-05026:
Bartlomiej Sobieski and six co-authors link hallucinations in diffusion image models to wobbles in the geometric surface the model has learned. Such models can produce samples that match training statistics yet break structural rules, like hands with too many fingers. The authors treat those failures as instabilities rather than simple sampling noise.

A filter based on those instabilities matches or beats a recent time-based filter, the team reports. Tracing the instabilities leads them to local intrinsic dimension as the main driver, and their corrective method, Intrinsic Quenching, directly lowers it. Across many benchmarks the method beat standard hallucination-reduction baselines and looks promising for anatomical consistency in medical imaging.
arxiv-2605-05426:
Open radio access networks let phone companies mix equipment from different vendors. Conrado Boeira and five co-authors measure how small network apps, called dApps, actually perform in that setting. Advice says to run them in containers, yet most real deployments still use bare-metal servers, with little data on resource use.

The team ran representative dApps both ways and compared delay, scaling, and resource needs. They found the main bottlenecks and tested a fix: moving work onto smart network cards. That offloading eased the bottlenecks and made the real-time apps respond faster, giving operators firmer ground for deployment choices.
arxiv-2605-05626:
Knowing what to say is only half of conversation; group chats also demand knowing when to stay silent. Vihaan Nama, Shreya Mendi, Zian Ye, and Brinnae Bent build When2Speak, a dataset for teaching language models that timing skill. Models that answer at every turn interrupt constantly and wreck coherence.

The dataset holds over 215,000 examples drawn from 16,000 synthetic conversations of two to six speakers. Each turn is labeled with a speak-or-stay-silent decision. A four-stage pipeline grounds the chats in real material, augments them structurally, and controls the transcription, so models can learn participation timing as a trainable behavior.
arxiv-2605-05726:
An AI agent with thousands of reusable skills faces a retrieval problem: which skill fits this request, within a tight context budget? Hongcheol Cho, Ryangkyung Kang, and Youngeun Kim introduce SkillRet, a large-scale benchmark for that selection task. Naming skills explicitly works in small libraries and collapses as ecosystems grow.

SkillRet gathers 17,810 public agent skills, organized with semantic tags and a two-level taxonomy of six major categories and eighteen subcategories. The benchmark measures how retrievers behave on a realistic, messy library. It gives agent builders a way to test skill selection before deployment.
arxiv-2605-06026:
Hiroki Kawabe and four co-authors design two fluid heat exchangers with topology optimization under turbulent flow. Their work pairs a cheap Darcy flow model with an expensive model based on the full flow equations. The cheap model is calibrated against the costly one, since gaps between them can be large, above all for pressure drops.

Optimization runs on the calibrated cheap model across varied inlet speeds and trade off settings, producing diverse candidate designs. The costly model then scores those designs with higher accuracy. The best layouts improved heat transfer while keeping pressure drops manageable. Their performance measure ran up to 22 percent above a reference design fitted with twisted tape inserts.
arxiv-2605-06226:
Tianyu Liu and fourteen co-authors introduce Hygieia, a multimodal AI agent for rare disease diagnosis and risk gene ranking. Rare diseases are hard to diagnose, and current workflows often mean long delays and low accuracy for patients. The system integrates phenotypic features, genetic profiles, and clinical records into one diagnostic process aimed at precision medicine.

A router based, knowledge enhanced design tailors strategy by disease category and works to limit hallucination. The agent prioritizes risk related genomic factors for rare diseases and reports confidence scores to support clinical judgment. Across diagnostic benchmarks it reached state of the art results in the authors' evaluation. In studies with clinicians at two medical schools, it beat physicians on diagnosis and helped experts work through real case records.
arxiv-2605-06426:
Diego Rossini and Lonneke van der Plas build a large pipeline for finding new words automatically. A neologism is a genuine lexical innovation, but most candidate tokens are names, foreign words, or noise. Their pipeline combines rule-based filtering with language model classification, guided by grammatical and extra-grammatical word formation.

Applied to 527 million Reddit posts from 2005 to 2024, it narrows 124.6 million unique tokens down to 1,021 candidates for expert checking. Several models vote on each candidate, and manual annotation confirms 599 as genuine innovations. The code and annotated list are public, and model disagreement itself shows how hard the task is.
arxiv-2605-06626:
Dmitry Treschev studies how a polynomial-like Hamiltonian system near a non-degenerate rest point can be perturbed into a completely integrable one. Hamiltonian systems describe motion at fixed energy, and complete integrability means enough conserved laws exist to solve the motion in principle. The starting system has a smooth energy function on a phase space.

Under nonresonance rules, Treschev proves a result for any chosen order M. A smooth small change exists that stays very small near the rest point to that order, yet makes the perturbed system completely integrable on the whole space. Small, carefully shaped changes can thus restore exact solvability. That is a striking result for Hamiltonian dynamics.
arxiv-2605-06726:
Obed Irakoze and Prasenjit Mitra classify wildlife species purely from their daily movement trajectories. Knowing which species produced a GPS track matters when identity is missing or uncertain. They train sequence models on large-scale trajectories from seven species hosted on the Movebank platform, testing on whole studies or regions held out from training to force real generalization.

Transformer models beat recurrent, convolutional, and temporal convolutional rivals by roughly eight to twenty-two points of balanced accuracy. On an elephant task the Transformer scores notably higher than all baselines. Richer movement features, including speed, direction, and turning, help rare species most, while hourly sampling beats finer sampling overall by reducing missing data.
arxiv-2605-06826:
Mohamed El Amine Seddik studies how attention pooling affects signal recovery in sequence models, using random matrix theory. Token vectors are drawn from a two-class Gaussian mixture and pooled with fixed attention weights, then summed up by a sample covariance matrix. As sizes grow he derives the limiting spread of eigenvalues, the outlier ones, and how eigenvectors align with the hidden signal.

Signal recovery passes through two sharp phase shifts governed by dimension ratios and attention-dependent numbers. The optimal attention weights turn out to be the top eigenvector of the position correlation matrix. As a special case, untuned causal attention beats plain mean pooling when early tokens carry more signal. Tests match the theory closely.
arxiv-2605-07526:
Pranjal Barik and three co-authors model what happens to a short-lived particle called the K*0 meson in gold-gold collisions at the RHIC accelerator. They use a computer model named AMPT that follows the collision through several stages. Their runs cover three collision energies from the Beam Energy Scan program.

The model shows that later collisions among ordinary particles hide many K*0 decays, cutting the counted yield, mostly at low sideways momentum. Its predicted ratios match recent measurements at all three energies. Surprisingly, runs without the late stage also fit the data, which challenges the usual story. The authors argue that the sideways flow direction of the meson is the sharper probe of that late stage.
arxiv-2605-07626:
Mohammed el Baraka and Siham Ezzouak develop a global arithmetic framework for studying endomorphism rings inside ordinary elliptic curve isogeny classes over finite fields. Classically, the endomorphism ring is viewed level by level on an isogeny volcano, where it stays constant along each level. They instead ask how these rings are distributed across a whole isogeny class at once.

Building on Deuring's correspondence, they express the distribution through weighted class numbers and give explicit formulas for exact and cumulative distributions of the rings. The approach recovers the volcano's vertical layering in averaged form. Varying the prime, they also derive a horizontal law: the natural density of primes whose curves admit a prescribed complex multiplication order, expressed through class field theory.
arxiv-2605-08126:
Marwa Ennaceur studies Rota-Baxter operators on the algebra of complex square matrices, with a heuristic nod to Toeplitz structures. The study classifies the operators that respect the C-star norm and works out the Lie brackets they induce, giving a clear structural picture of this operator family.

The algebra is then put to work in control theory. The classified operators deform the system matrices of discrete-time delayed systems under sliding mode control. Lyapunov-based matrix inequality conditions, rewritten in a tractable linear form, guarantee stability on the sliding surface and a bounded gain from uncertainty to state. The author is careful about the scope of each guarantee.
arxiv-2605-08626:
Liangqi Yuan and five coauthors survey how language models spread across phones, edge boxes, and cloud servers can work together. Cloud only service fails where connections drop, answers must be instant, or data must stay local, while single devices lack memory and power. Their collaborative intelligence view joins models at the task level through plain or structured messages.

Collaboration runs two ways: vertical splits between device and cloud, and horizontal teamwork among peer agents, often mixed in practice. The survey also covers learning how to route tasks and cooperate, plus open problems in scaling and trust. Networked AI research gains a map for sharing work under tight, uneven resources.
arxiv-2605-09126:
Vatsal Shah and co-author Jiahao Sun tackle a training problem in systems that learn across many machines without waiting for each other. Updates can arrive several rounds late, yet the usual outer optimizer ignores how old each update is. Their 2026 proposal, Cosine-Gated Adam-Decay, shrinks each incoming update by an age-based factor before it enters the Adam memory, and smoothly cuts off updates past a chosen delay.

The method reduces to plain Adam for fresh updates, adds only two settings, and extends to partial synchronization schedules. The authors prove a convergence bound whose stale-data term depends on their decay choice rather than the worst delay seen. In language model pretraining tests at three scales, their method stays stable across swept delays, while rival recipes grow risky at larger scale. The cosine cutoff acts as insurance when training gets big.
arxiv-2605-09326:
Singh and two colleagues simulate magnetically arrested disks around a non-spinning black hole with general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, and radiative cooling throughout. Cooling strength scales with mass accretion rate from one ten-millionth to one ten-thousandth of the Eddington rate, covering synchrotron and bremsstrahlung emission.

In the inner disk, piled-up magnetic field holds back gas accretion and forces gas into discrete interchange-driven filaments. The team finds, analytically and numerically, a transition accretion rate above which cooling outruns heating, assumed to come from local magnetic coupling. Above that rate, cooling cuts gas thermal pressure sharply, leaving much thinner and denser filaments and far higher radiative efficiency than at lower rates. Conventional scale-height measures mislead in MAD flows. The authors define scale height instead from the polar position of the density maximum, a more robust gauge of filamentary structure under strong fields and cooling.
arxiv-2605-09526:
Chidambaram and three colleagues introduce a moduli space of metric Möbius graphs, stretching ribbon graphs into the non orientable world. That single space holds both Riemann surface moduli and Klein surface moduli. Each metric Möbius graph carries a measure of non orientability. The authors count lattice points in this space, weighted by that measure, and prove a refined version of Norbury's recursion for the count.

Letting the mesh grow finer, they deduce a recursion for Euclidean volumes, yielding a refined Witten Kontsevich recursion. As an application, they define the refined Euler characteristic geometrically for the space and compute it in closed form. That computation answers a question posed by Goulden, Harer, and Jackson, tying refined counting to classical volume recursions.
arxiv-2605-09626:
Shapiro and Tahar revisit plane rectifiable curves, old and new. The classical notion, going back to Serret, Laguerre, and Humbert, concerns algebraic curves whose arc length varies algebraically with the endpoints. Arc length is rarely computable in closed form, and for a typical algebraic curve it does not depend algebraically on the endpoints at all. The famous exception is the ellipse, whose arc length theory led to elliptic functions, while the semicubic parabola gave an early explicit example.

The authors supply new criteria for algebraic rectifiability, connect the notion to quadratic differentials, and extend it to higher order differentials. A central classical result frames the story: a plane algebraic curve is algebraically rectifiable exactly when it forms the evolute of some algebraic curve. Recasting that problem in the language of meromorphic differentials on normalizations, the note connects a 19th century question to modern tools.
arxiv-2605-09726:
Gao and three colleagues proved a sobering limit for testing causal models with interference, where one person's treatment spills over to others. Researchers model such spillovers with exposure mappings, then run specification tests to check the model. Existing tests have weak power, and the paper shows that weakness cannot be fixed: for any test, the worst-case false-positive and false-negative rates must sum to one.

That total equals the error of a naive test that ignores the data and rejects at random, so no uniformly consistent test exists. The result holds for every exposure mapping, every sample size, and even alternatives far from the null. Informative testing, the authors conclude, must narrow the alternatives it targets, as their consistent test for no-interference against a network-linear-in-means model illustrates.
arxiv-2605-09826:
Juneja and nine colleagues built EnactToM, a benchmark for functional theory of mind in embodied agents: not just reporting what others believe, but acting well on implicit beliefs. Existing tests mostly ask direct belief questions, while real collaboration needs agents to use beliefs in action. EnactToM offers 300 embodied multi-agent tasks in a 3D household with partial observability, private information, and limited communication.

Each task is formally checked for solvability and required epistemic depth, and new tasks grow harder as models improve. On the hard split, all seven frontier models scored 0.0 percent on Pass^3 functional completion, while averaging 45.0 percent on literal belief probes. Manual analysis traced 93 percent of sampled failures to epistemic coordination breakdowns, like withheld information and ignored partner constraints.
arxiv-2605-10026:
Lu and two colleagues proposed MUSDA, a framework for multi-source, multi-modality unsupervised domain adaptation in 3D object detection for self-driving cars. Many annotated multi-modal datasets now exist, offering a chance to build detectors for new places without costly manual labels. Old methods often handle a single source domain or a single modality, limiting effectiveness in multi-source, multi-modal cases.

With several labeled source domains and one unlabeled target domain, MUSDA first adds hierarchical domain classifiers, aligning camera and LiDAR features at two levels for each source-target pair. A prototype graph between each domain pair then supports prototype-weighted multi-source fusion, pooling predictions from multiple source detection heads. On Waymo, nuScenes, and Lyft, MUSDA always beat state-of-the-art methods.
arxiv-2605-10226:
Pei-Yuan Cai and Yi Zhou probe a puzzle in flat superconductors, materials that conduct without resistance in a thin layer. Transport tests often show different transition temperatures in different directions. That raises a question: does the material truly split into two transitions, or merely look that way? Their 2026 paper builds a minimal baseline to tell the difference.

The model is a simple array of Josephson junctions with direction-dependent phase behavior, studied at rest and under current flow. At rest it shows a single BKT transition, driven by vortex pairs unbinding. Under current, direction-dependent couplings and energy loss distort resistance curves so that simple curve-shape tests fake a double transition. Stricter scaling tests still show one transition. A split that survives those tests, as reported at KTaO3 interfaces, must therefore come from physics beyond this clean baseline.
arxiv-2605-10626:
Keisuke Morita and Masayuki Ohzeki study sparse recovery with log-sum regularization. The log-sum rule reduces the shrinkage bias of the L1 rule and nears the L0 rule. But its uneven shape can make rebuilds unstable. Their 2026 paper eases this problem with tuned smoothing.

The strategy sets the smoothing setting so the proximal operator stays smooth. The authors build the message passing and derive the state loop. The fixed point of the loop predicts the MSE and the recovery phase shift in the noiseless limit. An ADMM algorithm is implemented to probe rebuild results. In the noiseless setting, the success boundary of ADMM agrees with the loop-predicted phase shift. The log-sum rule helps in sparse or high-measure-rate regimes. The L1 rule stays better at denser settings and lower measure rates.
arxiv-2605-10726: Chico Camargo argues that opinions are bundles of positions across many issues, not points on one left-right line. He builds a network from attitude profiles in a two-wave panel. The panel covers 1,194 people on ten issues. Densely occupied positions count as network-normative, or common in the population. Against three null models, movement into occupied regions beats chance by a wide margin, though the effect depends on grid resolution.
arxiv-2605-10826:
M. Koratzinos and six colleagues report the first canted-cosine-theta sextupole magnet built from high-temperature superconducting tape, a 2026 demonstrator for the Future Circular Collider's electron-positron stage. Sextupole magnets help steer and focus particle beams, and the usual copper versions draw heavy power in the collider's arcs.

This single-aperture, two-layer device winds ReBCO tape into tilted coils and was built and tested under cryogenic cold, with tapes from two makers qualified for the job. Swapping in superconducting sextupoles could cut losses and allow tighter nested layouts in the machine's short straight sections. Collider engineers get measured proof that the design works in hardware, not only on paper.
arxiv-2605-11326: Vinicius de Oliveira Rodrigues studies almost disjointness principles and Q-space cardinals in set theory. Banakh and Bazylevych had asked whether the cardinal adp equals dp or ap. Rodrigues proves in ZFC that adp equals dp. He defines a dual variant adp2 equal to ap. He introduces a tree analogue at equal to q2, concluding ap is at most q2. Assuming the continuum hypothesis, he builds forcing extensions where ap is strictly below q2, so the gap is consistent.
arxiv-2605-11926: Mengyi Gong, Rebecca Killick, and Andrew Hirons forecast daily water use in temperate trees to guide irrigation. Their pipeline joins sap flow gauges, weather station gauges, and statistical models, with weather readings driving sap flux density forecasts in an additive ensemble. Field data from nine tree species across the 2022, 2023, and 2024 growing seasons showed reliable daily forecasts, including discussion of heatwave stress and tree size effects.
arxiv-2605-12026: Alexandra Roberts and twelve colleagues propose a spectral vision transformer for fast token-making with limited data, aimed at medical imaging. Choosing a spectral basis brings spatial sameness and optimal signal-to-noise ratio, with lower cost versus spatial vision models. It matched or beat compact and standard vision models, attention CNNs, shifted window models, multi-layer nets, and logit models with fewer weights. Tests spanned fake, public, and hospital data, with code shared.
arxiv-2605-12126: Partha Ghose proposes a test of Leggett-Garg time patterns in single neurons, telling spread-like models from stickier random ones. Pure spread models meet the Leggett-Garg bounds, while steady-speed Kac-type random walks can break them with wavy time patterns. A break would not prove quantum links in the brain. It would show only that a plain spread picture fails, and that memory and context shape neural time patterns. Steady-speed random motion gives a plain route to such patterns, with no quantum claim needed.
arxiv-2605-12326: Niloy and Akimoto map the hidden difficulty of merging large language models by switching parameter groups on and off across layers. They frame this Data Flow Space merging as a mixed binary-and-continuous optimisation problem with up to 291 parameter groups and tangled dependencies between choices. Testing seven merging methods on Mistral-7B models, they cut the effective search space by about half, yet no method beats the stronger source model on the official tests.
arxiv-2605-12426: Ravfogel and three colleagues argue that transformers can memorise facts geometrically, not just as key-value pairs. The standard picture needs parameters that grow with the fact count, since weight matrices store pairs of embeddings. In a controlled test where a one-layer transformer must learn random subject-to-attribute maps, they prove a logarithmic embedding size suffices. Subject embeddings store sums of attribute vectors, and a small network picks the right attribute by gating. The account extends to multi-step chains of relational questions.
arxiv-2605-12526: Singh, Mondal and Menczer study toxic party speech on X during the 2024 United States presidential election. They use original posts and replies. A human-checked language model labels party alignment, while the Perspective API scores toxicity. They report an asymmetry in the data. Posts leaning Republican score as more toxic than posts leaning Democratic. Yet posts leaning Democratic draw more toxic replies. By comparing same-party and cross-party exchanges, the paper separates how partisans speak inside their own circles from how hard they engage the other side.
arxiv-2605-12726: Doda diagnoses a failure mode in final-token safety probes. Such probes read a single hidden state after prompt prefill. Jailbreak prompts can hide unsafe evidence across earlier user-token representations that the readout misses. Using SafeSwitch-style probes trained on clean harmful and benign prompts alone across three tuned models, he finds high recall on clean harmful prompts. Many jailbreaks are missed, and false positives appear on safety-adjacent benign prompts. Widening the probe bottleneck does not fix the mismatch, since missed jailbreaks differ along poorly captured directions.
arxiv-2605-12826: Zhao and five colleagues present FRAME, a method for image edit spotting that routes evidence as needed. Single methods suffer limited strength, split evidence, or weak reach across edit types. FRAME sorts check tools into a multi-path space, adaptively selects telling paths for each input image, and fuses matching evidence to lift spotting and placing. Moving beyond single-tool work and fixed fusion, it preserves clear cues from many sources. Tests show its value across diverse editing cases.
arxiv-2605-13026: Hong and seven co-authors ask why masked diffusion language models train far more slowly than autoregressive models, and how to speed them up. They trace the drag to locality bias: predictive information for a token sits mostly nearby. Their remedy, bell-shaped time sampling, lets models trained their way reach the same validation loss about four times faster on the One Billion Word Benchmark. Generative perplexity, zero-shot perplexity and downstream task scores improve faster too.
arxiv-2606-00026:
Van Steen tests whether psychology-informed features help AI detect depression in social media writing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Drawing on Beck's cognitive theory, which links depression to distorted thinking patterns, the study counts features such as first-person pronoun density, absolutist word use, and negative emotion ratios in Reddit posts. The dataset covers nearly 2,000 posts from depression-related and control groups, drawn from a public Kaggle set on suicide and depression detection.

Two pipelines were tested: a simple word-frequency baseline and a hybrid model. The hybrid paired DistilBERT language embeddings with holographic reduced representations, a compact vector method for encoding structure, then logistic regression. The hybrid clearly won, reaching a macro F1 score, a balanced accuracy measure, near 0.94 versus 0.80 for the simple model in their tests. Cross-validation showed the same gap, backing the claim that theory-driven features add signal beyond language embeddings alone.

arxiv-2606-04126:
Benjamin Goldblatt and co-authors introduce HighTide in 2026, an open-source benchmark suite for VLSI design, the process of laying out integrated circuits. Benchmarks in this field age quickly and often hide the reasoning behind their tuning choices.

The suite spans several design languages and manufacturing nodes, and builds designs from register-transfer code to final layout with an incremental build system backed by remote caching. Twelve agent skills assist curation across the design lifecycle, from flow tuning to maintenance, and per-design decision logs preserve why each choice was made. Compilation checks guard stable releases. The authors intend the suite to grow alongside the open hardware ecosystem rather than freeze as a one-time release.
arxiv-2606-04326:
Julian Skirzynski and colleagues build in 2026 synthetic benchmarks for concept bottleneck models, systems that predict outcomes through a layer of human-named concepts. These models promise interpretability, but almost no real datasets carry concept labels, so nobody can tell where they shine or fail.

Their benchmarks generate labeled data while dialing properties that plausibly drive performance: data modality, which concepts are provided, annotation quality, and concept completeness. They cover the two main use cases, decision support for humans and unsupervised automation of routine calls. Running representative model classes through the suite diagnosed concrete failure modes and showed how to target follow-up testing. The authors offer the generator as shared infrastructure for a field that has been evaluating on anecdotes.
arxiv-2606-04426:
Bauer, Keup, Kadmon, and Helias ask how brain circuits can code sensory information smoothly when their activity is chaotic, in a 2026 arXiv paper on neural networks. In chaotic networks, tiny input changes can push responses far apart, which seems at odds with the smooth population codes seen in cortex. The authors link microscopic chaos in recurrent networks to the geometry of the representations those networks form, using kernel methods and dynamical mean-field theory.

They show that chaotic dynamics roughen representations at small scales while keeping them smooth across larger stimulus changes. That mix acts as a built-in regularizer, improving generalization while preserving expressiveness. Chaotic networks also produce power-law spectral signatures, patterns where energy falls off in a steady ratio across frequencies, matching cortical recordings. The results explain how spiking networks sustain smooth population codes despite underlying chaos.
arxiv-2606-04726:
Lyubimtsev and Tuganbaev describe which triangular matrix rings have a strong form of centrality, in a 2026 arXiv algebra paper. Such rings are close to commutative in a precise sense. Formal triangular matrix rings, built from two rings and a bimodule arranged in triangular form, are a standard test class for ring-theoretic properties.

The authors describe the centrally essential rings within a large subclass of formal triangular matrix rings, and within a subclass of the three-by-three matrix ring over a base ring. The classification tells ring theorists exactly which of these matrix-like constructions keep the centrally essential property, connecting a global commutativity-like condition to the properties of the component rings and module. Results of this kind matter because triangular matrix rings provide counterexamples and boundary cases throughout ring theory, so knowing where a property survives helps map the concept's true scope.
arxiv-2606-04826:
Naskar, Robens, and Ziegler examine the kinematics of producing three Higgs bosons at once at the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2026 arXiv particle physics paper. Their setting is the Next-to-minimal Two Higgs Doublet Model, an extension of the Standard Model whose scalar sector has three neutral CP-even Higgs states. They analyze invariant mass and transverse momentum distributions to disentangle the production mechanisms.

They demonstrate that interference effects between diagrams can significantly alter the observable distributions. Simplified approximations that ignore interference can mislead searches for extended Higgs sectors. Fully differential studies, keeping the complete kinematic information, are important for probing such models.
arxiv-2606-04926:
Kumari and Ashokan present a 2026 arXiv study of many-body localization, where strong disorder keeps an interacting quantum system from settling into equilibrium. The contrast is the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, which says most such systems do settle and forget their starting state. Their test case is a disordered XXZ spin chain, a line of interacting quantum spins.

Using exact diagonalization, a method that solves small systems completely, the authors slowly ramp the interaction strength across the boundary between regimes. They compare linear, quadratic, and exponential ramps, tracking two entropy measures for chains of up to 14 spins in their simulations. Slow ramps left localized behavior largely intact, while faster ramps created more excitations and larger entropy growth. The quadratic ramp produced the smallest entropy changes among the three shapes tested.
arxiv-2606-05226:
A. Boumali, N. Jafari, and Manizheh Botshekananfard study Klein-Gordon and Dirac oscillators under a time-dependent apparent mass in this 2026 arXiv paper. The starting point is the Fock-Lorentz transformations, an extension of special relativity carrying an extra cosmological length scale. The authors propose a momentum-space dual of those transformations and derive a deformed relativistic mass shell.

On that world line, the relation equals the standard dispersion law of special relativity, but with an apparent mass drifting downward over time. Canonical quantization then yields Klein-Gordon and Dirac equations containing that varying mass. In the adiabatic regime the authors obtain exact instantaneous spectra for the one-dimensional oscillators, treating the Dirac case component by component to avoid double counting. For cosmological values of the scale, non-adiabatic corrections are negligible, and in the late limit the apparent mass tends to zero and the energy levels collapse toward zero.
arxiv-2606-05626:
Zhen Sun and colleagues keep a text-source detector current as new generators appear in a 2026 arXiv paper. Attribution means naming which model wrote a given text. New language models launch constantly, so detectors must learn new classes without forgetting old ones. Saving old examples for rehearsal costs storage and privacy. The team builds an update rule that needs no replay at all.

Their method, RidgeFT, trains an encoder once on the first generator set. For each new class it stores only compact summary statistics. The encoder then freezes, and new classes are added by closed-form ridge regression, a solved formula rather than fresh training. A calibration step suppresses variation that has nothing to do with the source. Across topics, backbones, and update orders, RidgeFT earned the best macro-F1 scores. It also improved both memory for old classes and pickup of new ones.
arxiv-2606-05926:
Zampini, Boffi, Dovletov, and Markowich move a flow problem's nonlinearity into a helper variable in a 2026 arXiv paper. Generalized Newtonian fluids, from blood to polymer melts, resist standard solvers because viscosity depends on the flow gradient itself. The framework introduces an auxiliary scalar holding the gradient's squared size. The state equation then becomes a chain of weighted linear problems, each uniformly elliptic.

At the continuous level the authors build an energy on a metric space matched to the material's growth law. They prove the scheme's convergence, with exponential rates, under that geometry. A finite element version follows through an explicit Riesz map, with global well-posedness for its dynamics. For p-Laplacian and p-Stokes models, rigorous convergence covers a wide exponent range. Operator splitting yields the Kačanov iteration as one special case. Numerical tests matched or beat Newton's method with mesh-independent iteration counts.
arxiv-2606-06126:
Umbach and colleagues evaluate a search-page intervention meant to deter abuse-material seeking and route people to help in a 2026 arXiv paper. Google Search shows a notice when queries seek child sexual abuse material. The study compares a revised notice stressing legal repercussions and therapeutic resources against the earlier reporting-focused version. Internal search logs supplied the data, analyzed with a difference-in-differences design.

The revised messaging reduced abuse-material queries within the session by three point eight percentage points versus the old design. Clicks through to linked help resources averaged under one percent of impressions. Small percentages at search scale mean many people reached support services. The authors read the results as evidence that a subset of seekers can be deterred and redirected. Search engines sit at an intervention point in this harm chain. Message design, the study shows, measurably changes what happens next.
arxiv-2606-06226:
Lucas Seaton and a large team of co-authors report an extreme quasar outflow in this 2026 arXiv paper on astronomy. Quasars are brilliant galactic cores powered by feeding black holes, and many drive gas outward at high speed. In the quasar SDSS J2318, the authors found absorption from carbon and silicon ions moving toward us at record pace. The gas reaches at least seventy seven thousand kilometers per second, about three tenths of light speed.

Its black hole weighs about one point six five billion Suns, and twenty years of photometry show brightness swings of half a magnitude. The outflow grew steadily stronger across three observing epochs spanning about two point two years in the quasar's own frame. Such speed challenges models, which must either accelerate gas to that pace while keeping its ions intact, or form the ions after acceleration.
arxiv-2606-06426:
Eugénie Terreaux and co-authors tackle signal counting in messy noise in this 2026 arXiv paper on statistical signal processing. Many sensors must decide how many sources hide in their data: radar targets, brain signals, spectral bands. The noise here is large dimensional, correlated, and non Gaussian, modeled as complex elliptically symmetric, a family allowing heavy tails. Classic criteria like AIC break down badly in that regime.

Their two stage framework first whitens the noise using a robust scatter estimate that respects its Toeplitz structure, then reads the signal count from eigenvalues using random matrix theory thresholds. They prove the estimators are consistent and derive explicit bounds separating signal from noise eigenvalues. Three whitening variants are offered, from plain covariance to distribution free Tyler estimation. Tests on synthetic data, hyperspectral images, EEG recordings, and financial series showed significant gains over AIC and unwhitened methods.
arxiv-2606-06526:
Sherin Muckatira and co-authors capture mathematics as it is actually made, collaboratively, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Benchmarks test whether models can solve finished problems, but real research advances through forum threads: partial attempts, spotted errors, repairs, and slow synthesis into a proof. CrowdMath draws on the MIT PRIMES and Art of Problem Solving program of the same name, whose discussions have produced published results.

The dataset holds one hundred sixty four expert annotated progress chains from 2016 to 2025. Each traces a thread from open problem to completed proof. Posts are labeled by role: partial progress, error, error identification, completion, and more. Six frontier models were benchmarked. They predicted the next post with eighty three to eighty eight percent accuracy, following the local flow well. But judging what a post contributes defeated them. The best reached only zero point four two macro F1 on role classification.
arxiv-2606-06626:
Exotic quantum phases are usually built by adding gain, loss, or contact with an environment. Stefan Dordevic and Vladimir Juricic show a stranger route in this 2026 arXiv paper. Start with an ordinary Hermitian lattice, one with no gain or loss. Then look at only a slice of it. The slice alone can behave as a non-Hermitian system with rich topology.

The trick works when the discarded part hides a zero mode, a state stuck at zero energy, that couples to the slice. In their exact example, a square lattice with an embedded zigzag strip, even sectors behave conventionally. Odd sectors take the resonant route: their complex energy bands braid around each other, crossing at exceptional points, and a complex Berry phase becomes the quantized marker of each phase. An electrical circuit version is also outlined, where transmission dips should reveal the transitions in the lab.
arxiv-2606-06926:
Finding the best moments in a two hour match is nothing like clipping a short video. Lee, Ki, Kang, and Kim build the first benchmark for that job in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their SVHighlights collection pairs full sports broadcasts with official highlight reels. That pairing generates labels cheaply, without hand scoring every clip.

The set holds three hundred twenty videos across many sports. Total footage runs past six hundred forty hours. Models trained on short clips fail on such long material. They also lack the context to judge what matters. The team's baseline, TF-SELECTOR, needs no training. It scores segments using vision, text, and audio together. Transcripts proved especially valuable in the ablations. The baseline beat current state of the art methods on the main measures. The authors hope the benchmark sparks work on long form video understanding.
arxiv-2606-07026:
Drones at low altitude need links that survive buildings, turns, and blocked paths. Celebi and co-authors steer those links with a smart wall in this 2026 arXiv paper. The wall is a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a panel that reflects signals with tunable phase shifts. Tuning every element for a moving drone is normally expensive.

Their stripe based method exploits a pattern in the surface's structure. Neighboring elements follow a phase gradient, which shrinks the search space sharply. Updates stay cheap even as the drone moves in three dimensions. The same reflections double as a passive sensor for tracking the drone. Two tracking schemes, Kalman aided and extremum seeking, handle smooth and jittery motion. Simulations beat conventional benchmarks on speed and efficiency. Signal quality stayed high despite phase errors and noise. Outdoor tests with a real prototype on a campus confirmed the idea works outside the lab.
arxiv-2606-07126:
How many triples can a hypergraph hold before a four cycle is forced to appear? Salia and Tompkins sharpen the answer in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Berge cycle links distinct vertices through distinct hyperedges, each edge containing consecutive vertices. The extremal number counts the most edges possible while avoiding the pattern.

For three uniform hypergraphs avoiding a Berge four cycle, the known ceiling had a specific leading constant. The authors lower it. Their bound allows at most n to the three halves divided by two plus root two edges, plus a linear error term. That improves the previous best constant, one over root ten. The graph version of the problem is classical, settled asymptotically by finite geometry constructions. Hypergraph versions resist the same methods, so each constant shaved off is hard won. The note is short, technical, and aimed at extremal combinatorics specialists.
arxiv-2606-07326:
Xia and co-authors present AnchorWorld, a system for simulating an interactive world seen through an agent's own eyes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Egocentric world models generate first-person video that responds to the user's actions, useful for training robots and embodied AI. Two weaknesses persist: body parts outside the camera view are hard to model, and users cannot easily customize how the world evolves. AnchorWorld attacks both using 3D human motion as the main control signal.

Extra views from outside the body teach the model where the full body sits in the scene, improving spatial grounding. For customization, users designate anchor views in a shared coordinate system and describe how each local scene should change over time. Experiments showed AnchorWorld beating leading baselines on their simulation benchmarks. Ablations, which remove one component at a time, confirmed both the external-view supervision and the anchor mechanism contributed to the gains.
arxiv-2606-07626:
Darshan, Rajesh, and Kumari build a LiDAR perception system for Indian urban traffic, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Autonomous driving detectors are developed for forward fields of view in orderly traffic, leaving their behavior under panoramic sensing unclear. Unstructured traffic adds occlusion, irregular motion, and mixed road users from trucks to cyclists. Their framework processes the panoramic point cloud sector by sector around the azimuth and extracts features with rotation-equivariant convolutions, so detections do not depend on which direction an object faces.

Evaluation used a dataset from an Ouster sensor collected across Indian city conditions. Detection stayed stable across classes, strongest for large vehicles: cars scored highest in their precision pairings, followed by buses and trucks. Pedestrians scored lowest, with cyclists and motorcyclists trailing, reflecting how much harder variable road users are in dense scenes. The authors present sector-wise panoramic scanning as a recipe for surround perception.
arxiv-2606-07826:
Chilla re-examines the EPR argument and draws a verdict about what it proves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The 1935 Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen argument claimed quantum mechanics must be incomplete. Chilla starts from von Neumann's formalism and adds Booleanity, requiring accounts to fit yes-no logic so results can be shared.

Under that constraint, he argues, classicality is already embedded inside the formalism. It need not wait for Planck's constant to shrink to zero. Applying the EPR criterion with locality and measurement independence reduces quantum mechanics to a classical model he calls Hilbert-space classical mechanics. On this reading, EPR exposes the classical boundaries of its own premises, not a gap in quantum theory. Chilla builds a quantum ontology on a split between the watching environment and the observed object. He also argues objective description should be a sufficient, not necessary, mark of physical reality, easing the Bohr-Einstein standoff.
arxiv-2606-08026:
L. Fortunato, A. Vitturi, and G. Singh propose a compact naming scheme for exotic atomic nuclei, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nuclear physics keeps discovering species with strange properties. Halo nuclei carry a diffuse outer cloud. Borromean nuclei fall apart if any one of three parts is removed. Clusterised nuclei are built from sub-units like alpha particles. No universal shorthand labels which traits a nucleus has.

Their ABC scheme names the three flagship traits: A for halo, B for Borromean structure, C for clusterisation. The definitions are categorical and informative. They extend easily to further letters as new features need labels. They limit the first chart to light isotopes, atomic number at most ten, where most such features appear. The proposal is deliberately modest, a first reasoned attempt at a shared vocabulary, offered so that catalogues of exotic nuclei can state a species' character at a glance.
arxiv-2606-08326:
Radicchi asks whether a future quantum internet could work at enormous scale, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Small quantum networks now exist, but communication reliability results covered only special layouts such as regular lattices, and practical protocols existed only for small networks. Radicchi takes a classical approach: an arbitrary quantum network is represented as an ordinary graph, and network theory methods assess whether communication across it is viable. On that basis he devises a family of quantum communication protocols for networks of arbitrary topology.

The protocols are designed for networks with as many as hundreds of millions of nodes. Systematic analysis on both real and synthetic graphs shows the protocols remain sustainable on heterogeneous networks, whose connections are unevenly spread. For random scale-free graphs, where a few hubs hold many links, Radicchi analytically proves that viable communication persists under stated conditions. The work removes topology restrictions that limited earlier theory.
arxiv-2606-08726:
Paudel, Jha, and Parakh test whether splitting a secret across sound and picture hides it better, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Steganography hides information inside ordinary media so the very existence of communication is concealed. Audiovisual media offer two streams, so a payload can be split across audio and video. The authors evaluate whether such split-payload hiding evades steganalysis, the detection science.

They create audiovisual samples with the hidden message divided between the audio and video tracks and test how well different detectors identify them. Single-mode detectors perform close to random guessing, demonstrating the benefit of splitting. A multimodal model initially appears more effective, but further checks show its improvement comes mostly from the video stream rather than genuinely fusing both modes. That caveat matters for defenders: a supposedly multimodal detector may be a unimodal one in disguise.
arxiv-2606-08826:
Lagman, Naval, and Reyes compare two deep learning architectures for sorting galaxies by shape, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Galaxy morphology, a galaxy's visual form, is basic astronomy data, and upcoming surveys will produce more images than people can classify. The team trained two convolutional neural networks, models that scan images for patterns, on the Galaxy10 DECals dataset of 17,736 labeled galaxy images. They rebalanced the ten classes and enlarged the set with spatial augmentation, then compared ResNet101 against InceptionV4.

Both networks reached about ninety percent accuracy, matching published results. ResNet101 came out ahead, with an overall accuracy of 89.5 percent and above seventy-five percent in every category. It trained more slowly per round, by about twenty percent, yet reached its best validation score sooner. With early stopping it finished in 86 minutes against 113 for its rival. Either architecture, they conclude, could anchor classification pipelines for coming surveys.
arxiv-2606-08926:
Moon and Ko demonstrate PROBE Web, a tool for judging knowledge graph completion models from more than one angle, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A knowledge graph stores facts as linked entities, and completion models predict missing links. Standard scorecards rank predictions with measures like mean reciprocal rank, but users disagree about what good means.
