A drug discovery team may prize confident accuracy, while others care that a model is not fooled by popular entities.

PROBE Web lets users retune the evaluation itself along two perspectives: predictive sharpness and robustness to popularity bias. Through an interface, they can run the standard toolkit, switch to perspective-aware scoring, inspect case studies of single predictions, and explore the landscape across models. The system is a demonstration, not a new model. By exposing strengths and weaknesses under different definitions of quality, it helps practitioners choose a model fitting their objective instead of a leaderboard's.
arxiv-2606-09026:
Pendharkar tests whether the shape of a half-finished solution betrays whether the solver will finish, in this 2026 arXiv paper. ARC-AGI tasks ask solvers to infer a grid transformation from a few examples. Symbolic solvers search, leaving intermediate grids behind. Pendharkar measured descriptors such as object counts and color entropy, halfway through. Across 44,800 runs, two solver architectures, and 400 tasks, the descriptors separated successes from failures.

One complexity descriptor carried the signal. Mid-run features discriminated outcomes, reaching 0.885 in area under the curve. A feature frozen on one solver predicted the other's success at 0.747 to 0.762. On pre-registered held-out tasks it reached 0.765 in the same metric. The signal was unexplained by solver capacity or score trend. Early stopping at the halfway point saved 33.6 percent of beam-search compute while keeping 98.9 percent of solutions. It exposed a coverage flaw: on 229 tasks the transformation library produced no valid first move.
arxiv-2606-09226:
Kaneko tests whether physics-based simulation fed with real observations could have predicted a major solar flare, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Solar flares threaten satellites, astronauts, and power grids, but forecasting them remains unreliable. He targets the X1.6 flare in active region NOAA AR 13663, erupted at 02:22 UT on 3 May 2024. His data-driven simulations drive the corona with the photospheric velocity field from magnetograms.

It reproduced the rapid energy-density rise at the flare's actual time and place. It revealed a two-step trigger: tether-cutting reconnection enabled a later breakout reconnection. When boundary input froze more than 1 hour before onset, the flare did not occur in simulation. Extrapolating the final observed field forward extended the lead time beyond 1 hour, flare reproduced. Exact prediction of flare magnitude remains open. The result sketches a working path: keep the driving field alive, and hour-ahead warnings gain a physical basis.
arxiv-2606-09526:
Stefano Catozi, Ugo Dal Lago, and Taro Sekiyama build a type system for a calculus where programs can raise and catch effects in this 2026 arXiv paper. The calculus is a lambda calculus, the spare math of functions, extended with algebraic effects and handlers. Handlers let a program pause on an effect, like a read or a throw, and resume with a rule. Intersection types sort terms by many traits at once.

Their system is behavioural: types track how a run unfolds. It keeps the classic wins of its kind, subject reduction and expansion. In effect, it marks out just the terms whose runs end. That mark turns reachability questions into type inference ones. A simpler type layer falls out of the main system. That layer is sound and, unlike a close rival, keeps its model-checking task decidable.
arxiv-2606-09726:
Hiroto Yanagisawa and his co-authors chart how two kinds of light scale in the odd cosmic specks called little red dots in this 2026 arXiv paper. The dots are compact young galaxies with broad hydrogen lines, seen by the Webb telescope. The team used spectra of thirty-seven of them, from redshifts near three to seven. They weighed broad H-alpha glow against total power, the bolometric brightness.

The two tracked each other tightly, which backs the view that one central engine drives both. Against nearby type 1 active galaxies, the dots shone far brighter in broad H-alpha for the same total power. The boost ran near fortyfold for H-alpha and near tenfold for H-beta. Cloud models with a photoionization code traced the boost to gas that wraps the engine almost fully. A thicker gas column helped as well.
arxiv-2606-10026:
Jeffreson and colleagues present the parent theory paper behind a new star formation recipe for galaxy simulations, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. Current cosmological simulations peg star formation rates empirically. The pressure-regulated, feedback-modulated theory instead links the local rate to a balance between gravity and stellar feedback in interstellar gas.

Implemented in the Arepo moving-mesh code, the model comes in two forms. A volumetric version serves simulations that resolve a galaxy's gas disc height. An integrated version reconstructs mid-plane conditions when they cannot be resolved. Tests on isolated Milky Way-like discs across a wide resolution range show shorter gas depletion times than the IllustrisTNG prescription, especially at high pressure and density. At high resolution both versions agree closely with TIGRESS, and the integrated version stays robust at every resolution tested.
arxiv-2606-10126:
Islam studies how to make personalized persuasive text fairer across demographic groups, in a 2026 arXiv paper on language model alignment. She frames fairness mitigation as a constrained multi-objective problem: cut demographic gaps while keeping texts personal and faithful. Her Pareto-guided teacher method builds revised drafts, screens them for feasibility, picks along a Pareto frontier, and can fine-tune with preference tuning.

Evaluation covers climate change and vaccine persuasion tasks on a demographic grid with matched gender and age pairs. A five-audit suite measures persuasion bias, formality gaps, emotional framing gaps, word association gaps, and personal touch. No single plan won on all goals: methods sat in varied regions of the fairness frontier, some cutting gaps more and others keeping texts more personal. Effects also carried over unevenly across domains and model families, favoring multi-audit model choice over single-metric tuning.
arxiv-2606-10526:
Moore and Winter work out the structure of a key quantity in hot nuclear matter in this 2026 arXiv paper in theoretical physics. The quantity is the two-point correlation function of the energy-momentum tensor, which encodes how energy and momentum fluctuations relate in the quark-gluon plasma. From such correlators, lattice calculations extract transport coefficients like shear and bulk viscosity.

The authors decompose the correlator into basic tensor structures that symmetry allows. Energy-momentum conservation then yields rules linking the component functions. The upshot is that the whole correlator can be represented by a smaller set of spectral functions, cutting redundant information. They give a recipe for applying this to lattice data, showing which component determines which transport coefficient.
arxiv-2606-10726:
Tapolcai and colleagues examine how Hungary judges its computer scientists in this 2026 arXiv paper on research evaluation. In computer science, top conferences carry prestige rivalling leading journals. Hungarian scientometrics remains journal-oriented, and this divergence distorts incentives in researcher evaluation. Linking four databases, iCore, DBLP, MTMT, and MTA-ATT, they mapped national papers at CORE A-star and A conferences, tracking their spread and authors' careers.

Two patterns emerge. In theoretical fields, conference publishing became common earlier than in applied fields. In applied fields, successful researchers more often continue abroad or in industry; a share of the top researchers work outside Hungary. The recommendation: count a CORE A-star paper as equal to a top D1 journal paper, and a CORE A paper as equal to a Q1 journal paper. The hosted library text is truncated, so this description follows the official arXiv abstract.
arxiv-2606-11026:
Varga and a large MINDS collaboration report a 2026 arXiv survey of planet-forming disks around T Tauri stars, young sun-like stars. Using mid-infrared Webb spectra, the team measured the silicate dust in twenty-six disks. Silicates, rocky minerals of silicon and oxygen, are the raw material of rocky planets, and their infrared features reveal grain growth and makeup.

A new tool called DustComp separates the spectra into mineral species. Magnesium-rich, iron-poor silicates fit well, with residuals typically within three percent. The average disk's dust is about sixty percent forsterite-type material, thirty percent enstatite-type, and ten percent silica by mass. Crystalline grains form five to twenty-four percent of the mass, averaging fourteen percent, and grains exceed two micrometers. Annealed silica, found firmly in nine disks, tracks stronger carbon dioxide emission, while forsterite-rich disks show stronger water emission, tying dust makeup to gas chemistry.
arxiv-2606-11226:
Padmanabhan presents a fast thermal modeling approach for automotive power electronics in a 2026 arXiv paper, first published as an SAE technical paper. Inverters full of MOSFET switches heat and cool rapidly as loads change, and full fluid dynamics simulation of every variant is slow. Designers need transient temperatures, how heat evolves over time, fast enough for early design iterations.

He develops a model by the Lumped Parameter Linear Superposition method, combining lumped thermal masses with superposition of responses. The case study is an inverter module with six MOSFETs in three phase pairs on a circuit board on a heat sink. Reference simulations in Ansys Icepak cover natural convection, forced convection at constant velocity, and varying flow velocity. Against those references, the new model matched component temperatures with error under five percent across a wide range of cases. It also compared favorably with a linear time-invariant reduced order model.
arxiv-2606-11426:
Stephan proves that Hill functions are exactly the sharpest possible biological response curves in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. Hill functions have long served as empirical fits. Martinez-Corral and co-authors postulated them as the universal Hopfield barrier for sharpness of input-output responses, based on numerics for Hill coefficients four and six. A Hopfield barrier limits how well biological systems process information without spending energy.

Stephan measures sharpness by the supremum of the derivative in semi-log scale. He proves any rational function with real coefficients between matching bounds has sharpness at most n over four. Equality holds if and only if the function is a Hill function with Hill coefficient n. Hill functions are thus the unique maximizers of sharpness, settling the mathematical question behind the barrier claim. The result closes a problem open since Hill introduced the functions in 1910.
arxiv-2606-11926:
Jiajie Jin leads a nineteen-author team building an AI agent that does research autonomously in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scientific progress loops through exploration, experiment and abstraction, and the authors ask whether an agent can run that loop autonomously over long horizons. Their framework, Arbor, separates strategy from execution.

A long-lived coordinator manages global strategy, while short-lived executors test individual ideas in isolated workspaces. The centrepiece is Hypothesis Tree Refinement: a persistent tree linking ideas, artifacts, evidence and distilled lessons, updated as results return. Verified improvements are admitted through a held-out gate. Evaluated on six real research tasks, Arbor achieved the best held-out result on all six. Its average relative gain was more than two and a half times that of two leading coding agents under identical budgets. On the MLE-Bench Lite suite it reached an any-medal rate above eighty-six percent.
arxiv-2606-12126:
Jiawei Niu leads an eleven-author team predicting patient outcomes from microscope slides in this 2026 arXiv paper. Computational pathology usually works one whole-slide image at a time, using multiple instance learning, where a slide is a bag of patches. Real pathologists, though, form conclusions by integrating evidence across all of a patient's slides. Forcing patient-level labels onto slide-level frameworks destabilises training.

Their framework, AGE-MIL, builds a patient-level anchor from the slide representations, capturing global pathological context. The anchor guides retrieval and integration of diagnostically relevant local patches across every slide. Patient risk is then modelled as an evidence accumulation process, which stabilises optimisation under weak supervision. Across six clinically relevant patient-level tasks from two independent cohorts, AGE-MIL consistently outperforms eight state-of-the-art multiple instance learning methods. The authors credit the explicit modelling of patient context for handling sparse diagnostic evidence.
arxiv-2606-12426:
Kotte audits AI labelers for social science and finds their politeness rewriting results, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Researchers increasingly use language models to annotate text, replacing human coders. Alignment training, though, bends labels toward socially desirable answers. Kotte tests three seven-billion-parameter models across six TweetEval tasks under four prompting styles, seventy-two combinations in all.

One model shows leniency bias, under-flagging offensive content with a false benign rate near 0.73 against very few false alarms on the reported cells. The other two overcorrect, over-applying harmful labels; one hits a hate-speech false alarm rate of 0.604 in its cell. All three flatten abortion stance, underestimating opposition by twenty-four to forty points. No prompting fix repairs every model; safety framing can worsen stance distortion. Most dangerously, one model's hate-speech total matches the true rate exactly, through errors canceling by accident. Aggregate validation can certify a broken labeler.
arxiv-2606-12526:
Fujiki and Tasuki find that a three-way entanglement signal after a disturbance is set by global choices, not local physics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study heavy local quenches, abrupt energy injections, in 2D holographic conformal field theories, where gravity in a curved bulk mirrors the quantum theory. Their diagnostic is genuine multi-entropy, a measure of three-party entanglement among intervals.

In the bulk, the measure comes from networks of geodesics. A perturbative analysis shows the first correction from a small-mass quench cancels, at all times. In the back-reacted geometry, a signal survives only through a mismatch: the three-way network picks one winding, while pairwise geodesics pick others. In the sharp quench limit, the signal's time course is fixed kinematically, logarithms of rational functions of time. It does not depend on the excitation's dimension. A boundary calculation with heavy-light vacuum blocks reproduces the formula.
arxiv-2606-12726:
Axline and colleagues demonstrate the first microwave-to-optical transducers made from thin-film lithium tantalate, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transduction converts quantum signals between microwave photons, used by superconducting qubits, and optical photons, which travel through fibre networks. The standard material, lithium niobate, suffers from bias drift that forces recalibration.

Lithium tantalate offers a comparable electro-optic response, meaning an electric field changes its refractive index, with better bias stability and power handling. The team fabricated superconducting microwave resonators coupled to optical resonators using wafer-scale lithography, producing hundreds of devices per wafer. Across 6 devices they show bidirectional conversion between C-band optical photons and microwave photons at 4.9 to 5.5 gigahertz, with single-photon coupling rates near 1 kilohertz, matching theory. The devices ran continuously for multiple days under a bias with minimal feedback. Added noise stayed below 1 photon for 100-microsecond pump pulses at the best on-chip efficiencies, near 0.04 percent.
arxiv-2606-13126:
Ordonez and Parnell present MiniPIC, a position-independent caching design for the vLLM inference engine, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented and agentic workloads prefill recurring inputs, called spans, such as documents and code files. Standard prefix caching cannot reuse their key-value entries unless requests share prefixes, while current position-independent caching versions require server changes or keep cache state outside the server, incurring transfer overhead.

MiniPIC is built from 2 ingredients. The first is a positional-encoding-free key-value cache, storing unrotated key vectors and applying rotary position embeddings inside attention using per-request positions. The second is 3 cache-reuse primitives that modify hashing behaviour and causal attention structure. On the 2WikiMultihopQA workload, MiniPIC with interleaved scheduling improves prefill throughput by 49 percent over baseline vLLM, reduces cached-span time-to-first-token by up to 2 orders of magnitude, and incurs only 5.7 percent worst-case overhead on uncached spans.
arxiv-2606-13326:
Jacob Halpern and colleagues assess a fusion experiment design in this 2026 arXiv paper. The proposal is a university-scale hybrid of a tokamak and a stellarator, the two magnetic confinement concepts for fusion energy. Its magnetic field comes from an axisymmetric array of planar dipole coils made with high-temperature superconductor. Because the coil array has few geometric degrees of freedom, the team optimises coil currents in a single stage. Starting from two-stage solutions, they obtain equilibria and coil sets agreeing within engineering limits.

Field error and coil current limits set minimum and maximum distances between coils and plasma. Those limits confine the plasma boundary to a fixed axisymmetric envelope. Inside that envelope, rotational transform, volume, coil current, and quasi-symmetry error trade off against one another. Tighter current limits spread the non-axisymmetric shaping more thinly. The study maps these trade-offs for a compact device.
arxiv-2606-13426:
Soen and colleagues speed up diffusion model sampling with a speculative scheme in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speculative decoding accelerates language models by letting a draft model propose tokens that a large model verifies, accepting or rejecting them without changing the output. Adapting the idea to diffusion models is difficult because checking requires sampling from a residual distribution, the leftover difference between draft and target. In discrete spaces that sampling is easy; in such space it is not, and adaptations either pay heavy costs or change the scheme.

The authors implement the sampling method for diffusions. Their advantage is enabling block checks, checking blocks of a draft at once, which raises how often drafts pass compared with step-by-step checking. They formalise and analyse the Free Drafter, a self-drafting heuristic that needs no trained draft model. The result is faster generation with the target model's output preserved.
arxiv-2606-13626:
Dezhi Yu, Lee, and Huang compare three families of models on Bach-style music in this 2026 arXiv paper. Working from a corpus of piano music in MIDI format, they train three families. First come autoregressive long short-term memory networks with attention. Then latent-variable models, including recurrent and vector-quantised variational autoencoders, and generative adversarial networks. Each family embodies a different philosophy: predict the next note, compress music into a latent code, or pit a generator against a critic. The comparison covers sequence modelling, latent codes, and the style coherence.

The autoregressive model produces the most coherent samples. Vector quantisation helps the latent-variable models by mitigating posterior collapse, where the decoder ignores the latent code, and yields more structured outputs than plain recurrent autoencoders. The adversarial approach captures local pitch patterns but is hard to train and generalises less reliably. The study maps each family's failure modes.
arxiv-2606-14526:
Schmid and co-authors find a new route to superradiance in a 2026 arXiv paper on light-matter interaction. Superradiance is a phase where many two-level atoms in a cavity emit light collectively. In the standard Dicke model its threshold is often experimentally out of reach, partly due to light's diamagnetic term.

The team adds a photonic Kerr nonlinearity, meaning the cavity light interacts with itself, inside the Dicke setting. A negative Kerr nonlinearity creates a low-threshold superradiant phase with spin inversion, where atoms sit in their excited state. That phase is unstable in a closed system, but cavity dissipation, controlled leakage of light, stabilizes the lit phase. The authors suggest the mechanism opens paths toward new lasers and bath-engineered quantum phases.
arxiv-2606-14626:
Bhatt and co-authors measure how deeply AI stories adapt to local cultures in a 2026 arXiv paper. A story can be localized shallowly, swapping in local names and places over a generic plot, or holistically, changing plots, values, and themes too. Their method finds the words that distinguish stories across nationalities, removes them, and checks how similar the remaining narratives are.

They generated stories with five models on one hundred twenty-five topics for one hundred ninety-three nationalities. Only a small subset of vocabulary, roughly nine to seventeen percent, accounted for the cross-national variation, and the stripped stories kept repeating shared multi-word sequences, evidence of one culturally agnostic template underneath. Checking the cultural markers themselves, the authors found markers from nineteen countries, mostly in the Global South, were offensive on average.
arxiv-2606-14826:
Salaris, Cassisi, and Bedin quantify a systematic error in star cluster ages in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clusters are dated from their white dwarf cooling sequences, the fading tracks of stellar remnants, but the conversion needs an initial-final mass relation linking a star's birth mass to its remnant mass. Different published relations could shift the inferred ages.

Using recent semi-empirical relations, the team computed theoretical luminosity functions with realistic errors for representative clusters at old, intermediate, and young ages. For old globular-cluster ages the relation choice shifted ages by at most about zero point six billion years, less at intermediate ages, and negligibly for young clusters. Ignoring the predicted metallicity dependence for old metal-poor clusters could underestimate ages by up to about zero point eight billion years, a systematic uncertainty the authors say belongs in every error budget.
arxiv-2606-14926:
Muhammad Ali, Omar Alsuwaidi, and Salman Khan rework a basic step inside image networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Convolutional networks shrink feature maps layer by layer. That shrinking step is called pooling. It builds robustness to small shifts and cuts computation. But pooling is lossy: the wrong choice discards the very signals later layers need.

Their method, FlexPooling, generalizes average pooling. It learns a weighted average over activations, trained jointly with the rest of the network. Each location's weights adapt to content instead of following a fixed rule. The authors also attach simple auxiliary classifiers inside the network. These small side heads guide early layers during training. The design aims to keep prominent information flowing to deeper layers. It stays simple enough to drop into standard convolutional pipelines.
arxiv-2606-15026:
Hagos and coauthors compare deep learning models for reading emotion from body signals in a 2026 study. Wearable sensors record heart rate, skin conductance, breathing, and temperature as feelings shift. The team tests three sequence models, LSTM, temporal convolutional networks, and Transformers, on the WESAD stress dataset. Signals come from wrist and chest devices, alone and combined.

Transformers score highest when both sensor sites feed the model, while temporal convolutional networks lead on wrist-only input. Ablation runs show the two sites carry complementary information, since early fusion beats either site alone. A late-fusion ensemble averaging all three models reaches the best overall accuracy and macro-F1 score. Amusement proves the hardest emotion to classify, likely because its signals overlap with other states. The authors caution that one laboratory dataset limits real-world claims. They frame the results as guidance for building robust wearable affect systems.
arxiv-2606-15126:
Huang and coauthors show that interactions can switch topological pumping of Rydberg electrons on and off in a 2026 study. Topological pumping moves charge in quantized steps as a system cycles through its parameters. How strong long-range interactions change that picture was unexplored. The team works with correlated Rydberg electrons in a synthetic lattice.

Dipolar exchange interactions shift the topological singularity, the point that sources the quantized transport, in parameter space. A fixed pumping path can therefore enclose the singularity or miss it, depending only on interaction strength. Tuning them alone drives the system through further topological transitions. Quantized transport emerges and then breaks down along the way. The behavior matches an effective Rice-Mele model with interaction-set onsite potentials. Checks on adiabaticity and tolerance to path imperfections support the reading. The authors present the platform as a route to interaction-controlled matter beyond weak-coupling regimes.
arxiv-2606-15226:
Jin and Zhou determine spreading speeds for nonlocal Fisher-KPP equations in a 2026 analysis paper. These equations model an invading population whose members disperse by long jumps, not just local diffusion. The jump kernel here changes with time and may favor one direction over the other. The question is how fast the invasion front advances rightward and leftward. For classical diffusion, that speed is set by the linearized equation at the front. The authors prove the same linear formula governs this harder setting.

Their proof uses comparison arguments, a refined maximum principle, and built sub- and super-solutions. The assumptions are mild: the kernel stays exponentially bounded and has uniform mean values. The result covers periodic and almost periodic time dependence as special cases. It even allows kernels whose support avoids a neighborhood of the origin. Ecologists gain a firm speed prediction for invasions under seasonal, directional dispersal.
arxiv-2606-15426:
Marcavillaca and coauthor develop inexact warped resolvent iterations in a 2026 optimization paper. The target is a structured monotone inclusion, a find-a-zero problem that encodes many convex optimization and saddle-point tasks. Splitting algorithms solve it through resolvents, steps usually assumed exact. Warped versions generalize them with a nonlinear warp, and this paper allows those steps to be computed inexactly, under a relative-error rule tied to the step size.

Geometrically the method reads as relaxed projections onto fresh separating cuts. Under mild assumptions the iterates converge weakly; adding Haugazeau-type steps onto halfspace intersections upgrades this to strong convergence, and a smoothness assumption yields a linear rate. The framework unifies named schemes, including Tseng's forward-backward-forward, Chambolle-Pock, and Condat-Vũ. Tests on synthetic saddle-point problems and CT reconstruction show the savings of tolerating inexact inner solves in large-scale problems.
arxiv-2606-15626:
Kalathoor and Oefelein turn to combustion noise in 2026, studying near-field source dynamics in a supersonic reacting hydrogen-air mixing layer. Bounded flows can lock into strong feedback tones, but open flows show broadband source activity spread across frequencies. Using time-resolved simulation data, they track pressure, heat-release, and dilatation fields to see how the sources organize.

Pressure and heat release prove only weakly coherent, and only inside selected low-frequency bands, with no collapse onto a single dominant mode. Combustion intermittency modulates the pressure response in those bands through burst-driven swings. Information-theoretic measures show pressure fluctuations share more statistical structure with heat release than with dilatation. A source-radiation projection finds a moderate low-frequency angular bias tied to where the heat release sits. The picture is of bounded, broadband source organization, a basis for later radiation calculations.
arxiv-2606-16026:
Hands and colleagues present a pipeline for classifying pathology reports in 2026, built to counter the drop when biomedical NLP models move between registries. A model trained on one registry's reports degrades on another's, because formatting, language, and terminology differ locally. The recipe trains in-domain, from routinely collected local data, with facility-stratified sampling, separate handling of registry-linked reports, and a production-matched holdout.

On a holdout of 418,000 reports, the Kentucky model reaches a false-negative rate of three per thousand. Its false-positive rate stays under ten percent, against the Seattle-trained baseline's ten per thousand and over eighteen percent, with a higher F1 score. A blinded audit of six hundred reports estimates positive prevalence well below the labels' implication, exposing label noise in rare sites. For registries, the operating point keeps missed cases rare while keeping reviewer workload in bounds.
arxiv-2606-16226:
Tabassum and colleagues predict in 2026 the best runtime settings for large parallel chemistry codes before burning supercomputer time. Coupled-cluster calculations scale across thousands of nodes, and run time depends on problem size, machine, and runtime parameters. Choosing settings by trial is expensive. The team builds machine learning predictors from past runs instead.

Two approaches combine gradient boosted regression trees, chosen from a rich suite of candidate models, with active and generative learning. Evaluated on coupled-cluster singles and doubles computations, the models reach a mean absolute percentage error as low as 0.023 with data in full. Accuracy also reaches a coefficient of determination as high as 99.9 percent in those tests. Active learning fights data scarcity: with only 20 to 25 percent of the original dataset, error stays near 0.2 in the reported results. Gradient boosting proves most accurate across the Aurora, Frontier, and Perlmutter machines. Better predictions mean fewer wasted supercomputer runs.
arxiv-2606-16726:
Agronah and Bolker tackle sample size planning for microbiome studies in a 2026 statistics paper. Choosing how many samples to collect is a basic design step. Too many wastes money, subject time and animal lives. Too few, the far more common failure, wastes even more, since real differences go undetected and weak results invite dubious practices like p-hacking.

Differential abundance studies ask which microbial taxa differ between groups, and their power depends on more than effect size alone. The average abundance of each taxon matters just as much, the authors show. Their method computes needed sample size from effect size, mean abundance and target power together. It ships as an R package and was tested against estimates from thirty real microbiome datasets. The sobering result: published studies are usually far smaller than the sizes needed for adequate power. The framework helps researchers plan studies that can actually answer their questions.
arxiv-2606-16826:
Zenan Wu and colleagues introduce ATOM-Bench in a 2026 robotics benchmark paper. General robot manipulation policies are sold as foundation models, but their failures are hard to diagnose. A policy can pass demonstrated tasks while lacking basic motor skills, or own the skills yet fail to recombine them in new orders.

The benchmark splits tabletop manipulation into motor atoms and instruction atoms, the smallest skill and language units. It holds thirty atomic tasks plus twenty-four held-out combined tasks, on both single-arm and dual-arm robots. Three thousand human demonstrations support fine-tuning, and all data are released. New scores separate weak atomic skill from weak composition, so a failure's cause is visible. Across five policies and thousands of physical rollouts, simple instruction grounding is learned well. Fine motor atoms, counting and logical filtering stay hard, and strong atomic scores do not reliably transfer to new combinations.
arxiv-2606-16926:
Csillag and colleagues make functional gradient descent practical in a 2026 optimization paper. Instead of tuning the parameters of a fixed network, this method improves the function itself, step by step in function space. The theory is clean, but true functional gradients are infinite-dimensional and cannot be stored.

Fixed approximations make the method run, at the cost of uncontrolled error. The new algorithm adapts how it represents the gradient as optimization proceeds, and the analysis counts that approximation openly. The result is the first usable version with general guarantees. It converges to a stationary point for smooth losses. Under an added Polyak-Lojasiewicz type condition, it reaches a global minimum, whatever approximations are chosen. Tests cover regression, solving partial differential equations and modern computer vision. Across settings the method beats both fixed-approximation functional descent and neural network baselines in efficiency and accuracy.
arxiv-2606-17126:
Choi, Byun and Lee give singing voice conversion finer expressive control in a 2026 audio machine learning paper. Conversion systems change who a song seems sung by; the harder part is style, especially vibrato, the wavering of pitch. Their earlier system controlled vibrato through the high-frequency pitch contour, but pitch and energy stayed entangled.

VibE-SVC2 separates control of pitch style and timbre style. An energy style converter cleans leftover style information from the energy contour. A zero-shot pitch converter mimics the pitch style of a reference recording. Vibrato rate can now be scaled independently of extent, a control the earlier model lacked. On the timbre side, the system handles varied phonation styles, down to vocal fry. Fry breaks ordinary pitch trackers with its subharmonics, so a correction algorithm refines the contour first. Evaluations show finer, more independent style control than prior methods, with naturalness and identity preserved.
arxiv-2606-17226:
Deakin, Chen, and Che present a 2026 arXiv paper on high-speed optical waveform generation. Coherent links need such waveforms, but standard modulators are lossy by design. They discard light in low-amplitude symbols, and their bandwidth caps symbol rates. The method studied here uses cascaded phase modulation plus dispersion, moving light in time instead.

Past work with these temporal unitary transforms reached only low rates and poor signal quality. It also needed heavy radio-frequency drive power to work. This team generated coherent signals at far higher rates than before. Error-free Nyquist signals were produced up to the highest rate tested, using modest electrical bandwidth. Signal quality fell with rate for practical loop reasons, not basic ones, which integrated platforms could remove.
arxiv-2606-17426:
Lin, Frei, and de la Peña present a 2026 arXiv paper on concentration inequalities for exchangeable data, where observations share a hidden common source instead of being independent. Classic bounds like McDiarmid's assume independence, so they break when items are only exchangeable, as benchmark questions grouped by domain tend to be. By conditioning on the de Finetti directing measure, the authors split any bounded-difference statistic's deviation into a sampling part and a latent mixture part with distinct behaviour.

When the latent part is suitably light-tailed, they prove a bound whose variance proxy adds both parts together in one formula. For zero-sum contrasts, such as a subsample mean minus the full population mean, the mixture term cancels exactly. That gives a tight bound with no mixture term at all, extending recent finite results to the infinite case. Applications quantify uncertainty in composite AI benchmarks such as MMLU.
arxiv-2606-17826:
Seo and colleagues tackle a scoring problem for speech recognition in hospitals outside the English-speaking world, in a 2026 paper. In clinical speech, one term can be written in several valid scripts, and standard scoring counts those variants as errors. That habit makes recognition systems look worse than they are, so the team built a benchmark named MultiClin to judge them more fairly.

Tests across many recognition models show that script-aware scoring gives a fairer picture of quality than single-reference scoring. The team also studied training data and found that mixed script mappings raise uncertainty and slow learning, with a half-and-half mapping giving the worst confusion. Unifying scripts in training gave the best results overall. Their data and code are public, aimed at safer tools for clinical dictation.
arxiv-2606-18126:
Yin proves that a basic question about teams of watchers can have no algorithmic answer, in a 2026 control theory paper. Several local agents observe one finite-state plant and send short symbolic messages to a fusion center, which must decide whether the plant's behavior matches a given specification language. With unlimited alphabets or classic monotone rules like AND and OR, versions of this problem can be decided. Yin asks what happens under tight communication limits.

Even in a stripped-down architecture, where each agent sends a single binary symbol and the center fuses them with exclusive-or, the existence of good local decision maps is undecidable. The proof reduces from the Thue word problem, a classic undecidable question about string rewriting. The same verdict extends to decentralized supervisory control, fault diagnosis, and fault prognosis under finite alphabets, exposing a hard boundary for distributed control design.
arxiv-2606-18226:
Klingborg and colleagues test which levers can stop online political talk from splitting into camps, in a 2026 modeling paper. Their computational model, grounded in psychology, follows opinions through a population whose members hold complex, overlapping identities. Into that world they introduce realistic interventions and watch whether polarization is prevented, or even reversed once entrenched.

Widening or narrowing the Overton window, the range of acceptable opinion, did surprisingly little. Tuning it could even spark the split. Shifting attention toward neglected topics, or raising the cost of breaking shared norms, often prevented splits but struggled to undo them. The strongest lever was amplifying voices of influence who model moderate, calm discourse and hold cross-cutting appeal. The hopeful result comes with a warning the authors stress: surface calm can hide latent extremism underneath.
arxiv-2606-18426:
Seneviratne and colleagues introduce VEGA, a method for training robot navigation policies from first-person video found online, in a 2026 robotics paper. Egocentric videos are plentiful and full of cluttered spaces, but they carry no robot-ready actions, goals, or obstacle-aware paths, so they cannot directly teach a navigation model.

VEGA reconstructs local scene geometry from monocular video, samples navigation goals expressed as text, images, or waypoints, and generates obstacle-aware trajectories through the rebuilt geometry. Those trajectories supervise a flow-matching vision-language-action policy, with geometry used only during training so the deployed robot needs its camera. The team releases a benchmark of a quarter-million scenes paired with millions of goals. On that benchmark VEGA cut collisions by about a third against the strongest baseline, and in real-world trials it improved success rates while reducing collisions and keeping wider clearance from obstacles.
arxiv-2606-18526:
Buono works out how to feed a generalized one-time pad with keys drawn from a quantum key distribution source without breaking its perfect secrecy, in a 2026 cryptography paper. The Mixed-Radix One-Time Pad encodes data in digit systems with mixed bases rather than bits. Its secrecy proof demands keys chosen perfectly uniformly over that mixed-radix space, while quantum sources deliver ordinary binary entropy.

He identifies Horner's method, the nested evaluation familiar from polynomials, and its inverse as the canonical bridge between a binary integer and a mixed-radix key tuple. Naively reducing random bits modulo the key space size biases the keys and voids the secrecy guarantee at any size, he proves. Rejection sampling with inverse Horner decomposition restores uniformity at a bounded expected bit cost. The paper extends the guarantee across many sessions under a key-rolling scheme.
arxiv-2606-18926:
Jurga and colleagues define blanket times in 2026, a new gauge for how fast an orbit in a dynamical system matches its long-run law. Cover times are known already. They gauge how fast an orbit fills the space and gets dense. Blanket times ask a stronger thing. They ask how fast time shares near each place match the true invariant measure.

The study looks at expanding maps on an interval with a finite set of branches. For these maps, the authors bound the mean blanket time in terms of scale and precision. When the invariant measure is smooth with respect to length, blanket and cover times match up to a fixed factor at all small scales. Proofs mix large-deviation bounds for hitting times with a fractal tool that cuts the measure into a finite model.
arxiv-2606-19026:
Evans and colleagues build a hybrid neural model in 2026 to predict errors in a leading high-resolution weather forecast system. Errors in the HRRR model often trace to boundary layer shifts, storms, and terrain-driven flows that change with height. Past work showed recurrent networks could predict such errors from surface data alone. Skill fell, though, during complex vertical change, when surface data miss what is happening aloft in the air column.

The new model joins a recurrent LSTM with a vision transformer that reads profiler data from the New York State Mesonet. It predicts hourly errors for rain, surface wind, and near-surface temperature at single stations. Adding profiler structure improves skill for all three targets over the LSTM alone. Gains are largest at short lead times and in active boundary layer periods. Rain error gains stand out most in the best cases.
arxiv-2606-19626:
Antonio Leitão Filho and four colleagues present TOTEN in 2026, a system that keeps technical quantities intact for AI pipelines. AI tools reasoning over engineering text need numbers, units, and symbols to arrive whole. Standard tokenizers split such entities into arbitrary fragments, and errors then spread downstream.

TOTEN types each text region by a formal ontology of engineering entities instead of statistical splitting. A classification function maps raw text into typed regions, and instantiators emit a self-describing structure. Three outside authorities anchor the typing: Pint for dimensions, Unicode data for typography, and RSLP for Portuguese word forms. Tests span an internal benchmark of 800 cases and four external Brazilian Portuguese corpora. TOTEN keeps every technical entity whole in all contrasts, beating eight rival systems. Number reconstruction reaches 0.775 to 0.904 on outside corpora, against 0.627 to 0.703 for the best rival.
arxiv-2606-19826:
Prashanti Nilayam and three colleagues stress-test mixed-model AI debates with hostile peers in 2026. Multi-model debate promises that diverse peers correct each other's errors. The same channel that carries correction also carries adversarial influence.

Panels mix honest and hostile agents across four model families and three reasoning benchmarks. Tracking focuses on answer revisions: how often agents switch, and whether switches help or harm. An honest unlike peer sharply cuts harmful revision among honest agents. A hostile peer reverses that gain just as sharply. For one Llama defender on hard maths, harmful revision drops from eighty-nine to thirty-five percent with an honest peer. Adding an honest peer beside an existing hostile one cuts losses of right answers from thirty-one to six percent. Diversity thus defends as well as endangers.
arxiv-2606-19926:
Guangyi Liu and nine colleagues build a mobile phone agent that manages its own context over long tasks in 2026. Phone agents fail long jobs by drowning in their own step history. ReAct-style prompting piles records up until key cross-app facts dilute away.

MemGUI-Agent treats context handling as actions chosen by the same policy that taps the screen. Three structured fields hold folded action history, folded screen state, and a recent step record. Critical facts survive while the prompt stays compact. A companion dataset holds nearly three thousand annotated trajectories for training. An eight-billion-parameter model trained on it leads open-data rivals of its size on MemGUI-Bench. It also generalises to the separate MobileWorld benchmark. Proactive housekeeping, not bigger context, is the design lesson.
arxiv-2606-20126:
Peter Šemrl describes the general form of order embeddings between domains of real symmetric matrices. His 2026 paper works with the Loewner order, where one matrix counts as below another when their difference is positive semidefinite. A matrix domain is an open, connected set of such matrices. An order embedding is a map that preserves this order exactly in both directions: the image of one matrix sits below the image of another precisely when the originals do.

Such maps are the natural symmetries of the ordered structure, and classifying them reveals how rigid it is. Šemrl determines the general form these embeddings must take on arbitrary matrix domains, for matrix sizes of two or more. The classification extends classical preserver problems in linear algebra and gives a complete toolkit for recognizing order-preserving transformations.
arxiv-2606-20526:
Saimun Habib, Vaishak Belle, and Fengxiang He give DeepProbLog a counterfactual semantics. Their 2026 paper addresses neurosymbolic systems that combine neural perception with probabilistic logic, where standard inference only correlates. Asking what would have happened under an intervention needs a causal semantics on top.

DeepSWIP materializes fixed-context neural predicates into ordinary ProbLog choices, applies Single World Intervention Programs, and computes them by weighted model counting over one transformed program. Under finite grounding and unique supported models, the method is exact relative to the learned causal model. Experiments on MPI3D check the result against a twin-network construction across 12,000 queries, with a 2.14-fold speedup from avoiding duplication. A traffic experiment shows how sloppy neural probabilities bias plug-in estimates and how a randomized-policy fix removes most of that bias.
arxiv-2606-20626:
Fabio Spagliardi and five colleagues make safety benchmarking cheaper with item response theory. Their 2026 paper notes that safety suites treat all items as equally informative for all models, a bad assumption for adversarial, heterogeneous items. Full evaluation would need on the order of a hundred thousand responses, most carrying little ranking signal.

Item response theory recovers interpretable structure on safety benchmarks, with ability estimates resolving differences among models. Items differ in difficulty and discrimination, so adaptive subsets can rank models with far fewer responses. The analysis points to evaluation that spends its budget on informative items. Safety comparison becomes a measurement problem with known tools, not an endurance test.
arxiv-2606-20826:
Benjamín Grinstein, Carlos Miró, and Pablo Quílez ask in 2026 whether a future solar axion experiment could tell one axion from many. Axions are hypothetical particles proposed to solve problems in particle physics. Many theory extensions predict several axion species. If two axions couple to photons, their combined helioscope signal may mimic one axion with different parameters. A detection alone might not reveal the count.

The team recasts bounds from the CAST experiment and projects reach for IAXO and its upgrade. They map where a signal could appear in two-axion parameter space. Spectral signatures of axion flavor oscillations are analyzed in near-degenerate and hierarchical mass cases. Detector energy resolution decides where two-axion and one-axion stories can be separated. Results extend to systems with many axions. Planning that discrimination now shapes how a discovery would be interpreted later.
arxiv-2606-20926:
Mohsen Moradi, Taejoon Kim, and Rémi Chou propose a learning-based decoder in 2026 for quantum low-density parity-check codes, strong candidates for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Decoding such codes is hard. Short cycles, degeneracy, and poor convergence limit standard belief-propagation decoders. Their method extends a reinforcement learning sequential decoder with list-based search. A learned policy picks which variable node to update next.

At each step, the decoder keeps the ordinary trajectory. It also explores a rival branch. That branch softly biases the updated values toward the second most likely symbol. Local messages are recomputed for that branch. Candidate paths are ranked and pruned by a new cumulative path metric. Numerical results test whether list search plus learned scheduling improves decoding. Better decoders matter because quantum error correction must run fast and accurately for real machines to scale.
arxiv-2606-21126:
Yuren Hao, Xiang Wan, and ChengXiang Zhai argue in 2026 that feedback alignment, a training method for neural networks, is judged by an insufficient pair of measures. The method replaces the backward weights of standard training with fixed random matrices. That promises training that is more plausible in brains and cheaper in hardware. Standard reporting uses task accuracy and cosine similarity to the standard gradient.

Two silent failure modes undermine that pair. In some designs the reference gradient collapses to the numerical floor, making cosine values meaningless. A pooled cosine also masks layer differences, hiding credit pooled at one end of the network. New checks cover scale stability, reference validity, and depth utility. Better tests matter because a method can look aligned on paper while its learning signal is weak in the layers that need it most.
arxiv-2606-21626:
Lorenzo Coccia, Matteo Padovan, and Giuseppe Vallone systematize the hunt for Tsirelson bounds in 2026, the ceilings on how strongly quantum mechanics lets separated parties correlate their measurement outcomes. For qubits the ceilings are well mapped; for high-dimensional systems, tight bounds have been hard to reach. Their method derives bipartite quantum and local bounds from sum-of-squares decompositions in a uniform way.

Applying it, they find new bounds and recover known ones for maximally entangled qubits and qudits. Bell tests now underpin device-independent randomness and cryptography, so certified ceilings are practical tools, not just foundations. One uniform method replaces case-by-case ingenuity, and it extends to higher-dimensional settings where richer correlations may yield stronger guarantees.
arxiv-2606-21726:
S. Akshay, Raghav Goyal, Aditya Neeraje, and Piyush Srivastava study control with an unusual goal in 2026: not where a stochastic system goes, but how concentrated its state distribution stays. Think drug molecules spreading through body compartments, where the measurable quantity is a concentration profile, a probability distribution, not any single molecule's path. Such entropy objectives for Markov decision processes are nonlinear, which makes synthesis hard.

The authors first show even relaxed versions of the problem are complexity-theoretically hard. They then build a sound, and conditionally relatively complete, method to verify and build strategies, merging convex duality with invariant synthesis. Memory and randomization get their own investigation: both can matter for meeting an entropy target. A prototype and small benchmarks show the approach working in practice.
arxiv-2606-21826:
Li and colleagues review dark energy research in the DESI era in 2026. DESI, a large sky survey, measures baryon acoustic oscillations, sound-wave patterns frozen into the distribution of galaxies, to trace how the universe has expanded. Combined with microwave background and supernova data, its results hint that dark energy may change over time rather than stay constant, as the standard model assumes.

The review weighs how strong that hint really is, showing it depends on the chosen parametrization and on which datasets are combined. Residual measurement errors and tensions between datasets could also mimic the signal. Several rival explanations can produce the same expansion history, including interacting dark energy, gravity coupled in non-minimal ways, and non-standard dark matter. Each option carries different consequences for known tensions over the expansion rate and the clumpiness of matter.
arxiv-2606-21926:
Huang and colleagues present A11YRepair in 2026, a system that fixes web accessibility violations rather than merely reporting them. Accessibility ensures people with disabilities can perceive and use web content, and the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines define the rules. Existing repair tools handle one bug at a time, yet one page often carries many related violations needing coordinated edits across files.

A11YRepair, driven by a large language model, first clusters violations that require coordinated edits, then splits each cluster by root cause so patches stay focused and consistent. Accessibility guideline knowledge guides both fault localization and patch writing. The team also built A11YBench, a benchmark of sixty real-world web projects holding 8,886 violations. A11YRepair resolved 76.8 percent of violations at an average cost of about two cents per issue, beating strong baselines. Some patches were merged into open-source projects of major technology firms.
arxiv-2606-22026:
Cabrera Martin and colleagues address, in 2026, the problem of adapting machine learning models when data distributions drift over time. Many tabular benchmarks lack any time structure. Drift methods therefore cannot be tested on them in a reproducible way. The authors build a simulation framework instead. It turns static datasets into controlled evolving streams, using structured perturbations inside clusters of the feature space.

Six strategies are compared across five benchmark datasets and many model families. They range from static learning to sliding-window and ADWIN-based retraining, global or cluster-local. Sliding-window retraining often scored best. But it paid heavily in computation and labelling. Global ADWIN updated less often while staying competitive. The proposed cluster-local method retrains only clusters where drift is detected. It cut retraining effort by up to seventy-five percent. Performance stayed close to the continuously adaptive baselines in both settings.
arxiv-2606-22126:
Qiu and colleagues argue, in 2026, that language models gain little from time series because current tasks reduce the data to curve fitting. Real temporal decisions instead need semantic context and stepwise reasoning. Their response is TSCognition, a multimodal benchmark built from fifteen public sources with about forty-one thousand question-answer samples.

The benchmark spans five cognitive tasks: decoding, grounding, inferring, extrapolating, and acting. Alongside it, the authors propose TSAlign, a framework that encodes series into compact patch-level representations. These are aligned with semantic directions in the model's embedding space through gated residual injection and multivariate fusion. In experiments TSAlign beats large language model, vision-language model, and time series question-answering baselines. It wins on both TSCognition and the public TimerBed benchmark, while substantially reducing computational cost.
arxiv-2606-22226:
Yachbes and Tardos quantify, in 2026, how much useful information a human can still receive from a misaligned AI agent, using Bayesian persuasion. In their model the AI observes the world state, a bit string, while the human knows only a prior and acts after seeing the agent's signal. The sender wants as many bits as possible guessed as one; the receiver wants to guess correctly.

They compare the receiver's utility from the prior alone against the best utility among signaling schemes that are optimal for the sender. The ratio is at most three halves for any prior. For priors close to the independent product prior, the sender-optimal scheme adds only a small multiple of the distance and the string length. A six-bit example attains a ratio of thirty-nine thirty-firsts, above five quarters. No universal five-quarters bound is therefore possible.
arxiv-2606-22426:
Yingdu Dong, Wenwen Jian, and Xiaoping Yuan study a Schrödinger operator with a random potential in this 2026 mathematics paper. The setting is one dimension on a fixed interval, with Dirichlet boundary conditions that pin the wavefunction to zero at both ends. The potential is Gaussian white noise, the standard model of jagged randomness, at a set strength.

The authors prove a high-energy expansion for the eigenvalues, the operator's energy levels. The leading term follows the clean interval pattern, while the next term is an integral over Brownian motion that records the noise's effect. A small remainder fades as the level index grows. As a consequence, almost surely all large levels are positive. They also derive formulas for the eigenfunctions, whose shapes stay close to sine waves. The work is theoretical, with no data involved. The proofs use Prüfer coordinates, Volterra expansions, and a Borel-Cantelli argument.
arxiv-2606-22526:
Paweł Szabłowski computes a conditional expectation involving Hermite polynomials in this 2026 mathematics paper. Hermite polynomials are a classical family tuned to the Gaussian distribution. Szabłowski asks for the expected value of a product of Hermite polynomials in some variables, given the value of one other variable.

The answer is a polynomial in the observed value, and its degree is exactly the sum of the indices of the polynomials in the product. The formula Szabłowski derives is iterative in the dimension, so each new variable builds on the previous case. Auxiliary formulas about the polynomials support the calculation. The work also revisits the Kibble-Slepian formula, which expands a multivariate normal density as a series of Hermite polynomials, and studies its coefficients. For dimensions two and three, the machinery yields exact, simple forms of those expansions, recasting known results from a fresh perspective.
arxiv-2606-22626:
Léo Roche and eight colleagues, including Stephan Reitzenstein, build an integrated quantum light source in this 2026 photonics paper. Their device couples an electrically driven micropillar laser to a ridge waveguide on one chip. Both parts contain indium gallium arsenide quantum dots, tiny islands that can emit single photons.

The laser uses a whispering-gallery mode, light circulating around the pillar's rim, and its glow leaks sideways into the waveguide. The team measured how lasing depends on the gap between pillar and waveguide. Guided light then travels to a second micropillar at the waveguide's end and excites its quantum dots optically. Under continuous excitation those dots emitted single photons with a very low multi-photon rate, the key purity test for such sources. Their colour could be tuned electrically through the quantum confined Stark effect. The authors present this as a step toward compact deterministic single-photon sources.
arxiv-2606-22826:
Devleena Das and five colleagues shrink the cost of testing language models in this 2026 paper. Every new model variant must be rerun on large benchmarks, which can take tens of hours on edge hardware. Existing subset methods cut that cost but need large calibration pools or extra learned predictors.

Their method, MINCE, uses Monte Carlo simulation on per-item logs from just a few calibration models. It finds the smallest subset size that keeps accuracy drift bounded, then fixes one randomly sampled subset of that size, with no prediction layer. MINCE cut one benchmark by fifty-four percent, another by eighty-nine percent, and a math benchmark by seventy percent. Maximum drift stayed under about two and a half points on full-precision models. Evaluation ran several times faster on graphics processors, and drift was far lower than a rival subset method using many more calibration models.
arxiv-2606-23226:
Zixu Li and colleagues recover pulse signals from facial videos under messy conditions in a 2026 paper. Remote photoplethysmography estimates the pulse from subtle color changes in face video, with no contact sensor needed. Changing light, expressions, and head movement swamp the faint pulse signal in real settings. Most methods model the signal as one unified waveform, coupling its parts together during reconstruction. Strong disturbance components then drown the weak pulse components. Their framework, PhysFlow, splits the work by frequency and by signal part.

Li and colleagues decompose the true pulse signal into trend and amplitude components, each serving as its own training target. Two learned velocity fields reconstruct the parts separately, cutting the interference between them. A rectified flow formulation rebuilds the waveform efficiently in a few equation-solving steps. The design aims for stable, reliable pulse readings where earlier methods wobble.
arxiv-2606-23426:
Mehdi Golafshan explains a counting result about words in a 2026 combinatorics paper. Two binary words are called 2-binomially equivalent when they share the same short subsequences in the same counts. Rigo and Salimov proved in 2015 that the number of classes of words of a given length is the nth cake number, a known counting sequence. Their proof gave no picture of why the count comes out that way. Golafshan builds one: a set of planes in three-dimensional space whose chambers match the classes one to one.

Golafshan shows the planes form the three-dimensional member of an endless family. In dimensions one, two, and three, the classes give back abelian equivalence, a natural middle equivalence, and binary 2-binomial equivalence itself. Higher dimensions give finer classes. The size of each class comes out of Gaussian binomial coefficients, which yields the full spread of class sizes.
arxiv-2606-23526:
Isidore Mohr and Claire Wang report on Composition, a community event series joining art, mathematics, and code, in a 2026 experience report. Composition is a free, twice-yearly meetup in the northeastern United States. Anyone may present work that connects art with mathematics or code and shows technical depth. Work in progress is welcome. Two events had run at the time of writing: a first edition in Brooklyn, New York in December 2025, and a second in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania in May 2026. The report covers all facets of running the series as a case study for community builders.

Mohr and Wang describe the event's structure and their approach to selecting speakers through an open submission process. They detail outreach for submissions and promotion, and the community response the series received. The paper is presented as a reference point for others building communities around art, mathematics, and code.
arxiv-2606-23926:
Singha and colleagues squeeze a relativistic double neutron star's orbit for a new test of general relativity, detecting the deformation of the orbit itself, in a 2026 paper on pulsar astronomy. PSR J1757-1854 spins every twenty one and a half milliseconds and orbits its companion every four point four hours on an eccentric path. Few systems decay faster under gravitational wave emission. The team combines archival timing with new, more sensitive MeerKAT observations, stretching the baseline to nine years.

The sharper timing improves the known relativistic parameters by a factor of two or more. It also yields the first detection here of the relativistic angular deformation of the orbit, making this only the third double neutron star with that measurement. The deformation rules out two of four possible spin orbit geometries, consistent with general relativity.
arxiv-2606-24026:
Khan and colleagues ask whether language model agents can explain what the inner parts of a neural network actually do. Mechanistic interpretability, the effort to reverse-engineer a model's internal circuits, can now locate those circuits automatically, but explaining each part still takes slow manual work. Their benchmark, released in 2026, gathers 84 partly artificial transformer circuits with 163 notes labelling what individual components do.

Alongside the benchmark, Khan's group builds HyVE, an agent that loops through watching a component, guessing its role, and testing that guess with causal checks. Tested across four language model backbones, the agent recovers useful explanations, though no single backbone wins everywhere. Failures tend to come late, from incomplete test plans or code errors. A case study on arithmetic inside Llama-3-8B shows the method also works on a normally trained model.
arxiv-2606-24926:
Tong Zhu and Zhigang Zheng show that a simple swarm of active particles can realise a topological principle from non Hermitian physics. Their model blends two classics: Vicsek flocking, where particles align headings, and Kuramoto synchronisation, where phases lock together. A phase lag in the local alignment frustrates the flock, driving bulk instabilities at a finite wavelength. Under collision boundaries, a robust one way flow appears along the edge.

A nonlinear saturation ansatz organises the explanation. The linearised hydrodynamics selects the unstable wavelength and the spectral topology. Particle dynamics then saturates the chosen mode. The continuum spectrum supports Chern numbers of plus and minus two, fixed by the dispersion matrix's spin structure. Strip spectral flow predicts chiral edge propagation from those numbers. Particle simulations agree in the nontrivial sectors. Zhu and Zheng present the model as a minimal active matter home for Chern bulk boundary physics.
arxiv-2606-25026:
Run-Yu Meng and Xiao-Bo Dong present WaveDM.jl, an open source Julia package for simulating wave dark matter on galaxy scales. Wave dark matter treats the dark matter as a wave obeying the Schrödinger Poisson equation. The package solves that equation with a pseudo spectral Fourier method. Its spectral solver is tightly integrated with the N body gravity solvers, so wave dark matter and ordinary baryonic matter evolve together in one simulation.

A multi level parallelisation framework unifies shared memory, distributed memory, and GPU processing. The same workflow scales from a single machine to multi node clusters without major code changes. A toolbox supports practical work: trajectory lookback, flexible initial condition generators, tidal force calculations, and real time visualisation. Because the core is a general nonlinear Schrödinger solver, the same code serves nonlinear optics and cold atom physics. Meng and Dong release it publicly.
arxiv-2606-25226:
Designing tiny structures that steer light, such as flat lenses, usually means running huge numbers of costly simulations. Shuo Huang and colleagues describe a 2026 approach called a dimension expansion network, which first expands a short list of design goals into a rich, structured code. That code then guides a neural network that designs the structure. Training runs directly through physics simulations, so no giant library of earlier designs is needed beforehand.

On metalens tests, the method matched the focusing strength of a standard optimisation technique while using about half as many simulations. It also handled anywhere from tens to thousands of target focal spots inside one region. On a light splitter test, just twenty one training targets were enough to reproduce any requested split of power between two outputs.
arxiv-2606-25326:
A fast moving detector in curved spacetime feels a warm bath where empty space should be. This is the Unruh and Hawking effect. Xiang Hao and colleagues use that warmth to charge a quantum battery in 2026. Their model links a fast moving detector to a massless field across de Sitter and anti de Sitter spacetimes. The useful stored energy is called ergotropy, the most work that can be drawn back out.

The team tracks how that stored energy settles under changed heat, boundary rules, and numbers of space dimensions. The end value rested only on speed up and spacetime curvature, one shared sign of global thermality for both spacetimes. The path there differed though. Hard speeding in de Sitter space gave strong swings, while in anti de Sitter space the boundary choice could raise storage. Extra dimensions gave a modest early boost and faster settling.
arxiv-2606-25826:
Does a network remember its past because of how it is wired, or because of how strongly its links pull? Elkaïoum Moutuou and Habib Benali test that question in 2026 across thirty four real networks, from gene regulation and neural circuits to ecology, society, and transport. A thermodynamic account of information flow measures how deeply earlier interactions stay woven into present behaviour. Shuffle the link strengths while keeping the wiring fixed, and the memory shallows. Real weights organise memory at greater depth than random ones, in every domain studied.

The memory patterns collapsed onto just four recurrent dynamical organisations, a strikingly low dimensional order. Targeted null models then separated the ingredients. Weight geometry governs memory depth. Middle scale structure shapes how memory spreads across scales. Directionality tunes how sensitive the cascade is to damage. The comparison doubles as a test for whether a network's weights carry genuine functional meaning.
arxiv-2606-26026:
Pavan Tanna, Simon Lock, Amy Bonsor, Simon Hodgkin, and Cathie Clarke ask whether planet-forming collisions can be caught in the act. Giant impacts between planet-sized bodies shape how planets and moons form. New surveys like Gaia and the Rubin Observatory's LSST scan the sky repeatedly. A fresh impact remnant should flash and then fade, which a survey could spot.

Hydrodynamic simulations supply the light curves. The team crashes Earth-composition planets with total masses from a fifth to four times Earth's. Remnants start between a tiny fraction and a tenth of the Sun's brightness. Fading runs roughly exponentially, over days to years depending on the case. Folding in impact rates gives a forecast. Gaia's full data release might catch up to fourteen such events, possibly none. LSST should find a comparable haul, constraining how often giant impacts occur.
arxiv-2606-26226:
Vaibhav Sharma and Sumiran Pujari turn a quantum spin liquid into a new kind of error-correcting code. The toric code is the canonical topological code, built from commuting checks. Their starting models modify the toric code in space until the stabilizer property breaks. In its place sits a large family of anticommuting local conserved quantities. The resulting ground-state degeneracy is extensive, and it becomes the code's subsystem degrees of freedom.

Topological order survives the conversion. The code inherits the spin liquid's many-body topology, making it a topological subsystem code. Square and kagome lattice versions are built in detail. Their checks measure four-body and three-body operators respectively. One quirk sets these codes apart: many local gauge qubits sit untouched by the checks, beyond the logical qubits themselves. The construction templates a whole category of codes for varied lattices and hardware.
arxiv-2606-26326:
Johannes Jahan and a large team present Calliope, the newest MUSES calculation engine release, for the matter created in heavy-ion collisions. Knowing that matter's equation of state, how pressure depends on temperature and density, is essential at every collision energy.

Calliope's modules span equations of state from lattice QCD calculations to models with or without a critical point, in up to four dimensions of chemical potentials. Workflows merge two equations of state consistently and invert them into inputs for fluid simulations. The team demonstrates a full viscous hydrodynamic run using an extended equation of state with a movable critical point.
arxiv-2606-26626:
Samangi Wadinambiarachchi, Jenny Waycott, and Greg Wadley explore how sketching changes AI-supported design work. Most creativity tools take text prompts and return polished, solution-shaped outputs. Designers, though, traditionally think by sketching, a reflective process where ideas evolve on paper. The authors built SketchifAI, a prototype that accepts sketches as input. They ask whether rougher input invites deeper reflection.

Design students used the prototype in a within-participants study. Each student tried text prompts, sketches, and sketches with tags. The team measured how well students felt they could express intent, how supported their creativity felt, and their divergent thinking output. Sketching tended to improve fluency, the flow of ideas. Evidence on variety, originality, and quality stayed inconclusive. Paradoxically, students still preferred text prompting strongly. The authors discuss designing tools that restore reflection through sketching.
arxiv-2606-26726:
Shao-Zhen Lin and Jean-François Rupprecht overturn an expectation about elongated cells in tissues. In packed cell sheets, shapes range from roundish to strongly stretched. Standard vertex models link stretching to fluidisation: give cells a stretched target shape and the tissue flows. The authors instead give cells an intrinsic elastic preference for stretched shapes, emerging on its own.

Stretching then rigidifies rather than fluidises. The tissue passes from an ordered round-celled solid to a disordered stretched-celled solid. Both sides of the transition keep a finite yield stress and shear stiffness. Shape and flow are thus decoupled in this setting. The authors caution against reading fluid-like mechanics from elongated cell shapes alone, a common inference in studies of embryos, wounds, and tumours.
arxiv-2606-27326:
Hansen and Wang show that when generative world models hallucinate, the failure is predictable from data coverage. World models render action-controllable futures for planning, yet fluent rollouts can drift from true dynamics. The team hypothesises that drift concentrates where training data barely covered the state-action space. A new dataset supplies hundreds of hours across hundreds of tasks with true actions and live simulators. A mid-size world model trains on it, in a machine learning study published in 2026.

Three hallucination modes appear, tied to distinct pipeline stages: perceptual, action-marginalised, and scene-diverging. Three light signals predict where failure will strike with good accuracy. Coverage-aware sampling closes gaps during training. Online, the same predictors act as curiosity rewards, steering data collection to weak spots. Fine-tuning then adapts the model to new environments, needing as few as fifty real trajectories in the reported recipe.
arxiv-2606-27426:
van Donkelaar, Mayer, and Capelo ask whether a young star cluster's birthplace stamps its spin forever. At high redshift, clusters form two ways in their simulation: inside galactic discs through gravitational instability, and in circumgalactic filaments, a channel they nickname cosmic wallflowers. Stellar kinematics supply rotation speeds and rotational support for both families at redshift seven point six in the MassiveBlackPS run. The families separate cleanly, in an astrophysics study published in 2026.

Disc clusters are strongly rotation-dominated and spin faster. Wallflowers rotate less and span a wide range of rotational support. A subset of slow wallflowers sits surprisingly close to Milky Way globular clusters in the spin-density plane, while disc clusters stay offset. Gas-rich wallflowers prefer the slow regime, marking them as natural proto-globular cluster candidates. Denser, faster wallflowers may instead feed massive black hole seeds. Environment and gas content together set a cluster's fate.
arxiv-2606-27526:
Pairs of dense objects rarely orbit in empty space. Black holes and neutron stars that spiral together sit inside gas, disks, and tidal fields. Lorenz Zwick and four colleagues built a framework in 2026 for these cases. It tracks how surroundings disturb relativistic binaries. Such binaries emit gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, when they merge.

Their method turns each disturbance into a resonant spectral projection. That filter keeps only disturbance parts that can build up over many orbits. Hansen coefficients supply the weights. The result is coupled ordinary differential equations for the orbital elements. The equations run on a coarse time grid. They include radiation reaction, the energy lost to the waves. Zwick's team tested two cases. One was a compact binary in a changing tidal field. The other was an extreme-mass-ratio inspiral in an accretion disk, where a small object circles a huge black hole.
arxiv-2606-27626:
Living systems hold their order through the interplay of their parts, with no central controller. Emmy Blumenthal and Gautam Reddy build a tractable model of this self-organised robustness in 2026. The model is a mean-field one, averaging over many interacting units. Robustness is framed as a search over responses to pushes.

They form a landscape that reshapes itself over time, which the authors call a seascape. Its shape is set self-consistently so the system returns to rest faster. The shared motion follows an optimised Wasserstein gradient flow toward a resting state. When the units can share only a little information, interactions tend to encode the modes that relax slowly and the modes that get pushed most often. Robust shared states come with flatter landscapes at rest. The model also predicts a continuum of in-between reservoir states.
arxiv-2606-28426:
Benjamin J. A. Héry, Lucas Tepper, and Roland R. Netz compare four exact ways to compress a complicated system into one variable's equation of motion. The Mori-Zwanzig formalism guarantees such generalized Langevin equations, each with a systematic force from a potential of mean force, a friction force with memory, and a random force. Exact does not mean identical, and the variants differ in instructive ways.

The memory kernel may or may not depend on the chosen observable, and the potential may or may not absorb the observable's effective kinetic energy.
