Héry and colleagues show that including the kinetic energy pays off when the observable's velocity obeys Wick's theorem, a Gaussian factorization rule. The equation then reproduces the correct joint distribution of position and velocity even before friction and noise contribute anything.
arxiv-2606-28526:
Doria Bonzi, Tom Bourgeade, Fabrice Lefèvre, and Irina Illina build a sparring partner for French medical students. Clinical exams called OSCEs stage short simulated consultations, but human standardized patients are scarce, limiting practice. The team first recorded a dataset of two hundred forty student-patient training dialogues in French.

On that foundation they built a controllable virtual patient driven by a language model, with retrieval grounding and a reflection loop keeping the patient faithful and true to the case. Their evaluation framework grades simulation quality, student performance, and language quality with a model acting as judge. The control modules mostly improved patient fidelity and the consistency of student scoring. An interactive prototype lets students rehearse with the virtual patient and receive automatic feedback immediately, multiplying scarce practice opportunities.
arxiv-2606-28926:
Liu, Tang and Huang offer a probabilistic explanation of in-context learning, the ability of language models to learn a task from examples placed in the prompt. This skill is widely used and strikingly effective, yet a general model with rigorous theory behind it has been missing. Their work builds a probability model of the process and derives how well in-context learning should perform under it.

The derivations cover both general parametric distributions and the widely used exponential family, a flexible class of probability laws. From the formulas, the authors explain how several factors shape performance. More demonstrations generally help. The model's sensitivity to its own parameters matters, because touchy models react more strongly to the examples given. Similarity between the demonstrations and the query also matters. Closer matches support better answers. The analysis turns folk wisdom about prompting into quantities one can reason about in advance.
arxiv-2606-29126:
Zhao, Zhou, Jha, Bastian and Shah propose HiComm, a communication module that helps cooperating AI agents share the right information in reinforcement learning. Agents under partial observability rely on messages, but most protocols send flat dense vectors, cut off from the structure of what the sender saw. In many settings observations are naturally hierarchical, organised in groups and entities, and that structure is useful guidance.

HiComm grounds messages in the sender's hierarchy, and the receiver drives the exchange. It issues a query, and a three-stage decoding selects a group, then a sender, then an entity in that group. The matching feature slice returns as the message. Communication becomes structured retrieval, not unstructured transmission. A differentiable trick for discrete choices and a light shared projection let HiComm attach to standard pipelines. Across cooperative tasks it matched or beat learned communication baselines while cutting communication volume up to twenty-three-fold.
arxiv-2606-29226:
Jahan reviews how self-similarity has been used to describe the proton's inner structure. Self-similarity means a pattern repeats at smaller and smaller scales, as in a fractal. The tools are parton distribution functions, which state how the proton's momentum is shared among its quarks and gluons. In deep inelastic scattering, where electrons bounce off protons, such models have matched key features of the data, above all at small x.

The review sets out these models and what they imply for structure functions and parton laws. It then asks whether they link to holographic QCD, a modern approach. Jahan finds qualitative matches between the scaling in the models and the geometry used in holography. He is clear that the link is interpretive, not derived from first principles. Still, it gives a fresh way to view fractal-like scaling in scattering data.
arxiv-2606-29526:
Liang and colleagues identify a neglected problem in reinforcement learning for large language models, the training that rewards better answers. Training and inference run on separate engines for speed and accuracy. Even with identical parameters, the two engines can give different odds for the same output. Updates that improve the training policy therefore may not improve the inference policy, the one actually deployed.

Earlier work tried to stabilize the training policy under this mismatch. Liang's team instead proposes Monotonic Inference Policy Improvement as the real objective. Their two-step framework, MIPU, builds sampler-based candidate updates. It then accepts only matched candidates that an inference-side gap proxy judges favourably. Experiments at two model scales, under high mismatch, show MIPU improving reasoning scores and training stability. The authors argue that deployment behaviour, not training-side scores, should define what such training optimizes.
arxiv-2606-29926:
Thomä and three colleagues propose a multi-sensor version of integrated sensing and communication, a future mobile network service. It uses radio signals both to communicate and to detect objects radar-style. The team's target use is protecting critical infrastructure, such as watching the low airspace over sensitive sites for unauthorised drones.

The design places three or more passive sniffing sensors near the protected site, linked to a distant illuminating base station. It locates targets with multistatic range-Doppler estimation under the cooperative passive coherent location principle. The authors weigh this multistatic layout against the common quasi-monostatic one, where a sniffer sits near the base station, and compare coverage and geometric dilution of precision. That measure captures how sensor geometry blurs position accuracy.
arxiv-2606-30026:
Yuxuan Fan and five colleagues test whether AI models truly understand art, or merely recognize it. Audiovisual art spans cinema, visual art, stage performance, and games. Meaning there comes from deliberate creative choices, like silence conveying grief. Their benchmark, MuseBench, probes reasoning about artistic intent directly. It goes beyond asking what a scene depicts.

MuseBench holds just over four thousand questions across four art domains. The questions were distilled from over ten thousand candidate video essays. Professional commentary in those essays pairs with visual demonstration. A four-phase pipeline filters shortcuts, adds tricky distractors, and validates with experts. Twenty-eight leading multimodal models were evaluated with no training on the task. The best scored under half marks, far below human experts. Game arts proved hardest for nearly every model tested. The authors blame weak stylistic vocabulary and cultural knowledge.
arxiv-2606-30226:
Marcelina Marjankowska, Valerio Modugno, and Paolo Barucca track how the curvature directions of a neural network's loss move during training. The Hessian matrix captures that bending across all its weights. Its eigenvalues say how strong the curvature is. Its eigenvectors say which parameters generate it. Most studies watch the eigenvalues and ignore the directions.

The authors train basic neural nets on a sorting task. They measure eigenvector change with two measures over time. Displacement tracks how far the leading ones drift overall. Localization, via the inverse participation ratio, shows concentration on few parameters. A random null model from the architecture provides the baseline comparison. The two optimizers behave very differently in these measures. SGD makes leading directions progressively more stable. Adam reorganizes its eigenvectors much more strongly throughout training. Adam also concentrates the bending onto a small subset of weights.
arxiv-2606-30826:
Lucas O'Brien settles a conjecture about the best shape for a free transport network. The average distance problem asks for a compact, connected set of bounded total length that minimises the average distance from points of a given distribution to the set. It models networks, like irrigation or roads, where travel on the set itself is free. Buttazzo, Oudet and Stepanov introduced the problem in 2002 and conjectured a topological description of its minimisers. Recent work by Kobayashi, Kim and O'Brien studied these regions through the barycentre field, a vector field tied to the cost.

Building on that tool, O'Brien proves the conjectured description in much greater generality. In particular, the conjecture holds in all dimensions for the case the original authors studied.
arxiv-2606-30926:
Peilin Chen and Xiaoxuan Yang design SpikON, a co-designed algorithm and chip for training spiking neural networks directly on edge hardware. Spiking networks, whose neurons communicate in brief pulses, promise energy-efficient, brain-inspired computing. Online supervised training methods work well but use operations that hardware handles poorly, blocking efficient deployment. SpikON adds learnable thresholds and weight centralisation over time to fix the algorithm side. A new training dataflow with cascade computation reuse lets forward and backward passes run concurrently and share work across timesteps, feeding a dual-parallel accelerator with a custom vector core.

The algorithm alone cut training latency by 32.2% and energy by 35.0% against the baseline, with no accuracy loss. The full co-design beat an Apple M4 GPU on training throughput by 7.2 times, and a TPU-like accelerator by 26.8 times.
arxiv-2606-31026:
Huanlin Gao and ten colleagues speed up diffusion image and video generation by predicting which computation steps can be safely skipped. Caching methods reuse intermediate results across denoising steps, but graph-based schedule searches assume steps contribute independently, an assumption that breaks down at very low step budgets. OTCache instead treats caching schedules across budgets as evolving smoothly in policy space, borrowing the language of optimal transport. It first finds a high-fidelity reference schedule under a generous budget, then runs a light anchor search at an extreme low budget, guided by a perceptual objective.

Schedules for any target budget are then predicted by blending between the reference and the anchor. On FLUX.1 it accelerated sampling 4.5 times, on Qwen-Image 4.7 times and on HunyuanVideo 3.66 times. It also improved fidelity over the strongest existing caching baselines, with no training required.
arxiv-2606-31526:
Ayala computes the exact number of labeled partial orders on 19 points, a count equal to the number of labeled T0 topologies on 19 points. The sequence had been known only up to 18 points, from work by Brinkmann and McKay. The new value is a 39-digit integer, and a Stirling transform turns it into the count of all labeled topologies on 19 points.

The route uses the Erné-Stege moment reduction, which writes the count as antichain sums over posets of at most 16 points. One hard moment over 16-point posets is avoided by growing the 15-point posets one element at a time, with a per-parent kernel priced by the parent's own antichain count. Several independent checks, including a modular residue prediction, confirm the result.
arxiv-2606-31726:
Joos and Kling ask whether scattered-photon coincidences can prove that photon pairs from para-positronium decay start out entangled. Positronium is a short-lived bound state of an electron and a positron. In the spin-zero case its two annihilation photons, each at 511 kiloelectronvolts, are predicted to form a maximally entangled Bell state. Ordinary polarimeters cannot handle such energies, so polarization must be read through Compton scattering.

Working with two-photon density matrices, the pair prove an exact equivalence. The predicted angular pattern of scattering coincidences appears if and only if the photons were in that Bell state before scattering. They also sketch a leaner counting scheme that avoids scanning all solid angles, and they study how finite detector resolution softens the signal.
arxiv-2606-31826:
Pai and six colleagues measure how much optical ghosts contaminate images from the LSST Camera at the Rubin Observatory. Ghosts are artifacts from light bouncing between lenses, filters and detectors. Even tiny surface reflectances matter when a bright star floods the camera, and the artifacts threaten faint, low-surface-brightness science.

Ray-tracing simulations tuned to commissioning observations give the scale of the problem. Averaged across all bands, about 0.57 percent of the focal plane is affected by ghosts in their estimate, inside the one-percent requirement. Data from the Collimated Beam Projector measure the reflectances of individual optical elements in place. The values generally confirm the roughly two-percent figures used in systems engineering predictions.
arxiv-2606-31926:
Nair and six colleagues hunt for the most luminous tidal disruption events in the mid-infrared. A tidal disruption event flares when a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and is torn apart. Infrared searches had mostly covered nearby events, leaving the rare, extremely bright end of the population unmeasured.

A systematic search of the NEOWISE archive, using a new selection rule based on how the W1 minus W2 color evolves, found ten infrared-bright events. Their peak luminosities exceed roughly three times ten to the forty-third power in erg per second. The inferred volumetric rate sits well below an extrapolation from fainter events, a suppression the team links to fewer disruptions around the largest black holes.
arxiv-2606-32026:
Wang and three colleagues make latent world models keep learning while they are being used. Such models predict future states in a compact latent space and support planning through model predictive control. Ordinarily the model is frozen after training, so when test conditions shift, through lighting changes or altered friction, its predictions drift and the planner optimizes the wrong objective.

AdaJEPA instead adapts inside the control loop itself. After executing the first planned action chunk, the model treats the observed transition as a self-supervised signal, updates itself, and replans with the refreshed model. As few as one gradient step per replanning step substantially improves planning success across goal-reaching tasks. Gains are strongest under distribution shift and when training data is limited.
arxiv-2608-00126: On discrete solutions of the Euler system of gas dynamics, arXiv 2608-00126. The Euler solutions. The work is kept for study. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
arxiv-2608-00226: Analytical Charge Density Profile of Vortex Core, arXiv 2608-00226. The vortex core. Scholars can read the full paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
arxiv-2608-00326: Learning to Coordinate Symbolic Tools: LLM Agents for Verified Sum-of-Squares, arXiv 2608-00326. The symbolic tools. The research is preserved here. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
bailey-epicurus-extant-remains-1926:
Epicurus taught in his Athens garden in the early third century BCE and wrote a great deal, yet almost all of it is lost. Cyril Bailey gathered all that survives into one Oxford volume in 1926. His edition gives the Greek text with his own English version, along with notes and a critical apparatus.

Inside are three letters, to Herodotus, Pythocles, and Menoeceus, that sum up his physics and his ethics. Next come the Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings, and the Vatican Sayings, found in a single manuscript. Bailey's notes explain the hard points. For English readers of its day, this volume was the standard Epicurus.
barrett-besterman-divining-rod-1926:
William F Barrett, a physicist, and Theodore Besterman published The Divining Rod in 1926, after years of study for the Society for Psychical Research. Their subject was dowsing, the old practice of finding water or metal with a forked rod that twists in the hands. Many well diggers swore by it.

Field tests, case reports, and past records fill the book, along with a study of how the rod moves. The authors looked for trickery, chance, and knowledge of the land that a dowser might not know he had. Their inquiry, among the last big SPR field studies, treats a folk craft with full scientific care.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol1-1826:
François Bernier, a French doctor, spent twelve years in India and served at the court of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Volume One of his Travels, in Brock's 1826 translation, reports what he saw between 1656 and 1668. It is the classic European account of Mughal India.

Bernier describes the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons, the wealth of Delhi, and the habits of the court. He writes as a trained observer of medicine, trade, and religion. His letters home shaped how Europe pictured India for a century. Few early travelers match his mix of access and clear prose.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol2-1826:
Volume Two of Bernier's Travels in the Mogul Empire continues his account of India under Aurangzeb. The French physician had traveled with the court and seen the empire at close range. Brock's translation completes the work in this volume.

The highlight is Bernier's trip to Kashmir with the emperor's camp, a rare early picture of that valley. He also writes on the Ganges delta, Hindu customs, and the burning of widows, which he condemns. His remarks on trade and land rent drew later thinkers on Asia. Together the two volumes remain a prime source on seventeenth-century India.
bible-tyndale-new-testament-1526:
William Tyndale put the New Testament into English and saw it printed in 1526, the first printed English New Testament. He worked from Greek, not Latin, and paid for the work with exile. Church leaders banned his text, yet copies spread fast across England.

Readers get the four Gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and others, and Revelation. Tyndale wrote in plain, strong English that later Bibles kept. Much of the King James wording starts here. His version changed how English people read Scripture and how English prose sounds. Its cadence rings through church and school to this day.
black-tertiary-man-asia-choukoutien-1926:
Davidson Black, a Canadian anatomist working in China, announced the Choukoutien discovery in Science in 1926. Fossil teeth had come from a cave deposit near Peking, now Beijing. Black saw them as evidence of very early humans in Asia.

He argues Asia may have been a center from which humans spread. The announcement launched the excavations that soon produced Peking Man. Those fossils, later classed as Homo erectus, became world famous. The originals were lost during wartime, adding mystery to the story. Black's short paper opened one of paleoanthropology's great chapters.
bolivian-constitution-1826:
Bolivia's first constitution was adopted in 1826, and it came almost straight from Simón Bolívar's own hand. The Liberator had freed the country that took his name. A congress in Chuquisaca asked him for a charter, and he sent his draft with a famous speech.

The text creates a president who holds office for life, with the right to name his successor. Beside him sit three chambers, including censors charged with guarding morals and the constitution itself. Bolívar argued that a new nation, torn by war, needed a fixed point of authority to survive. Chuquisaca adopted the charter, and Sucre became the first president under it. The lifetime presidency scared many, and the charter lasted only a few years. It remains Bolívar's political last will, written into law.
cather-my-mortal-enemy-1926:
My Mortal Enemy, published in 1926, is Cather's short, pitiless novella of Myra Henshawe, remembered by a younger woman who knew her in youth and in ruin. Myra had given up a fortune to elope with Oswald Henshawe for love.

Years later the couple live poor and diminished, and Myra's bitterness turns on the man she chose. Her dying words name him her mortal enemy. Cather strips the elopement romance to the bone in barely a hundred pages. The late style here is bare, hard, and unforgettable, among the most perfect things she wrote in fiction.
churchward-lost-continent-mu-1926:
Colonel James Churchward claimed a lost continent, Mu, once filled the Pacific Ocean. His 1926 book The Lost Continent of Mu calls it the motherland of man. He said old tablets in India taught him its story.

Churchward describes a rich, wise land that sank in a great quake. Its people, he argues, seeded Egypt, India, and the Americas. Maps, symbols, and stone marks serve as his proof. Scholars reject the tale for lack of hard evidence. Yet the book became a fringe classic, still read by seekers of lost worlds.
cia-0000009726:
A Neo Lao Hak Sat weekly bulletin, carrying photographs and details of American prisoners, leads an October 1971 CIA item. Neo Lao Hak Sat was the Pathet Lao's political front in Laos. Its bulletin was propaganda meant for Lao readers, yet it printed real captives' faces.

Enemy publications became unlikely sources for the prisoner accounting. A photograph in a propaganda sheet could prove a man alive and held. Analysts therefore read the other side's press with close, hostile care. This file records that practice: a weekly bulletin mined for names, faces, and dates the enemy never meant to give.
cia-0000009926:
Prison camp bunkers were being built for two American pilots captured in a place the title cuts off, a March 1972 item reports. Bunkers mean digging for permanence and protection from air attack. Captors who build for two named-value prisoners expect to hold them long.

Construction reports revealed the prison system's growth from the ground up. New bunkers also signaled where bombing could endanger the very men it meant to pressure. Officials logged the site for both reasons. This file preserves the building report as received, an entry in the strange architecture of captivity in the war's last year.
cia-0000012426:
The Penkovsky memoirs occupy a CIA paper from May 1963, as the spy's story moves toward print. The colonel was then on trial in Moscow, or just condemned by it. His papers and debriefings were being shaped into a book the agency had a hand in preparing. The file's literary turn had begun while its subject still faced a Soviet court.

The paper weighs the memoir as a publishing proposition, with editors and censors in its future. Such books carried a secret case into public argument. For readers, the memo shows the story's second life being planned before its first life had fully ended.
cia-0000012826:
What could the Soviet Union do, and what would it most likely do, through 1960? A CIA estimate from April 1955 answers both questions at mid-decade. Stalin was two years dead, and his successors were testing new lines abroad while building rockets and bombs at home. The estimate weighs Soviet strength across the board, from divisions to diplomacy.

The mid-fifties balance it strikes set a baseline for a generation of defense planning. It measures the bear's strength at the Cold War's heightening. For readers, the estimate shows the superpower contest being priced, in forces and intentions, by the men charged with knowing.
cia-0000013226:
Viet Cong policy toward American prisoners gets a full study in a CIA paper from September 1969. By then the southern doctrine had years of hard practice behind it. The paper compares the south's rules with Hanoi's rules. It marks the telling differences between the two systems. The south's camps were poorer and more mobile. They were often harsher too, run by cadres closer to the fighting and farther from any capital's control.

The study shows the system's southern face in its own terms. Policy in the jungle answered to local war more than to doctrine. For readers, the paper explains why captivity in the south was its own ordeal.
cia-0000013926: American pilot prisoners were put on parade in Hanoi, in a CIA note dated January 3, 1969. Parading captives through the capital was a show for crowds and cameras. Such displays broke the rules of war as the United States read them. The note records the parade as one more use of prisoners in the public contest.
cia-0000015326: A letter to George Wyllie from Herbert Scoville fills a CIA file dated June 4, 1959. It concerns a book, They Knew Too Much, per the clipped title. Scoville was one of the agency's top science men. A book about spy craft or saucers could pull even him into the mail. The Scoville letter now rests in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015426: The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena, known as NICAP, is the subject of a redacted CIA case dated January 1, 1965. NICAP was the leading civilian group studying saucer reports in that era. The agency watched its work and kept a case on it. Part of the case was cut before release, leaving the group's name and the date as the firm facts.
cia-0000020326: The private life of Carlos Castillo Armas fills a CIA record dated in 1957. Castillo Armas ruled Guatemala after a 1954 coup backed by the United States. Agencies kept personal files on foreign leaders, habits and all, as part of knowing their man. That the file survives from the year of his death gives it a grim edge for later readers.
cia-0000021526: American pilots held near Ban Na Kay, in Houa Phan Province, died there, a CIA record dated in 1966 reports. Ban Na Kay gives the deaths a place on the map of northeast Laos. No names appear in the title, so the record stands for unnamed men. Such reports closed cases in the worst way and were kept with the same care as hopeful ones.
cia-0000022626: Technical comments on photographs of prisoners of war fill a CIA record dated in 1968. Photo staff judged focus, angle, and detail before matchers trusted a picture. Their notes told other analysts how far a given image could be pushed. Craft remarks like these underpinned the whole comparison effort, where a weak picture could mislead a hopeful search.
cia-0000044426:
A Jesuit priest explained the events leading up to the killings, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. He spoke as an insider of the community that was attacked. Few accounts of the case can match a survivor's nearness to it.

Inside, his account walks through the days before the murders. Warnings, fears, and pressures take shape in his telling. Such testimony later mattered to investigators and historians alike. The file preserves the road to the crime as one of its targets lived it. That is the closest view of the case that any reader can get.
cia-0000045926: Diplomats offered views on the photograph said to show American prisoners still held in Southeast Asia. A CIA item dated June 6, 1991, gathered their comments. The picture was then at the center of a fierce public argument over men missing from the Vietnam War. Their careful reactions show governments trying to judge the claim without raising false hope.
cia-0000049226:
Controlling right-wing terrorism in El Salvador is the stated problem of a CIA paper from 1985, preserved in the Truth Commission file series. Four years into the civil war, death squads tied to the far right remained the government's shame and Washington's leverage problem. The paper addresses the question its title asks outright.

Papers of this kind weighed what pressure could do: aid conditions, public naming, and private warnings to the men who protected the squads. They also weighed the risk that pressure would crack the government the aid was meant to save. The paper survives as a record of the dilemma at the center of the war's politics.
cia-0000049326: El Salvador: Politics of Terrorism is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000049326, dated January 5, 1980, marked for the Truth Commission. The paper treats terrorism in El Salvador as a political subject. Readers are left with a brief dated agency item whose title frames the topic, preserved without the fuller argument that a longer study would supply.
cia-0000102926: Division of international relief supplies and indications of Vietnamese forced labor, in cut-short heading form, are declassified CIA document 0000102926, dated June 2, 1982. Two topics share one title, relief supplies and a labor hint. Readers find a short double-subject record, unusual in a cluster otherwise devoted to Soviet labor alone.
cia-0000112826: Schmalfuss - Subversive Activities is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112826, dated September 2, 1945. The title pairs a name and a charge: Schmalfuss, subversive activities. A companion October file holds a statement made to clear the same name. The brief record is the charge side of that pair, filed in the autumn of 1945 as released there.
cia-0000119726:
A September 1956 CIA item reports Hungary heralding a new era of independent communism. The heading misspells heralds as herals in the original file. Budapest's leaders were speaking the language of a national road to socialism, modeled on Yugoslavia's defiance of Moscow.

Such talk marked real distance from the Kremlin, and the agency noted it as it spread. Within weeks, the hopes behind the phrase would drive Hungarians into the streets, and Soviet tanks would answer them. The item captures the hopeful moment at its height. A small country's leaders still believed they could bend communism to a national shape without breaking with it fatally.
cia-0000124326: A May 1952 CIA document concerns the identification of American airmen captured in Korea. Putting names to captured men was slow work built from fragments of reports. Each confirmed name brought news to a waiting family, and the paper preserves the identifications as they were made. Identification work joined photographs, letters, and camp gossip into names, and each settled name changed a family's status from dreadful uncertainty to fact, welcome or grim.
cia-0000132426: A banking order from the Cuban National Bank fills a CIA item dated January 2, 1960. The bank had forbidden the rediscounting of crop loans by foreign lenders, though the headline breaks off at the word fore. Finance was becoming one of the revolution's weapons against outside influence. The short item reports the move and its place in Havana's tightening control of the economy.
cia-0000132626: Leftist pressure shaping Mexico's stand on Cuba fills a CIA document dated June 3, 1960. Mexico City was caught between Washington's demands and its own restless left. Mexico would keep its ties with Havana long after most neighbors cut theirs. The short document weighs the pressures on the Mexican government and explains the stand they produced.
cia-0000135726: The catalog places this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document at 6 February 1961, with the date flagged as estimated. February was final-training time for the exile brigade. Estimated dates in this series come from the declassification record, not necessarily from the page itself. No subject is named for the item. It is kept in Spanish as released, a piece of brigade paperwork whose exact day, like its contents, the record leaves open.
cia-0000135826: A meeting record in the declassified CIA files, dated 2 August 1953, covers conferences with a person whose name is deleted. Guatemala in these years meant PBSUCCESS, the secret CIA effort against President Jacobo Arbenz and the government he led. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136126: A CIA cable from 3 April 1954, now declassified, deals with Sherwood radio broadcasting, the loud voice of the propaganda arm, cabled to a deleted name. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136226: On 3 May 1954, the agency filed a cable, now declassified, on joint planning to be initiated, asked for BRODFROST and LANGEVIN as teams pulled together. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.

He asked for an immediate air attack on government troops moving toward Quetzaltepeque from Ipala, and urgently requested an air drop of supplies and rifles at Vado Hondo. He also warned that bombardment of Zacapa would be light and the enemy had many reinforcements and motor equipment. The older description's Europe and Hitler framing is wrong; this is Guatemala.
cia-0000136626: This Spanish document, dated 2 February 1961, is filed with the 2506 Brigade papers in the CIA's declassified release. The brigade was then in the last phase of training for the Cuba landing. The catalog record states no subject for the item. It survives in the original Spanish, one of the brigade's February records, and it is described here by the facts the record carries: date, language, and collection.
cia-0000137326: Land and industry seizures lead this CIA briefing. It served the 14 January 1960 National Security Council meeting. Governments take over property without legal notice. No promise of compensation is made. National Bank president Che Guevara is solidifying his power. He places his own proteges in key economic posts. Four teams of Cuban diplomats are now traveling. They visit over thirty countries across four regions. They promote a conference of hungry nations. Foreign Minister Roa met Nasser three times in Cairo.
cia-03169426: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/06/04, a CIA publication. The June briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06701426: KIDNAPPING AND ASSASSINATION OF ARGENTINE AMBASSADOR TO VENEZUELA BY A GROUP A, a CIA document. The Caracas killing. This file preserves that declassified paper. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-1:
Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, was Charles I's closest adviser through the English Civil War. His History of the Rebellion tells that war from inside the king's council. The history was published in 1702 to 1704, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1826, which runs to eight volumes.

Clarendon blends memoir with history: he knew the actors, sat in their councils, and weighed their characters. His portraits of the age's great men remain famous for their shrewdness and grace. The royalist cause has no fuller or finer advocate. Volume one begins the grandest English narrative of the civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-2:
Volume two continues Clarendon's History of the Rebellion in the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his own years at the heart of royalist power, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. The work runs to eight volumes in this edition, each thick with council, camp, and character.

Clarendon's strength is the portrait: friend and foe alike stand forth as living men with mixed motives. He defends the king's cause while blaming royal errors with striking candor. The narrative carries the war's early campaigns in stately, rolling prose. For the inner story of Charles I's court at war, no source stands beside Clarendon. Volume two deepens that story.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-3:
The Oxford edition of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion reaches volume three of eight. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, had served Charles I as chancellor and chief counselor before exile and disgrace. His history, published in 1702 to 1704, grew from notes and memory gathered across a lifetime in high politics.

Volume three holds the war's middle passage, where negotiation and battle chased each other year by year. Clarendon writes with a minister's grasp of paper, money, and men. His judgments on the great figures of the age shaped how later centuries saw them. The book is at once a royalist brief and a work of literature, and this volume keeps both alive.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-4:
Volume four of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion follows the Oxford edition of 1826, though this volume comes from the 1827 printing of the same edition. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his place in Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes. The 1826 scan from Toronto could not be had, so the matched 1827 printing serves.

The fourth volume stands mid-war, where Clarendon's double gift shows best: narrative of events and portraits of the men who drove them. His account of the king's cause is partisan, learned, and deeply felt. No other royalist history matches its access or its art. The set reads whole with this volume in its proper place.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-5:
Volume five continues the 1826 Oxford Clarendon, the History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde wrote the work across his years of power and exile, and it appeared in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes in this edition. Few historians have written about events in which they played so large a part.

That nearness gives the narrative its weight: decisions of the king's council are told by a man who sat in it. Clarendon's measured prose hides strong feeling for the lost royalist cause. His character sketches, generous and severe by turns, remain models of the art. Volume five carries the war toward its end, with the council chamber always in view.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-6:
Clarendon's History of the Rebellion moves through volume six of the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, began the history during the war itself, at the urging of friends who saw it slipping into legend. The published work of 1702 to 1704 fills eight volumes in this edition.

The later volumes trace the royalist cause through defeat, exile, and the long wait for restoration. Clarendon never writes as a mere partisan: he scores his own side's blunders with care. His great gift, the lifelike portrait, stays sharp to the end. Readers meet the English Civil War here as tragedy told by a chief actor. Volume six keeps that telling grave and full.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-7:
Volume seven of the 1826 Oxford edition brings Clarendon's History of the Rebellion near its close. Edward Hyde wrote the history as the chief minister and counselor of Charles I, and its publication ran from 1702 to 1704. The eight-volume Oxford set is the classic form of the work.

In these later pages the war's outcome is sealed, and Clarendon turns to judgment: of men, of measures, of the causes that ruined a kingdom. His prose keeps its stately balance even in bitterness. No other royalist source matches his access to the king's mind and councils. Volume seven holds the penultimate share of the greatest memoir-history of the English civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-8:
Volume eight completes the Oxford edition of 1826 of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, wrote the work from inside Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. Eight volumes hold the whole of his vast, personal history.

The closing volume ends the story of a kingdom torn apart and a cause lost and, in time, restored. Clarendon's portraits and judgments set the terms in which the civil wars were debated for two centuries. His book stands as the great royalist memoir-history, literary and documentary at once. To close volume eight is to finish the fullest inside account of England's great rebellion.
constitution-barbados-2026:
Barbados has used this constitution since independence in 1966, and the hosted text carries amendments through 2026. Early chapters declare the constitution supreme, define citizenship, and protect fundamental rights and freedoms of the individual. For most of its life the charter provided for a Governor-General acting for the British monarch as head of state.

That changed in 2021, when Barbados became a republic and a president replaced the Governor-General, which is the office this text now describes. A prime minister leads the government, drawn from Parliament. Parliament pairs an elected House of Assembly with an appointed Senate. Remaining chapters cover the courts, the public service, and finance. The republic change made Barbados the world's newest republic at that time.
constitution-kazakhstan-2026:
Kazakhstan adopted this constitution in 1995, four years after the Soviet Union ended, and the hosted text is a current version through 2026. Early sections give the bases of the state. Kazakhstan is a single, democratic republic. Kazakh is the state language, while Russian is used on equal terms in state bodies. Astana is named the capital.

A president with wide powers heads the state and names the prime minister and government. Parliament pairs a Senate with a Mazhilis, the lower house. Later sections cover the courts, a Constitutional Court restored by changes in 2022, local rule, and public finance. Those 2022 changes, passed after deadly unrest, cut some presidential powers and barred the president from party membership while in office.
cooper-last-of-the-mohicans-1826:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Last of the Mohicans in 1826, the second Leatherstocking tale and his most famous book. Cooper set it in 1757, during the French and Indian War, around the fall of Fort William Henry. He claimed the story grew from a visit to Lake George with British tourists.

Hawkeye, the white scout raised beside the Mohicans Chingachgook and his son Uncas, guides two sisters through a war-torn forest. The Huron villain Magua pursues them with patience and hatred. Captures, rescues, and massacres follow across glens and caverns Cooper made iconic. The title's tragedy gathers force as the old order of the forest dies with Uncas. The novel became the archetypal American adventure and the most translated early American book.
cross-true-masonic-chart-1826:
Jeremy L Cross published The True Masonic Chart in 1826, and it became a well known American guide to lodge ritual. Cross was a traveling Masonic teacher who helped spread a shared form of work across many lodges. His chart used pictures as memory aids for members.

Rows of symbols, tools, and scenes, called hieroglyphic emblems, helped Masons recall the lessons of each degree. The text around them gave the order and sense of the ritual without printing every secret word. For historians, the chart shows how American Masonry taught itself, and how pictures carried meaning that words alone were not meant to hold.
cummings-is-5-1926:
E. E. Cummings published is 5 in 1926, his second major collection of poems. By then his experiments with broken lines, scattered type, and lowercase letters were becoming famous. He divided the book into sections that move from satire to love poems.

The best-known piece here, anyone lived in a pretty how town, tells a whole life in a few musical, looping lines. Other poems mock politicians and professors, then soften into tender songs about lovers and seasons. Cummings plays with grammar the way jazz musicians play with rhythm. The collection shows him at his most beloved and most daring at once.
defoe-history-of-the-devil-1726:
Daniel Defoe, the English writer of Robinson Crusoe, published his History of the Devil at London in 1726. The full title adds 'as well ancient as modern,' and the book runs in two parts. Defoe treats Satan as a figure with a long public career.

He traces the devil through the Bible, Milton's Paradise Lost, the Crusades, and the age of witch trials. Then he jokes that Satan has moved on to softer prey: fine ladies, wits, and fools of fashion. The result is part history, part satire, and pure Defoe.
defoe-political-history-of-the-devil-172:
Daniel Defoe, the novelist of Robinson Crusoe, published The Political History of the Devil in 1726. The book traces Satan's career from the Fall through the witchcraft panics of Defoe's own recent past. It is the great Augustan synthesis of demonology and skepticism, belief and doubt in one shrewd mind.

Defoe mocks credulous tales of pacts and apparitions while still treating the Devil as a real political schemer in human affairs. He sorts scripture, history, and street gossip with a journalist's nose for a weak story. The result reads like a skeptical sermon, funny and unsettling by turns.
