Later drug generations overcame resistance and intolerance, bringing life expectancy for responders close to that of the wider public. Goals have shifted toward quality of life and treatment-free remission, which landmark stop-treatment studies show about half of eligible patients can maintain. Remaining challenges include resistance, safety, and widening access. The authors survey newer drugs, combinations, and immune approaches that may push more patients toward functional cure.
pmc-13233826: Yuping Ye and co-authors issued a 2026 author correction in Scientific Reports. The notice is a correction only, fixing the ethics approval details of their earlier study on hospital information system based psychological nursing for cesarean section patients. The approval number and date were misstated in the ethics section and in the study flowchart. The corrected approval carries a new number dated 17 February 2022, from the ethics committee of Foshan Women and Children Hospital. Figure details were updated to match, and the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13235526:
Sara Y. Tartof and a large team estimated in 2026 how well an RSV vaccine protects older adults across two seasons. The study used health records from a large Southern California care system during two winter seasons. Adults aged sixty and older hospitalized or seen in emergency care for respiratory illness were tested for the virus. Those testing positive formed cases, with carefully chosen negative patients as controls.

Protection against severe RSV illness reached about eighty percent in the first season after vaccination. Second-season protection stayed in the mid-seventies in the primary analysis presented. Benefits persisted for the oldest adults and for people with frailty, risk factors, or weakened immunity. Protection seemed to fade faster in immunocompromised adults, though estimates there were imprecise. The authors, in a manufacturer-funded study, see substantial public health benefit from vaccinating older adults.
pmc-13236926:
Gergely Jocsak and team reviewed in 2026 how hormone-disrupting agents can disturb synapses, the junctions where brain cells signal each other. The agents include bisphenols, phthalates, farm pesticides, PCBs, heavy metals, and flame retardants. Synapses grow stronger or weaker with use, and that tuning underlies learning and memory, with hormones helping to set it.

The agents meddle with hormone circuits, cell receptors, and the marks that control genes. They disturb signal flow, calcium balance, and the small spines on receiving cells. The review also ties exposure to energy failure in cells, oxidative stress, inflammation, and a leakier blood-brain barrier. Exposure while the brain is still forming worries the team most, since effects may pass to later generations. Stronger rules on these agents are their closing call.
pmc-13238126:
Takaaki Hiranaka and colleagues followed 33 knees after a shinbone realignment operation in 2026, asking whether a tilted joint line afterward harms the outer knee cartilage. The operation, medial opening wedge high tibial osteotomy, shifts weight away from worn inner cartilage but can leave the joint line oblique. Quantitative MRI measured cartilage quality before surgery and a year later.

Thirteen knees ended with excessive tilt and twenty stayed in the acceptable range, though overall leg alignment matched between groups. The tilted group showed early degenerative change in the outer tibial cartilage on MRI and reported worse symptom, quality-of-life, and sport scores. The authors advise keeping the joint line within range during planning. Alignment of the whole leg alone, they show, does not tell the whole story.
pmc-13239026:
Ebud Ayele Dagnazgi and team measured eye damage from vitamin A lack among pregnant women in Ethiopia's Tigray Region in 2026, checking 1,355 women in antenatal care at public hospitals in 2024. Unlike most earlier work, the study covered the full clinical range of xerophthalmia rather than night blindness alone. One in four women, about 25 percent, had the condition.

Risk climbed with poor sanitation, missed iron pills, fewer antenatal visits, low vegetable intake, thin arms, and alcohol use during pregnancy. Not owning livestock and having a past miscarriage carried especially strong links. The authors call the share a critical public health concern. Their factor list points to nutrition, clean water, and antenatal contact as the levers most worth pulling.
pmc-13239326:
Brenda Apiyo Odoi and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study of bacteria living in and on the seeds of Kenyan rattlepods, plants in the genus Crotalaria. Seed microbes can help plants take up nutrients and grow, yet the bacteria carried by these widely eaten plants had not been described before.

The team cultured 118 isolates from the seeds and used gene sequencing to name 20 of them, finding mostly Bacillus and Proteus types. Several isolates made strong amounts of enzymes that break down protein, starch, fat, and plant fibre. One isolate matched known species poorly and may be new to science. The results point to seed bacteria as a possible source of useful enzymes for industry.
pmc-13239426:
Edward R Bader and co-authors examine rural and urban gaps in epilepsy care in a 2026 United States hospital study. Rural patients often live far from neurologists and specialist epilepsy centres, and the team asked whether that distance shows up in outcomes during admission.

Using a national inpatient database from 2016 to 2021, they analysed more than eight hundred thousand epilepsy admissions. Patients from the most rural counties faced nearly double the odds of dying in hospital compared with the most urban patients. They also arrived more often in prolonged seizure emergencies and stayed longer, while receiving brain-wave testing less often. Notably, these gaps faded among patients with private insurance.
pmc-13240226:
Liseth's team at Mayo Clinic combined CAR T cells with a cancer-killing virus to strengthen treatment of solid tumors. CAR T therapy often falters in solid tumors through fatigue and fading staying power. The team used vesicular stomatitis virus to wake the T cells' own native receptor. That waking happens next to the built-in synthetic receptor.

The pairing produced a subset of virus-primed CAR T cells with stronger killing behavior. Single-cell reads showed these cells grew in clones and switched on effector genes. Their active states and protein profiles differed from unprimed CAR T cells. Helper CD4 T cells proved pivotal in making the primed group, hinting at a new lever for tuning cell therapy.
pmc-13240826:
Pieter Francsois Fouche and co-authors report a 2026 study of blood pressure around the start of adrenaline infusions after cardiac arrest. Low pressure after the heart restarts is common and tied to worse outcomes. Records came from emergency cases in Victoria, Australia, across five years.

Only adults who regained a pulse, reached hospital with a pulse, and started the infusion within an hour were included. Minute-by-minute monitor data showed pressure falling before the infusion began. After the start, pressure climbed steadily over the next twenty minutes for both measures tracked. The authors say the pattern defines how patients respond in the field. It can also inform future trials on timing and pressure targets.
pmc-13241426:
Moran's team at James Cook built a barramundi muscle cell line and watched its genes switch over. Barramundi is a prized farmed fish of the tropics with little cell data. Expression of key muscle regulators was tracked for fourteen days. Sampling covered the explant stage, early passages, and myoblast change.

Key genes switched on in patterns matching their known jobs in muscle growth. The cells duly changed form, proof of a true muscle line. Waves followed the culture's own shifts, including each passage. Moran offers the line as a base for studying fish muscle growth.
pmc-13241526:
Pei and co-workers in Japan alloyed a symmetric gold cluster with silver to make a chiral metal cluster atom by atom. Subnanometer clusters change their behavior sharply with each atom swapped. Starting from a carbon-centered cluster of six gold atoms, they added silver trifluoroacetate. The product holds four gold and six silver ions around the central carbon.

Calculations mapped the bonding between carbon, gold, and silver in the new cage-like structure. Using handed ligands, the team produced either mirror form of the cluster cleanly. Both forms glow red to near-infrared and show distinct chiroptical responses. The route etches gold out while silver moves in, opening a path to tailor-made light-emitting clusters.
pmc-13241626:
Giulia Escobar and Marcela V Maus present a 2026 review of combination strategies to make engineered T cell therapy work in pancreatic cancer. This cancer resists immunotherapy through dense scar-like tissue and a suppressive local environment. Engineered cells must enter the tumor and stay active once inside.

The authors discuss their recent preclinical work with cells aimed at mesothelin, a protein found on these tumors. One drug raised target levels on tumor cells by blocking its shedding. Another drug steered T cells toward a more helpful state. Blocking the PD-1 brake restored cell function in tumors carrying its partner protein. Combining such approaches, they argue, beats seeking a single fix.
pmc-13242426:
Maggie Yu and co-authors asked whether a sense of self-mastery shields people with multiple sclerosis from the effects of stressful life events. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. They analyzed survey answers from 948 people with the disease across several countries. Stressful events were counted and weighted, mastery was split into low, middle, and high levels, and both were compared with quality of life and fatigue.

Among people with low or moderate mastery, heavier stress loads came with clearly lower mental quality of life. Stress also raised the odds of severe fatigue several-fold, mainly in the low-mastery group. Among high-mastery respondents, those links largely vanished. The snapshot design cannot prove cause and effect, and the authors call for follow-up over time. Still, they suggest that building mastery could soften the harm stress does to people living with multiple sclerosis.
pmc-13242826:
Lingling Dong and co-authors report a 2026 single-cell atlas of lung tissue in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The disease mixes persistent inflammation with structural remodeling, and the cells sustaining that state are unclear. New single-cell data were merged with public datasets from healthy and diseased lungs.

Fibroblasts, the scaffold-building cells, stood out. They sent the strongest outgoing signals among lung tissue cells, and their signaling rose most in disease. Across fibroblast subgroups, diseased cells shared an inflammatory, immune-recruiting state tied to injury and scarring. Control networks inside the cells were extensively rewired. The authors propose fibroblasts as underappreciated immune regulators in this disease and as targets for future therapy research.
pmc-13243226:
Marissa Di Napoli and colleagues test whether a new liver scoring rule closed a sex gap in 2026. The MELD 3.0 rule, adopted in 2023, was meant to judge disease severity more fairly for women awaiting transplant. Earlier rules had left women at higher risk of dying while they waited.

The team studied 95,211 adults on the United States waitlist from 2017 to 2024. Women still faced a higher risk of death within 180 days than men under the new rule. Risk also rose steeply with age, and older patients with high scores had the worst odds of survival. The authors call for further change so the waitlist treats women more fairly.
pmc-13243326:
Natália Albino Pires and colleagues piloted a tablet app that uses heritage to stir autobiographical memory in older adults. Their study appeared in the Journal of Cross-Cultural Gerontology in 2026. Reminiscence therapy is known to work with music and crafts, but traditional dance and oral storytelling had barely been tried as triggers. The team built a selection protocol and a prototype, LONG-REMI, then field-tested them in six centers in Spain and Portugal.

Fifty-six adults aged sixty-five and over took part, some with mild or moderate cognitive decline and some without. Dance clips and traditional tales were matched to each person's background by the app's support tools. Both heritage forms evoked memories and sparked communication in both groups. The authors call the approach reproducible and ready for larger trials. Heritage, they argue, is not decoration: it is identity material that therapy can put to work.
pmc-13243426:
Yuan Gao and co-authors gauge how ready Chinese nurses feel for new infectious diseases in a 2026 survey built around mpox. Nurses stand at the front line for spotting cases and stopping spread. A recent mpox outbreak gave a real test of that readiness.

The online survey drew 387 nurses from 24 regions between January and March 2024. Most nurses scored well on mpox knowledge, and nearly all held positive attitudes toward control work. Nurses with higher rank and those who had workplace training on mpox knew more. Knowledge and attitudes also rose together. The authors call for steady, structured training so readiness does not fade between outbreaks.
pmc-13244626:
Jean Marie Annoni and colleagues ran a worldwide project in which people with aphasia set the research agenda for their condition. Their report appeared in Research Involvement and Engagement in 2026. Aphasia's burdens reach far past language into emotional and social life, yet researchers choose the questions. This initiative, started by a person with aphasia and three laypeople, involved more than one hundred patients from fourteen countries, working in many languages.

A three-phase process generated topics, refined them in national co-design sessions, and voted them into priorities, with eleven countries joining the vote. Inclusive methods, under a framework built for lay involvement, let people with severe language difficulty lead rather than attend. The agenda confirmed earlier findings and sharpened one demand above all: public awareness must rise. The authors present the project as proof that priority setting can be co-created across languages when access is designed in.
pmc-13245426:
Li and co-authors charted the yearly hormone cycle of an endangered turtle in this 2026 PeerJ study. The Beale's eyed turtle, found only in southeastern China, is critically endangered, yet its reproductive physiology was almost undocumented, a gap that hampers captive breeding. The team measured three sex hormones in blood from captive turtles across a full year using standard immunoassays.

Males showed two testosterone peaks, in spring and late summer, matching mating seasons and a pattern of sperm production after mating. Females peaked in estradiol in April, tied to egg-yolk formation for a single yearly clutch, with progesterone cresting around ovulation in June. The authors offer the profiles as a reference calendar for managing breeding of this rare species in captivity, while noting their small sample.
pmc-13246126:
Chen and co-authors studied a risky intensive-care maneuver after one of the most dangerous heart operations, in this 2026 Critical Care Explorations paper. Patients who develop severe lung failure after repair of an acute type A aortic dissection are often too unstable to turn face-down, the prone position that helps failing lungs. The team reviewed seventy-eight such patients at one heart center.

Fifty-eight patients were proned and twenty stayed on their backs. Oxygen levels in the proned group rose quickly, within hours, and patients turned within forty-eight hours of lung failure spent less time on the ventilator. No safety disaster emerged. The authors back early, protocol-guided proning for selected patients, with prospective trials to confirm.
pmc-13246326:
Taner Yılmaz measures campers' confidence in their outdoor skills in a 2026 survey study from Türkiye. Camping involves risk and self-reliance, so belief in one's own skill shapes safe behavior. Practice-based studies of that belief among campers remain rare.

Face-to-face surveys gathered 317 volunteer campers across Antalya, Muğla, and İzmir. Men reported higher confidence than women, and university graduates scored above high school graduates. Regular exercise stood out as one of the strongest links with confidence across every subscale. More camping trips also went with higher confidence, and income played a smaller part. The author argues that guided early trips could build confidence in new campers.
pmc-13246726:
Arad Jain and co-authors overview exercise as a counter to immune aging in a 2026 narrative review. Activity levels have fallen worldwide while immune systems age into chronic low-grade inflammation. Lab and clinical proof now ties regular movement to slower immune decline.

Exercise trims inflammation, cuts harmful web release from white cells, and reshapes T cell and natural killer cell pools. It also slows autoimmune flares, steadies metabolism, and helps immune cells watch for tumors. Around tumors, movement can normalize blood vessels and restore cell function. Carefully dosed multi-part programs seem safe for older adults. The authors call for studies that fine-tune the prescription.
pmc-13246926:
Delgado Casanova and colleagues followed a common breast-biopsy finding to see whether it really needs surgery, in this 2026 Breast Cancer Research and Treatment study. A radial sclerosing lesion is a benign, star-shaped scar-like area that mimics cancer on imaging; historically, surgeons removed such lesions to be safe. Their hospital reviewed four hundred nineteen lesions in three hundred ninety patients diagnosed by needle biopsy from 2020 to 2025.

Lesions that went on to repeat biopsy or surgical removal, sixty-three in all, turned up no cancer at all. Across the whole group, the estimated chance of cancer appearing at the lesion site within three years was zero. The authors support watching these lesions with imaging when biopsy sampling and imaging agree, sparing many women an operation.
pmc-13247426:
Xiaohu Yang and co-authors scan a United States safety database for heart rhythm risks from antifungal drugs in 2026. Systemic antifungals save lives in deep infections, yet some may disturb the heart's electrical timing. Real-world reports offer a wide lens on that risk.

The team mined 42,393 reports with four statistical screens for lopsided reporting. Itraconazole, fluconazole, and posaconazole drew the strongest rhythm signals across the checks. Fluconazole stood out for fast rhythms and a dangerous twisting rhythm pattern. Three other drugs showed no signal on any screen. The authors advise matching drug choice to each patient's heart risk and current medicines.
pmc-13247526:
Ya-Wei Weng and co-authors build models that flag thinking problems in people living with HIV in a 2026 study. Even with good virus control, many patients lose sharpness in planning and flexible thought. Blood proteins that govern tissue enzymes may carry part of the story.

The study enrolled 169 middle-aged patients in Taiwan who took card sorting tests and lab panels. About one in ten showed executive impairment. One protein, TIMP-1, sorted patients best on its own. Joining lab values with clinical facts such as years since diagnosis lifted accuracy a lot. The best model reached strong scores in cross-checks. Such tools could target brain screening where it helps most.
pmc-13249026:
Monteiro and colleagues checked eye-measuring machines in patients with implanted helper lenses, in this 2026 research letter from Porto, Portugal. Two modern biometers map the eye's inner surfaces automatically before cataract surgery. An extra lens inside the eye, placed earlier to correct vision, can confuse that mapping, so the team reviewed one hundred such eyes.

Both devices misdrew the eye's surfaces in roughly a quarter of eyes, mistaking the implanted lens for the natural one. Errors shrank the measured chamber depth and inflated lens thickness, and one lens style caused most mistakes. One machine sometimes refused to guess, forcing manual checks. The authors warn surgeons to inspect every scan in these eyes.
pmc-13249926:
Goodwin and colleagues show that invisible structure steers how people hunt through a cluttered display, in a 2026 perception study. Across six online experiments, participants foraged for many copies of two target types among distractors, while the screen was visibly divided into segments holding equal numbers of objects. The divisions carried no hint about where targets hid, since targets were spread evenly.

Even so, searchers kept working inside one segment rather than hopping to the next, a systematic style the layout alone induced. That style cost speed but improved memory for where things had been. Stronger visual structure strengthened the effect. The authors warn that display design silently choreographs search behavior, in the lab and in everyday scenes.
pmc-13250026:
Anne McMunn and Jeroen Spijker introduce a 2026 journal collection on unpaid care in later life across Europe. People live longer now, but extra years are not always healthy years, so more older people need help from family and friends.

The editors argue for a life course view: what shapes who ends up giving care, and how heavily, is built across a whole working and family life. Women still give more care, and for longer, though the gap narrows among older couples. Carers also tend to be worse off money-wise. The collection's papers trace how jobs, partnerships, and money earlier in life lead into caring roles.
pmc-13250326:
Salam Melhem, Hadeel Bouzia, and Nour Moosa report a misleading belly pain case in this 2026 report. An eight-year-old boy had one day of worsening right-sided pain, and an ultrasound first suggested early appendicitis, a very common cause of such pain in children.

Keyhole surgery told a different story: a twisted, bleeding lump of the fatty apron inside the belly, near the upper colon, while the appendix was only mildly red. Surgeons removed the lump and the appendix, and lab tests confirmed the fatty tissue had twisted on itself with no appendicitis present. The boy recovered well. The authors back keyhole checks when scans disagree with symptoms.
pmc-13250626:
Yuhei Suzuki and co-authors describe a cancer returning after 24 quiet years in this 2026 case report. A 55-year-old woman had fluid around her right lung and swollen glands under her breastbone, found after a stem cell transplant for a blood disease.

At age 31 she had surgery and radiation for a windpipe cancer called adenoid cystic carcinoma, a slow type known for late returns. A needle sample taken through the airway proved the swollen gland was the same cancer back again, not her blood disease. Because this cancer grows slowly, speed of growth cannot rule it out, and the authors urge tissue checks whenever it is suspected.
pmc-13251226:
Angelika Bolte and co-authors crack a hidden genetic case in this 2026 study. Their patient, a Syrian child with severe developmental regression, had clear chemical signs of Sandhoff disease, a storage disorder, but standard gene tests found no cause.

Deep gene reading using long-read methods found the answer buried inside a gene called HEXB: a change deep in a non-coding stretch that switches on a false segment, breaking the gene's message. Both copies carried it, a pattern the team calls a candidate founder variant in the region. The case shows why hidden variants may be missed in Middle Eastern patients and hints at future splice-fixing therapies.
pmc-13252726:
Quan Zhou and colleagues link arm function, exercise, and thinking in older Chinese adults in this 2026 study. The group studied lives apart from their children, a fast-growing group as China ages, and their mental sharpness is a growing concern.

Data came from a 2018 national longevity survey covering 5,060 such adults, with an average age near 79. About 15 percent had cognitive impairment. Restricted upper limb function more than doubled the odds of impairment, while regular exercise lowered them. Exercise explained only a small slice of the arm-brain link, about six percent. The authors treat exercise as a minor pathway, not the main story.
pmc-13253826:
Marwa Abdeltawab Ahmed and colleagues test a nano form of a farm insecticide in a 2026 mouse study. Chlorpyrifos is known to harm male fertility, and its nano-emulsion form may enter the body more easily. Forty male albino mice got one of three daily doses, or none, by mouth for 35 days.

At the top dose, fertility fell to zero and sperm survival dropped from 74% to 43.1%. Testosterone fell from 4.2 to 1.8 nanograms per milliliter, while stress and DNA damage markers rose. Tissue checks showed shrunken tubes and harmed testis structure, which the authors link to oxidative stress, meaning cell damage from reactive oxygen.
pmc-13254226:
Lizhi Wu and co-authors review how microplastics combine with other pollutants in a 2026 paper. Microplastics are tiny plastic bits now found worldwide. On their own they can harm cells, immunity, and the brain, hormone, and reproductive systems. They can also carry other pollutants on their surfaces, changing those pollutants' effects.

The review covers combined effects with heavy metals, organic pollutants, plastic additives, antibiotics, and viruses, plus the mechanisms behind them. The authors urge future work on realistic exposure scenes, long-term effects, and combined exposure risks, to guide public awareness and policy on plastic pollution.
pmc-13254426:
Shuhong Mei and a large team model a frustrating stroke outcome in a 2026 multicenter study. Futile recanalization means a vessel reopens after clot removal, yet the patient still has major disability at 90 days. The study covered 350 stroke patients, with a model built in 260 and checked in 90 from another center.

In all, 152 patients, or 43.43 percent, had futile recanalization. Predictors were higher stroke severity, lower early CT score, high blood sugar at admission, poor backup blood flow, and longer time to reopening. Their scoring chart reached accuracy values of 0.84 to 0.86 in testing, with fair calibration.
pmc-13254726:
Peng and colleagues combined bulk, single-cell, and spatial data to position the chemokine-like factor CKLF as a driver of liver cancer growth. CKLF was more abundant in hepatocellular carcinoma tissue than in normal liver, and high levels tracked with later stage, distinct molecular subtypes, and shorter survival. The factor appeared in tumor cells and in infiltrating immune cells alike.

Laboratory tests supported a causal role: silencing CKLF slowed proliferation, movement, and colony growth in liver cancer cell models. Forcing the Ras pathway on partly reversed those effects, placing CKLF upstream of AKT and ERK signaling. The authors propose CKLF as both a prognostic marker and a drug target.
pmc-13255626:
Hairui Zhao and colleagues report a 2026 year-long field experiment on methane release from the shoreline wetland of Qinghai Lake, China's largest salt lake. Alpine wetlands store much carbon, and warming plus changing water levels could unlock more methane. The team combined experimental warming with different flooding depths and measured gas fluxes across seasons.

Under flooding alone, emissions peaked in autumn. Warming reshaped the yearly pattern and produced unusually high winter emissions. Warming with deep flooding boosted summer and autumn release yet suppressed winter release. Soil carbon and nitrogen measures tracked emissions closely only in autumn. The authors highlight autumn as a key season when carbon and nitrogen move together, and they warn that future warming with wetter conditions may raise methane loss from such wetlands.
pmc-13256226: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas on acute viral hepatitis in hospitalized children in North India. The work covered clinical, blood-test, ultrasound, and cause-related findings. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published study, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship cannot be verified. The notice gives no patient findings, so the retracted work is described here only by its subject and the reasons for withdrawal.
pmc-13257626:
Chen Chen and colleagues argue that history, not just chemistry, shapes magnesium hydrides used to store hydrogen. These materials offer high capacity from a cheap, abundant metal. Yet samples with the same label often behave very differently. Their 2026 Perspective blames hidden states written in by making and using the material.

Defects, leftover strain, unstable structures, and changed catalysts all steer how hydrogen enters and moves. That makes each sample's reaction path depend on its past, which the authors say explains the field's reproducibility troubles. They propose recording processing history as standard metadata. Designing around reaction pathways, they argue, beats hunting for better compositions alone.
pmc-13258926:
Andrey Smirnov, Ilya Nedospasov, and Iren Kuznetsova study a backward acoustic wave for liquid sensing in a 2026 physics paper. The wave travels through a piezoelectric crystal plate loaded with liquid on one side. Theory, simulation, and bench tests were combined for the first time on this wave type.

Liquid electrical and density traits each shifted sensor readings in separate, readable ways. Resonance frequency and quality factor carried the two signals independently. That separation supports sensors that report several liquid traits at once. Results matter both for wave physics and for practical sensor design. Engineers building compact liquid analyzers gain a new wave platform to exploit.
pmc-13259126:
Yodthong Baimark and co-authors blend a shrimp-shell derivative into corn-based plastic to help it rot faster. Poly(L-lactic acid) is biodegradable in name but lingers far too long in soil and packaging waste streams. Their 2026 fix stirs in thermoplastic chitosan, plasticized with lactic acid itself.

A small chitosan dose made films stretch further before breaking and toughened them noticeably. Higher doses reversed those gains, so the sweet spot sat low. Wetter surfaces and far greater soil-burial weight loss followed as chitosan content rose. After a year underground, the richest blend lost dozens of times more mass than plain film, suiting single-use packaging.
pmc-13259226:
Paolo Miguel Siazon and coauthors examine the overlooked stalk of cannabis resin glands in a 2026 molecular study. The gland head makes cannabinoids, while the stalk was long treated as mere support. Proteins and gene activity were compared between isolated heads and stalks.

Thousands more genes ran hot in stalks than proteins alone suggested. Stalk cells carried vessel like and skin like signatures together. Head genes centered on making and storing special compounds. Stalk genes centered on transport, growth, sugar movement, and hormone signals. Breeding for higher resin yield may need to target stalk supply lines, not heads alone.
pmc-13259426:
Walid M. Shewakh and coauthors anneal printed PLA parts to map strength against crystal structure in a 2026 study. A compact experimental grid crossed three oven temperatures with three holding times, five copies per cell. Strength tests ran beside calorimetry and diffraction measurements.

Every annealed condition beat the unheated strength baseline. The best gain came from the mildest heat held for the middle duration. Crystallinity climbed highest at the hottest, longest setting, yet strength peaked elsewhere. Disordered crystals dominated the strongest parts, while stiffer parts shifted toward ordered crystals. Desktop printing users gain a practical annealing recipe with the trade off explained.
pmc-13259826:
Vladimir Suvorov proposed in 2026 that qualia, the felt sense of a situation, can be treated as control tools for self-driving systems. His paper argues that breaking a scene into separate objects and searching many action plans makes open-world driving too slow. Living agents instead judge a whole scene at once, and he asks how a machine could do the same.

He defines an event phase space, a low-dimension map where safe states act as stable attractors and danger sits at the borders between them. Tests used the CARLA driving simulator with parked-car blocking scenes, running 1,000 episodes per controller across five seeds. An alarm built from the learned field cut collisions in stress scenes and beat time-to-collision pipelines by a wide margin. The model ran in under two milliseconds per choice with only a few thousand parameters.
pmc-13260226:
Lisa Linnenbrink-Garcia and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article making the case for many-sided motivation interventions built into everyday classrooms. Most earlier programs targeted one slice of motivation, such as showing students why a subject is useful, without changing the classroom context. The authors survey approaches to supporting student motivation, then argue for programs that combine several theories at once. They also introduce complex dynamic systems thinking as a guide for understanding motivation in schools.

Two programs that worked are described in detail. One targeted reading motivation and engagement in primary and middle school classrooms. The other targeted science motivation and engagement at middle school level. Both were embedded in normal teaching rather than delivered as add-ons. The authors close by weighing the practical challenges of such broad programs against their promise for lasting student engagement.
pmc-13260426:
Stefan Stepic and co-authors studied in 2026 how variants in two casein genes relate to milk quality in Serbian water buffalo. Caseins are the main proteins in milk, and their gene variants can change protein content and cheese-making traits. Their team genotyped 130 buffalo and checked raw milk composition in 42 of them.

One variant in the alpha-S1 casein gene tracked with richer protein and casein in milk. Looking at two variants together as a haplotype sharpened the picture further. One combined pattern showed clearly higher casein and protein than the reference pattern. Single-variant tests gave weaker signals than the paired analysis. The authors suggest breeders could use these markers when selecting buffalo for richer milk. Small herds in Serbia raise buffalo mainly for milk and butter.
pmc-13260626:
Jiaqi Huang and colleagues studied in 2026 how day-to-day temperature swings relate to deaths in Chengdu, in southwest China. Most climate-health work targets heatwaves and cold spells, while wobbling temperatures get less attention. Their team used ten years of daily weather and death records, splitting variability into swings within a day and shifts between days.

Total and within-day variability each tracked with higher daily mortality, while between-day variability pointed the other way. Within-day swings carried the main burden, linked with roughly twenty-seven thousand attributable deaths over the study years. Respiratory deaths, women, and people aged sixty-five and over proved most vulnerable. The effect also grew stronger in cold seasons. The authors urge local adaptation plans to treat within-day swings as a distinct risk.
pmc-13261426:
Daniel Rosenkranz and colleagues refined in 2026 a classic color-based test for iodine in urine, aiming at large population surveys. Iodine status guides thyroid health programs, and urine carries most of the body's iodine output. Their team adjusted reagent amounts, digestion heat, and reaction conditions through four versions of the Sandell-Kolthoff method.

The final version measured accurately across its range, with recovery near the true value and variation under three percent. Checks against two reference methods, including mass spectrometry, agreed closely. Samples kept cold for short periods stayed stable, yet repeated freezing and thawing cut measured iodine noticeably. A surprise hazard emerged: urine touching test dipsticks picked up outside iodine and inflated readings many times over. The authors offer the tuned method as a cheap, validated tool for big monitoring programs.
pmc-13261926:
Sarper İçen and Şefika Nurhüda Karaca Cengiz present a 2026 exploratory study of impulsivity and internet gaming disorder symptoms in teenage boys with ADHD. Adolescents with ADHD face elevated risk of problem gaming. It was unclear whether different sides of impulsivity, such as acting without planning, relate to different gaming symptoms.

The study recruited 45 male adolescents aged 12 to 17 from two psychiatry clinics in Türkiye. Most gamed over four hours daily, 73.3% on weekdays and 75.6% on weekends. Gaming symptom scores rose with non-planning impulsivity (ρ = 0.56), attentional impulsivity (ρ = 0.52), and motor impulsivity (ρ = 0.45). When all three were modeled together, only non-planning impulsivity stayed independently associated with symptom severity. Age showed no significant correlation with impulsivity or gaming severity. The authors frame these as exploratory links needing confirmation in larger samples.
pmc-13262026:
Yukihiro Matsumoto and co-authors probed in 2026 tiny structural flaws inside a metal-organic framework thin film using a nanoscale infrared method. Such films promise sensors and filters, yet bulk measurements hide local defects. Their team combined an atomic force microscope with nano-FTIR to read coordination bonding spot by spot in a film called NAFS-1.

The maps exposed patchiness that wide-area tools miss. Some zones held carboxyl groups that never linked to metal, while raised features elsewhere showed strong coordination. Skipping the usual water rinse after film transfer made the film less uniform overall, even though average bonding improved. The authors say local checks like these are essential for judging film quality. The findings also illuminate how these films assemble at the air-liquid boundary where they form.
pmc-13262826:
Ifeoma Jovita Nduka and co-authors model whether breast X-ray screening is worth its cost in Nigeria in a 2026 journal article. Mammography is the standard screening test, but Nigeria has no national screening program and use is low. The team simulated yearly and two-yearly screening for women from age 40 over a lifetime, from the health provider's viewpoint.

Yearly screening cost 238.60 US dollars per woman in their model and averted about 1.060 disability-adjusted life years, a measure of healthy years lost. Its cost per healthy year gained fell well below the study's pay threshold. The authors call yearly screening the best value among the options modeled, while warning the result depends on model assumptions and is not a final policy directive.
pmc-13263326:
Aiping Wu and co-authors publish a 2026 correction notice for their Scientific Reports article on liraglutide, a diabetes drug, and artery disease linked to high cholesterol. The original paper reported that the drug reduces adhesion between vessel-lining cells and white blood cells.

The notice fixes labeling mistakes made while assembling figures. Panels in Figure 6 carried the wrong condition labels and now show the correct ones for treated and untreated cells. Figure 8 also contained incorrect data, which has been replaced with data matching the main text. Readers can view the original, incorrect figures in the notice for the record. The article itself has been corrected.
pmc-13263626:
Olivia Klapec and colleagues lay out a randomized trial to settle whether fruit-flavored e-cigarettes help smokers quit better than the flavors regulators allow. Pod fruit flavors were restricted despite hints they aid switching. Their 2026 protocol recruits daily smokers with repeated failed quit attempts who want to switch.

Participants draw fruit, menthol, or tobacco pods for six weeks, plus a structured switching plan. Lab sessions first measure how rewarding each flavor feels against real cigarettes. Daily cigarette counts through the switch and at twenty-six weeks form the main outcome, verified by breath carbon monoxide. The design also tests whether reward explains any flavor advantage.
pmc-13263726:
Xiang-ting Shi and colleagues introduce a new primrose from Guizhou, Primula xingyiensis, and fit it into its section. Section Carolinella primroses are hairy, powder-free plants with bell-shaped calyces. Their 2026 description rests on the newcomer's gracile build and unusual flowers.

Slender stems, small leaves furred on both sides, and long-styled single-form flowers set it apart. Its corolla stretches seven to eight times the calyx length, a striking proportion. The authors supply distribution details, a conservation assessment, and a key to every known species in the section. The key turns the paper into a field tool, not just an announcement.
pmc-13263826:
Lijuan Huang and colleagues asked in 2026 whether people with more muscle for their height carry more kidney stones, in a large Chinese health screening cohort. Stones appeared in about four percent of those screened. After adjustment, each step up in the muscle index carried a modest rise in stone odds. The top muscle quartile showed roughly seventy percent higher odds than the bottom quartile. The link held across most subgroups but vanished among participants with diabetes. Because the study froze one moment in time, the authors refuse any causal claim. They suggest muscle index deserves a place in screening assessments while prospective work tests the direction of effect.
pmc-13264126:
Jiahui Zeng and colleagues examine ultrasound-assisted extraction of uranium and rare earth elements from low-grade material in a 2026 paper. Low-grade resources and tailings could supplement supply if metals can be leached out efficiently and with less waste left behind.

The study focus, signaled by its keywords, combines alkali pretreatment, acid leaching and ultrasound to co-extract both uranium and rare earths together. Understanding how sound waves enhance the leaching steps could improve recovery from poor ores. Readers should note the excerpt centers on background and aims rather than final recovery figures.
pmc-13264426:
João Castro Mendes and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a hip replacement that lasted well for 16 years despite a shaky start. The patient had a hip socket shaped wrong from birth and bad joint wear. Surgeons used a metal support ring, but part of it was left with poor bone cover.

The patient was a 59-year-old man treated in 2010. Surgeons packed ground bone from his own thigh bone head around the bare part of the ring. At 16 years he had no pain and full use of the hip. Scans showed the graft had joined the bone, with no loosening. The authors say such grafts can make up for weak first cover.
pmc-13264526:
Jennifer C Wong wrote a 2026 commentary on a mouse study of Dravet syndrome, a severe form of epilepsy that starts in early life. The condition also brings slow development, poor body temperature control, and bad sleep. Wong sums up work by Fadila and colleagues on how sleep and temperature link in this illness.

In the mouse model, core body temperature was lower than normal. Healthy mice cooled as they fell asleep, but the Dravet mice did not. Warmth helped healthy mice sleep, yet not the sick ones. Restoring the faulty gene in the brain, or stimulating a brain area that controls heat, brought back the warmth effect. Wong highlights the hypothalamus as a key site.
pmc-13264626:
Manar T Ali and colleagues published a 2026 study of Sphagneticola trilobata, an ornamental plant used in folk medicine. They compared the chemistry of its flowerheads and leaves for the first time in full. The goal was to explain why the two parts differ in antioxidant power, the ability to block cell damage from reactive molecules.

Using advanced chemical profiling, they tentatively named 86 compounds, and 18 were new records for this plant. Flowerheads were rich in flavonoids and phenolic acids, while leaves held more terpene compounds. In three lab tests, flowerheads showed clearly stronger antioxidant action. Four compounds stood out as markers of that strength. The authors suggest flowerheads as a source of natural antioxidants for drugs or cosmetics.
pmc-13264726:
Mustafa Khanbhai, Michael Faheem and Shweta Aggarwal describe a combined mastectomy and reconstruction technique for high-risk patients in a 2026 surgical paper. Standard implant or free-flap reconstruction can be unsafe for patients with obesity and multiple illnesses because of long operations and complication risk. A flap from the side chest wall, fed by a perforator artery, adds outer fullness.

pmc-13264926:
Nelson Ositadimma Oranye and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of school and community mental health programmes. The review targets children aged five to nineteen in marginalised or underserved groups. School pressures can cause distress, which often hits these children hardest. Where a programme runs may affect how well it works.

Reviewers will search major databases for randomised trials of programmes that aim to prevent depression, anxiety, and stress. Two reviewers will screen studies and extract data independently. Quality checks, pooled analyses, and subgroup comparisons are planned. The goal is fair evidence on which setting serves underserved children better.
pmc-13266226:
Dana C Ross and colleagues trial an online hybrid therapy for adults with trauma symptoms from childhood interpersonal harm, published in 2026. Many affected adults face barriers to trauma-specific care. The Trauma PORTAL blends self-paced learning modules with optional virtual group sessions. The Ontario trial randomised participants against usual care.

Eight modules and eight weekly group sessions formed the intervention. The main outcome was self-reported symptom severity at eight weeks. Clinician ratings, emotion regulation, mood, and self-compassion were secondary outcomes. Assessors were masked to group assignment. People with lived experience helped develop the programme, broadening access by design.
pmc-13266726:
Yu Wang and colleagues build in 2026 a model that grades severity of Pneumocystis pneumonia in adults living with HIV, using chest CT scans. Standard grading relies on blood oxygen measures, which may miss how unevenly the lungs are involved. The single-center study included 96 confirmed cases, split into training and test groups.

A radiomics model, which turns scan patterns into numbers, used ten selected features from both lungs. It separated mild from moderate-to-severe disease well in training and test sets, performing at least as well as a model based on blood tests and CD4 count. The authors stress that the small sample needs outside validation before clinical use.
pmc-13266826:
Andrei I Gritsiuta and Roman V Petrov survey in 2026 the complications that follow lung removal surgery and how teams can limit their harm. About a quarter of patients in large registries face at least one complication.

Risk rises with the amount of lung removed, and whole-lung removal carries far higher death rates than lobe removal. Longer hospital stays add cost and strain for patients and systems alike. The authors argue that modern practice must anticipate problems, sort patients by risk, prevent what can be prevented, and rescue patients quickly when decline begins.
pmc-13267426:
Colin Church and colleagues report a 2026 phase 2 trial of an inhaled powder for high blood pressure in scarred lungs. The drug is a long-acting form of treprostinil, which widens lung blood vessels. Adults with pulmonary hypertension tied to interstitial lung disease were given the powder or a placebo once a day for 16 weeks.

The trial enrolled 29 patients on the drug and 10 on placebo. Most reached the top daily dose, and side effects matched those known for inhaled forms, such as cough and breathlessness. Serious side effects were less common in the drug group than in the placebo group. Fewer treated patients worsened during the trial. Walking distance and a heart strain marker also trended better, leading the authors to back further study.
pmc-13267926:
Liyong Shi and colleagues wrote a 2026 study building a risk chart for obstructive sleep apnea. In this disorder the throat closes repeatedly during sleep. Five factors made the final chart: age, sex, body mass index, platelet width spread, and a fat-sugar index from blood tests. Men, older adults, and heavier patients carried higher risk, as did those with higher values on both blood measures. The chart sorted patients with fair accuracy in both groups and matched real rates well. The authors call it an exploratory aid for sorting who most needs the full sleep study.
pmc-13268726:
Gyungah Kim and Won-Young Kim summarize in 2026 the newest Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, which reshape care from before hospital arrival through recovery after discharge. Fluid guidance keeps an early weight-based volume but stresses judging each patient's traits and rechecking often to avoid too little or too much. Pressor drugs may start alongside fluids in unstable shock. The authors present the update as practical for rich and poor settings alike.
pmc-13269226:
Heming Zheng, Yunmei Fang, and Wenfu Pan diagnose in 2026 why donated medical equipment so often sits idle in remote clinics: policy pays for devices but not for keeping them running. Using a time-driven costing model, they priced five years of operation and maintenance for portable ultrasound machines donated to a high-altitude county hospital. Travel and logistics alone swallowed most of the support budget.

When that cost is invisible, devices are delivered and abandoned, wasting money and deepening rural health gaps. The authors propose judging donations by full life-cycle cost and funding service capacity, training, and consumables alongside the hardware itself.
pmc-13269326:
Nurun N Fancy and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on two variants of the TREM2 gene that raise Alzheimer's disease risk. Immune cells from risk variant carriers responded less to rising amyloid, and brain support pathways were reduced. The two risk variants differed from each other: one raised cleanup-related genes, the other changed inflammation genes. The authors say the variants act through distinct routes.
pmc-13269826:
Cristiane Rose Rossi Mazzoni and co-authors published a trial report in 2026 on physiotherapy for pain right after cesarean birth in a Brazilian teaching hospital. Forty women were assigned at random to a posture-guidance protocol or standard care. Pain during movements was scored before and 24 hours later.

The authors class the simple protocol as effective early help.
pmc-13270226:
Quan-Ying Dong and co-authors revise in 2026 a group of insect-parasitizing fungi from Yunnan, China, that prey mostly on beetle larvae. pmc-13270626:
Amira S. Eissa led a 2026 journal article on coatings for titanium implants, tested in rabbits. The coatings joined carbon nanotubes, tiny tubes prized for their large surface area, with hydroxyapatite, a mineral that helps bone grow onto a surface. The question was whether they speed early bone bonding.

Thirty rabbits received uncoated discs, nanotube-coated discs, or discs with nanotubes plus one percent hydroxyapatite, set into jaw defects. After four weeks, both coated types showed more bone touching the implant and more new bone area than uncoated discs. Adding the mineral gave no extra gain over nanotubes alone within that period.
pmc-13271126:
Tao Chen is lead author of a 2026 journal article on delivering curcumin, a plant compound, through the nose to treat depression. Standard antidepressants often work poorly, and curcumin itself reaches the brain badly. The authors packed pure curcumin into tiny fat-based particles that self-assemble, aiming them at the brain.

The particles were evenly round, about 116 nanometres wide, and loaded the drug efficiently with slow release. Cell uptake reached 41.47 percent, more than double plain curcumin, and the particles protected stressed cells with stronger anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. In a mouse depression model, the nasal particles eased depressive-like behaviour more effectively, the authors report, offering a promising brain-targeted approach.
pmc-13271426:
Marion Dagenais is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study titled I See What Others Don't See When They Look at Me, on body perception disturbances in chronic non-cancer pain. Such disturbances, like feeling a limb is the wrong size, are well known in one pain syndrome but little studied across chronic pain in general.

The team interviewed 15 adults, aged 26 to 76, with conditions including fibromyalgia, muscle and joint pain, migraine, and endometriosis. Every participant reported some disturbance. Six themes emerged. They covered distorted body features, altered position awareness, and attention shifting toward or away from pain. They also covered troubled emotions about the body, neglect-like symptoms, and a disturbed sense of control over one's own body.
pmc-13271826:
Paul Leighton is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on interviews, of patient experiences of Dupuytren's contracture, a condition that bends fingers toward the palm, and its treatment. Participants came from the DISC trial, which compared surgery with collagenase, an injected enzyme that breaks down the cord causing the bend.

Forty-five participants were interviewed three to six months after treatment. Most had lived with the contracture for a long time, seeking help only when practical tasks grew hard or appearance bothered them. Most reported improvement whatever the treatment. Collagenase patients more often said they would choose it again over surgery, accepting an imperfect result for an easier experience, and many would accept repeated treatments.
pmc-13271926:
Zhen Li and colleagues profile in 2026 the killing molecules carried by immune cells in patients awaiting liver and bile duct surgery. Two proteins, perforin and granzyme B, let killer T cells and natural killer cells destroy target cells. Whether disease type or personal factors shape their levels was unknown.

The team tested six marker combinations in 245 surgical inpatients across six disease groups. Natural killer cells carried the markers most strongly, and levels did not differ by disease once age was considered. All markers rose with age, pointing to immune aging as the main driver. One marker did separate severe from milder pancreas inflammation cases fairly well.
pmc-13272026:
Zinnia Sen Yen Lai and coauthors describe in 2026 a woman whose genetic syndrome showed two features not previously reported with it. HIST1H1E syndrome, caused by a shifted reading frame in one gene copy, affects development and intellect. Eye problems noted before were limited to squint and focusing errors.

The 51-year-old woman had intellectual disability, repeated falls, and worsening vision. Examination found pale optic discs in both eyes, patchy field loss, and thinning of retinal nerve layers on scans. Brain imaging showed shrinkage of the optic nerves and the cerebellum. Gene sequencing confirmed the syndrome variant, widening its known picture toward nerve degeneration.
pmc-13272226:
Jacopo Pasquini is lead author of a 2026 review on the noradrenergic system in Parkinson's disease. Noradrenaline activity in the brain shapes behaviour, thinking, movement, arousal, and sleep, and this review summarises imaging evidence on how that system fails in Parkinson's and what symptoms follow.

Brain scans show loss of signal in the locus coeruleus, a small noradrenaline hub, and positron emission scans show noradrenergic nerve loss across deep and surface brain areas. More severe noradrenergic dysfunction tracks with cognitive decline, apathy, acting out dreams in sleep, and autonomic problems, while tremor-dominant Parkinson's keeps better transmission. Noradrenergic failure also feeds tremor and freezing of gait. Drug treatment for these features still lags, the authors note.
pmc-13272326:
Sihan Li and coauthors test in 2026 whether tumor tissue type changes how well first-line immune checkpoint drugs work in advanced lung cancer. These drugs are now standard first treatment, yet squamous and non-squamous tumors may respond differently to particular regimens. A network method can rank many drug combinations never compared directly.

The analysis pooled 41 phase three trials with 23,871 patients and 31 drug regimens. Rankings differed sharply by tissue type; one chemo-immunotherapy pair topped the non-squamous list while placing differently in squamous disease. The authors advise matching regimen choice to histology rather than treating lung cancer as one uniform group.
pmc-13272726:
Harsh Agrawal leads a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing one-stent and two-stent methods for treating heart artery branch points. In the provisional method, one stent is placed first and a second only if needed. Earlier long-term reviews had favored that simpler approach.

The team pooled 15 randomised trials with 6,978 patients, searching major databases through September 2025. Risks of death, heart attack, repeat treatment, stent clots, and major events did not differ clearly between methods. The authors say choice should depend on the lesion shape, case complexity, and operator skill, and warn that their result does not prove the two methods are equal.
pmc-13273026:
Siwar Belhaj Salem leads a 2026 case report of a healthy 24-year-old man whose community-acquired pneumonia first appeared as belly pain. He arrived with severe pain in the upper right abdomen and fever. Pneumonia usually causes cough, chest pain, and breathlessness, so belly pain can mislead clinicians.

His condition worsened, with breathlessness and a productive cough emerging. Examination and a chest X-ray showed a right lower lobe infiltrate, and sputum tests pointed to Streptococcus pneumoniae. He recovered with intravenous fluoroquinolone treatment and oral antibiotics on discharge. The authors stress that pneumonia belongs in the diagnosis list for acute belly pain to avoid delay.
pmc-13273726:
Jian Lu and co-authors tested a synthetic compound against bone loss in a 2026 study. After menopause, falling estrogen speeds the cells that eat bone, called osteoclasts, and bones thin. A signaling step in which the protein TRAF6 tags itself helps drive that overactivity, making it a drug target.

Their compound, SN-2, blocked osteoclast formation from precursor cells in a dose dependent way and reduced the rings these cells use to dissolve bone. It stopped the TRAF6 self tagging, weakened its grip on a partner kinase, and quieted two downstream pathways. In mice that had their ovaries removed to mimic menopause, SN-2 eased bone loss, improved femur strength measures, and curbed osteoclast formation. The authors propose it for diseases of excess bone resorption.
pmc-13274026:
Ahmed A Abd-Rabou and Amr E Edris present a 2026 journal article on tiny oil droplets carrying plant compounds against colon cancer cells. They combined quercetin, a plant chemical, with cold-pressed orange peel oil. The mix was made to form a nanoemulsion, droplets so small they spread evenly in water.

Orange oil proved to be eighty-nine percent d-limonene, and the droplets trapped over ninety-three percent of both compounds. In lab tests on two colorectal cancer cell lines, the formulated mix killed more cancer cells and raised cell-death signals more than the plain compounds. A version built with two surfactants worked best, lowering some growth proteins while raising a death-promoting one.
pmc-13274126:
Nina B Masters and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on uptake of the Shingrix shingles vaccine in newly eligible adults. The two-dose vaccine has been advised for healthy adults from age fifty since 2017. The team used linked health records and claims to track who started and finished the series.

Among 153,899 adults who turned fifty between 2018 and 2024, only 9.9 percent got a first dose within a year. That share climbed from 2.6 percent for the 2018 group to 14.0 percent for 2024. Getting a flu shot in the fiftieth year was the strongest single predictor of starting. Black adults, rural residents, and Medicaid enrollees had lower uptake.
pmc-13275226:
Daniele Fabbri and co-authors reviewed the role of European Apodemus mice in vector borne zoonoses in a 2026 narrative review. These wood mice are among the most widespread small mammals in Europe and host many ticks and other vectors. They help maintain bacteria, viruses, and protozoa that can infect people.

The review finds their roles vary sharply by pathogen. They are confirmed reservoirs for some Borrelia types and for Neoehrlichia mikurensis, while for other agents their part is indirect or depends on habitat and local conditions. Crowding, community mix, forest cover, and climate all shape contact between mice, vectors, and people. The authors warn that carriage rates alone do not prove reservoir strength, and they argue for a One Health view.
pmc-13275626:
Benhard Christopher Simanjuntak and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of treating a small urine leak after hypospadias repair in children without surgery. Hypospadias is a birth defect of the urethra, and a fistula, a tiny leaking channel, is a known complication usually fixed by another operation. The review gathered studies of tissue adhesives, fibrin glue, or reinserting a catheter for leaks up to two millimeters wide in patients under eighteen.

Only five studies covering seventy-three patients qualified, and differences between them blocked any pooled success rate. Individual closure rates in the main series ran from 53.8 to 62.5 percent, best for leaks found within fourteen days of catheter removal. Side effects were minor, and one trial priced glue treatment at about 9.3 percent of surgery's cost, but most studies carried high bias risk.
pmc-13276226:
Rahma Esmael and co-authors present a 2026 hospital study on deaths among adults on breathing machines in eastern Ethiopia. Mechanical ventilation keeps critically ill patients alive, but death rates stay high where resources are scarce. Which factors shorten survival in such settings was poorly documented.

The team reviewed records of five hundred eighty-six ventilated adults at one large hospital. Deaths occurred at a rate of roughly seven per one hundred patient-days. Low platelet counts, heart and circulation failure during ventilation, and needing resuscitation all raised the risk of dying sooner. So did use of blood-pressure-raising drugs and higher oxygen levels at the start. A feeding tube into the stomach was linked to lower risk. The authors urge close watching and care of the highest-risk patients.
pmc-13276326:
Wujin Li and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on stopping lung cancer spread with a broccoli compound delivered in nanoparticles. Sulforaphane, found in cruciferous vegetables, can slow metastasis, the spread of cancer, but it breaks down too easily for clinic use. The team traced how it works in non-small cell lung cancer.

They found a gene switch called SPI1 turns up a small RNA that drives cancer cells to invade and migrate. Sulforaphane binds the switch directly and quiets the small RNA, blunting spread. To protect the fragile compound, the team loaded it into porous silica nanoparticles coated with two targeting molecules. The particles stayed stable, entered tumor cells well, and homed to tumors. In mouse models they fought metastasis better than the free compound. The authors see clinical potential in the delivery system.
pmc-13276426:
Yi-Tian Fu and colleagues map the genetics of Toxoplasma gondii in China in a 2026 study. The parasite infects people and many animals, and older typing methods blur fine genetic differences. Sharper typing can reveal hidden diversity and how strains move between hosts.

Ninety-six samples from pigs, cats, sheep, birds, bats, and captive wildlife across twelve provinces were typed at sixteen markers. One lineage, ToxoDB number 9, dominated yet varied widely within itself. A North American forest lineage turned up in a captive caracal, far outside its known range. Genetic patterns showed much mixing with little geographic structure, which supports routine molecular monitoring.
pmc-13276726:
Haejin Hong and colleagues sort stress-exposed adults into distinct types using machine learning, in a 2026 study. People react to stress in very different ways, and standard diagnoses may miss those patterns. A data-driven grouping could match support to the biology each group carries.

Eight hundred nine adults gave clinical data, blood samples, and structural brain scans. Clustering found three groups: a multi-risk group with depression, anxiety, and poor sleep; an alcohol-focused group; and a resilient low-risk group. Classifiers separated the groups well using biology alone. The multi-risk group showed frontal brain changes and disturbed cortisol, while the alcohol group showed metabolic shifts and different frontal patterns.
pmc-13277226:
Christine Raouf George Mikhail leads a 2026 survey of recurring mouth ulcers among dental students in Egypt. The condition, called recurrent aphthous stomatitis, causes repeated painful sores inside the mouth. Among 150 fourth-year students at King Salman International University, 128 answered questions on health, habits, and stress.

About sixty-nine percent had experienced the ulcers. A family history of the sores was by far the strongest predictor, pointing to a genetic link. Having other dental problems and daily toothbrushing also raised the odds, a brushing link the authors say needs more study. Stress scores, though, showed no firm tie to the ulcers in this group, despite stress often being blamed.
pmc-13277426:
Xiujiao Wei and Qinghong Duan present a 2026 case report of a young man who suddenly lost movement in all four limbs after neck massage. The healthy 33-year-old had a week of neck pain that worsened over three days of massage. Exam found limp paralysis of the legs, weakness in the arms, and loss of feeling below the upper chest.

A first CT scan looked normal, but detail was blurred near the shoulders. An emergency MRI showed a blood collection pressing on the spinal cord from the neck to the upper back, and he had urgent surgery to relieve the pressure. A normal CT does not rule out such compression, the authors warn, and massage on a painful neck deserves caution.
pmc-13277626:
Evangelos Danopoulos and co-authors appraise policy recommendations inside climate research papers in a 2026 systematic review. Studies on green energy and transport increasingly end with advice for policymakers. Whether that advice is communicated with the same rigour as the findings had never been checked.

Four databases were searched for work published since 2019, and twenty-three studies passed screening. A critical appraisal tool rated the policy recommendations poor in every included study. Papers leaned toward advocacy over neutral information, and uncertainties were rarely disclosed honestly. Findings and conclusions were communicated far better than the recommendations themselves. The authors propose a reporting guideline for evidence-based policy advice in journals.
pmc-13277826:
Arnaud Duport leads a 2026 protocol for a study of how movement changes as short-term pain becomes lasting pain. Long-term pain affects over thirty percent of people worldwide, and altered movement may help pain persist. The plan follows 150 healthy adults given a controlled muscle pain injection in a forearm muscle, across four visits.

Researchers will track wrist movement patterns and muscle activity, plus brain excitability measured with magnetic pulses and scalp recordings. Self-reports will cover pain, fear of movement, beliefs, and coping. The study has no results yet, as a protocol. Its aim is to find brain and movement markers that could guide more personal pain treatment later.
pmc-13278326:
Kazuma Iwasaki leads a 2026 case report of a sinus cyst that appeared twenty-eight years after repair of a cheekbone fracture. A cyst grew in the left maxillary sinus of a patient with worsening left cheek pain. At the original injury, a displaced wall of the sinus and an untreated eye socket floor fracture had formed a bony partition, sealing off a mucus-lined cavity.

Infection of the old metal plate was first suspected, but pain persisted after plate removal. Scans then showed the partition and an expanding cyst eroding bone. Surgeons removed the partition with nose specialists, reopening drainage into the sinus, and rebuilt the eye socket floor with hip bone. Pain resolved and no recurrence appeared at one year.
pmc-13278426:
Elisa Liberati leads a 2026 protocol for a qualitative study of MDMA, a psychedelic drug being tested as an aid to psychotherapy for post-traumatic stress disorder. Trial results are encouraging, but how the drug works on the mind is poorly understood. About twenty-five experienced psychodynamic therapists will receive two MDMA doses under controlled conditions and report their experiences in depth. As a protocol, the study reports no results yet.

Interviews before, during, and after sessions, plus daily journals, will feed a model of the drug's psychological mechanisms. Standard measures of reflective functioning add a further lens. Treating therapists as expert observers of their own minds is the design's distinctive bet, the authors explain.
pmc-13278926:
Kenneth Maiese reviews agitation, anxiety, and Alzheimer disease through the lens of ageing biology in a 2026 article. Mood problems in dementia strain patients and carers, and current treatments ease symptoms without stopping disease. Ageing populations mean far more people will face both conditions together.

The review gathers work on autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and related cell-death pathways. Gut microbes, diabetes-linked metabolism, the APOE gene, oxidative stress, and inflamed support cells all enter the picture. Newer angles include GLP-1 drugs and artificial intelligence for diagnosis and drug hunting. Maiese argues that shared underlying pathways, rather than symptoms alone, offer the best route to treatments that change disease course.
pmc-13279426:
Gabriella Bottari and colleagues published a 2026 case series describing the first use of a low-volume blood purification cartridge in newborns and small infants with septic shock. Hemoadsorption devices, which filter inflammatory and toxic substances from blood, were designed for adults and can endanger tiny patients. The series covers four children treated in intensive care: two newborns weighing under four kilograms and two infants, all on standard antibiotics and circulation drugs, with kidney support alongside.

Two of the four children also needed ECMO, a heart-lung support circuit, for severe organ failure. Three of the four survived, and no major adverse events were blamed on the cartridge. The one death was judged unrelated. The authors are careful to claim feasibility and safety only, since every child received many treatments at once. They call for larger studies before the technique can be recommended for the smallest patients in septic shock.
pmc-13279526:
Yunhui Xiang and colleagues published a 2026 review on Disease X, the placeholder name for a future pandemic from a pathogen nobody has yet identified. A 2026 Nipah virus outbreak in West Bengal, India, opens the review, an example of how known priority threats keep resurfacing. COVID-19 showed what an unknown pathogen can do, the authors argue, yet the world still lacks a coordinated, pre-emptive strategy.

Their framework rests on a One Health continuum linking surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment across human, animal, and environmental settings. Signals at any interface feed real-time tracking and immune profiling. That intelligence would trigger non-drug interventions at the right moment, steer mathematical models, and direct rapid countermeasures where they matter. Resilient infrastructure, fair data sharing, and governance built on global collaboration complete the design. The authors present preparedness as an operating system to run continuously, not a plan drafted after disaster begins.
pmc-13279626:
Raphaël Ouellet and colleagues published a 2026 study of how people with disabilities took part in an inclusive ultra-trail project. Over two years, a mixed team trained at trail events across Quebec. The team then attempted a 105-kilometer ultra-trail on Réunion Island. The study asked how far members felt choice, belonging, challenge, engagement, skill growth, and meaning. Twenty-three people took part, three with disabilities. The team used interviews and field observation.

Four themes organized the accounts. One covered the human experience of a diverse group. Another covered keeping commitment through a long preparation. A third covered the pull of motives and feelings around joining. A fourth covered the meaning of raising public awareness. Real inclusion, a meaningful role, and a supportive group climate helped involvement. The authors urge trail programs to build on those lived elements.
pmc-13280126:
Feifei Yuan and colleagues report a 2026 study of newborn muscle vesicles to rejuvenate aged muscle. Muscle aging leads to sarcopenia, loss of muscle mass and strength, tied to cell aging and power core flaws. Newborn muscle regrows strongly, and its extracellular vesicles, tiny cell sent parcels, may carry that power. The team isolated such vesicles for the first time and loaded them in a bilayer microneedle patch for aged mice.

In dish tests, the vesicles eased fat acid driven cell aging, power flaws and fat build in muscle cells. In aged mice, the patch boosted power core function and cut muscle aging, scarring and fat deposits. A small RNA in the vesicles, miR-542-3p, drove the effect by two routes. It curbed a fat gene pair and woke a fuel pathway via a second target. Needle patch delivery puts the cure right in the muscle.
pmc-13280226:
Attia A. Yaseen and colleagues report a 2026 study of plant nanofibers in edible films for bread packaging. Cellulose nanofibers were made from sunflower heads and pomegranate peels by chemical and physical steps. The fibres joined carboxymethyl cellulose films with clove, cumin or cinnamon oils. The aim was active packaging, films that guard food and fight germs. Microscope checks showed even fibres six to fifteen nanometres wide.

Crystal shares were near sixty nine percent for sunflower and near seventy three percent for pomegranate fibres. Clove oil held the top phenol level and cell guard acts, while cinnamon oil fought germs best. At ten percent sunflower fibre load, film tensile strength rose by one hundred seventy four percent. Stiffness rose by two hundred fifty six percent as well. Bread was coated with the best films to test real use. Farm waste fibres can armour food films.
pmc-13280526:
Yuxiu Huang and team give a 2026 bioinformatics analysis of NCAPH in endometrial cancer. NCAPH is a part of the condensin complex, a protein set that packs chromosomes for cell division. New evidence links it to mitosis control and tumour growth. Its levels and clinical weight in endometrial cancer were not well mapped. The study checks its levels, mutation map, co expressed gene nets and prognostic weight in an integrated way.

Levels were checked in pan cancer and endometrial cohorts from two large databases, TCGA and GTEx. Mutation checks used an R software tool for genome files. Co expressed genes fed functional enrichment checks. Gene set scores weighed links between NCAPH levels and pathway scores. An immune resource checked links with tumour infiltrating immune cell counts. Survival checks weighed prognostic weight. Such data maps can nominate NCAPH as a marker worth lab proof.
pmc-13280626:
Laith N AL-Eitan and colleagues published a genetics study in 2026 on breast cancer risk in women in Jordan. They looked at three genes with key jobs in the body. One gene helps control blood pressure, one helps cells handle stress damage, and one helps run the daily body clock.

The team tested blood from three hundred women with breast cancer and three hundred healthy women. One form of the blood pressure gene was linked to a much higher risk of breast cancer. The other two genes showed no such link. The authors say that gene form could one day serve as a warning marker, though more work is needed.
pmc-13280726:
Wang Bo and colleagues published a 2026 paper presenting DuoMod-Net, a learning framework for medical image segmentation when few images are labeled and rare structures dominate. In scans of the abdomen, background pixels and common organs swamp small organs, biasing training twice over: gradients favor the majority, and rare classes get thin feature representations. Their design attacks both problems with two components.

The first rebalances the loss on a logarithmic scale, treating the background as a neutral pivot so foreground organs keep their differences. The second exploits disagreement between models as a geometric signal, expanding the feature space during training so decision boundaries retreat to safer positions. That expansion is removed when the model is deployed. Tested with 5, 10, or 20 percent of data labeled, the system improved rare-class accuracy, cut catastrophic misses, and generalized to unseen datasets without retraining. The authors aim it at clinics where annotation is scarcest.
pmc-13280926:
Linling Chen and Yongjia Wu published a 2026 retrospective study of chest CT scanning for COVID-19 care when PCR testing was scarce. Fifty symptomatic patients treated between December 2022 and June 2023 received non-contrast chest scans, read by radiologists who graded the likelihood that findings represented COVID-19 and their severity. The team compared scan impressions with PCR results and recorded how the imaging steered management in emergency and intensive care.

Patients averaged 67.2 years old, and about two thirds were men. Ground-glass opacity, a hazy lung pattern, was the commonest finding at 56.8 percent, usually spread across several lobes on both sides and toward the lung edges. Two scan phenotypes emerged. The authors report high sensitivity for CT against PCR and argue scans done within five days of symptom onset sharpen precision. Severity scoring, they conclude, also helped forecast how sick patients would become and guide treatment intensity.
pmc-13281426:
Franziska E Müller and colleagues studied a serotonin switch in heart attack repair in a 2026 paper. Serotonin is best known for mood, but it also steers immune cells. After a heart attack, swelling must be tuned well for the heart to heal. The team blocked a heart artery in mice and read the damaged zone. They also checked blood cells from human heart attack patients. A serotonin receptor, a switch on cells, spiked in the wound in the first days.

The switch was rich on macrophages, the immune cells that clean wounds. Mice bred without the switch had weaker hearts two weeks on, with more swelling.
