A drug that turns the switch on helped more mice live, though heart strength in survivors did not rise. Two gene markers shifted with the switch in both mice and patients. The authors name the switch a tuning knob for post-attack swelling.
pmc-13281726:
G N Duminda Guruge and colleagues hunted risk factors for small babies in Sri Lanka in a 2026 study. Babies born small for their stage face higher risks of illness and death. The Anuradhapura district has the country's highest share of low-weight births. The team read midwife pregnancy records from 2014 to 2017 in two health areas. One hundred thirty-six mothers of small babies were matched with two hundred seventy-two mothers of average-size babies.

Five mother traits stood out on their own. Weighing little before pregnancy raised risk, and so did being very short. Risk rose at both weight extremes, thin and heavy alike. The strongest flag was a past low-weight baby, which raised odds close to fourfold. Hints tied to kin marriage, anemia, and missed folic acid faded once other factors were weighed. The authors urge food and care support before and during pregnancy.
pmc-13282126:
Jeong A Lee and co-authors report a 2026 case of heart valve surgery done through a small chest cut instead of reopening the breastbone. The patient, a forty-year-old man, had leaking of the pulmonary valve, the valve leading from the heart to the lungs. Such leaks can follow childhood repair of birth heart defects. Reopening the breastbone risks harming the heart where scar tissue sticks tightly behind it.

Surgeons worked through a small cut on the left front of the chest. They fitted a biological replacement valve, twenty-seven millimetres wide, above the natural valve ring using interrupted stitches. Tying knots behind the valve is hard in the tight space, so they used an automated fastener tool for those stitches. The authors say the case shows the small-cut approach is workable and repeatable. The fastener made the hardest stitches simpler and safer to secure.
pmc-13282926:
José Gonzalo Bravo Quiroz and colleagues described in 2026 an unusual throat growth in an 18-year-old woman. She had a lasting lump feeling in her throat, a hoarse voice, and pain on swallowing. A scope found a smooth, pale lump on the arytenoid cartilage. That cartilage is a small structure at the back of the voice box. The lump did not look like the common contact sore seen there.

Surgeons removed the lump with a blue laser during a direct look at the voice box. Lab study showed a lobular capillary hemangioma. It is a benign tangle of small blood vessels, also called pyogenic granuloma. Her symptoms cleared fully within weeks, with no return at the last check. The report urges lab proof for odd-looking throat lumps.
pmc-13283426:
Testosterone shots coincided with retinal fluid in a prolactinoma patient, Vivek Jha and colleagues caution in a 2026 case. The man had low sex drive and erection problems from a prolactin-secreting tumor. Low testosterone from the tumor led to hormone replacement as part of care.

He took a prolactin-lowering drug weekly plus testosterone shots every two weeks. After three months he developed painless blurred vision in the left eye. Scans showed fluid under the retina at the macula in that eye. Dye tests showed a focal leak with a classic smoke-stack pattern. The right eye stayed normal on all imaging checks in the report. No steroid use or other known risk factors were present.
pmc-13283826:
Jingyi Wang and a large team surveyed Chinese college dragon boat athletes in 2026 about injuries. Dragon boat racing is a traditional paddling sport with hard, repeating one-sided strokes. A nationwide electronic survey in 2024 enrolled 443 athletes, 277 men and 166 women, who recalled injuries from the prior year in detail.

About one in four athletes reported at least one injury, and 172 injury events were logged. Women had clearly higher injury rates than men per session and per training hour. Long-term overuse injuries outnumbered sudden ones. The shoulder and waist were the top sites, and most injuries came during water training, mainly in the pull and catch phases of the stroke. Most injuries were mild. The authors point prevention work at shoulder and waist protection.
pmc-13284026:
More forest and more varied landscapes support richer orchid bee life in Brazils savanna, find Fernanda G de Sousa and colleagues in 2026. Habitat loss from farming and pasture threatens pollinators and their services. Orchid bees were sampled with scent baits across varied land covers.

Sampling covered 20 landscapes across forest, savanna, edges, and farm matrix sites. A total of 728 orchid bees from 14 species were collected. Richness and numbers rose with forest cover and landscape variety. Species mix also shifted mainly with forest cover in the models. Patch shape added explanatory power for richness counts. Keeping natural cover anchors pollinator diversity.
pmc-13284426:
Mustafa Attiyah Hadid and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how synthetic biology can turn bacteria into targeted cancer treatments. Normal cancer drugs often harm healthy tissue, while engineered microbes can sense tumor signals, enter low-oxygen zones, and release toxins on site. The review compares chassis such as Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Clostridium, and Bifidobacterium.

Methods covered include toxin delivery, prodrug conversion, immune tuning, and surface display that helps bacteria bind tumors. Tools such as CRISPR/Cas9 editing, genetic logic circuits, and kill switches aim to raise safety and control. The authors weigh current clinical hurdles and argue that careful chassis choice plus precise killing designs will shape the next stage of bacterial cancer therapy.
pmc-13284826:
Lucía Ferrer Clavería and co-authors describe a 2026 allergy case of anaphylaxis after eating dragon fruit. The patient needed hospital care one hour after eating the fruit and had prior hay fever from Salsola kali pollen. Tests included skin checks with fresh fruits and pollens, plus blood measures of specific IgE by two systems.

Results confirmed sensitivity to dragon fruit, several pollens, and peach. Lab work showed the patient IgE bound many dragon fruit proteins. Blocking tests showed Salsola extract nearly erased that binding, and peach peel erased it fully. The authors conclude cross-reaction with pollen and peach likely drove the allergy, a warning as new foods spread to sensitized people.
pmc-13285026:
Mustapha Muhammad Nasiru, Aliyu Idris Muhammad, and Evans Frimpong Boateng introduce a journal collection, in a 2026 editorial, on adding nutrients to food without using heat-based processing. Heat can damage fragile vitamins and minerals, which limits how well fortified foods work. Gentler methods promise to protect nutrients while keeping food safe.

The editorial surveys methods such as high pressure, pulsed electric fields, ultrasound, and cold plasma. Contributions in the collection cover iron for dairy foods, vitamin D in sugar, and juice fortified with bee bread. Other pieces link laboratory data about genes and metabolism to meals shaped for one person. Sustainability and consumer acceptance also receive attention.
pmc-13285926:
Maiara Campolina de Miranda and co-authors test venom peptides against the fungi behind sporotrichosis in a 2026 laboratory study. The skin infection, often caught from soil or cats, faces long drug courses and growing resistance. Peptides drawn from spider and bee venoms offer a fresh line of attack worth probing in the dish.

Seven peptides faced two Sporothrix species, and all of them halted fungal growth at low doses in test wells. Melittin from bee venom hit hardest, tearing fungal membranes while stirring oxidative stress inside the cells. Paired with the standard drug itraconazole, melittin worked better than either agent alone. A skin formula built on melittin proved gentler on human cells and safe at the lowest dose in mice, a first step toward local treatment.
pmc-13286026:
Xuan An and colleagues trace how a cytokine receptor drives fiery cell death in smoke-damaged lungs in a 2026 animal and cell study. COPD lungs lose the small air sac cells that keep breathing surfaces working, and a bursting form of cell death called pyroptosis speeds that loss. The team asked whether the receptor for interleukin-17, found on those very cells, pulls the trigger.

Mice bred without the receptor in their air sac cells suffered far less lung damage under cigarette smoke than normal mice. In dish-grown cells, dialing the receptor down shut two separate death pathways that smoke normally switches on. The signal protein alone lit only one of the two paths, which hints at a split control scheme. Blocking the receptor now stands out as a candidate way to slow the slide into COPD.
pmc-13286226:
Shun Nakahara and colleagues pool trial proof on inhaled nitric oxide for scarred lung disease in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. The gas relaxes lung vessels and might ease the breathlessness that interstitial lung disease brings, yet single trials have disagreed. Four randomized trials that set the gas against placebo were gathered and merged, with walking distance as the headline measure.

The pooled set held 274 patients, most of them on the gas, watched for a median of twelve weeks. Walking distance barely differed between gas and placebo groups once the trials were merged. Daily active minutes and total side effects also sat close between the arms, with wide margins around each estimate. On this proof the authors see no case for routine use, while granting that small trials leave room for doubt.
pmc-13286326:
Hongying Yu and co-authors fuse language models with classic prediction tools for lung cancer spread in a 2026 methods study. Whether cancer has reached the lymph nodes decides the first treatment move, yet judging that before surgery stays hard. Statistical models read the numbers well but ignore textbook knowledge, while large language models hold the knowledge and guess loosely. Their framework feeds both the patient data and the machine scores into the language models as prompts.

Records from 767 patients at a Beijing cancer hospital tested the blend. Three language models each judged every case five times, and voting rules merged the calls. The combined system beat the plain statistical models on the headline accuracy curve. Wording and reasoning settings shifted the balance between catching cases and crying wolf. The authors offer the design as a template for mixing stored medical knowledge with patient data.
pmc-13286926:
Lin Cai and a very large team report a phase 3 trial of SSGJ-608, an antibody drug that blocks the immune signal IL-17A, in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The 2026 trial randomized 770 patients in China to one of two schedules: a smaller dose every two weeks after a loading dose, or a double dose every four weeks.

After twelve weeks, both schedules cleared skin at similar high rates, with more than nine in ten patients reaching the main improvement threshold. Complete clearance arrived for roughly half of each group. Patients who had already failed a similar drug class still responded well. Common side effects involved blood fats, infections of the upper airway, and a liver enzyme. No new safety signals appeared.
pmc-13287026:
Sharon Saldanha and colleagues compare the protein film that saliva lays down on titanium implant posts in patients with no teeth against those with some teeth remaining. The 2026 study took one healing abutment from each of sixteen implant patients after time in the mouth and identified the proteins stuck to it. That film shapes bacterial growth and tissue reactions around implants.

Three proteins appeared consistently in both groups: alpha-amylase, albumin, and an antibody type. Overall profiles did not differ significantly between groups. Plaque scores, however, did associate with group membership. Local hygiene, the authors conclude, may matter more than how many teeth a patient has when it comes to the chemical environment around an implant.
pmc-13287126:
Elham Behrangi and co-authors report laser-opened skin as a drug route for stubborn fungal infections in a 2026 case series. Five patients with confirmed skin dermatophytosis had failed at least six months of oral antifungals, the standard rescue now blunted by rising resistance. At a Tehran clinic they received up to three monthly sessions of ablative fractional laser, which drills microscopic channels, followed by clotrimazole and terbinafine creams soaking through the openings.

Every patient scored the maximum on the dermatologist's improvement scale, the top grade of significant improvement, based on standardized photographs. Itching eased dramatically and satisfaction ran high across the group, aged 39 to 57. The sessions were well tolerated with no serious side effects during follow-up of up to six months. The authors propose laser-assisted delivery as a practical option when pills stop working.
pmc-13287326:
Miki Ikeda and colleagues describe in 2026 a girl aged seven carrying changes in two genes at once, SCN9A and PRRT2. The first affects a sodium channel tied to pain signalling. The second is linked to sudden movement episodes. Together they produced a mixed clinical picture.

The child had attacks of extreme pain, areas of reduced feeling, heat sensitivity, and repeated head-drop episodes that resisted treatment. Easy tiredness and low muscle tone were also present. The team read the movement attacks as a non-triggered paroxysmal disorder. They suggest the overlap may also include small fibre nerve damage, given her cold, bluish feet.
pmc-13287926:
Chong Chen and colleagues review cisplatin resistance in ovarian cancer through the lens of metal balance, in a 2026 article. Cisplatin is a platinum drug that anchors ovarian cancer treatment, yet tumors often learn to resist it. The review focuses on how cancer cells handle copper and iron inside their mitochondria, the cell's energy hubs. Both metals drive chemical stress reactions that can either protect the cell or kill it.

Too much copper can trigger a death pathway called cuproptosis, in which key energy proteins clump together. Disturbed iron handling drives a different death route, ferroptosis, through damage to cell fats. The authors connect these pathways with the metabolic rewiring that resistant tumors undergo. They argue that pushing metal balance off center could restore sensitivity to platinum drugs. The piece maps research leads rather than reporting a new trial.
pmc-13288726:
Wen Chen, Wencheng Zhou, and Songjun Liu review iron-driven cell death in women's diseases in 2026. The death type is ferroptosis. It was named in 2012. Iron fuels a buildup of lipid peroxides. Past a toxic point, the cell dies. Failed cystine import can start the chain.

Early lab models tie it to major diseases. Womb lining overgrowth is one. Endometrial cancer and endometriosis also feature. Ovarian cancer completes the set. The review sums up control machinery for each. It weighs what the paths mean for care. Knowing the switches could open drug targets. Such drugs might push sick cells to die this way.
pmc-13288926:
Sabina E W Leonard and co-authors harvest norovirus antibodies from healthy donors in a 2026 study. Noroviruses cause most acute stomach flu outbreaks, yet no licensed vaccine or antiviral exists. Their many genotypes make broad protection hard to achieve. The team used a method called LIBRA-seq to link each immune cell's receptor code to the antigen it binds. A diverse panel of capsid pieces screened blood cells from healthy people.

Twenty-five norovirus-specific monoclonal antibodies were produced from the screen. Some bound only one genotype, while others crossed many group II genotypes. Competition tests showed the antibodies target both shared and distinct spots on the capsid piece. Several broad antibodies blocked the virus piece from attaching to blood group sugars, a step in infection. Blocking strength varied by genotype even for broad binders. The panel gives vaccine testers defined tools for judging future candidates.
pmc-13289026:
Lovisa Lesand and colleagues study family diabetes and hand disease in Sweden. The Malmo Diet and Cancer cohort supplied the data. It holds 30,446 adults aged 45 to 73. Kin links came from a national register. Hand diagnoses came from hospital records.

In all, 4,150 people had a hand diagnosis. That is 14 percent of the group. Own diabetes raised hand risk in raw counts. Kin diabetes also raised it at first. After full checks, only own diabetes held. Two kin links still stood out. A sibling with diabetes tied to one stiff-hand disease. A child with diabetes tied to carpal tunnel.
pmc-13289326:
Kenni Wojujutari Ajele and Erhabor Sunday Idemudia carried out a 2026 meta-analysis on confidence in self-care among adults with type 2 diabetes. Self-efficacy means believing one can handle daily tasks. The authors pooled work linking that belief to self-care habits and to HbA1c, a blood marker of long-term sugar control.

Searches of six databases from 2007 to 2024 found 62 studies with 19 231 people for pooling. Higher confidence tied to better self-care and to lower HbA1c values across studies. Diabetes-specific confidence scales showed the tightest link with self-care of all tools. Links ran stronger soon after diagnosis and in some low-income East Asian groups. The authors argue that building confidence should be a direct goal of diabetes support.
pmc-13290526:
Filmmakers' happiness with AI tools runs through how efficient and in-control the tools leave them feeling, Wenyu Jiang and Jiaqi Zheng report in 2026. The study models creative satisfaction as the outcome of tool functionality, human-AI collaboration, and learning cost.

Four mediation paths emerged: functionality raised satisfaction by way of efficiency gains, autonomy gains, or both, and collaboration worked through the same two channels. Gender split the picture. Female directors leaned more on tool functionality and smooth collaboration, while male directors weighted autonomy more heavily. How often a filmmaker used generative video tools, and how open they were to new technology, also shaped satisfaction. The authors offer the map to designers tuning AI tools for creative work.
pmc-13290626:
Ikue Kondo and colleagues relate mouth function to mild cognitive impairment in older Japanese adults in a 2026 study. Participants lived in a rural city in Niigata Prefecture and were aged sixty or older. Six mouth measures were taken, covering tongue coating, moisture, chewing, swallowing, tongue speed, and tongue pressure. Thinking was scored with a standard screening test, with low scores marking impairment.

Of 303 participants, 179 met the impairment cutoff. Three measures stayed linked to impairment after full adjustment. Fast tongue repetition, strong tongue pressure, and good chewing each lowered the odds of impairment. Tongue repetition speed also tracked test scores most closely of all six measures. Mouth moisture, coating, and the swallowing checklist showed no clear link. The authors suggest that a multidomain mouth check could flag older adults at risk of decline. They call for follow-up studies to test whether training the mouth protects the mind.
pmc-13291226:
Gene data alone can miss how proteins link in a network. Osama Mahmoud and colleagues build a 2026 method to fix that gap for brain tumor outlook. Glioblastoma is a fast, deadly brain cancer. Clear warning signals from gene data are hard to find.

Their method blends gene levels with trusted protein link maps. A model was built and locked using one atlas of cases. It was then tested on a separate Chinese atlas. Scores held up modestly outside the training set. One gene stood out as the strongest driver. High-risk tumors showed inflammation and low oxygen traits. The authors say the tool ranks risk, but needs tuning before clinic use.
pmc-13291326:
Engineered immune cells can hunt the cells that shield tumors. Thomas Landkildehus Lisle and colleagues write a 2026 letter on this plan. Many tumors hide behind a checkpoint flag called PD-L1. Natural T cells that strike that flag exist in people.

Such cells were found in healthy donors and patients. They can kill tumor and immune cells bearing the flag. A past vaccine trial using them worked well. Shots plus checkpoint drugs gave high response rates. Delivered cells may beat shots in strength and control. The team built a defined receptor from these cells. That step moves the idea toward a cell therapy product.
pmc-13292426:
Jiayin Xing and a large team compare a 2026 storytelling study across two cultures, asking whether autism shapes narrative the same way in the United States and Hong Kong. Participants narrated a wordless picture book on an eye-tracker. The US group held 56 autistic and 49 control native English speakers. Hong Kong added 24 autistic and 52 control native Cantonese speakers, matched for age.

Autistic storytellers in both cultures skipped key story parts and showed rigid gaze patterns toward social material. Cultural differences surfaced too: only the US autistic group used fewer descriptions and fewer explanations of characters' thoughts and feelings. Less social attention tracked with thinner mental-state description everywhere. The authors read the shared narrative structure problems as core to autism, while the mental-state language gap looks culturally shaped.
pmc-13292826:
Prashant Changoer and colleagues report a 2026 study of gene testing in advanced thyroid cancer at a Dutch medical center. Gene panels are used more often to guide drug choice, yet real-world benefit data remain thin.

Records covered 103 patients tested between 2014 and 2024, at diagnosis or when disease worsened. The most common changes were in TP53, found in 39.8% of patients, plus NRAS, BRAF, PTEN, and RET. Changes that could guide drugs appeared in 62.1% of patients, based on the scale the authors used. Sixteen patients got matched drugs, and over half saw tumors shrink. The authors back wider use of gene-guided care.
pmc-13292926:
Xinyu Sun and colleagues report, in 2026, a tougher way to store digital data in DNA-like strands. DNA can hold vast data in tiny space, but long strands break down fast and are hard to make at length.

The team paired circular single-stranded DNA with a lab-made cousin called FANA, picked after stress tests against heat, chemicals, and enzymes. A trained computer model helped improve an enzyme that builds FANA about 4.4 times faster than before, a gain the authors report. Hybrids resisted damage well, and stored data were read back fully even after decay. Stored genes also worked inside mammalian cells.
pmc-13293426:
Qianyao Yuan and co-authors compare, in a 2026 study, scans and tissue traits of a rare lung cancer that mixes two cell types. Adenosquamous carcinoma holds both glandular and squamous parts, acts aggressively, and is hard to spot before surgery.

Scans and records covered 27 patients with the mixed cancer, plus 40 each with pure glandular or pure squamous cancer, matched by age, sex, and smoking. Mixed tumors sat more toward the lung edge than squamous ones and spread to lymph nodes more often. Against glandular ones, they were larger and more often solid. A combined scan-plus-tissue model split the types best, aiding pre-surgery calls.
pmc-13293726:
Chadi Bourimi and co-authors untangle, in a 2026 case report, repeated urethral bleeding during sex in a 39-year-old man with no injury or fracture. Bleeding during erection usually hints at a torn penis cover or urethra, neither of which fit here.

The man was using outside testosterone. A scope showed a small focal defect in the urethra lining, and dynamic MRI found a 4 mm blood pocket with early leak from a tiny branch of a deep penile artery. With bleeding stopped on its own and the patient stable, doctors chose watchful care. Healing was complete at three months with good function.
pmc-13293926:
Xiaowei Li and coauthors survey 4,456 college students from five universities in Sichuan Province for a 2026 study on short video addiction and resilience. Mean age was 20.34 years, and 52.1% were female. Students rated video addiction, belief in a just world, meaning in life, and resilience, and the team tested chain pathways between them.

Heavier addiction predicted lower resilience. Three indirect paths mattered: through just-world belief alone, through meaning alone, and through belief then meaning in order. Together indirect paths made up 62.5% of the total link. Meaning in life was the closest correlate of resilience, which points to layered campus support.
pmc-13294126:
Yingling Luo and Tao Quan chart passing networks by pitch zone at the UEFA Women's Euro 2025 in a 2026 social network analysis. The field was split into 48 zones, and six network measures were compared by match outcome, tournament stage, score state, and match half. Four situational lenses show how space use shifts under pressure.

Winning sides built stronger bridging links and used the flanks more. As play moved from groups to knockouts, hubs shifted from the defensive third toward midfield, with steadier circulation up front. Trailing teams crowded central zones but lost local structure, while second halves showed weaker connectivity overall. Drills on wide link play follow from the patterns.
pmc-13294226:
Wang Tao and colleagues frame diabetic nerve damage as an energy failure in a 2026 review. Long nerve fibers in the common stocking-glove pattern need heavy energy supply, and high blood sugar alone no longer explains their decay. Glucose, fat, and amino acid handling all go off balance, starving both neurons and their Schwann support cells.

Anatomy, energy pathways, and fiber-support teamwork are integrated into one account of how supply and demand drift apart. Fixing a single pathway is unlikely to stop or reverse damage, the authors argue. Restoring overall energy balance in both cell types offers the stronger path to preserving nerve function.
pmc-13294426:
Marco Finocchiaro and coauthors catalog staph germs on healthy eyes in a 2026 typing study. Eye swabs from 49 adults aged 18 to 77 gave 120 germ samples. Of these, 68 proved to be staph by mass tests and gene tests. Drug strength, clone prints, and key genes were charted across three staph types.

One type, Staphylococcus aureus, made up 74% of staph finds in the reported share. Shield rates ran high for three common drugs. Close to half the strains shrugged off many drugs at once. Clone prints were highly mixed, with one clone at times shared across adults. Healthy eyes can hold drug-tough germs.
pmc-13295426:
Shakta Mani Satyam and colleagues propose a big-picture framework linking three problems usually studied apart: stubborn infections, immune dysfunction, and thinning bones, in a 2026 review. Their organizing idea casts metabolism as a shared control panel, and metformin, the familiar diabetes drug, as a hand on its dials. Metformin touches energy production in mitochondria, a master fuel sensor called AMPK, oxidative balance, and cellular recycling, all pathways implicated in both microbial persistence and bone turnover.

The authors are careful about the evidence ladder. Some mechanisms are experimentally solid, others are context-dependent hints from cell and animal work, and the combined infection-plus-bone benefit has never been tested in a proper prospective trial. Early findings suggest metformin can cramp microbes, cool excessive inflammation, and nudge bone remodeling, but each effect depends on setting. The framework is offered as a scaffold for testable hypotheses, not a proven model.
pmc-13296526:
Diana Tatarciuc and a large team map RNA-based lipid-lowering therapies against the heart risk that remains after standard treatment, in a 2026 scoping review. Genes for several blood-fat proteins drive this residual risk, and traditional drugs cannot reach some of them. The review searched four databases and kept thirty studies from over a thousand records.

RNA drugs silenced their targets strongly in the kept studies, with deep cuts in lipoprotein(a), triglycerides, and LDL cholesterol reported. Effects lasted months after each injection, and delivery chemistry aimed the drugs at liver cells. Injection-site reactions were the commonest side effect. The authors frame these agents as precise tools for risk pathways that older drugs leave untouched.
pmc-13296626:
Agnieszka J. Szczepek introduces a special journal issue on hearing impairment in a 2026 editorial. Eleven contributions trace the auditory pathway from the inner ear to the brain's cortex. Hearing loss, the editorial stresses, reaches beyond thresholds into communication, emotion, and thinking.

One pair of contributions examines how the stress hormone corticosterone alters hearing synapses, with effects that differ by sex in mouse cochlea work. Other pieces tackle sudden hearing loss, using an inner-ear protein test to detect fluid leaks behind some cases labelled unexplained. Reviews and clinical studies fill out the issue. Together they argue for integrated auditory health that joins molecular, clinical, and brain-level research.
pmc-13296926:
Shinichi Kinami and colleagues review local resection for early stomach cancer in East Asia in a 2026 article. Full stomach removal with lymph node clearance controls cancer well but leaves lasting digestive and nutritional problems. Early cancers spread to nodes rarely, so smaller operations may suit carefully chosen patients.

Sentinel node biopsy, done during surgery, can confirm that nearby nodes are clear before a limited resection proceeds. One important complication is delayed stomach emptying after the operation. Stomach shape changes seem to contribute, and meticulous closure technique can reduce the problem. The review weighs where local resection now stands and what still blocks wider adoption.
pmc-13297726:
Alexis T. Mickle and colleagues ask Canadian patients with early-stage cancer what they value when judging a new treatment, in a 2026 survey. Trials lean on overall survival, yet patients may weigh other outcomes too. One hundred three respondents chose between paired mock treatments that varied survival at five years, spread risk at two years, tissue clearance, and side effects short and long.

Higher survival drew the strongest pull, as expected. Lower spread risk and fewer side effects, above all lasting ones, also swayed choices clearly. Nearly half backed access to a drug that delays spread even before any survival gain is proven. Trial design and drug approval should count delay and comfort beside survival, the authors argue.
pmc-13298026:
Ruijun Chen and co-authors examine what resistant dextrin does to cooked Chinese rice, in a 2026 food science study. Two dextrin products were added during cooking to one japonica and one early indica variety at several levels. Measurements covered cooking behaviour, texture, taste scores, pasting, gelatinisation, protein structure, and microstructure.

Adding dextrin shortened cooking time, raised hardness, chewiness, and springiness, and lifted sensory scores as the dose grew, while several viscosity measures fell. Higher additions changed protein secondary structure and encouraged new gel-like structures in the cooked grains. The authors conclude the ingredient can shape texture and eating quality, which matters for developing functional rice products.
pmc-13298126:
Pengcheng Li and colleagues propose a way to divide road networks into control subareas for coordinated traffic signals, in a 2026 transport study. Older methods lean on local correlation or fixed layout, which can miss how congestion states spread under changing loads. Their approach uses a state-guided coloured random walk plus path entropy to model that propagation.

Subareas are chosen to minimise mismatch between node-level and subarea-level path responses. A microsimulation with dynamic loading compared the method against two established alternatives across five measures covering delay, congestion, stops, and queues. The new method scored best on every measure, which the authors read as better balance and fewer bottlenecks.
pmc-13298726:
Yalan Feng and a team catalogue the MYB transcription factor family in balloon flower, a traditional medicinal plant, in a 2026 genome study. These factors regulate growth, metabolism, and stress responses, yet the family was unmapped in this species. Computational searches plus manual checks identified 170 members, grouped into subgroups and set against a model plant.

Promoters carried many hormone and stress response elements, and several genes responded to a jasmonate treatment in both sequencing and targeted tests. Three candidates emerged as likely regulators of flavonoid production, and all three proteins sat in the cell nucleus during testing. Functional proof remains future work.
pmc-13299726:
Oğuz Tavşan and colleagues compare root canal treatment against gum treatment for quality of life and sleep, in a 2026 prospective study. Patients completed standard oral health and sleep questionnaires before treatment and three weeks after. Seventy-four people received endodontic care and ninety received periodontal care at the study clinics.

Both treatments significantly improved oral quality-of-life scores and most sleep components. One domain favoured gum treatment, another favoured root canal treatment, and overall scores showed no significant difference between groups. Sleep medication use stayed unchanged in the gum group. The authors present both options as supporting short-term patient-reported gains for centred decision-making.
pmc-13299926:
Yufeng Liu and Suhong Liu build a fine-grained mosquito habitat map for chikungunya risk in the western Greater Bay Area after its 2025 outbreak, in a 2026 remote sensing study. Satellite indicators fed a weighted suitability index at ten-metre resolution, with weights learned by contrasting street-level case locations against random background points.

Humidity and water conditions weighed more heavily than vegetation or temperature. Case locations generally scored higher than background points, and a global risk map agreed moderately at broad scale. Leftover mismatch pointed to human activity, transport links, and healthcare access as missing drivers. The authors offer the framework for targeted surveillance and vector control.
pmc-13300026:
Sixteen seasons of United States influenza hospital data form the basis of a 2026 analysis by Hayden D. Hedman. Working with FluSurv-NET records from 2009–2010 through 2024–2025, Hedman split the timeline into pre-pandemic, disruption, and recovery phases. The aim was to measure how burden, seasonal timing, and racial gaps changed across the COVID-19 years.

Peak weekly hospitalization rates nearly doubled after the pandemic, rising from 5.1 to 11.1 per 100,000 people. Seasonal peaks also arrived earlier, and yearly patterns grew far more regular. Black patients faced rates roughly twice those of White patients in every phase. Forecasting and anomaly tools both flagged recent seasons as departures from pre-pandemic expectations.
pmc-13300926:
A cheap index built from two routine blood values may flag completely blocked heart arteries, Yan Li and colleagues report in a 2026 retrospective study. They reviewed 1,157 coronary angiography patients treated at Beijing Chaoyang Hospital between January 2024 and January 2026. The triglyceride–glucose index, a stand-in for insulin resistance, was compared between 317 patients with chronic total occlusion and 840 without.

Patients with a blocked artery averaged a TyG index of 8.98 against 8.79 in the others. Each step up in the index raised occlusion odds, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.377 overall. The link held across age, sex, and health subgroups, bending rather than running straight in dose-response curves.
pmc-13301126:
Life at the edge of survival invents unusual chemistry, and Daniela Giordano introduces a 2026 special issue of Marine Drugs devoted to bioactive molecules from extreme environments. The editorial frames the third edition of a series running since 2019, set against a MarinLit catalogue now listing 44,710 marine compounds.

Hydrothermal vents, briny basins, polar seas, and the deep ocean push organisms toward novel defenses and signals with drug, cosmetic, and industrial promise. The issue gathers eleven contributions, eight original studies and three reviews, spanning those harsh habitats. Giordano's overview threads the papers together and points readers toward the work closest to their own questions, while noting how much remains unexplored.
pmc-13301326:
L Dinshaw and co-authors apply focal pulsed field ablation to dangerous rhythms arising in the wall between the ventricles in a 2026 case series. Septal ventricular tachycardia in scarred hearts resists drugs and sits deep, where heat based burns struggle to reach. Eight consecutive patients with structural heart disease, three quarters of them with non ischemic muscle disease, received monopolar pulsed field deliveries through a catheter at twenty-five amperes.

Every procedure succeeded acutely, with the target rhythm stopped in all eight patients. Procedures averaged about 118 minutes with roughly fifty-nine applications each, brisk for this difficult territory. One patient developed a slower ventricular rhythm within three months, and one suffered a pericardial tamponade, the series's major complication. The authors present focal pulsed field energy as fast and effective for a subgroup that badly needs options, while the single tamponade keeps the safety ledger honest.
pmc-13301926:
K Misonou and colleagues report, in a 2026 Japanese study, on giving very elderly pacemaker patients a leadless device instead of replacing a worn-out battery unit. Opening the chest pocket for a generator swap carries infection risk when skin is fragile or dementia is present. A leadless device sits inside the heart and avoids the pocket entirely.

Seventy-one consecutive patients received the swap approach between 2017 and 2025, at an average age close to ninety. Most procedures took under twenty minutes, and the paced trace width barely changed after implantation. Two complications occurred, one fluid build-up around the heart and one threshold rise needing a new device, with no infections seen. Hospital stay averaged about three days, shorter than typical generator replacement.
pmc-13302026:
Operating early on a squeezed cervical cord paid off for most patients in a 2026 Italian case series by Michele Incerti and colleagues. Fifty-one people had neck spine surgery for degenerative cervical myelopathy at the Policlinico di Monza between 2020 and 2023. Three quarters started with mild cord scores, and recovery was tracked with neurological scales and the SF-36 survey.

At follow-up, sixty-five percent had recovered fully, twenty-nine percent improved, and the rest held steady, with nobody worse. A mild starting score independently predicted complete recovery in adjusted analysis. Quality-of-life gains showed in mood, social life, pain, and general health, strongest in mild cases. Complications were few, at 5.8 percent, and limited to passing swallowing trouble.
pmc-13302426:
Curved magnetic fields could let MRI scanners image just the region that matters, Emre Kopanoglu and colleagues propose in a 2026 methods study. Nonlinear gradients encode space along two directions at once, so standard slice pulses can excite rounded sub-volumes directly. The team worked out the smallest field of view a study must encode and tested a Z2 harmonic field in simulations and phantom scans.

Against one-dimensional slice selection, scan time fell while tissue heating, measured as SAR, stayed unchanged. Against two-dimensional selective pulses, the method won on SAR, echo time, and scan time together. Faster reduced-volume imaging without exotic pulses is the practical promise for SAR-limited sequences.
pmc-13302826:
Salvatore Altavilla and co-authors report, in a 2026 observational study, risk-based screening for gut carriage of bacteria resistant to last-resort carbapenem antibiotics before hospital admission. In regions where such bacteria circulate widely, spotting carriers early guides isolation and bed planning. Screening targeted patients with preset risk factors rather than everyone.

The programme ran through 2025 at one centre in a high-burden European setting. Of nearly two thousand seven hundred admission candidates, about eleven hundred qualified for rectal swab testing. Testing confirmed 191 unique carriers, roughly eighteen percent of those screened. The KPC resistance gene dominated, followed by NDM and a smaller group carrying both, giving planners a clear local picture.
pmc-13303626:
Ling Wang and co-authors offer a 2026 critical review proposing city fountains that grow microalgae to capture carbon. Algae systems can store carbon dioxide and yield useful biomass, but costly, energy-hungry reactor designs limit their spread.

Retrofitting existing fountains would reuse public infrastructure in busy places, cutting setup costs. Fountain-style growing methods may raise biomass output, while visible displays could teach passersby about carbon and prompt greener habits. The review weighs gains for developers, city governments, and residents, and draws on work in suspended cultures, building-mounted reactors, and landscape design. A shared plan for wider city use is laid out.
pmc-13303726:
Wei Zhang and Jianlou Yang report a 2026 randomized trial of planned exercise for mental health in Chinese college students. Stress, anxiety, and low mood are common in this group, but strong trial proof for structured programs has been scarce.

A total of 120 students with mild to moderate symptoms were split among team sports, solo aerobic exercise, and a waitlist group. Both active groups trained three times weekly for eight weeks in hour-long supervised sessions. Depression and anxiety scores fell sharply in both exercise groups and held at one-month follow-up. Resilience rose as well, and team and solo formats worked about equally well.
pmc-13303926:
Hongzhan Ju and co-authors study gadolinium doping in permalloy films for spin electronics in a 2026 physics report. Permalloy damps magnetic motion very weakly, which saves power but limits fast-switching devices that need stronger braking.

Films pairing platinum with permalloy-gadolinium mixes were made by sputtering and probed with spin-torque resonance tests. Adding gadolinium raised damping step by step, peaking at a mid-level dose with more than double the pure value. Charge-to-spin conversion also improved sharply, reaching its best level at a higher dose. Rare earth tuning thus gives device designers two useful dials at once.
pmc-13304026:
Masahiro Iinuma and co-authors link, in a 2026 retrospective study, nutrition scores to bone strength in older patients who broke a hip through fragility. Malnutrition is common in this group and shadows poor recovery, yet its tie to bone density and turnover was under-mapped. Three blood-based nutrition indexes were set against scans and bone markers.

The study covered 108 surgical patients with proximal thigh fractures. Better nutrition scores tracked with denser bone at the femoral neck, though not at the spine. Patients classed as malnourished also carried lower vitamin D and higher bone turnover markers, a pattern of faster bone loss. All three indexes stayed tied to hip density after adjusting for age, sex, and body size.
pmc-13305326:
Berthe Sabine Mapoko Esson and co-authors present a 2026 case of sudden limb blood loss in a patient with Kaposi's sarcoma, a vessel-born tumor. Blocked limb arteries in cancer patients are usually blamed on body-wide clotting effects of the tumor.

The 51-year-old man had purple skin patches and nodules on both legs for six months and a matching mouth lesion. New HIV treatment had just started. His left leg developed dry gangrene that worsened over time. Because this tumor grows from vessel lining cells, the authors ask whether it can harm limb arteries directly rather than through general clotting.
pmc-13305526:
Kuo-Cheng Lu leads a 2026 review of body-clock disruption and melatonin in chronic kidney disease. The kidney runs its own daily clock guiding filtering, salt handling, and blood pressure rhythm, and kidney failure steadily breaks that timing.

Built-up toxins, oxidative stress, and inflammation suppress clock genes while night melatonin output fades, removing a key repair signal. Melatonin pathways that fight oxidation, calm inflammation, and limit scarring are traced in detail. Nightly supplements improved sleep in dialysis patients in early studies, but proof that they slow kidney decline is still missing.
pmc-13305726:
Braulio Mark Valencia set out a 2026 protocol for mapping what is known about genetic testing in everyday primary care. Rather than testing a treatment, the plan describes how a Campbell evidence and gap map will be built and judged.

Steps cover a systematic search for studies, a visual summary of where evidence clusters, and a clear account of empty areas that need new work. The finished map is meant to help researchers, clinicians and policymakers judge the current landscape at a glance. It should also guide choices about bringing genomic tools into routine front-line care.
pmc-13306026:
Rumbidzai Mugwira tried to recover phosphorus from bay mud dredged at Malmfjärden, Kalmar, in a 2026 early-stage study. The goal was strong phosphorus release with as little metal contamination as possible.

Single washes used citric acid, sulphuric acid, sodium hydroxide or EDTA at two strengths, with acidity also varied in some runs. Stronger mixes and more acidic settings usually pulled out more in the reported results, and sulphuric acid at pH 1 freed the most phosphorus at 46.4% of content. EDTA also performed well, and a two-step wash was tested to balance yield against purity.
pmc-13306126:
Yazhen Zhang proposed a recovery framework after bleeding inside the brain in a 2026 synthesis linking bone, tea and exercise signals. Brain bleeding stroke has few preventive options and a hard recovery path, so the authors seek shared routes that protect vessels.

Tea chemicals, notably EGCG, and exercise products such as lactate and short-chain fatty acids act on common stress and inflammation pathways in the evidence reviewed. Gut microbe shifts toward calming profiles may further steady vessel walls and brain blood flow. Patient education sits inside the plan, aiming to turn daily habits into part of rehabilitation.
pmc-13307526:
Omar Bahlaoui and colleagues report in 2026 a thirty-three-year-old woman whose abdominal pain revealed Behçet's disease through a rare vein aneurysm. Imaging showed a clotted, sac-like swelling of the superior mesenteric vein reaching toward the portal junction. She also had recurring mouth ulcers, skin lesions, joint pain, and a positive skin prick response.

Blood clotting disorder tests came back negative, and eye examination was normal. Treatment began with high-dose steroids, then intravenous cyclophosphamide and oral prednisone to suppress the vessel inflammation. Blood thinners were adjusted several times as control proved unstable. Scans showed the swelling and clot shrinking gradually, with partial reopening of the portal vein. A biologic drug was planned because scarring threatened future portal pressure problems.
pmc-13307726:
Jian Sun and colleagues map in 2026 where HIV integrase touches the viral RNA element called TAR inside the virus core. Earlier work using sequencing and protein footprinting found contact points in the protein's tail domain. Crosslinking and magnetic resonance methods now extend that map.

Several newly found basic building blocks in the tail domain proved critical for RNA binding. Changing them damaged viral replication and produced malformed mature virus cores. Integrase is best known for stitching viral DNA into host chromosomes, the step blocked by several approved drugs. Its RNA contacts belong to a later, structural job in particle assembly. The authors argue that knowing both jobs sharpens drug design. A protein with two essential roles may offer two chances to disable the virus.
pmc-13307826:
Lauren R Finka and co-authors survey in 2026 how cat shelters across the United Kingdom and Ireland assess cats and adopters, manage behaviour, and decide new homes. Their study, part two of a sector wide pair, drew 393 replies from staff and volunteers who do that daily work.

Replies showed that checks on cats and on would be adopters were routine, and that results guided care and homing choices for each cat. How standard or fair those checks were stayed unclear, and practice varied a lot from place to place. Some habits carried a risk of poor welfare for cats. The authors flag clear spots where shared, kinder methods could lift outcomes for cats and staff alike.
pmc-13308326:
Christopher Chadwick and co-authors study in 2026 how flu vaccine know how has been shared between makers, and what helps such sharing succeed for pandemic readiness. They mixed surveys and talks with 24 makers and global experts, plus written records, and charted 18 sharing cases in depth.

Of those cases, 15 transfers finished and 13 led to an approved vaccine for use in people. Past sharing skill, private firm control, and direct two party deals all tracked with faster finish and approval times. State backing for local making and buying ranked as the top aid. Know how also spilled into COVID-19 and routine shots, which widened the gain.
pmc-13308726:
Jie Yang and co-authors run in 2026 a randomised trial of esketamine, given as a single push or as a slow drip, to ward off low mood after caesarean birth. In all, 503 women with no low mood before birth were split among push, drip, and salt water control groups for the test.

At six weeks, low mood struck 9.15 percent of the push group versus 19.33 percent of the control group in the trial. The drip group sat close to the push group, with no firm gap between the two drug routes. Push dosing brought less dizziness and sickness during surgery than drip dosing did overall. Both routes worked alike, so the simpler push may win on comfort.
pmc-13308926:
Nandita Gawande and co-authors give a 2026 account of a rare face case of Schweninger-Buzzi anetoderma, a skin state where elastic tissue fades and loose sacs form. The usual form dots the trunk and upper arms with no symptoms, and face spread is scarce in past reports.

Their patient, a woman aged 36 years, had a soft cheek lump for three years that bulged when she tipped her face left. No drug, hurt, or swelling came before it, and no kin shared the mark in her tale. Naming face anetoderma for what it is can spare needless tests and calm fears about looks, which weigh most on young women.
pmc-13309526:
Sieun Jeon and co-authors present a 2026 study of a soft robot material that reads, stores, and acts on light-based commands. Most soft robots move when told, while the thinking stays in outside electronics. Here, liquid crystal networks joined with silk protein fold command storage, coded display, and movement into one soft body.

Light patterns written into the material can be hidden, shown, and then used to drive shape change without a separate controller. Tests show the platform holding coded images and bending on cue from stored commands. The authors frame the design as a step toward soft machines that process information in their own material. Engineers working on gentle robots and smart materials are the main audience.
pmc-13310626:
Mark A. Phillips and colleagues deliver the cystic fibrosis gene in 2026 to human airway cells using particles derived from parainfluenza virus 5. The particles carried either a marker gene or a corrected copy of CFTR, the chloride channel gene broken in cystic fibrosis. Tests used primary airway cell cultures grown from both healthy and cystic fibrosis donors.

Applied to the airway surface, the particles mainly entered ciliated cells, with lesser entry into secretory and basal cells. Marker expression faded gradually over a month. Correcting roughly fifteen percent of cystic fibrosis cells restored channel-driven electrical current to healthy levels. At least a tenth of patients cannot use current modulator drugs, leaving gene delivery their main hope. The authors present the viral particle platform as a flexible carrier for respiratory gene cargoes. Persistence and repeat dosing remain the open questions.
pmc-13310726:
Roma Patel and co-editors open a 2026 collection on gene based causes of diabetes. Doctors once treated diabetes as one illness, yet patients with the same blood sugar can differ in the body paths that drive harm. Faults may sit in insulin cells, fat tissue, immune control, or gene switches that turn traits on and off.

Studies in the set span groups in China, India, Pakistan, Qatar, Russia, Sri Lanka, Brazil, and Latin America. Work covers immune signals, gene switches, and gut health, plus tests in diabetic mice. One line links three genes to both immune control and gut function. Together the set pushes care toward types defined by cause.
pmc-13310826:
Venkata Avinash Addanki and co-authors study tiny leaf blister mites on rose family plants in a 2026 paper. Mites that feed on apple, pear, and rowan trees were long seen as one wide ranging pest. New proof hints at hidden species tied to single hosts, which body measures alone may miss.

Gene data from two markers and measures of 28 body traits were joined in one test. Family trees showed strong host based splits, with up to seven deep lines. Apple mites stood apart in body form, while pear and rowan mites overlapped and looked cryptic. Pest control should treat the group as host tied species.
pmc-13310926:
Karen Gambina reports a 2026 case of a triple immune side effect after cancer immunotherapy. A woman aged 77 years got a PD-1 blocking drug for bladder cancer and then grew weak with drooping lids and slurred speech. Tests pointed to joint harm of heart muscle, skeletal muscle, and nerve muscle signaling at once.

Strong steroids, a second immune calming drug, and antibody infusions cleared her symptoms. Blood cell profiling before, during, and after care showed memory killer cells surged at flare. A worn effector cell subset tracked disease activity and shrank with steroids. Cell tracking may guide care for rare immune harms.
pmc-13311326:
Tessho Maruyama and Makoto Kaneko mine American cancer registry data in 2026 for survivors who develop three or more separate primary cancers, focusing on sites linked to human papillomavirus. Registries covering 1975 to 2022 held 15.9 million cancer cases. The team mapped how often higher-order multiple primaries occur and whether risk between particular sites persists over time.

About 2.8 million cases, roughly eighteen percent, involved multiple primaries, and higher-order cases made up around four to five percent of diagnoses. Most virus-related sites carried significantly elevated risk of further primaries. That risk persisted at least ten years after the first cancer. Two-way links appeared between specific sites, including anus to tonsil and tongue to vulva at long latencies. Follow-up organised organ by organ may miss this cross-site pattern. The authors argue for integrated, long-term surveillance and prevention planning in this survivor group.
pmc-13311826:
Lisa Büttgen and colleagues offer a 2026 systematic review of traits that might show how resilient a chicken is to short shocks such as germs or heat. A resilient bird dips briefly, then bounces back.

The search, run with AI-assisted screening, settled on 33 relevant studies. Most were small or mid-size trials, and most used immune challenges or heat stress as the test shock. Studied traits centered on production measures and immune or disease signs, with about half also tracking genes. Behavior traits were barely studied. The review maps a young field that breeding programs hope to use.
pmc-13311926:
Ji-Won Park and colleagues, in 2026, report a study on a low-weight beta-glucan from the fungus Aureobasidium pullulans against colon cancer cells. Beta-glucans have many body effects, but their anti-cancer routes were unclear.

Treated SW480 colon cancer cells lost viability in a dose and time pattern, with half-maximal doses falling as exposure lengthened. Death signs included active caspases, lost mitochondrial voltage, and freed cytochrome c, marking the intrinsic death path. Blocking caspases rescued cells only partly, so other death routes also ran. Self-eating markers rose too, and a key survival pathway quieted. The compound attacks on several fronts at once.
pmc-13312026:
Aleksander Lühr Hansen and co-authors ask, in a 2026 Danish study, whether the root cause behind a person's type 2 diabetes changes how the disease looks and what harm follows. They sorted 7,867 newly diagnosed adults from a national cohort by whether genes, low birthweight, or lifestyle seemed the main driver.

Groups formed by genes alone differed from the rest: those classed as intrauterine or lifestyle cases had lower insulin sensitivity, higher triglycerides, and more inflammation at diagnosis. Over ten years, major cardiovascular events struck 14.8 percent of the intrauterine group, 13.2 percent of the lifestyle group, and 11.5 percent of the genetic group. The split suggests that cause-based grouping could sharpen risk prediction and care.
pmc-13312126:
Dae Kwan Ko and Federica Brandizzi present a 2026 protocol for running the NEEDLE gene discovery pipeline in plant species that lack a model organism's resources. Finding the transcription factors that switch key genes on or off is central to understanding gene regulation, yet non-model plants have few ready tools for the job.

The protocol covers setting up the computing environment, preparing data, running the analysis, and reading the outputs. NEEDLE chains together RNA sequencing processing, co-expression network analysis, a tree-based network inference method, and promoter conservation checks to rank candidate regulators. The walkthrough uses sorghum stem development, with 11 samples, as its example. The authors note that six or more meaningful samples generally give stable networks, and that the pipeline transfers to other species with suitable data.
pmc-13312526:
Christina Darwish and colleagues report a 2026 case of a patient diagnosed with two B-cell cancers at the same time: Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Blinatumomab, a bispecific T-cell engager aimed at CD19, is approved for the acute leukemia but had barely been explored as treatment for the chronic one.

Given as consolidation therapy for the acute disease, the drug cleared the patient's measurable residual disease. Follow-up checks showed the chronic leukemia clone had been eradicated as well, leaving both diseases in deep remission. The authors note the acute leukemia masked whether the chronic clone would ever have needed treatment on its own. They present the case as evidence that CD19-directed immune therapy can reach across both conditions when they collide in one patient.
pmc-13312826:
Wen-Li Deng and co-authors test, in a 2026 prospective study, whether fine-grained retinal function testing beats the standard letter chart at catching early gains from treatment for diabetic macular oedema. This swelling of the central retina is a leading cause of vision loss, and first-line anti-VEGF injections can improve the retina in ways a coarse acuity score misses.

Fifty-eight patients received conbercept injections and were checked the day before, a day after, and a month after treatment with acuity, retinal imaging, and microperimetry, which maps sensitivity point by point. Microperimetry showed far larger effect sizes and detected improvement within a day. Among 26 patients whose acuity never changed, it still revealed clear functional gains at one month. Starting fixation measures and a triglyceride-glucose index helped predict who would benefit, information the authors say can guide expectations.
pmc-13313226:
Marta Tkachuk and Nataliya Matiytsiv review the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster as a test animal for organophosphate poisoning in work published in 2026. These chemicals cause fast nerve toxicity, stress damage, DNA harm, and slow nerve decay by blocking an enzyme called neuropathy target esterase.

The review covers three kinds of fly tests. Plain flies get the chemicals in food or vapor, and staff score survival, movement, climbing, and enzyme and stress markers. DNA harm is checked with the SMART test and the comet assay. A mutant fly called swiss cheese, whose gene matches the human PNPLA6 gene, models the slow nerve disease apart from the fast nerve effects. Together the tests sort hazards and help find guards against both harm paths.
pmc-13313826:
Saddam Khalid Hummadi tests, in a 2026 animal study, whether a plant-extract ointment can heal wounds in diabetic rats. Diabetic wounds are a stubborn problem in veterinary care, healing slowly and infecting easily. Thirty-two male rats were made diabetic by removing part of the pancreas. Each received a full-thickness skin wound. One group was treated with a standard antibiotic. The other received an ointment blending 20 percent Boswellia serrata extract and 10 percent fenugreek seed extract, for twenty-one days.

The herbal group outperformed the control at every check. Microscopy showed faster new blood vessel growth and a better inflammatory response. Collagen was stronger and more mature, and skin and hair follicles regrew more fully. Gene activity matched the picture, with two growth-promoting genes turned up and an inflammatory gene turned down across the treatment period. The author concludes the ointment improved diabetic wound healing in this model.
pmc-13313926:
Ansam Hussein Ali and co-authors test, in a 2026 feeding trial, whether nano-encapsulated plant oils can protect the gut of freshly weaned lambs. Weaning stresses young lambs, loosening the intestinal barrier and blunting digestion just as feed intake wobbles. Sixty-four Awassi lambs, 45 days old, were split into four groups. They received plain feed, nano-encapsulated black seed oil, nano-encapsulated thyme oil, or both oils together, at 200 milligrams per kilogram of feed for 56 days.

The combination clearly won. Gut barrier proteins rose between 2.5 and 3.1 fold over controls in the combined group. Digestive enzyme activity jumped by roughly seventy to eighty percent. Intestinal leakiness fell by 58 percent on the marker ratio used. Daily weight gain improved by 24 percent in that group. The authors conclude the two encapsulated oils act synergistically. They propose them as a practical feed strategy for the fragile post-weaning window.
pmc-13314426:
Giorgia Corli and a large team test the heart harm of a synthetic stimulant in animals in a study from 2026. The drug, 4,4 prime-DMAR, belongs to the aminorex class, acts like amphetamine, and has shown up in poisonings and deaths in adults and teens.

The drug comes in two mirror forms, cis and trans, with unlike effects in the body. The team gave the cis form alone and mixed with the trans form to living animals and tracked heart and breathing action. Such stimulants can speed the heart, strain breathing, and trigger sudden cardiac death, yet lab study of those harms is thin. By splitting the two forms, the work shows which shape drives the acute heart risk, data that can guide care of poisoned patients and drug policy.
pmc-13315426:
Andrea K. Blanchard and co-authors used national survey data in 2026 to track fairness in mother and newborn care in urban India over two decades. They pooled household surveys from 2002 to 2008 and family health surveys run from 2015 to 2021, covering about 200,000 births. Groups were compared by wealth, at public and private care sources.

Coverage of pregnancy, birth, and after-birth care rose a lot, and newborn survival improved to a lesser degree. The team used several inequality measures to judge whether gaps by wealth narrowed, and how the National Urban Health Mission era, begun in 2013, lines up with those shifts.
pmc-13315826:
Yazan Mohsen and colleagues study in 2026 whether recorded sleep apnea marks a distinct group among atrial fibrillation patients treated with ablation. Blocked breathing in sleep is common with this rhythm disorder and may shape both its form and the chance of return after vein isolation treatment.

The main registry held 2,559 first ablation patients treated from late 2021 to mid 2025, with a nested active group of 666 patients given week-long rhythm checks. Documented apnea appeared in 10.5 percent of the registry group and about 10.1 percent of the active subset. Outcomes centered on repeat ablation or shock treatment at the same center.
pmc-13316126:
Arndt Schmidt and colleagues test in 2026 a simpler way to count plant and arthropod interactions from environmental DNA on single flowers and leaves. DNA sampling finds which species are present with ease, but judging how abundant each is remains weak, and replicate filtering methods are slow and costly.

Skipping filtration, the team extracted DNA directly from individual flowers and leaves and compared isolation methods with a standard filtration protocol. Simple precipitation was enough to recover community-level arthropod DNA from single flowers. Using how often a species appears across replicates as a stand-in for abundance could make semi-quantitative monitoring practical. Less lab work per sample means more sites can be checked.
pmc-13316226:
Galit Karpov and colleagues followed teenagers in 2026 to see how emotion processing develops differently in anxiety and mood disorders shaped by childhood adversity. Anxiety and depression peak in onset during adolescence, when frontal brain systems mature, and poor emotion regulation is a shared symptom that adversity worsens.

Youth aged 10 to 17 years, 65 with internalizing disorders and 74 comparison peers, did an emotional working memory task and a rethinking task during scans at start and one year later. Mixed models tracked group and age differences in frontal activity. Disorder youth showed altered development in the left ventral anterior insula. Age shaped some of these paths as the teens grew.
pmc-13316426:
Ludovica Monti and her team, publishing in 2026, map folded DNA structures called G-quadruplexes across the genome of Trypanosoma brucei. That parasite causes African sleeping sickness. The folded structures, formed in guanine-rich stretches, may regulate genes, but where they sit in this species was largely unknown.

Computer analysis across 64 related species showed wide variation in how common these structures are. The team then produced the first chromatin-based genome-wide map in T. brucei, using antibody capture followed by sequencing. Structures clustered in coding regions and near where genes switch on and off, a pattern unlike human maps. A drug that locks the folds changed how genes carrying them behave, which backs a gene-control role and a possible treatment target.
pmc-13316626:
Philip J Batterham and co-authors evaluated, in a 2026 mixed methods study, what helps a one-session digital mental health program, called Helipad, take root in workplaces. The program aims to guide staff toward proper help, and the team drew lessons from a cluster trial.

Interviews with 16 people and survey data from 344 staff showed Helipad beat plain written education on appeal, fit, and ease of use. Workplaces that pushed harder, with extra emails, meetings, and delivery through learning systems, got more staff to join. Ratings held across workplace types. Users praised the wide content but flagged a hard problem: reaching staff who feel no need for support. Leader backing and paid time to finish were key tips.
pmc-13320026:
Huada Tang and co-authors map brain lesions in a rare energy failure illness in a 2026 study of scans from a Beijing hospital. In MELAS, spells that mimic strokes leave swelling in the outer brain layer that can fade again, yet how those patches spread and where they stop was unclear. Records and scans from more than a decade of care were pooled to trace the pattern.

A total of 61 scans from 55 patients were split by fine brain maps, and a math split found eight patch families. Patches favored the back side lobes and tracked with maps of cell link density. Spread looked free inside a zone but held back at zone edges, as if borders fence the harm. The map may help doctors read new spells in this illness.
pmc-13320326:
Murilo Augusto Ferreira and co-authors tell of a single patient seen in 2026 whose rare fat cancer of the sperm cord mimicked a trapped groin hernia. A 55 year old man with a past hernia repair came in with a stuck scrotal mass that looked like the hernia had come back and jammed. Such fat cancers grow slowly and painlessly, so they are often read as far more common groin lumps.

A first surgery found no hernia at all, and scans then pointed to a fatty growth. Wide removal with the testicle on that side gave tissue proof of the cancer. Full removal with clear edges is the gold path for this tumor, and long watch must follow since return is a real risk even years later.
pmc-13320426:
Aragaw Zemene Sendekie and co-authors test fungi that live on seaweed off Kenya for germ killing power in a 2026 study. Sea living fungi are a rich but barely tapped well of new drug leads. Fungi were grown from red and green algae at one coastal site and screened against tough drug proof germs that sicken people.

From 330 fungal strains first sorted by shape, nine active strains were named by gene reads. Extracts in two solvents killed germs across wide zones in dish tests and at low doses in broth, and scope views showed torn germ walls that point to a membrane attack. Extracts also broke up germ films, though most cuts were modest. Two lead extracts held a broad mix of active compounds on chemical scans.
pmc-13320626:
Huan Zhang and a large team uncover, in 2026, how Brucella bacteria use one of their proteins to calm the immune system and settle into chronic infection. Brucellosis is a major animal and human disease worldwide. The bacteria provoke the anti-inflammatory signal IL-10, which limits immune damage but also helps the germ persist.

A bacterial enzyme called PrpA was shown to make macrophages release IL-10 by activating a signalling chain inside the cells. Removing a link in that chain weakened bacterial killing and lowered several immune signals. Mice infected with a Brucella strain lacking PrpA mounted stronger defences, with more protective antibodies and T cells. That mutant strain also protected mice better than its parent against a virulent challenge, making it a vaccine candidate.
pmc-13323026:
Tianhui Niu and co-authors profile gene changes in a rare cervical cancer tied to Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, in a 2026 single-patient study. Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma is aggressive and unrelated to HPV, and its appearance in this inherited syndrome is exceptionally rare.

Targeted sequencing and tissue staining covered one well-described patient with stage IB3 disease. Testing found an inherited STK11 change plus tumour changes in KRAS and ERBB3, and strong staining for Claudin18.2 and MUC6 confirmed the gastric character, while p16 stayed negative. Claudin18.2 gives a proven target from gastric cancer care, and ERBB signals offer another lead. The authors propose routine molecular profiling for this cancer type.
pmc-13323226:
Shanshan Han and co-authors build a survival model for breast cancer that joins immune and inflammation signs, in a 2026 single-centre study of 503 surgically treated patients from 2020 to 2025. Recurrence risk varies widely, and standard clinical factors miss part of the immune picture.

Stromal immune cell levels in tissue and a blood-based inflammation index defined three immune types, from favourable to poor. During follow-up, 107 patients had a disease-free survival event in the cohort records. A random survival forest beat Cox and boosting models on accuracy across five years in their comparisons. Staining for CD8 and CD163 supported the grouping, and nodal stage carried the largest weight in the forest model.
pmc-13325126:
Supanit Chungyampin and colleagues make magnetic alginate beads that carry a copper catalyst in a 2026 materials study. The beads let a liquid-phase reaction run and then be fished out with a magnet for reuse.

Beads formed by gelation trapped copper on titanium dioxide plus magnetite inside a sodium alginate shell. Raising magnetite content changed swelling, density, and how well the cargo stayed inside. A mid-level recipe balanced strength against access to the catalyst. In acetic acid hydrogenation, the best bead made 18.69 mg per liter of ethanol, while too little copper starved the reaction and too much clumped. Reuse slowly lowered output, likely from fouling and copper loss.
pmc-13325326:
Ioannis Panagopoulos and colleagues scan fusion genes across sites in high-grade serous ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. These cancers cause most ovarian cancer deaths, and fused genes can flag targets or predict behavior.

RNA sequencing from several tumor sites in each patient showed wide variation between cancers. Most fusions were one-offs, unique to a single tumor, rather than shared events. Protein kinases appeared among fusion partners far more often than chance suggests. Several kinase fusions kept their working catalytic parts intact, which may leave them druggable. Fusion patterns also widened the known reach of DNA repair faults in these tumors. The diversity complicates any one-size marker plan.
pmc-13325726:
Zeen Feng and Yalin Sun report a ten-year result after laser surgery for a misplaced urinary opening in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 50-year-old woman, had doubled kidney drainage systems on both sides and an ectopic ureterocele.

The cyst-like swelling caused repeat urinary infections and urgent leaks. A thulium laser cut through the urethra opened the ureterocele with little heat spread. Ten years on, the upper kidney cortex had thickened from 0.52 cm to 1.14 cm on imaging. Swelling of the kidney had cleared, and symptoms never returned. No second operation was needed. The case backs laser incision as a kidney-sparing fix for adults.
pmc-13325826:
Wendi Guo and co-authors map the cell network behind vessel invasion in endometrial cancer in a 2026 study. Lymphovascular space invasion predicts spread and poor outcomes in the endometrioid type, yet its team mechanics were unclear.

Single-cell sequencing covered three invasion-positive tumors, two negative ones, and two healthy samples. Positive tumors held a restless epithelial subset marked by low oxygen, partial transition traits, and progesterone resistance. Support cells and macrophages jointly rebuilt the matrix and grew new vessels. Signals through LGALS9 quieted T cells inside the niche. Nine genes in cancer cells tied to prognosis were named. The invasion front paired oxygen-starved tumor cells with PD-L1 rich immune cells.
pmc-13328026:
Laura Hertner and co-authors argue for measuring social suffering apart from depression in a 2026 study of displaced Syrians in Lebanon. Standard screens capture illness symptoms, but much burden grows from injustice, poverty, and broken social worlds. They used survey data from 1,228 Syrians gathered in late 2023, comparing a new feeling broken or destroyed scale with a standard depression questionnaire.

The new scale held together well, with a Cronbach's alpha of 0.822 in its first Lebanese use, and it correlated only moderately with depression scores, at 0.56 in their sample, marking it as a related but distinct measure. It also reacted more sharply to poverty and neighborhood quality. Aid programs that treat symptoms alone may miss the social wounds driving distress.
pmc-13328426:
Emily Denise Fischman and co-authors test a SUMO pathway blocker against the sleeping sickness parasite in a 2026 study. Trypanosoma brucei causes African trypanosomiasis, and current drugs suffer toxicity and creeping resistance. The parasite needs SUMO tagging for cell division and surface switching, so the team applied ML-792, a blocker of its activating enzyme.

The drug cut overall SUMO tagging and nuclear SUMO levels. It slowed parasite growth in proportion to dose, with potency in the micromolar range. It also scrambled cell cycle patterns, leaving abnormal nucleus and kinetoplast pairings. Blocking one enzyme thus jams several vital processes at once. The SUMO pathway earns a place on the target list for safer antitrypanosomal drugs.
pmc-13329326:
Anjana Roy and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a review of tools that assess Agni in Ayurveda. Agni covers digestion and metabolic factors that vary from person to person. Many questionnaires and clinician tools claim to grade its strength, but their quality is unclear.

The review will search several databases and Ayurveda sources for studies in adults aged 18 or older. Two reviewers will screen and extract data, with a third settling disputes. Checks will cover how well each tool measures what it claims, how steady its scores are, and how practical it is in clinics and research. Quality frameworks named in the plan include QUADAS-2 and COSMIN. Results will be summed up in words and tables.
pmc-13330526:
Özge Karabıyık Acar and colleagues report hormone-making cells inside thyroid tissue in a 2026 study. After full parathyroid removal, parathyroid hormone rarely falls to zero, and the source was unclear. The team soaked fresh tissues in saline for 30 minutes and measured hormone in the fluid from thyroid, other tissues, and healthy parathyroid glands.

Groups held 46 thyroid samples, 46 other tissue samples, and 7 parathyroid samples. Thyroid fluid held far more hormone than other tissues, though far less than parathyroid fluid, in the reported values. Staining showed thyroid-like cells bearing hormone granules. The authors propose a new cell population in thyroid tissue as one source of leftover hormone.
pmc-13330626:
Dominic Santoleri and colleagues probe how a common gene variant shifts liver fat and cholesterol in a 2026 mouse study. The variant affects GKRP, a protein that controls glucokinase, the liver enzyme that starts glucose handling. Mouse models swapped in the human variant form or the standard form after removing the mouse gene.

Variant mice held less GKRP and glucokinase protein and showed higher blood cholesterol in the reported results. Removing liver glucokinase alone copied key effects, with more liver cholesterol and fat plus higher fat-making gene activity. Adding a backup enzyme reversed the pattern. Weak glucose handling thus seems to drive the lipid changes, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331226:
Elizabeth Escamilla-Chávez and colleagues present an operative video of neck spine fusion in a 2026 article. A 33-year-old man fell from over 3 metres and suffered many injuries, including a type II odontoid fracture with the peg shifted back by up to 5 mm into the canal. Ligaments at the skull and neck junction had torn, yet the cord stayed unharmed.

Front screw fixing was ruled out by fracture shape and ligament damage. The team used the Goel-Harms method, placing screws in the first and second neck vertebrae from behind.
