Alignment was restored during surgery without vessel or nerve harm. Afterward the patient stayed neurologically intact, pain eased a lot, and scans showed stable fixing.
pmc-13331826:
Yao Wang and colleagues investigate the protein KIF7 in clear cell kidney cancer in a 2026 study built from tumor data banks, tissue arrays, and cell experiments. KIF7 levels were much higher in tumor tissue than in nearby normal tissue, and high levels tracked with later stage and shorter survival.

pmc-13333226:

pmc-13333426:

pmc-13336426:

pmc-13336626:

pmc-13337126:

pmc-13337426:

pmc-13339626:

pmc-13341426:

pmc-13341526:

pmc-13341826:

pmc-13342226:

pmc-13343126:

pmc-13343226:
Hui Ye and co-authors look for blood markers of postpartum depression in twin pregnancies, in a 2026 retrospective study. pmc-13343526:
Dorota Górniak and co-authors compare survival playbooks of local and worldwide bacteria in Antarctic microbial mats in 2026. pmc-13345726:

pmc-13346026:

pmc-13349726:

pmc-13349826:

pmc-13349926:

pmc-13350426:

pmc-13350526:

pmc-13352426:

pmc-13352626:

pmc-13353926:

pmc-13354126:

pmc-13354526:

pmc-13355826:

pmc-13363826:

pmc-13365726:

pmc-13371826:

pmc-13373826:

pmc-13374126:

pmc-13374326:

pmc-13383826:

pmc-13385926:

pmc-13387626:

pmc-13388526:

pmc-13402226:

pmc-13402326:

pmc-13402626:

pmc-13402926:

pmc-13403026:

pmc-13403526:

pmc-13403726:

pmc-13404826:

Exclusive breastfeeding varied with age, birth weight, delivery mode and nursery admission. Timing of the first feed, pre-milk feeds and vaccination status also showed links.
pmc-13405126:

Costs were compared between the bottom and top of each social gradient where the data allowed. Rural versus urban living and ethnic group formed separate comparisons. The review shows where diabetes spending falls hardest, informing fairer funding choices.
pmc-13406426:

pmc-13407226:

pmc-13407726:

pmc-13407826:

pmc-13408226:

pmc-13408926:

pmc-13409826:

pmc-13411326:

pmc-13411626:

pmc-13411826:

pmc-13411926:

pmc-13413026:

pmc-13413226:

pmc-13413726:

pmc-13413826:

pmc-13415126:

pmc-13415826:

pmc-13416126:

pmc-13416626:

pmc-13417026:

pmc-13419226:

pmc-13419326:

pmc-13419426:

pmc-13420126:

pmc-13420326:

pmc-13420426:

pmc-13421226:

pmc-13421326:

pmc-13424526:

pmc-13424726:

pmc-13425026:

pmc-13425526:

pmc-13425626:

pmc-13426026:

pmc-13426426:

pmc-13427526:

pmc-13427926:

Recordings confirmed the team's starting suspicion in about 85 percent of cases.

Based on the findings, about half the patients went on to surgery that removes the seizure zone. A heat treatment delivered through the same electrodes helped about three quarters of treated patients at one year, though full seizure freedom was uncommon. Responses to that heat step then guided later choices. Serious lasting harm was rare, near 1 percent. Clinicians gain a staged framework rather than a single yes-or-no test.
pmc-13428026:
Liu and colleagues report a 2026 case of familial chylomicronemia syndrome in an infant, a rare inherited disorder where the blood cannot clear dietary fat, leaving triglyceride levels dangerously high. The baby, a girl admitted at forty-one days old, was diagnosed by genetic testing that found two faulty copies of the lipoprotein lipase gene, the main fat-clearing enzyme.

Treatment centered on a strict low-fat diet supplemented with medium-chain triglycerides, fats that bypass the broken clearing pathway. Over one year of follow-up, her triglyceride levels improved markedly. She also showed catch-up growth, closing the gap toward normal infant size. The authors stress that early genetic diagnosis matters because diet started in infancy can control the disorder and help prevent its feared complication, repeated pancreas inflammation.
pmc-13428126:
Mondaza-Hernandez and colleagues published a 2026 study on drug response markers in sarcoma. Soft tissue sarcoma covers many rare cancers with few good drug options. Pazopanib is a standard second drug, yet patients respond in uneven ways. The team compared tumor samples taken before and after pazopanib treatment.

Gene profiling found 38 genes whose activity changed after treatment ended. One gene, SERPINE1, rose more than fourfold and tracked with poorer survival. Lab tests in sarcoma cell lines backed the gene findings with protein checks. The drug also shifted immune-related cells within tumors in their analysis. The authors frame SERPINE1 as a lead for bigger validation studies ahead. Patient selection for pazopanib could sharpen if the marker holds up.
pmc-13428426:
Christoph Beger and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 paper, a software suite that helps medical teams define patient types precisely and find them in data. Phenotyping, describing the observable traits that define a condition, is often done by hand and varies between groups. Their TOP framework lets users define traits formally, organize them into a structured hierarchy, and build disease models. A sample case built around a liver failure score shows the machinery in action.

Queries generated by the suite can pull matching patients from records automatically. Built-in testing checks that definitions behave as intended. Eleven users rated the experience, scoring appeal and practical quality clearly on the positive side of the scale. The authors claim gains in speed, scale, and reproducibility for studies that depend on exact patient definitions, a need precision medicine keeps sharpening.
pmc-13428626:
Qihua Qiu and Jaesang Sung check, in a 2026 study, whether laws raising the tobacco purchase age to 21 change young adults' body weight. Tobacco 21 laws cut youth smoking by blocking initiation, and quitting smoking often brings weight gain, which raised the question. The team used national behavior survey data from 2009 to 2019 for 18 to 20 year olds. A difference-in-differences design compared states as the laws rolled out at staggered times.

Average weight and overweight rates barely moved overall. Obesity did dip slightly, driven by small losses among those just above the obesity line. The dip appeared in the first year after adoption, then faded. Effects concentrated among never smokers, which fits prevention rather than quitting as the channel. Reported exercise rose and diets improved in the same window, suggesting wider lifestyle ripples.
pmc-13429126:
Yi Jiao Angelina Tian and colleagues sift, in a 2026 scoping review, which qualities in the doctor-patient relationship actually move patients to follow treatment. Sticking with treatment saves lives and money, and good relationships are often credited. The team searched three databases for empirical studies from 2015 to early 2025 that tied a specific relational quality to adherence. Forty-eight studies qualified across many designs and settings.

Six qualities recurred: communication, shared decision-making, trust, empathy, continuity of care, and agreement between doctor and patient on the plan. Communication led the list, especially what is said, how it is said, and how often. Few studies defined or measured these qualities the same way, which the authors call the field's main gap. Digital care and subspecialization may also be thinning the very relationships that adherence depends on.
pmc-13429226:
Tuğba Yanık-Yalçın and co-authors distill, in a 2026 consensus report, what Türkiye's infection control leaders see as their system's weak points. The material comes from the seventh national symposium on healthcare-associated infections, whose recorded sessions were transcribed and thematically analyzed. Participants led infection prevention programs across the country. Antibiotic resistance frames the whole discussion, since resistant infections now kill millions globally each year.

Five barrier themes recurred: reporting pressure that bends the data, habits and culture that resist change, thin training and staffing, patchy standardization, and committee decisions that stall before reaching the ward. Suggested fixes include visible leadership backing, simpler data systems, and behavior-change strategies built to last. The report reads as an insider map of why good rules fail in practice, drawn from the people charged with enforcing them.
pmc-13429626:
Zinat Gordi and colleagues design a sun-light catalyst to break down BPA, a chemical that can upset hormones and that turns up all over the world. Their mix joins a two-metal cage-like solid with tiny bits of titanium dioxide, so it can soak up plain daylight.

Tests showed the two parts had joined well and that the mix took in more light than each part alone. A planned set of trials tuned acid level, dose, and start levels, and the best set broke down 95.3 percent of the BPA. The break-down ran at a steady first-order rate, which gives water teams a sun-powered way to clean up a tough pollutant.
pmc-13430526:
Juan Mendoza Turmero and co-authors made tiny bone-like mineral particles in 2026 with the help of high-pitched sound waves, a route they frame as kind to the environment. The team varied how long the sound ran, from a quarter hour to a full hour. They also varied the liquid mix, pairing water with one of three other liquids.

Tests of shape and makeup showed a form of the mineral much like the one in real bone, with size and shape tied to the liquid used. All batches held up well under heat and gave strong yields. Blood tests showed low harm for one mix, with no block to clot cell action. One mix cut the growth of a common germ film the most, which hints at use in bone repair materials.
pmc-13431026:
Wei Ding and colleagues tested whether a heart ultrasound measure can foretell serious heart events in people on long-term kidney dialysis. The measure, peak strain dispersion, gauges how unevenly the heart's main chamber squeezes across its walls.

The team matched 336 dialysis patients into high and low measure groups using a cut-off set before the study. Over a median of about 47 months, major heart events struck about 38 percent of the high group versus about 20 percent of the low group. High readings also doubled the risk of heart death and raised overall death risk after adjustments. Ding suggests adding the measure to routine heart checks for dialysis patients, pending wider tests.
pmc-13431426:
Priyanka Kumari Nahak wrote a 2026 letter that questions a pooled review of exercise therapy for forward head posture in people with neck pain. The letter praises the review team for gathering proof on a shared and growing problem, and for hewing to set reporting rules. Posture of this kind links to pain, lost function, and poorer daily life.

One worry targets who got into the pooled counts. The review said it would bar studies that paired exercise with other care, yet several pooled studies set exercise against active care such as standard therapy or posture lessons. The pooled figures thus mix unlike contests. A second worry notes very wide spread in results across studies for head angle, pain, and neck function. The letter warns that such spread can bend what the pooled figures truly mean.
pmc-13434126:
Ning Zuo and colleagues study fair access to AI help in English classes. AI tools have spread fast in language teaching, yet not all learners gain alike. Past work stressed devices and wifi, while skill, voice, and choice got less care.

Surveys from 220 college English learners, checked with standard tools, were read with stats that test links, middlemen, and group gaps. Skill with digital tools and with AI strongly predicted how much learners joined in and steered their own learning, and those two traits in turn shaped outcomes. Teachers get proof that AI lessons must teach AI skill itself, not just hand out software.
pmc-13434226:
Mohan Ajmeera, P Chiranjeevi, and A Krishna Mohan present TriAttnNet in 2026, a vision model that spots cotton pests and sorts leaf disease from photos. Small data sets, uneven class counts, and repeated traits make the task hard in the field. Their pipeline cleans images first and then adds made up images to widen training.

A segmentation step marks the leaf area of interest before sorting begins. The main model weighs space, channel, and context cues at once. Reported accuracy reached 98.66 percent, above two strong rival models named in the study. Farm advisers get a fast aid, though field trials beyond test images still matter most.
pmc-13434426:
Chuan Li and coauthors build a water based battery that still works at deep cold in 2026. Dual ion designs store charge in graphite at high voltage, yet they once needed costly, thick salt mixes that fail when cold. A gel rich in polar molecules replaces the thick mix here.

The gel holds only dilute salts yet stays stable past a wide voltage span at minus 40 degrees. High voltage scans wake the graphite to take in the charge carrying ions. Cells gave high plateaus at minus 20 and minus 40 degrees. Cold stores and polar sites gain a safer battery option.
pmc-13434726:
Michael G Connor's team traced in 2026 how pneumococcus, the bacterium behind pneumonia and ear infections, bends host immunity through a protein called COMMD2. They compared a mild, commensal-like strain with an invasive strain, mapping which proteins cling to p65, a hub of the NF-kB immune pathway. The invasive strain drove COMMD2 to join p65 and p62, a complex that ships p65 out for breakdown.

Removing COMMD2 changed the host immune response, marking it as needed for the bacterium's quieting trick. The paper thus lays out one route by which a harmful strain damps inflammation while a mild strain does not. Infection teams get a precise target for follow-up, and a frame for why the same species can live quietly or turn dangerous.
pmc-13434826:
R D Dowling's team presented BAGEL in 2026, a statistical model for tracing how blood stem cells mature into specialized types. Cell maturation runs as a smooth path, not a set of jumps, and modern single-cell gene data now let researchers watch that path in fine detail. BAGEL treats maturation as continuous, using Bayesian tools with Gaussian processes and Gibbs sampling to infer each path and its branch points.

A second part of the tool projects data from many studies into one view, so teams can compare cell paths within and across species. Although the paper centers on blood formation, the authors say the method should work for other single-cell data sets too. Biologists get a flexible, visual route to map how cells choose their fate.
pmc-13435726:
Rainer Gosert and a large team compare two shop bought antibody tests for RSV in 2026. Blood from 462 people spans healthy adults, pregnant women, children, and transplant patients with vaccine shots. Both kits hunt total IgG and IgA against the virus.

Agreement on IgG calls ran high at 83.8 percent. One kit still read higher values and more positives across the board. Both kits tracked the sharper pre fusion antibody well, most in children. IgA showed rarely and matched less well. The kits are not swaps for each other, the team warns. Clinics must stick with one kit when tracking change.
pmc-13436526:
Pausas, Valbuena, and Beltrán-Marcos report how fire reached beech forest in Spain, a damp, shady woodland long seen as a fire barrier. Beech canopies shade out undergrowth, and high altitude summer fires were once rare. During a fifteen day heatwave in summer 2025, lightning lit the Barniedo fire in León. It burned 19,100 hectares across shrubland, oak, and beech. Their 2026 report reads satellite severity maps and field signs to judge the damage.

Fire raced through shrubland as crown fire, then slowed to a creeping litter fire inside beech stands. The barrier effect is real but not absolute. About a third of the beech was untouched or barely scorched, with nearly all trees surviving. Another third burned as a low intensity, high severity ground fire that killed most trees. The last third came out mixed. Fire regimes, the authors warn, are climbing into forests new to fire.
pmc-13436926:
Verónica Fuentes-Santamaría, Carmen María Díaz García, and Juan Carlos Alvarado review the research linking hearing loss with a higher risk of dementia, including Alzheimer disease. Their 2026 critical review weighs what is known, what stays unclear, and how doctors should read the link in daily care. Studies show risk rising as hearing gets worse, yet a direct cause has not been proven.

Several paths may connect the two conditions, the authors explain. The brain may lose input, reorganize itself, and work harder to follow speech. Lonely and withdrawn daily life may add further harm, since hearing loss often cuts people off from others. Problems with central hearing may also signal early weakness in the brain itself. Hearing tests for older adults and hearing aids may help, the review concludes, though firm proof that treatment protects memory is still missing.
pmc-13437226:
Patrick Terrence Brooks's team profiled early immune recovery in 2026 among seventy-seven adults one month after donor stem cell transplant. Post-transplant troubles are largely immune-driven, so a day twenty-eight blood profile may flag who thrives, relapses, or develops graft-versus-host disease. High-resolution cell typing plus cytokine release after stimulation mapped innate and adaptive compartments, activation, and checkpoint markers.

Higher overall immune counts and stronger cytokine responses went with better survival. Stronger innate subsets went with less relapse, while high PD-1 on helper T cells and activation on killer T cells went with poorer survival. Transplant teams get an early, functional snapshot for monitoring and for picking immune targets. Validation in larger groups is needed before clinical use.
pmc-13437526:
Shen Jiang, Teng Zhang, and Xiaona Gu tested a new rinse for skin burns from metallic sodium, a chemical that reacts fiercely with water and leaves strong alkali in wounds. Their 2026 study made a wash from glycine and a chelating salt, then tested it in sixty rats. The five groups were no rinse, plain water, boric acid, a commercial fluid, and the new wash. Each wound was rinsed for fifteen minutes starting three minutes after exposure.

The new wash pulled wound alkalinity down fast, reaching near-neutral levels by rinsing's end. By day fourteen, those wounds had healed more than the no-rinse, water, and boric acid groups. Markers of vessel growth and repair ran higher, two harsh inflammatory signals fell, and a calming signal rose highest. The authors present the wash as a promising emergency rinse, while noting direct proof of sodium removal is still missing.
pmc-13437926:
Stahl and colleagues test an idea about malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, aggressive cancers arising in people with neurofibromatosis type 1. Many of these tumors lose a gene silencing complex called PRC2. Earlier work hinted the cells survive only by methylating their DNA heavily, so removing methylation might kill them. Their 2026 study maps DNA methylation and gene activity in tumor lines and engineered human Schwann cells with and without PRC2. It then applies two methylation blocking drugs.

Losing PRC2 did not change global DNA methylation at all, undercutting the premise. Both drugs stripped methylation, yet they split in effect. Azacitidine killed tumor cells directly and stirred RNA processing genes. Decitabine caused no direct killing and stirred immune response genes instead. Methylation loss alone does not kill these tumor cells. The authors suggest pairing such drugs with other treatments rather than relying on them alone.
pmc-13438426:
Ashley Blawas and colleagues strapped heart monitors to blue and humpback whales to learn how the heart keeps up with lunge feeding. A rorqual whale surges open-mouthed into prey, then slows to filter tons of water through its baleen while gliding. Diving animals usually brake the heart to save oxygen, and how that brake bends during such bursts was unknown. Their 2026 study read heart rate across whole feeding dives.

Heart rates stayed high through the lunge and, strikingly, held up during the filtering glide that follows, keeping blood flowing to muscles largely stopped. The pattern resembles a sprinter more than a saver: the lunge seems to run partly on oxygen-free energy, building a debt filtering time only partly repays. The authors read this cardiac flexibility as the unlock for the rorqual style. Their tags turn a long theoretical debate about dive heart control into measured fact.
pmc-13439026:
Kate M Bermingham and colleagues present a 2026 report on building and testing a digital food questionnaire for everyday eating habits. Their PREDICT questionnaire holds 265 food items and is filled in online by each person. Diet tools often miss foods people eat now, so the team drew items from two older questionnaires plus cohort data from the United States and the United Kingdom.

Over one month, 68 people completed the new questionnaire and six 24-hour recalls for comparison. Agreement was fair to good, with food group links ranging from weak for legumes to strong for meat. Most people fell in the same or a nearby quarter rank for diet quality on both tools. The authors conclude that the new tool gives a usable picture of modern diets for large nutrition studies.
pmc-13440726:
Sabrina Ee-Ying Ong and colleagues pool trials of therapies meant to repair social functioning in traumatised teenagers, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. Posttraumatic stress symptoms often sour friendships, family ties, and trust, yet therapy research usually grades symptom relief alone. Searches found seventeen studies yielding thirty-five effect sizes on interpersonal functioning. Intervention type, delivery mode, and session count were tested as possible moderators of benefit.

Gains right after treatment were small but reliable across studies. Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy produced the largest effect of any approach. Formats mixing solo sessions with joint or group work beat group-only delivery. At three months, the pooled effect grew to medium size on the few available measures. More sessions did not change immediate gains, though they tracked with stronger follow-up results. The authors ask for trials that target social mechanisms directly and track them longer.
pmc-13441826:
Ping Li and colleagues pool studies on a nutrition-and-inflammation score as a survival predictor for lung cancer patients on immune checkpoint drugs, publishing a 2026 meta-analysis. The prognostic nutritional index blends albumin and lymphocyte counts from routine blood work. Fourteen observational studies covering 2,106 patients with non-small cell lung cancer treated with PD-1 or PD-L1 blockers were pooled with standard quality grading.

Patients with higher scores at baseline lived markedly longer overall and went longer without progression. The pattern held across study regions, spanning China, Turkey, Japan, and the United Kingdom, and across the score cutoffs used. Survival pooling showed heavy statistical heterogeneity, yet sensitivity checks kept the result standing. Signs of publication bias appeared, and correction for missing studies barely moved the estimate. The authors nominate the index as a cheap candidate marker for immunotherapy prognosis.
pmc-13442426:
Erin Karissa and colleagues map where microbe hunters have found actinomycetes across Indonesia in a 2026 review. These thread-like microbes make many drug-like compounds, yet most past finds in the island nation came from plain soil. The review builds a family tree from gene reads for 152 strains drawn from soils, caves, hot areas, mangroves, seas, and plants.

Most strains fell in one genus, Streptomyces, long known as a rich source of new compounds. Just 44 microbe products from the country have firm or likely structures so far, a small count next to world reports. The authors note that few strains get full DNA reads and public deposits. They urge wider hunts in odd habitats, paired with gene work, to lift both name accuracy and drug finds.
pmc-13442626:
Yaojie Zheng's team better gel tests in 2026 for gauging the 11S to 7S ratio in soybean storage proteins, a key quality trait for breeding, handling, and allergy work. Standard SDS-PAGE is cheap and easy, yet pull-out spread and fuzzy bands limit numeric trust. Two known pull-out methods were compared across three types, then merged into a new buffer method with sugar, binder, cutting agent, and protein-cutting blocker.

The new method gave clearer bands, lower error spread, higher stat gap, and strong straight-line fit between band strength and protein amount, with steady ratios across runs. Across fourteen breeding lines, ratios ranged from about 1.29 to 2.20, sorting types well. Soybean breeders get a reliable, low-cost ratio assay for selection and handling.
pmc-13443026:
Ruben Munoz-Cabrera and colleagues map smart computer tools onto HIV care tasks in a 2026 review. Virus care now spans test, drug choice, and long watch phases, each with rich but messy data. Their review covered more than 50 studies from 2017 to November 2025, sorted by care scope, data type, source, and tool type.

The map pairs each clinic task with the tool class that fits it best, from plain math models to neural nets and text tools. Drug care has tamed the virus for many, yet gaps in speed and reach keep tools welcome. Source banks and their limits get blunt notes for each task. The authors aim the frame at clinicians who must pick tools without deep tech training. They stress fit to task over raw model power.
pmc-13443626:
Yi-Xuan Wang and colleagues join whole-genome reads with blood chemical scans in up to 199,138 UK Biobank members in a 2026 study. Blood metabolites mark how genes shape health, yet array-based gene work missed much of their code. The team mapped gene control of 313 blood chemicals at full genome depth.

Single-variant hunts found 36,105 solo signals, with a 22.20 percent share new to science in their count. Fine maps pinned 12,361 likely cause links with sharper aim than array work. Rare variant group tests added 1,527 gene-trait pairs. Twin checks with disease genes gave 245 likely cause links, such as omega-3 fats with gallstone risk. Protein picks with matched effects named 410 drug target leads, all shared in an open web resource.
pmc-13443926:
Hussam Osman reviews smart computer tools in blood lab diagnosis in a 2026 paper. Blood work leans on hand scope reads and expert eyes, which vary between labs and tire with load. The review sweeps four databases for tools that read cell shapes, flow data, chromosome maps, and gene marks.

Deep learning nets scored well at cell shape reads, from blood smears to marrow slides, and caught faint odd marks. Flow tools sped gate work and flagged rare events. Gene tools aided chromosome sorts and variant calls, while triage tools helped plan care steps. Blocks span messy data, thin proof, cost, and rule gaps, with African labs in sharp focus. The author urges shared data and staged proof before wide trust.
pmc-13444126:
Wang Pei and colleagues assess a 2026 survey of nurses' knowledge and confidence in spotting adult sepsis at two hospitals in eastern China, where early recognition saves lives but skills vary. The team surveyed 355 registered nurses with a 15-item knowledge test aligned to Sepsis-3, a confidence scale, and an open question on support needs.

Average knowledge reached 10.04 out of 15, with gaps in early signs and shock care, while confidence averaged 17.22 out of 25 and correlated only weakly with knowledge. Nurses in emergency, intensive, and respiratory critical care outscored ward nurses, and education, seniority, and exposure predicted knowledge. The authors call for structured training, simulation, and standard workflows, especially on general wards.
pmc-13446326:
Valérie Dormal and colleagues test strawberry leaf extract in older adults who feel their memory slipping, in a 2026 randomized trial with a placebo arm and blinded dosing. Plant compounds called ellagitannins, rich in strawberry leaves, show guard effects on the brain in lab work. The trial asked whether the extract lifts memory and eases felt stress in daily life.

Treated adults beat the placebo group on a paired-associates learning test, a standard probe of episode memory. Gains also showed in word memory and working memory tasks. After twelve weeks the treated group reported lower felt stress than at the start. The extract was safe and well borne in this group, and the authors frame it as a gentle option for aging minds.
pmc-13447226:
Junjie Zhong leads a team studying an ovary response index in older fertility patients in a 2026 review of treatment cycles in Yulin, China. The index combines eggs collected and drug dose to show how sensitively ovaries respond. Women aged thirty-five and older often respond poorly, so a simple guide to likely outcomes would help counselling.

More than a thousand fresh embryo transfer cycles from 2021 to 2023 were split into low, middle and high index thirds. Higher index patients needed less drug, produced more eggs and had more good embryos, with higher pregnancy test rates. Live birth rates did not differ across the groups, however. Once age and a hormone marker of egg supply were taken into account, the index no longer predicted pregnancy on its own.
pmc-13447826:
Xavier Bosch-Capblanch leads a team mapping stakeholder positions around introducing the RTS,S malaria vaccine in Ghana in a 2026 study. New health technologies fail without the right actors engaged at the right stage, from research through regulation to delivery. A partnership framework supplied the stages, and members of a research consortium reported where they and others sit along that chain.

Thirty-one stakeholders answered a questionnaire, with a workshop held to validate the map. Most involvement clustered near service delivery, the final stage, rather than earlier research and regulatory steps. A small number of actors held the highest interest and influence over introduction. High vaccine demand beside thin domestic research capacity mirrors wider African patterns, the authors note, and broader inclusion plus stronger upstream capacity would firm the path for future technologies.
pmc-13448026:
Sen Wang and colleagues build a machine learning model to predict kidney injury after off-pump heart bypass surgery in a 2026 study. Kidney injury complicates roughly a quarter of heart operations and raises death risk and cost. Off-pump bypass, done without a heart-lung machine, still carries substantial risk, so early warning from routine data could guide protective care.

Records for nine hundred thirty-eight patients treated between mid 2023 and early 2025 were analysed, and about twenty-two percent developed kidney injury. Features drawn from before surgery plus time-series signals during surgery fed several models. A gradient boosting model won on held-out validation with very strong discrimination. Explanation analysis ranked a kidney filtration marker first and a heart strain marker second among predictors, giving clinicians a ranked risk picture.
pmc-13448126:
Nishimura presents a 2026 commentary on a nationwide study of repeat lumbar surgery after spinal fusion in patients with Parkinson disease. Parkinson's brings stiff posture, weak back muscles, bone thinning, and balance problems, all hostile to fusion surgery. The commented study used matched nationwide data to compare later surgery rates, a design the commentary examines for what it can and cannot prove.

Life expectancy in Parkinson's keeps improving with better medical therapy, so more patients will face elective spine surgery and live long enough to need revision. The commentary's value lies in framing: which risks belong to the disease, which to surgical choice, and where matched data blur the two. Surgeons counseling Parkinson's patients need exactly that separation before quoting reoperation odds, and patients deserve prognosis built on their disease's mechanics, not generic fusion statistics.
pmc-13448526:
Elizabeth E. Manning and coauthors test a 2026 mouse study of threat bias in a leading fixated-driven illness model, male Sapap3 knockout mice, using a platform dodging task with facing and response blocking. Split cohorts trained under high or low shock strength were tested for dodging learning, fading, and reward seeking under conflict.

Knockout mice held back reward seeking more and froze more during warning tones, showing raised threat alertness under conflict. Dodging faded more strongly after facing therapy only under low shock training, with early signs of reduced fore-brain action. The region may mediate therapy effects and threat-reward balance in OCD.
pmc-13448826:
Darren Gray and a large team report in 2026 a village-level trial in Central Java, Indonesia, testing whether better latrines plus hygiene education can curb intestinal worm infections. Eight village clusters with 2,155 participants took part between October 2016 and October 2017. Intervention villages got mass deworming drugs, an improved pit latrine called the BALatrine, and community hygiene teaching, while control villages received the drugs alone.

Stool samples checked twelve months later showed infection starting near 13 percent in both arms. The combined intervention cut the odds of any worm infection sharply, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.22. Protection reached full effectiveness against roundworm and 95 percent against hookworm, though the drop in whipworm did not reach statistical significance. The authors argue sanitation and education deserve a central place beside drug campaigns.
pmc-13449326:
Yuan Yuan and colleagues examined a possible new lever against liver cancer in 2026, focused on the gene ETV4. Hepatocellular carcinoma often runs through the RAF, MEK, and ERK signaling chain, and the drug sorafenib blocks RAF. Yet blocking RAF can paradoxically switch the chain back on, which helps explain why some tumors resist sorafenib. Since ETV4 sits downstream of ERK, silencing it might bypass that rebound.

Using a liver tumor cell line and a normal liver cell line for comparison, the team knocked ETV4 down with small interfering RNA and measured cell behavior. The experiments test whether lowering ETV4 slows growth and spread in tumor cells while sparing normal cells. The paper offers an early laboratory case for ETV4 as a target worth testing further in drug-resistant liver cancer.
pmc-13449526:
Nurul Adilah-Amrannudin and co-authors investigate in 2026 insecticide resistance in the mosquito Aedes albopictus across northern Peninsular Malaysia, where spray programs are losing their bite. Mosquitoes from four localities in Penang and Perlis faced World Health Organization bioassays against five insecticides, from larvicides to pyrethroids. Survivors then had three segments of their sodium channel gene sequenced, the very target pyrethroids attack, and computer docking tested how mutations change drug binding.

Every strain showed some resistance to every insecticide tried. Alongside the known F1534L change, the team found new mutations, A1022S and A1022P, E1041K, P1585R, and F1695L, scattered across the channel. Family-tree and haplotype analyses suggested the resistance changes arose multiple times rather than spreading from one source. Docking showed the new variants alter how pyrethroids grip the channel, tying genotype to the survival phenotype and giving control programs a molecular watch list.
pmc-13450526:
Keyu Li and colleagues mapped genes for leaf angle in maize in 2026, a trait that shapes how much light dense plantings capture. Upright leaves let more light reach lower leaves, supporting high-density planting and higher yields. The genetic basis of leaf angle in southeast Chinese breeding lines was not fully mapped.

A panel of 212 inbred lines was genotyped with a 60,000-marker array, and five association models were run. Fourteen significant markers and 342 nearby candidate genes emerged, with six markers stable across models, including four novel loci. Eleven high-confidence genes at those loci point to hormone signaling and leaf development pathways. Breeders gain targets for shaping maize canopies for denser planting.
pmc-13452226:
Liu and colleagues built in 2026 a neural network, MD-Mamba, that classifies breast cancer tissue images into four classes from normal to invasive cancer. Standard image networks see only small neighborhoods at once and can miss the broad tissue patterns pathologists rely on. Their design joins a state-space model, which reads long-range order cheaply, with widened convolutions that view the tissue at several scales at once.

A two-path attention stage then spotlights diagnostic regions and reweights features, which also makes the model's choices easier to inspect. On the BACH benchmark of four hundred microscopy images, the model reached accuracy above ninety-six percent and classified every malignant image correctly in its test run. Part-removal studies showed each block of the design adds to the score.
pmc-13452326:
Pileggi and colleagues published a 2026 study on how stomach bypass surgery rewires women's muscles. Roux-en-Y bypass shrinks the stomach and reroutes food to aid weight loss. The team tracked 41 women before surgery and one year afterward. They read gene tags and gene activity in thigh muscle samples.

Over 8,000 gene regions changed their chemical tags after the surgery. More than 2,000 genes also changed how strongly they switched on. Muscle-building and protein-making genes turned up, aiding strength and repair. Energy-factory genes eased down even as those factories grew in number. Pre-surgery muscle traits partly predicted who lost the most weight. Weight loss and fat loss were marked across the full group. Muscle samples came from the thigh muscle of each participant studied.
pmc-13453026:
Kim surveyed Seoul-area baby boomers in 2026 on a Korean policy that would build retirement communities offering housing and care in one place, often outside big cities. South Korea became a super-aged society in late 2024, and the policy hopes to draw city retirees to smaller regions. The plan rested on an old web survey that missed offline elders, so fresh face-to-face data were gathered.

Willingness to join came in high, at about four in five respondents. Most wanted to stay within an hour of the capital and near medical care. Low-rise, mid-size apartments were favored, as were mixed rental and owned units. Respondents were mostly educated and middle class, which Kim reads as a sign that support should reach beyond low-income groups.
pmc-13453726:
Yuanyang Ye and four co-authors report a brain tumor that hid behind a large bleed and was first read as a stroke from high blood pressure. Their 2026 case report follows a 60 year old man whose CT scan showed an 87.1 millilitre bleed deep in the right side of his brain. Surgeons drained the blood, and he went home with a pressure related diagnosis.

Two months later he returned with a bulging skull flap and rising pressure, yet scans showed only a fluid filled cyst. Three spinal taps then told the true story: the fluid teemed with odd cells bearing cancer marks, and its chemistry ran far from normal. Tissue proof later confirmed a grade IV glioblastoma that had spread along the brain's lining. The authors urge spinal fluid cell checks when a bleed behaves oddly.
pmc-13453826:
Aida Sehle and Joachim Liepert test a gait training aid that triggers the leg's flexor reflex with electric pulses in people years past a stroke. The reflex bends the hip, knee, and ankle together, which can help a stiff leg swing through. Their 2026 pilot covers five patients a mean of 3.8 years after stroke, in 15 training sessions over five weeks.

Walking tests ran with and without the pulses, at two baselines, right after training, and at 3 and 12 months. Both the ten metre walk and the two minute walk improved after training, and the gains still showed at three months. Walking with the reflex on also beat walking with it off at the checks. Users rated the device highly, and blinded video review saw safer, faster gait. The authors call for a randomized trial to split training gains from device gains.
pmc-13454026:
Yanting Shi and five co-authors report Sweet syndrome, a painful skin flare of fever and tender plaques, arising in a woman whose ulcerative colitis seemed quiet. Their 2026 case report follows a 60 year old woman on anti TNF therapy whose bowel scope had suggested remission. A skin biopsy showed the dense neutrophil crowd typical of the syndrome, and infection tests came back clean.

A fresh colonoscopy then told another story: the bowel was in fact actively inflamed, which likely drove the skin flare. The anti TNF drug infliximab failed, so the team switched to upadacitinib, a JAK inhibitor, at 45 milligrams a day. Pain eased within a week and the plaque healed fully by week eight, with the bowel healed at follow up. A lower dose then held both conditions in remission.
pmc-13454226:
Shanshan Chen and eight co-authors describe staged nursing care for a 13 year old girl with the worst grade of mouth sores after a stem cell transplant. The girl, treated for transfusion dependent thalassemia, developed sores on day six that reached grade 4 by day seventeen, with bleeding, a locked jaw, and no ability to eat. Her blood counts were wiped out and platelet transfusions kept failing.

The nursing path split care into phases, mixing constant checks with behavior tools such as tell show do coaching and music distraction. Caregiver help made mouth rinsing and ultraviolet treatment possible despite severe pain. The sores eased to grade 1 by discharge at day 32 and cleared by day 84, while pain fell from 8 to 0. Anxiety and nutrition risk scores also improved. The authors note that many measures ran at once, so no single one can take credit.
pmc-13454326:
Zeinab Zaheri Abdehvand and others joined two satellite eyes in 2026 for fine soil-fertility maps in Khuzestan wheat fields. Soil-fertility maps steer fertiliser use, but field-scale maps need both fine colour detail and fine ground detail. Three plans were tried with forest models.

EnMAP colour-rich data alone scored zero point eight four, Sentinel-2 data scored zero point seven two, and joined data scored zero point nine zero with ground detail down to ten metres. The fertility score joined eight soil traits, such as organic matter, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, salt, iron, carbonate, and texture. Near sixty-one percent of the land fell in the mid-fertility class. Farm advisers gain a joined-data map for precise wheat care.
pmc-13454726:
Agata Bronisławska and six colleagues review, in 2026, macrohormones, oversized hormone complexes that fool laboratory tests. A macrohormone forms when a normal hormone sticks to an antibody, creating a molecule too large to act yet still counted by assays. The result can be a false high reading in a healthy person.

The best-known case involves prolactin, and a simple chemical settling test can unmask it. Reports now cover many other hormones, from thyroid and growth signals to insulin and calcitonin. Each can send doctors toward scans and drugs a patient never needed. The authors urge testing for macrohormones whenever symptoms and lab values disagree. That single check, they argue, can prevent overdiagnosis and spare patients needless treatment.
pmc-13454826:
Bayar A. Qasim and five colleagues describe, in a 2026 case report, a twelve-year-old girl whose knock-knees traced back to a hormone disorder, not a bone problem. Overactive parathyroid glands are rare in children. Her legs bent further despite corrective surgery and supplements, and she had earlier suffered high calcium during a pancreas attack.

Blood tests showed calcium far above normal and parathyroid hormone at roughly fifteen times healthy levels, with very low vitamin D. Neck imaging found a small tumor on one gland, and X-rays showed cystic, soap-bubble lesions in her bones. Tissue checks confirmed the classic bone disease of hormone excess. Burning the tumor away with a radiofrequency needle normalized her calcium and hormone levels. Her lesions nearly vanished on follow-up scans, and the leg bend improved markedly. The authors urge hormone checks before bone surgery in such children.
pmc-13455426:
Yuki Kondo and colleagues test a workshop that teaches pharmacists to size up drug interactions with numbers in a 2026 study. Drug interactions cause many adverse events, and a framework called PISCS can estimate how much one drug changes another's exposure, yet most pharmacists had little chance to practise it. Workshops at two Japanese pharmacy conferences enrolled 45 pharmacists, who rated their confidence before and after case-based sessions.

Before training, 60.0 percent knew of PISCS but 55.6 percent had never used it in practice. Afterward, confidence rose in every domain, including finding interaction data, predicting exposure change and proposing prescription changes, and 95.6 percent called the workshop useful for practice. The study shows confidence gains, not proven prescribing change, but it offers a ready model for turning a quantitative tool into daily pharmacy work.
pmc-13456526:
Bevens and co-authors study the teamwork behind universal depression screening in this 2026 qualitative study inside a large pediatric hospital network. Many hospital systems now screen every young patient for depression. Yet nobody had examined how the workflow survives day to day in practice. So the team ran focus groups with the staff who run it.

Eight focus groups gathered 37 nurses, physicians, and behavioral health staff from participating units. Six barriers and five proposed solutions emerged, organized along the care cascade from screening through assessment to planning what happens after a positive result. Staff flagged screening questionnaire wording that fits younger and neurodivergent patients poorly, rigid separation between medical and mental health roles, and missing infrastructure for follow-up referrals. Their fixes include adapting the language, cross-training staff, and creating dedicated follow-up roles.
pmc-13457126:
Marco Öchsner and six colleagues test, in a 2026 imaging study, one brain tumor model that keeps working when a key scan type is missing. Glioblastoma outlining software usually expects a full MRI set, including the FLAIR sequence that lights up swelling. Real clinics sometimes lack it. The team trained a standard segmentation network while randomly blanking the FLAIR channel, a trick called targeted dropout.

With the full scan set, the dropout model matched the ordinary one, scoring about 95 percent overlap with expert outlines. When FLAIR was removed at test time, the ordinary model sagged to about 81 percent, while the dropout model held near 93 percent. Whole-tumor volume error shrank from a forty-six milliliter miss to under one. A separate model trained only on three sequences did just as well, though. The authors credit adapting to fewer inputs, by dropout or by design, as the real fix.
pmc-13457226:
Claire Nancy Walker, Michael Lambert, and Karen Estelle Welman take stock of how elite athletes in non-motorised surface water sports are monitored in training and competition. Coaches track workload to sharpen performance and cut injury risk, but sports such as sailing, rowing, and canoeing add wind and water loads that land-based tools were never built to capture. Their 2026 scoping review searched four databases and kept 22 papers.

Heart-rate measures of internal load dominated, appearing in 71 percent of the studies, while GPS-based external load measures appeared in 47 percent. Both families of metrics were borrowed from land and ergometer settings and remain unvalidated against the environmental strain that defines these sports. Youth athletes and women were notably underrepresented in the literature. The authors advise reading every metric against the day's conditions and call for monitoring methods designed for the water, plus broader coverage of sailors and canoeists.
pmc-13457526:
Ruoxi Yang and co-authors ran a head-to-head comparison of two imaging scans for finding and staging pancreatic cancer. Their 2026 prospective study scanned 97 patients suspected of having the disease with both a newer tracer scan, FAPI PET/CT, and the standard FDG PET/CT scan. The FAPI scan targets a protein abundant around pancreatic tumors. Of the group, 88 patients were confirmed to have pancreatic cancer by pathology or follow-up imaging.

The FAPI scan lit up primary tumors much more strongly than the standard scan. It separated cancer from background tissue better in lymph nodes, liver, peritoneum, and bone as well. Overall diagnostic accuracy reached 93.2 percent for the FAPI scan against 72.7 percent for the standard scan in this cohort. Using it changed the recorded stage of seven patients and altered treatment plans for six, including patients moved from surgery to non-surgical care.
pmc-13457926:
Libby R. Copeland-Halperin, Lauren O'Brien, and Michelle Copeland share lessons from a case series of lower leg liposculpture, a contouring operation many surgeons avoid. Fat that ignores diet and exercise can thicken ankles, calves, and inner knees, yet the region's nerves, lymphatics, and veins punish careless technique. Their 2026 retrospective review covers both-legs cases from 2021 to 2025 that combined laser, power-assisted, and fine-cannula liposuction.

Of 40 lower leg cases, 30 sculpted all three zones. Surgeons removed an average of 793 cubic centimeters per leg in sessions lasting about 115 minutes. Follow-up averaged just over four months. Three patients had problems: skin darkening, a thickened scar, and a pressure injury with cellulitis plus lingering swelling. The authors argue that careful checks before surgery, honest advice, and careful aftercare let a multimodal approach reshape the lower leg with limited harm. They pass along practical lessons for colleagues attempting it.
pmc-13458526:
Yanru Wang and a large collaboration test two sister crystals as wafer-thin sources of entangled light. Quantum technologies run on entangled photons, usually made in bulky crystals that resist shrinking onto chips. Their 2026 study compares spontaneous parametric down-conversion, where one pump photon splits into two, inside the van der Waals ferroelectrics NbOBr2 and NbOI2, tying performance back to each crystal's structure and optics.

The iodide compound proved the better near-infrared source, extending the working wavelength range of this material family. It directly produced polarization-entangled photon pairs with a concurrence of 0.90, give or take 0.05, a strong entanglement score for so thin a source. The bromide still worked, giving the pair a useful contrast for design rules. Beyond adding two candidates to the source library, the authors extract guidance for engineering integrated quantum photonic materials, where ferroelectric layering may let builders tune entanglement into the stack itself.
pmc-13458726:
Mateusz Kciuk and colleagues test new sulfa compounds against bowel cancer cells in a 2026 study. Bowel cancer ranks third in incidence and second in cancer deaths worldwide, and new drug scaffolds remain needed. A series of pyrazolo-triazine and pyrazolo-tetrazolo-triazine sulfa drugs was tested for cell-killing power and mechanism, with four leads, MM134, MM136, MM137 and MM139, studied in depth.

Adding a tetrazole ring raised cell-killing power up to 50-fold and focus to between 3.6-fold and 9.2-fold versus non-tetrazole cousins, with lead half-kill levels from about a tenth to about one micromolar. Leads damaged DNA, blocked growth, triggered death and rotting features, and bound directly with double-strand DNA. MM137 killed cells in 3D cell balls at 5 micromolar, marking that series as hopeful leads for animal testing.
pmc-13458826:
Javier Melchor Duart Clemente and three colleagues wrote this 2026 letter on complications of ACDF. The operation, anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, removes damaged neck discs and fuses the spine bones with plates. They respond to a paper by Mundis comparing one long plate against several segmental plates in long neck fusions. The letter pushes the biomechanical side of the argument further.

Mundis proposed that a single long plate is less stiff, especially in rotation. Stress then piles up at the lowest segment, raising failure risk there. The letter writers agree this distal instability helps explain failed fusion at that level. They add points the original paper left aside. Plate design matters, because dynamic plates that allow slight movement share load differently from rigid ones. Shorter plates generally behave better, too. Weighing the mechanical environment, they argue, could prevent complications rather than merely explain them.
pmc-13459426:
Ali Aydilek and Yusuf Erdem studied whether the size of the back fragment in a three bone ankle fracture predicts how well patients walk and function after surgery. Their 2026 review covered seventy two patients operated on for trimalleolar fractures between 2017 and 2022. Patients were split by whether the posterior malleolar fragment covered under or over a quarter of the joint surface. Outcomes combined standard foot and quality of life scores with smartphone based gait analysis, benchmarked against seventy two matched healthy controls.

Patients with larger fragments developed worse post traumatic arthritis grades over follow up. The smaller fragment group scored better on physical function and sports activity scales. Other foot scores and pain ratings did not differ between the fragment groups, however. Against healthy controls, both patient groups walked with clearly impaired speed, step timing, step length, and cadence. Gait stayed abnormal regardless of fragment size.
pmc-13460226:
Jiayi Xu and co-authors map in 2026 research linking idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis with interleukins, a family of immune signaling proteins. Interest in this pairing has grown because some interleukin pathways drive scarring while others might be druggable. Searching two databases, the team gathered 832 papers and fifteen clinical studies, then charted themes, cited links, and keyword bursts with mapping software spanning 1999 to 2025.

Attention to the field is rising steadily, led by the United States and China. Mechanism studies and treatment strategy work dominate the themes, and bursting keywords include the antifibrotic drug pirfenidone alongside diagnosis and fibrosis itself. The authors present interleukins as promising markers and offer their map to guide lab checks and patient grouping for future trials.
pmc-13460526:
Katie Louise Saxby and colleagues tested in 2026 whether metformin, the common diabetes drug, actually protects against abdominal aortic aneurysm, a dangerous ballooning of the main artery. No proven drug treatment exists to slow these aneurysms. Their approach paired an observational analysis in UK Biobank, with 2,972 aneurysm cases matched against about eighty-nine thousand controls. It also used Mendelian randomization, a genetic technique that mimics a trial using inherited variants tied to metformin's targets.

People reporting metformin use had roughly half the aneurysm risk of others. The genetic analysis agreed, estimating about a forty-three percent risk reduction for an effect equal to a prescribed dose, and the signal appeared only for metformin's own targets. The authors call for clinical trials of the drug in aneurysm patients.
pmc-13460726:
Nezahat Merve Ata Soylu leads a Turkish team that studied in 2026 whether ordinary blood count markers can flag children likely to suffer preoperative anxiety or emergence agitation. That agitation is the confused, thrashing state some children enter while waking from anesthesia. Their prospective study enrolled 350 children aged five to twelve, rating anxiety in the waiting room and agitation in recovery with standard scales, alongside pain scores timed after surgery.

About thirty-seven percent developed agitation, and those children showed higher white cell and platelet counts with lower lymphocytes before surgery. Composite inflammation ratios ran higher across the board. In adjusted models, younger age, worse pain, and a high systemic immune inflammation index predicted agitation on their own. Anxious parents joined the predictors for preoperative anxiety.
pmc-13461026:
Prabhat Kaphle and colleagues present in 2026 a 30-year-old Bangladeshi man whose vomiting of blood traced back to a hidden hepatitis B infection. Occult infection means the usual surface antigen test reads negative while viral DNA still circulates, quietly injuring the liver. His first tests were doubly misleading: surface antigen and core antibody both came back negative. His liver ultrasound showed no cirrhosis or lesions, yet his esophagus held swollen varicose veins that had burst.

Viral DNA testing finally confirmed the hidden infection as the driver of his portal hypertension. Bleeding was stopped with transfusions and fluids, a beta blocker was started, and repeated endoscopic banding sessions tied off the veins. Follow-up showed stable varices with no new bleeding, and the authors stress DNA testing whenever portal hypertension lacks an explanation.
pmc-13461326:
Fan Bu and co-authors review in 2026 drug treatment for sleep disturbance after breast cancer surgery, a common yet overlooked complication that feeds pain, fatigue, low mood, and slow recovery. Sleep problems in this setting arrive in different flavors, so the review matches drugs to patterns rather than prescribing one answer. Short courses of sleeping pills fit brief insomnia driven by nighttime hyperarousal, while melatonin style drugs suit a scrambled body clock.

Pain-heavy presentations point instead toward gabapentinoid drugs and layered pain control. Safety checks run throughout: total sedative load, breathing risks when opioids are aboard, next-day grogginess, and interactions with hormone therapy such as avoiding strong metabolic blockers with tamoxifen. Talk therapy for insomnia anchors the non-drug side, supported selectively by light therapy, exercise, mindfulness, and acupuncture.
pmc-13461526:
Sakata and colleagues examine a signaling protein called SMAD4 in mouth cancer in this 2026 study. SMAD4 helps relay signals from transforming growth factor beta, a molecule that can restrain tumors, but its role in oral squamous cell carcinoma was little studied. The team stained tumor samples from 90 patients who had received chemotherapy and radiation before surgery, and ran cell experiments on drug sensitivity.

Tumors with low SMAD4 were significantly more likely to have spread to lymph nodes. They also responded poorly to the pre-surgery treatment. And they carried a worse outlook for the patient. In lab cells, lowering SMAD4 made cancers harder to kill with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, two standard drugs, and raised levels of cIAP2, a protein that blocks cell death. The authors caution that SMAD4 alone may not predict outcomes independently.
pmc-13461626:
Khreich and Ayoub used in 2026 machine learning to predict wellbeing in empty-nest parents, those whose children have left home. Worked examples that turn prediction methods into psychology questions are scarce, so the pair used the empty nest as a demonstration case. They drew on a large European survey of over forty-three thousand parents aged 45 and older, matched the two parent groups fairly, and hunted for robust predictors among 77 candidates.

Khreich found the two groups barely differed in happiness or life satisfaction, even after matching. Health status and a sense of freedom and control predicted happiness most strongly. Life satisfaction drew on a wider set, spanning personal resources, social ties, trust in institutions, and social capital. Most predictors worked alike in both groups, with only a modest set of group-specific effects. The authors conclude wellbeing in later life rides on factors that cross family setups.
pmc-13462226:
Kenneth A Winter and colleagues introduce, in a 2026 study, a task measuring test anxiety by what it does to performance, not by self-report. Every existing tool for test anxiety is a survey, which cannot show functional harm. Their task, PEAT, times how much negative judgment disrupts a person's work. Scores came from 573 participants, and four checks tested whether the task measures the right thing.

Students sorted as highly test anxious showed a sharper cortisol rise under evaluation than low-anxiety peers. Brain recordings showed altered engagement with test-related threat, but not general threats. In a response-control task, high-anxiety students made more errors after negative feedback, while accuracy held. Scores showed no link to attention deficit diagnoses or medication use. The authors read the combined behavior, body, and brain evidence as support for a measure of test anxiety that impairs function.
pmc-13462326:
Zhitao Yao and colleagues studied jaw joint fracture healing in rats in 2026, asking how a small chemical mark on RNA shapes bone repair. The mark, called m6A, is added by an enzyme named METTL3, and its role in jaw healing was unclear. The team tracked healing at one and five weeks with scans and lab tests of bone and cartilage markers.

Raising METTL3 sped bone healing and bone-cell growth, while lowering it slowed repair, broke bone structure, and pushed cells toward cartilage instead. In lab-grown stem cells, silencing METTL3 cut cell survival and bone growth and damped a growth signal path known as TGF-beta/Smad. A target named IGF-BP3 emerged, with its message made more stable by the mark, pointing to a route that might one day aid jaw fracture care.
pmc-13462726:
Johanna Saia Pope and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 concept study, what the term health misinformation means in current writing. False health claims are a growing worry in a digital age, yet the label is fuzzy. The team ran the first phase of a three-phase concept analysis. It combined a systematic trawl of literature from 2016 to 2022, a stratified random sample of texts, and a theme-by-theme reading of how authors use the term.

Writers traced the problem to fast technology change, actors profiting from false claims, and cultural strains such as fragmentation and fading trust in authorities. They depicted misinformation as a scourge marked by falseness or deceit, persuasive tricks, and power to break agreement. Harms reach individuals, communities, and social systems. Disagreements surfaced across the literature, which the article does not hide. Later phases will add interviews and combine both strands into a tighter shared definition.
pmc-13463126:
Breed and colleagues in Australia asked in 2026 what the broad public knows and feels about gene guided drug choice. The field, pharmacogenomics, reads a patient's genes to pick drugs and doses that fit. Uptake in clinics has lagged, though the gains are clear. The team ran a land wide poll of 772 adults, then sat down with 21 for long talks. Both sets weighed care, trust, and cost.

Three in four polled had never heard of the field. One in sixteen both knew it and felt sure of the facts. Talks gave five strands: grasp, trust, whole care, clinic worth, and reach. Folk backed the idea once it was laid plain. Cost and murk held them back. The authors urge plain words, open talk, and price fixes first.
pmc-13464726:
Lennart von Fritsch leads a large team that asks whether surgery serves pancreatic cancer patients aged eighty and older. Case counts in this age group rose from 2015 to 2023 across Germany. Tumors were often caught earlier in older patients, yet their outcomes still trailed younger groups.

Death rates after treatment ran higher for the oldest patients. Many who had surgery never went on to receive chemotherapy afterward, leaving the weaker half of the standard pairing. Surgery alone or chemo alone landed survival close to comfort-only care in this group. Giving chemo first, the authors suggest, could reveal who is fit enough to gain from the full combined push.
pmc-13464826:
Li and co-authors presented in 2026 the case of a 33-year-old man who healed without another operation. After surgery to repair a detached retina, his eye developed a full-thickness macular hole. That is a defect in the central retina. The team paired the case with a review of more than 30 published instances of spontaneous closure.

The man's hole sealed itself within three months while his vision improved. He was managed with anti-inflammatory eye drops and watchful waiting. The review found holes form when membranes on the retina's surface pull sideways. Swelling, surgical trauma, and inflammation worsen the pull, and high-altitude exposure is a surprising extra risk. Closure favors small holes, where retinal support tissue can bridge the gap as swelling resolves. That happens in roughly one in twenty to one in six cases. Patience can therefore precede surgery for quiet, small holes.
pmc-13465026:
Carson C. Edwards and six co-authors test whether oxidative DNA damage can foretell treatment response in high-grade serous ovarian cancer. Platinum chemotherapy helps some patients and fails others, with return of disease common inside two years. A fresh damage-reading method let the team score tumor damage directly.

High oxidative damage tracked with cancer recurrence after treatment. Damage levels also matched the tumor's skill at homologous recombination, a DNA repair route that blunts platinum drugs. Tumors rich in oxidative damage showed quieter IDO1 and TGF-beta immune-damping signals. Immune cell mixes inside tumors shifted alongside the damage scores. The authors propose damage scoring as a guide for forecasting survival and picking therapy.
pmc-13465526:
Hui Jin and seven co-authors benchmark six ways to encode DNA letters for models that predict what non-coding variants do. Letter changes outside genes steer regulation and disease, yet turning them into numbers shapes every model downstream. Six encoding styles, from plain categories to meaning-rich embeddings, faced three trait-linked tasks.

Nine learning models, from classic methods to deep nets, each ran the full encoding set under repeated, controlled trials. No single winner emerged; instead, encoding, model type, and data preparation bent results together. Readability, richness, and computing cost each pulled the choice a different way. The standardized frame gives genomics teams a fair test track for picking encodings before they commit to a pipeline.
pmc-13465726:
Mateusz Szczupak and colleagues ask whether inflammation markers in the blood can predict how severe the after-effects of intensive care will be, in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Those after-effects, grouped as post-intensive care syndrome, span weaker bodies, foggy thinking, and mental health strain. The main analysis covered 267 adults treated in one intensive care unit.

Blood levels of C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and interleukin-6 were drawn at set points during the hospital stay. Patients then filled a syndrome questionnaire at discharge and again two and three months later, with the three-month score as the main target. Models adjusted for age, sex, reason for admission, and other basic factors when testing the links.
pmc-13465926:
Lucia Maria Procopciuc, Adriana Corina Hangan, and Roxana Liana Lucaciu review the two-way traffic between gut and brain in metabolic syndrome, publishing in 2026. The syndrome bundles belly obesity, insulin resistance, unhealthy blood fats, and high blood pressure into one risk pattern. Microbes in the gut sit at the center of the review's account.

Imbalanced gut communities, a leakier gut wall, and steady low-grade inflammation form the core chain the authors describe. Microbial products such as short-chain fatty acids and bacterial wall fragments carry signals along nerve, hormone, and immune routes. Inherited traits and gene switches also shape how each person responds, which points toward care tailored to the individual.
pmc-13466126:
Ren and co-authors reviewed a 2026 account of ionizing irradiation as a green processing tool for rice and rice products. Radiation extends shelf life and improves safety without heat or chemical residues left behind. Its effects run through rice starch, whose layered structure from molecule to granule sets cooking and eating quality.

The review covers three common radiation types and how each reshapes starch structure across those scales. Ren connects the structural changes to physical properties, sensory quality, and storage stability of finished rice products. Current industrial uses and technical limits are weighed critically alongside proposed fixes for the field. The authors close with future directions grounded in the starch structure to quality relationship that organisers of processing could apply.
pmc-13466226:
Maxat Toishimanov and co-authors scan blood chemistry for early molecular signs along the road from normal sugar control to type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 study of 188 people. Groups covered 48 controls, 113 people with prediabetes, and 27 with diabetes, sorted by standard diagnostic rules. A broad, untargeted instrument read hundreds of small molecules in each serum sample.

Patterns shifted step by step across the three groups, with amino acid, fat, and organic acid signals changing most. Diabetes samples showed wide drops in several of those molecule families. None of the single signals survived strict correction for multiple testing, so the authors label the work exploratory and a guide for sharper follow-up studies.
pmc-13466326:
Halava and colleagues surveyed Finnish specialists in 2026 on how well their training taught communication and teamwork, two core roles in the CanMEDS framework for doctors. The survey ran twice, in 2018 and 2023. This analysis kept 2,772 doctors who finished training after 2007. They were grouped by graduation era and by five specialty families, from surgery to general practice. Each rated whether teaching and supervision had been adequate.

Most were satisfied. About 72 percent rated communication teaching adequate, and about 62 percent said the same for teamwork. The oldest cohort, trained in 2008 to 2012, reported gaps far more often than the next cohort. Surgeons and other operative specialists complained most about communication teaching. Teamwork teaching in leadership and consultation also improved between cohorts. In psychiatry, child specialists reported fewer gaps than adult ones. The authors read the trend as real progress, with operative fields still lagging on people skills.
pmc-13466726:
Sher and Niv pooled in 2026 the evidence on estrogen receptor beta in colorectal cancer. This receptor, a protein that responds to the hormone estrogen, sits in healthy colon tissue and may act as a tumor suppressor. Its loss has been tied to advanced disease. The team searched three databases to the end of 2025 for case-control studies. They compared receptor levels in tumor tissue with healthy tissue, and early with late stage tumors.

Sher found only six studies, split into thirteen sub-studies. Receptor presence was far lower in advanced tumors than in healthy tissue or early tumors, with positivity in about half of all-stage tumor samples against about three quarters in the comparison group. Results varied a lot between studies, but dropping any one study did not shake the pattern, and publication bias was not significant. The authors float receptor activation as a possible new treatment route.
pmc-13467026:
Karakaya and colleagues examined in 2026 whether blood vitamin D levels relate to gestational diabetes, the blood sugar disorder that appears in pregnancy. They reviewed records of 92 pregnant women at a tertiary hospital. Each had taken a full diagnostic glucose tolerance test after a positive screening test, and 44 had gestational diabetes while 48 did not.

Women with the condition were older on average, about 38 years versus about 29 years for the others. Their vitamin D levels were also lower, at about 14 units against about 19 units in the comparison group. In adjusted analysis, older age raised the odds of gestational diabetes, while higher vitamin D lowered them, and both links held independently. The authors call the findings observational and ask for larger prospective studies.
pmc-13467226:
Magdalena Rudziewicz and colleagues expose 3D-printed cement and alkali-activated blocks to laboratory storage, open air, and freeze-thaw cycles, then test how strength and direction-dependence change, in a 2026 study. Alkali-activated mixes shrank far more than cement ones as they reacted. Strength was measured along and across the printed layers.

Open air exposure raised crushing strength by up to about a fifth, while freeze-thaw left the across-layer strength largely intact. Bending strength told a split story: activated mixes started much stronger yet lost ground after weathering, dropping toward the plain mixes' range. Direction differences grew sharply for the activated family after exposure, a warning for printed walls designed as if uniform.
pmc-13467926:
Fan and colleagues reviewed in 2026 fruit-specific promoters, DNA switches that turn genes on only in fruit tissue or at set stages of fruit growth. Breeders use these switches to improve fruit quality, nutrition, and shelf life without switching genes on across the whole plant, a flaw of always-on promoters. The review sorts the switches by timing and maps how they are controlled.

Fan groups the promoters into four classes: early fruit, ripening, whole development, and dual-stage types. Control runs through short DNA elements, two big transcription factor families, and chemical marks on DNA and its packing proteins. New tools include precise editing of the switch elements themselves with CRISPR. Weak strength, leaky tissue targeting, and poor transfer between species remain the main limits. The authors look to AI-assisted design and single-cell methods for tunable synthetic switches.
pmc-13468026:
Peifeng Yu and colleagues examine in 2026 a melon gene, CmVQ23, that helps plants resist Verticillium wilt, a soil fungus that devastates melon and many other crops. The gene had surfaced in earlier mapping work, so the team inserted it into Arabidopsis, a standard test plant, to see what it does. The gene product settled mainly in the cell nucleus, consistent with a role as a helper for transcription factors that switch defense genes on.

Arabidopsis plants carrying the melon gene showed much lower disease scores after infection and restricted the fungus spread. The same plants grew differently, bolting later and staying shorter, a reminder that defense can cost growth. Mechanistically, the gene boosted reactive oxygen bursts and deliberate cell death at infection sites, two classic plant defense moves. A resistance gene that works across species is a valuable lead for breeding wilt-resistant melons.
pmc-13468126:
Moisès Bernabeu, Saioa Manzano-Morales, Marina Marcet-Houben, and Toni Gabaldón trace in 2026 the ancestries of eukaryotic genes to re-examine how cells arose. The standard story joins an Asgard archaeon host with an alphaproteobacterium that became the mitochondrion, yet other bacterial partners and even viruses may have contributed. Using phylogenomic methods across the known diversity of cells and viruses, the team rebuilt the protein set of the last eukaryotic common ancestor and traced each family origin.

The analysis found strong evidence for several waves of gene transfer from diverse bacteria, some apparently arriving before the mitochondrial symbiosis. The authors inferred what the major donor groups were like and what functions their genes gave the emerging cell. Giant viruses of one group seem to have facilitated transfers. The picture that emerges is messier and richer than a two-partner merger: early eukaryotes were built from many contributions.
pmc-13468926:
Ha and co-authors describe how often nerve damage shows up in ANCA-associated vasculitis, in this 2026 single-centre cohort study. In these diseases the immune system attacks small blood vessels. From 323 patients with the condition, they selected 97 for closer study. These patients had symptoms suggesting vasculitic peripheral neuropathy. Each received nerve conduction studies, electrical tests of nerve function, within three months of diagnosis.

The tests supported a neuropathy diagnosis in 55 patients, which is 56.7 percent of those examined, and a mixed pattern of nerve injury accounted for 83.6 percent of confirmed cases. The peroneal nerve in the leg was affected most often, in 70.9 percent of cases, and nerve biopsies taken from 12 patients agreed with the electrical findings in 75 percent of comparisons. The authors conclude the electrical tests add objective evidence when vasculitis-related nerve damage is suspected.
pmc-13469426:
Che and co-authors pooled the evidence in this 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on diaphragmatic dysfunction, weakening of the main breathing muscle, in patients kept alive on mechanical ventilators. Searching seven databases through July 2025, they gathered case-control, cohort, and cross-sectional studies that reported risk factors for the condition.

Eleven studies covering 5,272 ventilated patients met the criteria. Infection or sepsis stood out as the strongest risk factor, with pooled odds 2.65 times higher among affected patients, followed by worse severity scores, older age, and higher body mass index. Two factors protected patients instead: higher blood albumin, a marker of nutrition, and stronger hand grip strength, a simple measure of overall muscle condition. The authors argue for early screening of high-risk patients plus better nutrition and infection control on intensive care units.
pmc-13469826:
Budhwani and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for adapting Healthy Choices, a counseling program for young people with HIV, into Spanish for the Dominican Republic. The four-session program blends motivational interviewing, a talk method that builds a person's own reasons to change, with brief thinking-and-behavior skills. 

The team will adapt the program with local input, then run a pilot randomized trial with rollout strategies to test whether delivery is feasible and acceptable. Outcomes include stigma, self-management of care, and alcohol use, plus early signs of effect on health and viral control. Young people with HIV often drop out of care early, so retention is a core concern.  A successful pilot would justify a larger trial.
pmc-13470326:
Xiao and colleagues examined in 2026 the role of GLI1, a switch protein in the Hedgehog signaling pathway, in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, an aggressive blood cancer. The team measured GLI1 in tumor tissue and tested blocking or boosting it in two lymphoma cell lines, then confirmed effects in mouse tumors.

GLI1 was abnormally active in lymphoma tissue and tracked with two stemness-related proteins, Bmi1 and SOX2. A GLI-blocking drug slowed cell growth, paused the cell cycle, triggered cell death, and reversed changes linked to spread. Lab tests proved GLI1 binds Bmi1 directly, and blocking Bmi1 undid GLI1's tumor-promoting effects. In mice, the GLI blocker shrank tumors in volume and weight with good tolerance. The authors propose the GLI1-Bmi1 axis as a new treatment target.
pmc-13471626:
Song and co-authors traced how a chemical tag on RNA helps breast cancer cells burn sugar faster and hide from the immune system.
