Their 2026 study focused on NSUN2, an enzyme that writes m5C marks on RNA, and its target TPI1, a glycolysis enzyme, testing the chain in breast cancer cells and tumor-bearing mice.

Both NSUN2 and TPI1 ran high in breast cancer cells. In patient tissue samples split into groups of 25 high and 25 low expressers, high NSUN2 tracked with larger tumors at a significance of p 0.024 in the correlation table. Silencing NSUN2 slowed cell growth, glycolysis, and immune evasion, while restoring TPI1 reversed every one of those effects. The mechanism ran through the reader protein YBX1 and raised PD-L1, the immune brake, in step.
pmc-13471726:
Xu and colleagues set out in 2026 a standard platform for making and testing QLEDs, light-emitting diodes built from quantum dots. These devices have hit record performance, but fabrication is a steep barrier for newcomers and varied testing methods make results hard to compare. Their protocol covers making the electron transport material, processing thin films in an optimised way, and measuring devices by one shared method.

Xu had researchers with different experience levels run the protocol independently to check it holds up in fresh hands. They also wrote detailed troubleshooting guidance and named the main sources of variation between devices. The aim is a lower entry threshold, more reliable experiments, and fair performance claims across labs. The authors present the platform as shared infrastructure to speed wider adoption of QLED technology in displays and lighting research.
pmc-13472126:
Huang and colleagues built a computing framework in 2026 to predict how fast electric charge hops through peptoids, short chain-like molecules that can be programmed to fold and stack in set patterns. Soft solar materials need such charge movement to work, but their constant flexing makes rates hard to foresee. The test system carried iron-porphyrin units, ring-shaped groups that give or take electrons.

The framework joins atom-level motion simulations with quantum calculations and a standard rate rule, with no values tuned to the test system. Predicted hopping rates swung by several orders of magnitude, meaning thousands of times over, as the chains changed shape. The swing traced back to how strongly the iron-porphyrin pairs linked electronically, which depended on their spacing and facing. The authors offer the method as a general way to link a soft material's structure to its charge flow for solar design.
pmc-13472226:
Xuan Wu, Shiling Chen, and Zhouping Tang review in 2026 twenty years of treatment trials for bleeding inside the upper brain, a stroke type with high death and disability. Starting from a landmark 2005 surgery trial, randomized studies have tested operations, drugs, and physiological management one at a time. Most returned neutral or modest results on functional recovery, a record the authors read as lessons rather than pure failure.

Recent trials hint that benefit hides in careful patient selection, very early action, and bundled protocol care rather than any single intervention. Timing remains unsettled, and sex linked biological differences are barely studied despite plausible effects on bleeding and recovery. The authors close by urging time sensitive, mechanism informed, anatomy tailored, and sex aware combined strategies for the next trial generation.
pmc-13472626:
Bentian Yu and co-authors stabilize in 2026 wind blown loess soil using cement like binders made entirely from industrial waste. Tuff powder, fly ash, and furnace slag, woken by alkaline solutions, replaced cement and lime completely in their best recipe, at set shares with measured alkali doses. Cement production drives heavy carbon emissions, so a waste based binder attacks both a disposal problem and a climate problem.

Strength, soaking, and shear tests, backed by X-ray, microscope, and magnetic resonance checks, showed two mechanisms working together. Waste grains physically filled the pores while alkali triggered gels glued the soil, improving compaction, strength, and water resistance. Alkali strength needed care, balancing early pore refinement against long term pore stability. Carbon emissions fell by roughly three quarters to nearly nine tenths against cement stabilized loess.
pmc-13472726:
Pankaew and colleagues build AstroLogics, a framework for reading ensembles of Boolean network models, the on off logic maps biologists use to model gene regulation. Inference tools rarely return one model; they return crowds, which labs collapse into one answer and discard the diversity. Their 2026 study presents software that compares models by behavior instead of wiring. It measures distances between their transition graphs and clusters models that act alike.

Graph analysis is too slow for ensembles, so the framework leans on a simulator that samples model behavior with a Monte Carlo method, estimating what each network does. Per cluster it extracts the rules setting the cluster apart, naming the structures behind each behavior. Use cases show the tool sorting ensembles into groups reading as cell fates or signaling styles. Treating the crowd as data, the authors argue, turns model uncertainty from an embarrassment into a map of biologies.
pmc-13472826:
Dellwig and colleagues reviewed cases of canine paroxysmal dyskinesia in 2026, an episodic movement disorder in dogs that causes brief bouts of abnormal movement while the dog stays conscious. Telling the disorder apart from focal epilepsy is hard, so the team classified causes in seventy dogs seen at a referral center between 2012 and 2023.

Suspected idiopathic cases, meaning no cause found, made up about sixty-one percent of the group. Genetic forms accounted for about twenty-three percent, and gluten-sensitive cases for about thirteen percent. Reactive and structural causes were rare, at about one percent each. Age at onset and the body pattern of signs did not separate the cause groups, though body weight did differ. The authors recommend a tiered workup, adding breed genetic tests and early gluten checks.
pmc-13473126:
Song and colleagues report a 2026 study linking pesticide breakdown products in urine to heart disease death in older Americans. Organophosphate pesticides are widespread at low doses, but the biology between exposure and fatal heart disease is murky. The team studied 502 adults aged fifty and over from a national survey with urine tests, DNA methylation profiles, and death follow-up.

Of four pesticide metabolites tested, only one, DETP, linked to heart disease mortality after full adjustment, with risk about a third higher per standard rise in level. DETP also tied to five DNA methylation aging markers. Two markers hinted at carrying part of the effect, but that mediation did not survive strict correction.  The study names a specific metabolite, not pesticides in general, as the one to watch.
pmc-13473626:
Bu and co-authors report a troubling finding for supplement culture: two popular antioxidants help liver cancer spread by guarding a metastasis-driving protein from breakdown. Their 2026 study shows glutathione and N-acetylcysteine lowering reactive oxygen species in hepatocellular carcinoma cells, and that calmer chemistry stabilizes BACH1, a gene-switch factor normally broken down quickly.

With BACH1 preserved, cancer cells moved faster in culture and spread more in animals, while deleting BACH1 blunted both behaviors and eased cell stress responses. The protein works metabolically: it switches on glycolysis genes at their promoter sites while switching off mitochondrial breathing genes, locking in the sugar-burning Warburg pattern that fuels movement. Broad chemical profiling confirmed the rewired chemistry. The authors frame antioxidant use during liver cancer as a risk worth re-examining.
pmc-13474726:
Jiahui Ye and co-authors measure tongue strength and rest position in teens in 2026 across jaw growth patterns. A group of 182 teens aged eleven to seventeen was sorted into three bite classes by jaw angle. Tongue push strength was read with a handheld gauge. Rest position came from side head X-rays scored with set indexes.

Teens with a forward lower jaw showed far weaker tongue push than the other two classes. Part of the link between tongue strength and jaw angle ran through tongue tip position. A tree model picked low tongue strength as the first split for flagging the forward-jaw class. Tongue checks may help orthodontists spot growth risk early.
pmc-13474826:
Hongli Ma and colleagues sort two look-alike immune cell types in the stroked mouse brain in 2026. Resident brain guards and incoming blood-derived helpers both flood the injury zone, yet their jobs differ. A gene-tagged mouse line let the team label resident cells before stroke struck. Single-cell gene reading then separated the two crowds by place and time.

Incoming helpers filled the core early but were gone by thirty days, leaving none in lasting scar tissue. Gene states for the two crowds stayed distinct at one and two weeks. A growth factor rose in both crowds after stroke. Removing it from blood-line cells at set days changed recovery in two opposite ways.
pmc-13476226:
Hassan Abdikadir Hussein and Abdimalik Ali Warsame study clean cooking and remittances in Somalia in 2026 and their links to environmental harm. Data ran from 1990 to 2022, tracking footprints, clean fuel access, and money sent home by workers abroad. Burst-detection tests flagged years when each series spiked. Time-varying causal checks and a flexible learning model followed.

Clean cooking access drove footprint changes in two spans, peaking near 2019 to 2020. Remittances also drove footprint shifts in two earlier spans. The learning model found both factors cut the footprint on net. Solar stoves, biogas, and better clay stoves earn policy backing from the results.
pmc-13476926:
Muhammad Rashid and co-authors compare two mutagen tools in 2026 for widening the gene pool of Basmati rice. Seeds of two prized types were treated with gamma rays or a chemical mutagen across dose ranges. Four generations of selection followed, watching survival, fertility, and yield traits. Harsh doses cut sprouting, growth, and fertility in a dose-wise pattern.

Thousands of promising mutants narrowed to 753 stable lines by the fourth generation. Grain yield per plant rose by about a quarter versus the prior generation. Tiller count and grain weight showed high heritability with strong gains. One mild chemical dose on one type gave the top yield line.
pmc-13478026:
Yuyang Pang and coauthors published a 2026 real-world comparison of four substitute chemotherapy plans used before stem cell transplant in lymphoma. The standard plan relies on carmustine, a drug hit by shortages, so centers swap in bendamustine or semustine. The team reviewed 80 patients transplanted between 2018 and 2023 at their center.

Toxicity profiles differed by plan. The semustine plan called SEAM produced the most rises in a heart stress marker. Every patient on the bendamustine plan developed fever with low white cell counts, and that group needed more platelet transfusions and stayed in hospital longer, a median of about 29 days. Survival, response, and transplant-related death were also compared, giving centers practical guidance when the standard drug is unavailable.
pmc-13478526:
Laith Al-Shdifat and nine colleagues surveyed in 2026 Jordanian pharmacists on cranberry extract supplements. Cranberry products are widely sold for urinary tract health, yet pharmacist knowledge and advice habits had not been mapped in Jordan.

Of 409 replies, most respondents were under 35, based in central Jordan, and working in community pharmacies. Average knowledge scored 7.65 out of 14, with 57.9 percent below the low-knowledge cutoff, while attitudes and practice scores sat near the middle of their scales. Community pharmacy work and research-based sources predicted higher knowledge, and higher knowledge plus warmer attitudes predicted safer practice. Gaps on safety, interactions, dose limits, and pregnancy advice point to training needs, though online recruitment tempers the reach of the findings.
pmc-13478626:
Wang and colleagues tested two small-molecule drugs in 2026 that block DHX33, an RNA helicase enzyme that cancer cells use to run many growth genes. Blocking an enzyme's motor action is not the same as removing the protein, so the team asked whether the drugs copy the effect of switching the gene off. They treated human cancer cells with the compounds BCD38 and KY386, then compared gene activity changes against cells where DHX33 was knocked down.

The inhibitors changed activity for a subset of genes, and that subset largely matched the knockdown pattern in the cancer cells tested. The affected genes were selectively turned down and are involved in cancer progression, both in cell culture and in animal work the authors cite. KY386 is the stronger of the two compounds against cancer growth, and the match with knockdown implies the enzyme's cancer role depends on its helicase motor activity itself.
pmc-13479426:
Mingze Sun and coauthors published a 2026 longitudinal study of eating disorder symptoms among Chinese college students. Symptoms were measured four times at six-month intervals with a short form of a standard eating questionnaire. The sample held 5,608 students, and each wave also captured sleep, mood, body image concerns, self-control, family functioning, school belonging, and online victimization.

Growth mixture modeling separated students into three change patterns. One group, about seven percent, started low and decreased further, while other groups followed distinct higher or shifting paths described in the analysis. Regression models then tested which clinical, personal, and environmental factors predicted membership in each trajectory. The design moves beyond counting symptoms once, showing counselors which students are on worsening paths and what accompanies those paths.
pmc-13479926:
Jong Won Shin and coauthors published a 2026 prospective cohort study of two blood antioxidants and stomach cancer risk in Korean men. Bilirubin and albumin both fight oxidative damage, and a combined index called ALBI may capture overall oxidative stress. The data came from the KCPS-II cohort of 83,371 men free of cancer at the start.

Over an average follow-up of about thirteen years, 1,162 men developed stomach cancer. Analyses were split by smoking history, since smoking drives both oxidative stress and this cancer. Among men who had ever smoked, higher bilirubin was linked to lower risk, with each standard step up tied to about twenty percent lower hazard. The authors test whether these cheap routine blood values can refine risk prediction for a common cancer.
pmc-13480226:
Faisal Naffa' and co-authors report a 2026 case where an old pacemaker silently broke the timing of a new leadless one. A woman aged seventy-two with complete heart block got a leadless device in 2024 while her older wired system stayed in place by her choice. She soon felt tired and breathless on effort, first blamed on infection and slow heart response.

Device checks showed the two parts of the leadless system spoke to each other only nine percent of the time, wrecking their sync. Sleuthing traced the fault to a breathing sensor still active in the retained older unit, which sent signals that jammed the new link. Switching that sensor off restored full sync and cleared her symptoms. The case, billed as a first of its kind, urges full checks of every implanted unit before a leadless device goes in.
pmc-13480526:
Dingqiao Ji and co-authors report a 2026 tweak that lifts a light-driven material for making hydrogen peroxide. The base material is a carbon-nitrogen network that normally holds sodium ions. The team swapped in organic ions borrowed from solar cell chemistry, such as methylammonium, at up to one per network cell, keeping the crystal form intact.

The methylammonium version led the pack, making peroxide at a rate forty-two percent above the sodium form under violet light. Extra oxygen pressure pushed output to among the highest values on record for such systems. Charge studies suggest the organic ions cradle photo-charges and shuttle protons in step with electrons, which speeds the reaction. Swapping the quiet counter-ion, long treated as filler, turns out to be a strong design lever for solar chemistry.
pmc-13481326:
Yeo and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a stubborn bile duct narrowing cured with a drug-coated balloon. The patient, a 72-year-old woman, had a surgical join between bile duct and bowel after surgery for bile duct cancer. The join kept narrowing despite standard balloon stretching by scope and through the skin, and she returned ten times over three years with bile duct infections.

Doctors then stretched the narrowing with a balloon coated in paclitaxel, a drug that slows scar tissue growth, borrowed from heart artery practice. The join stayed open for the following two years, with no further hospital visits. Recurrent benign narrowing is a grinding problem: each infection risks the liver. One durable result in one patient cannot set practice, but it justifies testing coated balloons in more of these hard cases.
pmc-13483426:
Claudine K. Nkera-Gutabara and co-authors describe a 2026 project that handed personal gut microbiome results back to women in three African communities. The work sat inside a larger health study whose gut arm covered 1,801 women aged forty-two to eighty-six. Feedback meetings ran in Agincourt and Soweto in South Africa and in Nairobi, Kenya, with 778 women taking part.

Sessions used small groups, home visits, picture metaphors, pocket microscopes, and local languages. Women grasped their reports best when explanations grew from local culture; heavy English bred confusion. Most felt pleased and planned diet or lifestyle changes, though long waits between sampling and feedback frustrated many. Trust rose with openness yet hinged on fewer repeat blood draws and faster answers. The whole effort cost roughly twenty-nine to fifty-nine dollars per person, a workable price for returning complex results at scale.
pmc-13483626:
Helmbrecht and colleagues reviewed why brain injuries around birth so often fail to heal, arguing that inflammation which never switches off is the core problem. Their 2026 review covers injuries from early birth, infection, stroke, and oxygen loss, all of which trigger immune reactions in a baby's developing brain. Unlike a healing wound, this inflammation can smolder and prime the brain to overreact to later challenges.

Three signal proteins, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IL-1-beta, stay raised in the persistent state the authors describe. Microglia, the brain's immune cells, keep the process going through constant crosstalk with other cells. The review maps vulnerable windows across pregnancy, birth, and the newborn weeks. Helmbrecht argues treatments should aim at resolving inflammation, actively ending it, rather than only blocking its start.
pmc-13483826:
Shuai Zhang and others test whether a bile-acid dock called TGR5 protects mice from memory damage caused by chronic stress. In 2026, the study restrains normal and receptor-deficient male mice for twenty-one days. It then tests anxiety, spatial learning, gut and brain tissue damage, stress hormones, gut microbes, and electrical signal in the hippocampus. The gut-brain axis is the proposed route linking stress to cognition.

Chronic stress impaired learning and memory, damaged the memory center CA1 region and the colon, and shifted gut microbes and bile acids. Mice lacking TGR5 fared worse, with stronger brain swelling, lower mood signal, and severely weakened junction strengthening. The authors conclude that TGR5 normally restrains swelling in both brain and gut, making it a candidate target for stress-related memory problems.
pmc-13486826:
Taghizadeh and team calculated how much change on three thinking-skills tests counts as genuinely meaningful for Parkinson's patients with cognitive impairment. A score can shift by chance or practice, so trials need a minimal clinically important difference before claiming a treatment helped thinking. Their 2026 study tested 105 patients before and after a twelve-week dual-task training program, anchoring score changes to patients' own global ratings of improvement.

The anchor method set meaningful change at about eight points on the Parkinson-specific cognitive scale used. The second scale needed about three points, and the common screening test about two points by the same method. Cutoffs from a statistical curve analysis came out slightly lower for all three tests. Taghizadeh offers both sets of benchmarks so future cognitive trials in Parkinson's can judge results consistently.
pmc-13487226:
Jinshan Cui traces kidney damage after restored blood flow to a tagging enzyme that destroys a brake on stress signaling. Published in 2026, profiling of human and mouse acute kidney injury finds TRIM29 sharply raised. The enzyme grabs DUSP10, a phosphatase that normally quiets two stress kinases, and marks it for shredding at one specific site.

With the brake gone, stress kinase firing persists and fans inflammatory signaling plus tubular cell death. Mice lacking TRIM29 were markedly protected, showing better kidney function, less structural damage, and less inflammatory infiltration after the same insult. Blood-flow restoration injury drives much hospital kidney failure, yet few drug targets exist. The enzyme-to-brake contact surface offers a precise place to intervene.
pmc-13487426:
Yılmaz and colleagues mapped genetic variation in 2026 across the alpine plant Heldreichia bupleurifolia in Turkey, which grows in three leaf forms along a west-to-east range. Leaf shape is a key adaptive trait, but its genetic and environmental roots in wild populations are murky. Sampling 131 plants from twenty populations, the team generated over sixty thousand gene markers and joined genetic clustering with field records of rock type.

Three genetic clusters followed the geographic gradient and only partly matched the named subspecies. Two classification methods separated the leaf forms perfectly and flagged 167 candidate loci in protein-coding regions, enriched for ion balance and membrane pathways. Lobed populations grew only on volcanic rock, while the other forms sat on limestone. The authors read the pattern as substrate-driven selection and urge joining genome and ecology in alpine conservation, while noting the links are correlative.
pmc-13490026:
Wang and colleagues tested whether a low dose of interleukin-2, an immune messenger, can calm the autoimmune side effects that cancer immunotherapy sometimes triggers. The side effects arise when checkpoint drugs unleash immunity against healthy tissue, and current treatment blunts the cancer attack too. Their 2026 study profiled 26 gut-cancer patients before and after checkpoint therapy, then treated two mouse models with the low-dose regimen.

Patients who developed side effects showed helper T-cell activity genes surging early, outpacing the regulatory genes that normally restore balance. In mice, low-dose interleukin-2 restored that balance, reduced tissue inflammation, and lowered autoantibody production in the experiments described. Crucially, the treatment did not significantly weaken the checkpoint drugs' antitumor effect in the tumor-bearing model. Wang proposes the approach as a gentler alternative to broad immune suppression.
pmc-13490426:
Huang and colleagues coupled live system identification with predictive control to keep ships on course through wind, waves, and currents. Fixed controllers falter as a ship's handling drifts with load and weather. Their 2026 controller re-estimates the ship's maneuvering parameters continuously using a forgetting-factor least-squares method, which weights recent data more. It then feeds the fresh model into an optimizer that plans rudder moves within limits.

Simulations in calm water and under combined wind, wave, and current disturbance favored the adaptive controller over a standard PID controller and a robust adaptive rival. It responded faster, settled with smaller steady errors, and tracked changing courses more accurately in the reported runs. Disturbances showed up as parameter drift that the identifier absorbed automatically. Huang presents the loop as a practical route to precise automatic steering.
pmc-13490726:
Rathin Gosavi and colleagues argue for surgery first in removable colorectal liver metastases in a 2026 perspective piece. Cancer spread confined to the liver can be cured by removal in a sizable share of patients. Yet chemotherapy around surgery remains routine, despite trials never showing a clear survival gain in this setting, unlike in earlier-stage colon cancer. The authors weigh why that gap exists and what harms routine chemotherapy carries, from liver injury to losing the surgical window when tumors grow through treatment.

Chemotherapy still fits complex cases needing shrinkage, staged operations, or control of disease elsewhere, and heat ablation suits some small deposits in their account. Blood tests for tumor DNA may soon sort who truly needs drugs. Selective use is the plea.
pmc-13491326:
Miller and colleagues put an Apple Vision Pro headset between ultrasound operators and the vein, testing whether seeing the scan inside the procedure view makes vascular access easier. Clinicians normally glance away at a monitor while their hands work blind, causing failed first attempts. Their 2026 study gathered hands-on feedback from twenty-one participants who tried the passthrough augmented-reality setup, where the headset overlays the ultrasound image onto the real working field.

About fifty-two percent of participants rated the experience neutral or positive overall in the feedback collected. Praised points included image quality, the natural interaction, and ditching bulky carts and monitors from the bedside. Setup burden drew the commonest complaint, which the authors suggest assigning personal devices could ease. Even the harshest raters liked the concept itself. Miller calls the approach promising pending technical polish and clinical trials.
pmc-13491626:
Jiajin Zhang, Liyu Huang, and Sijia Wu propose in 2026 a network approach to RNA editing in non-small cell lung cancer. RNA editing changes letters in RNA copies of genes, and single changes have mostly been studied one at a time. The authors argue that groups of edits acting together may matter more, so they built modules of coordinated editing events.

Applied to this lung cancer, the framework found more than a dozen modules tied to immune control and to spread of the disease. Editing appeared to alter how small regulatory RNAs handle two genes, EIF2AK2 and PRKAR2A, and to affect a transcription factor called AHR plus a binding protein named DDX3X. The work offers a map for studying editing as a system rather than as isolated events.
pmc-13492026:
Valentine Dushimiyimana leads a large Rwandan team presenting in 2026 the protocol and baseline profile of NCOHIRWA, a ten-year cohort tracking heart and metabolic disease among people living with HIV. Rwanda faces a double burden as HIV care succeeds and chronic diseases rise, yet local evidence on who develops hypertension or diabetes is thin. Twelve health facilities enrolled adults from March 2021 onward.

Baseline data cover 1,546 participants, about four fifths of them living with HIV and the rest HIV-free comparators. Median ages sat in the early forties for both groups, and women made up nearly two thirds of the cohort. Overweight, obesity, smoking history, and family history of hypertension were all common at entry. The authors say the cohort is now positioned to reveal which biological, social, and health-system factors drive new disease.
pmc-13492426:
Andor Bik and five colleagues present in 2026 two patients who received a defibrillator lead placed surgically outside the blood vessels, because a vein-threaded lead was judged undesirable. Both patients also needed resynchronization pacing for failing hearts plus protection against dangerous rhythms after earlier cardiac arrests or inherited disease. Standard manufacturer guidance discourages pairing this extravascular defibrillator with pacing therapy, fearing oversensing and inappropriate shocks.

The first patient, a sixty-four-year-old man with inherited heart muscle thickening, had already lived through an arrest, device upgrades, and repeated shocks before the hybrid approach. The combined system, part endocardial and part epicardial pacing alongside the extravascular shock lead, proved technically workable in both cases. The authors stress extensive testing during implant and follow-up, and they caution that the strategy suits only selected patients.
pmc-13493826:
Meiting Wei and others test whether learning from short social-media-style videos harms memory and brain coordination. In 2026, the study runs three tests comparing short videos with long videos under incidental and intentional learning states, testing immediate memory, forgetting, and neural synchrony across viewers. Short videos switch rapidly and fragment content.

Short-video learners scored lower on immediate memory in both states and forgot faster when told to remember. Brain synchrony fell in regions for visuospatial focus, episodic memory, and mental control, while rising in areas for bottom-up focus, and coupling between visual, attentional, and control networks weakened. The authors conclude that fragmented video boosts automatic focus at the cost of deep learning.
pmc-13494026:
Miftakhov and colleagues study how astrocytes, the support cells of the brain, help strengthen memories, and whether that help fails in Alzheimer's disease. The team used designer receptors, switched on by a drug, to switch on one pathway in astrocytes of healthy mice and of 5xFAD mice, a genetic Alzheimer's model. They then measured synapse strengthening in brain slices.

Dose mattered: strong doses inflated signals even in tissue lacking the designer receptor, an off-target warning for the field, while a low dose left baseline signals untouched. At that careful dose, switching on astrocytes strongly boosted long-term potentiation, the strengthening of synapses thought to underlie learning, in healthy tissue. In the advanced Alzheimer's model, the same boost was compromised. The authors say the lost astrocyte help may be one thread in memory failure.
pmc-13495226:
Ali Mehri leads a 2026 interview study of nutrition literacy among primary school students in Sabzevar, Iran.
