Little proof from poorer countries shows how children build this skill across school, home, and community. The team interviewed 32 children aged ten to twelve from three schools in unlike income areas.

The children mostly showed basic skill: they could name unhealthy foods and some risks, above all around processed food and safety. Yet knowing rarely changed eating. Parental control, simple good-versus-bad food labels, taste, peer habits, ease, and skipped breakfasts all steered choices, and processed snacks were common. Higher skills, such as weighing claims, were rare. The authors call for joint action by schools, families, and food settings to close the gap between knowing and doing.
pmc-13495326:
Leticia Emefa Obobi and co-authors explore, in a 2026 interview study, how pregnant teenagers in rural Ghana eat and what shapes their diets. A pregnant teen must feed her own growth and the baby's, a double demand often unmet in poor rural areas. The team spoke at length with eleven pregnant adolescents aged sixteen to nineteen in North Dayi District.

Three themes stood out. Diets centered on starchy staples such as banku, kenkey, rice, and fufu, with little variety and irregular meals. Nutrition knowledge was very thin: most could not say what a balanced diet is, despite attending pregnancy clinics. Money limits, food taboos, little say at home, and clinic advice that skips diet blocked better eating, and cravings went unmet for cost. The authors call for food aid, teen-friendly nutrition teaching, and clinic counseling that treats diet as core care.
pmc-13495426:
Amirreza Radfar and colleagues study, in a 2026 paper, which patient traits go with dying in hospital after a brain bleed in southern Iran. Such bleeds, called intracerebral hemorrhage, kill many patients, above all in poorer countries. The team reviewed records of 1,796 patients admitted to a large referral hospital in Shiraz between 2018 and 2021.

Those who died were older on average than survivors. Sex, home area, and stay length did not split the groups on their own. Six ongoing conditions each raised the odds of death independently: cancer, heart disease, kidney disease, COVID-19 infection, high blood pressure, and diabetes. Several carried many-fold higher odds. The authors say spotting these conditions early can sharpen risk sorting in like settings, while finer severity measures are still needed for sharper prediction.
pmc-13495526:
Brooke D Conway Kleven leads a large team testing, in a 2026 study, whether thinking scores, blood markers, and brain scans together identify traumatic encephalopathy syndrome in athletes. The syndrome flags people at risk of CTE, the brain disease tied to repeated head impacts, but diagnosis still rests on symptoms alone. The team studied 158 professional fighters and 149 former football players from two long-running projects.

They built three combined scores, one each for cognition, blood markers of brain injury, and scan measures of brain structure. Models using all three beat any single score at sorting who met the syndrome criteria in both groups. Scans added most for fighters, while blood markers spoke loudest for football players. The authors say the syndrome carries a shared biological fingerprint across sports, a step toward tests that rest on more than symptoms.
pmc-13498426:
Akio Shibata and co-authors review in 2026 a method that fixes a drainage tube directly to nearby teeth when treating large cysts in the jaw. Draining a cyst slowly shrinks it and avoids bigger surgery, yet tubes often slip or rub the mouth lining. Wiring the tube to adjacent teeth was meant to keep it stable over many months of treatment.

Records for 20 patients treated between 2013 and 2023 were examined with jaw X-rays and image software to track shrinkage. Results ranged from strong shrinkage in nearly half the group to poor response in a smaller share. Lesions in the jaw body and upper jaw did best, tubes placed centrally worked more steadily, and prior infection predicted weaker shrinkage.
pmc-13499226:
Charlton and colleagues study pregnancy outcomes in women with long-term immune diseases in this 2026 United Kingdom cohort study. The diseases include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and bowel disease, and they often strike during the childbearing years. Yet doctors have little evidence on whether their drugs are safe in pregnancy. The team used a national primary care database covering 2000 to 2020, matching pregnancies in women with five such diseases against pregnancies in women without them.

The risk of losing a pregnancy was much the same for most diseases. It was slightly higher for bowel disease and psoriasis, with an adjusted hazard ratio near 1.18 for bowel disease. Major birth defects showed no clear rise, apart from a borderline signal in the bowel disease group. Three drugs, azathioprine, mesalazine, and sulfasalazine, showed no sign of raising pregnancy loss. The authors urge care in reading that signal, since other factors may explain it.
pmc-13500226:
Hamza A Ashfaq and colleagues report in 2026 a bleeding problem repeatedly blamed on the wrong source in a woman with advanced rectal cancer. Her stoma is a surgically created bowel opening on the abdomen. Swollen veins around a stoma, called peristomal varices, form when high pressure in the portal vein system, worsened by liver metastases, opens collateral channels through the wall. Their patient was a 72-year-old woman with stage IV rectal cancer whose recurrent stoma bleeding was first attributed to small bowel bleeding.

A multidisciplinary re-review of her CT angiography revealed abnormal vessels around the stoma matching portal collaterals, redirecting the diagnosis. Treatment then targeted the pressure itself with a vessel-tightening drug and a non-selective beta blocker, achieving brief control of bleeding. The authors urge teams to reconsider scans when standard gut bleeding workups come back empty in patients with portal hypertension and a stoma.
pmc-13500426:
Michael D Schaller and Peter H Mathers survey graduate students on whether responsible conduct of research training proves useful in real dissertation work. In 2026, the study runs two one-time surveys at a mid-sized United States university: eighty-three first-year doctoral students in a semester-long course and seventy-four past people reflecting later. Funding agencies mandate such training amid integrity concerns.

Current students found gains in knowledge and self-efficacy, while alumni named certain lessons that helped them steer clear of ethical challenges early in their careers. The authors conclude that students value research integrity training and apply it quickly, closing a gap between end-of-course effectiveness and real-world usefulness.
pmc-13501826:
Nawal A. Alharbi leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 retrospective comparison of two hysterectomy styles for placenta accreta spectrum, where the placenta grows too deeply into the womb and can cause catastrophic bleeding. At a Saudi tertiary referral centre, women had caesarean hysterectomy for the condition between 2018 and 2023. They were split by whether surgeons removed the whole uterus or left the cervix, the subtotal approach. Adjusted models accounted for urgency, disease severity, prior caesareans, and the operating surgeon.

Subtotal surgery came out ahead on every main outcome. Measured blood loss was far lower, with an adjusted geometric mean ratio of 0.36 against total hysterectomy, and operating time was shorter at a ratio of 0.54. Bladder injury odds were also lower, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.19 in the subtotal group. The authors back the subtotal option for selected cases while flagging selection bias in retrospective data.
pmc-13501926:
Beat Greiter and a Swiss team report a cohort study, published in 2026. It describes Lyme arthritis in European children. This is joint inflammation caused by tick-borne Borrelia bacteria. Most earlier child cohorts came from the United States. The team reviewed 107 cases. All were treated at the University Children's Hospital Zurich. The cases spanned 2006 to 2020.

About a quarter of the children still had arthritis two months after antibiotics. This course linked to older age. Longer symptoms before care also played a role. Delayed Lyme-specific treatment mattered too. Among children with persistent arthritis, most were later diagnosed with juvenile idiopathic arthritis. That is a chronic childhood joint disease. The finding shows how hard the two conditions are to separate early.
pmc-13503426:
Nilufer Akgun-Unal leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 study of how epilepsy injures the heart, and whether the compound resveratrol can protect it. Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy is tied to myocardial scarring, calcium mishandling, and autonomic failure. Using a pentylenetetrazol kindling model at 35 milligrams per kilogram, the team tracked seizures on brain recordings. Then they tested heart muscle strips, stained tissue for fibrosis, and measured signals for calcium pumps and cell death.

Kindled rats seized harder and their heart muscle weakened: contractile force and power fell across frequencies, and contraction stretched out at the fastest rate. Sections showed degeneration and scarring, calcium content climbed, the calcium pump SERCA2a message dropped, death signals rose, and the protein SIRT1 faded. Resveratrol at five milligrams per kilogram cut seizure severity, restored pump expression and performance, and reactivated SIRT1. The authors propose it as therapy against epilepsy's cardiac fallout.
pmc-13503626:
Alberto Jose Sanjuanelo Fontalvo and four colleagues present a 2026 case report of Sheehan syndrome found two decades after childbirth. The syndrome starts when heavy bleeding at birth starves the pituitary gland of blood and kills part of it. The woman in the report was 52 years old.

She had a year of deep tiredness, sleepiness, poor appetite, and a loss of 13 kilos. Her last birth, at home 21 years before, had heavy bleeding, and she never made milk or had periods again. Blood tests showed very low sodium and low thyroid and adrenal hormones. Brain scans showed an empty sella, the space where the gland sits. Steroid drugs were given before thyroid pills, and her sodium and health soon improved.
pmc-13503926:
Li Chuang and four colleagues build a camera system that watches classroom behavior of students with special needs, in a 2026 paper. Teachers in mixed classes must track dozens of students at once, and hand observation is slow and swayed by judgment. Fine cues like posture and head direction can flag who needs help.

The system pairs pose tracking from a standard camera with simple sound cues like voice activity. It was tested on data from a mock inclusive classroom with patterns typical of autism and attention disorders. It flagged states such as attention and social contact with mean accuracy near 85 percent. That beat hand observation baselines by a wide margin. The authors offer it as a support tool for teachers, not a replacement.
pmc-13505126:
Jiang and colleagues built in 2026 a machine learning model to predict death in tumor-related sepsis, where cancer patients develop a life-threatening response to infection. Current scoring systems judge these patients poorly. The team drew 3,777 cases from a large United States intensive care database, used three machine learning methods to pick key variables, and built four rival models for comparison.

Jiang found the best model used just nine variables and beat the classic APACHE II, SOFA, and LODS scores on discrimination. Its accuracy held steady between the training and test sets. Checks in two outside data sets, one American and one from a hospital in Guangxi, China, showed a modest drop but consistent performance. The team turned the model into a paper nomogram, a chart that converts patient values into a risk estimate, for bedside use.
pmc-13505526:
Yuan and colleagues produced the first single-cell atlas of the ovary of the Chinese pond turtle, Mauremys reevesii, in a 2026 sequencing study. Turtle reproductive biology has centered on temperature-driven sex determination. That focus leaves the ovary's cell makeup and its signaling largely unknown, a gap that limits ecology and conservation planning for these animals. The team sequenced RNA from ovarian cells and grouped them by gene activity.

Yuan resolved six lineages, including egg cells, the granulosa cells that nurse them, immune cells, vessel cells, and fibroblasts, and reconstructed the signaling web between them. Cross-species comparison confirmed classic markers. Two signaling proteins, WNT4 and WNT6, emerged as specific signatures of turtle granulosa cells, verified by tissue staining, and another protein marked the eggs. The authors present the atlas as a foundation for understanding turtle reproduction and for conservation of pond turtles and relatives.
pmc-13506626:
Kosuke Yoshida and colleagues report 2026 results on lighter chemotherapy for a narrow group of high-risk pregnancy-related tumors treated at Nagoya University Hospital. Records span 268 patients treated from 1991 to 2023, scored by both the world FIGO system and the Japanese system. Forty-nine patients fell in the high-risk range.

Seventeen patients with FIGO scores of 7 to 8 split by Japanese scoring into invasive mole and choriocarcinoma groups. All seven invasive mole patients got reduced treatment and reached full remission. The authors suggest careful scoring can spare some patients stronger multi-drug treatment that they may not need, though wider checks are still required.
pmc-13507226:
Yunshuo Wu and colleagues report 2026 work on a low-heat method to destroy nitrous oxide using methane as the helper gas. Nitrous oxide is a potent warming gas and ozone harm agent, and standard cleanup of factory exhaust needs heat above 400 degrees Celsius. Their platinum catalyst sits on a zeolite support.

Conversion reached near total at 150 degrees, with a very high reaction rate per unit of platinum. Studies credit freshly formed platinum particles that cycle single oxygen atoms quickly. Cost modeling for adipic acid plants in China suggests abatement costs could fall by about three fifths. Two warming gases are tackled in one step.
pmc-13508326:
Hugo Talibart and Dimitri Gilis build a large AI model that turns molecules into map points and back again, giving chemists a smooth space to search for new drugs, in 2026 work. Chemical space is vast and choppy, which makes hunting for molecules with the right traits hard. Their system, a transformer-based autoencoder, squeezes each small molecule into a fixed-length code. A new training goal forces distances between codes to mirror real chemical similarity. That keeps neighbors on the map chemically alike, so sliding between points yields sensible new molecules.

The model rebuilt its input molecules correctly 97 percent of the time, and every molecule it created was chemically valid. On standard molecule improvement tasks it held its own against rival generators. The team released free code and ready-trained models as an installable package, so drug designers can use or retrain the tool directly.
pmc-13508426:
Timothy Wilson leads a nine-author team comparing lung microbes in rheumatoid arthritis patients with and without lung scarring, in 2026 work. Lung fibrosis is a feared turn in this joint disease, and its triggers are unclear. The study enrolled 54 patients from joint and lung clinics, 22 with fibrosis shown on detailed scans and 32 without. Coughed-up sputum was read with gene sequencing to census its bacteria. Three separate statistical methods checked for group differences, with corrections for false alarms.

The fibrosis group was older, more often male, and had smoked more. Overall microbe variety in sputum ran lower in that group. One ordinary mouth-and-airway bacterium, Lautropia, fell short in every analysis method. After adjusting for age, sex, and smoking, fibrosis stayed firmly tied to undetectable levels of that bacterium. The authors call for long-term studies to test whether losing this microbe comes before fibrosis.
pmc-13509626:
Yuting Zhu and colleagues report an imaging study in mice, published in 2026. It builds a quantitative scan method for judging liver reserve. This is how much working capacity a liver has left. The team used a liver-specific MRI contrast agent. T1 mapping was also used. It times how tissue relaxes after magnetisation. Five kinds of mouse liver were tracked. They ran from healthy to fibrotic and fatty. Each handled the agent differently.

Each condition produced a distinct enhancement pattern. Transporter proteins set the pattern. They pull the agent into liver cells. Mice lacking those transporters barely enhanced at all. The imaging measure agreed with independent dye-clearance tests of liver function. This supports it as a molecular imaging marker of liver reserve. Later clinical translation is the goal.
pmc-13510126:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of hearing loss that the standard test definition misses.  The team reanalyzed two adult population samples, about thirty-one hundred people in Germany and over ten thousand in the United States.

Among adults classed as normal by the standard average, about a third in the German sample had raised thresholds at high frequencies, the range first hit by age and noise. Lopsided loss between ears was also counted, and the American data included self-rated hearing trouble, letting the team check whether these hidden profiles matched self-reported hearing trouble. A third of 'normal' hearers carrying loss means screening misses early, preventable damage.
pmc-13511126:
Fulya Ozcan, Filip Vujovic and Ramin M. Farahani published this 2026 perspective proposing a function-first approach to mitochondrial quality control, the systems that keep the cell's powerhouses sound. Classic accounts catalogue molecular repair machines, but the authors argue stress is sensed as a functional wobble: in energy output, redox balance, acidity, heat or protein folding. These domains act as sensory portals that switch on the control machinery.

Their framework describes a cascade: a stress is converted into signals such as reactive oxygen build-up, membrane voltage loss, shifted metabolites and altered lipids or DNA. Those signals spread through the cell and recruit repair, remodelling and disposal pathways, including proteases, antioxidant systems, organelle reshaping, mitophagy and vesicle export. Reprogramming circuits then retune respiration and defence. The same stress can yield different outcomes depending on the mitochondrion's state, they note. The authors offer the cascade as a unifying map for the field.
pmc-13512326:
Claudia Gyimah, Prasamsa Pudasaini, Allison LeMahieu, Phillip Schulte, and Yewande E. Odeyemi externally test a machine learning model that flags hospital patients with community-acquired pneumonia who are unlikely to worsen, in 2026 work. The model was built earlier at Mayo sites and uses data from the first six hours of admission. Validation used a large public intensive care database from a Boston hospital, with no retuning of the model.

The combined outcome covered need for stronger breathing support or death in hospital. Sorting power in the new database came close to the original cohort of 4379 patients, dipping only slightly. Accuracy and the key error trade-offs also held near their original values, and the negative predictive strength stayed high, which matters for spotting low-risk patients safely. Results for secondary outcomes matched as well. The authors say the model travels reasonably across hospitals.
pmc-13517026:
Abdallah and co-authors described a 2026 case report of a rare benign brain tumour inside the brain tissue of a seventeen-year-old boy. Schwannomas usually grow on nerves, so one arising within the brain itself, unconnected to any cranial nerve, is exceptionally rare. Its scans often mimic aggressive gliomas, making diagnosis before surgery very hard.

The boy arrived with new right sided visual trouble and swollen optic discs in both eyes. Abdallah's imaging showed a lobulated, contrast taking mass in the left back brain with heavy surrounding swelling, raising fears of glioblastoma. Surgeons removed the whole tumour through the back of the skull. Tissue tests found spindle cells with no division or death, plus strong S100 and SOX10 staining, confirming a harmless grade one schwannoma.
pmc-13520226:
Jinri Weng and five colleagues hunt in 2026 for hub genes linking low oxygen and immunity in atrial fibrillation, the commonest heart rhythm disorder. Public gene datasets were mined by combining differential expression, co-expression networks, and protein interaction mapping. Thirteen candidate genes tied to both hypoxia and immune response emerged.

Five stood out: IL6, JUN, FOS, FOSL2, and MAFF, each expressed higher in fibrillation patients than in people with normal rhythm, a result confirmed by PCR tests on patient blood. Four of the five are transcription factors that bind the IL6 gene's switch region. Enrichment analysis tied the set to cAMP and calcium signaling, and their levels tracked with altered immune cell mixes in heart tissue. Drug targets may follow, the authors suggest.
pmc-13520326:
Yike Zhang, Haozhe Wang and Tianhang Luo combine in 2026 evidence from 101 studies on early stomach cancer to guide a choice between scope-based removal and major stomach surgery. Spread to nearby lymph nodes is the key risk, since scope treatment cannot remove those nodes.

Spread of cancer into small vessels raised the odds of node involvement most strongly, while shallow invasion, small size and a well-differentiated pattern lowered the odds. Nerve invasion and ulceration also raised risk. Quality and certainty checks accompany each factor. Surgeons and patients gain a ranked list for judging when the gentler scope option is reasonably safe.
pmc-13520826:
Haya Elayan and colleagues simulate in 2026 when extra data helps or harms clinical risk models. Extra sets may come from other times, lands or care settings. Rules say models should use target group data. Spare sets still tempt model builders.

Fake target and helper groups varied in likeness and size. Four build plans were compared on fit, sorting skill and stability. Borrowing data helped in most runs. Recalibration often beat target-only builds. One recalibration variant proved shaky. A weighting plan stayed steady across most scenes. A Swedish heart registry case shows the lessons at work in real care.
pmc-13522526:
Jiarui Wang leads a team reporting light-activated memory switching at very low temperatures in a 2026 physics study. Memory devices that work in the cold are needed for cryogenic computing and for systems linking quantum and classical hardware. The device uses a layered material whose defects respond to both light and electric fields, a combination rarely controlled in the cold.

After a pulse of light, the device switched repeatably from high to low resistance and held that state long after the light ended. Its switching threshold could be tuned by voltage pulses, extra light pulses, and electrostatic gating. The device also mimicked synapse-like behavior. The authors attribute the effect to charged defects and present the device as a flexible platform for cold optoelectronics.
pmc-13523426:
A Brugués and colleagues review fifteen years of thyroid surgery at a Swiss hospital for links to low calcium after surgery in a 2026 study. Among more than six hundred thyroid operations, three hundred twenty-two total thyroid removals formed the analysis set. Records covered how many parathyroid glands surgeons spotted during surgery, whether any were removed by accident, and whether removed tissue was reimplanted.

Temporary low calcium affected over two fifths of total thyroidectomy patients, while persistent low calcium was rare. The number of glands identified during surgery did not predict temporary problems. Accidental removal, found in about one fifth of cases, tracked a modestly higher rate that was not statistically significant. Reimplantation cases had significantly higher rates, likely reflecting glands already at risk. The authors stress the multifactorial nature of calcium disturbance.
pmc-13523526:
Luke Ojo and others map, in a 2026 scoping review, sexual and reproductive health services for young people living with disabilities in sub-Saharan Africa between 2013 and 2024. This group faces marked inequities in using such services. The review gathered evidence on services offered, use rates, barriers, helpers, and quality across the region.

Sixteen studies from eight countries were included, with Ethiopia and Tanzania contributing most, and designs were mainly cross-sectional. Services spanned prevention, treatment, counseling and education, and support such as violence counseling. Use ranged from low to moderate. Stigma, negative provider attitudes, communication barriers including missing sign language, physical inaccessibility, and weak privacy were the commonest barriers. Education, family and peer support, and positive provider attitudes helped. Quality was most often reported as poor.
pmc-13524926:
Ulku Baykal presents, in a 2026 data resource paper, the first full transcriptome for Erysiphe corylacearum, the fungus behind hazelnut powdery mildew. The disease causes heavy damage in Türkiye's Black Sea region, the heartland of world hazelnut supply. Gene resources for this obligate parasite, which lives only on its host, were very limited.

RNA was sequenced from infected hazelnut leaves, with epidermal peeling used to enrich fungal material and limit host contamination. Over 66 million paired reads gave an initial set of about 135,000 unigenes, and a cleaned archive file holds 100,863 transcript sequences. Matches covered 71 percent of the initial set, including genes tied to pathogenicity and reproduction. A cleaned set of sequence variants is offered as a starting point for markers and tests.
pmc-13526526:
Choe and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how three subtypes of radial glia, the main stem cells of the developing human cortex, arise and behave in lab-grown cortical organoids. These mini-brain models, grown from human stem cells, reproduce much of its cell diversity. Two subtypes appear readily in organoids, but the third, truncated radial glia, was defined only recently and had never been mapped in organoids.

The review sets out the biology, signals, and offspring of each subtype. Outer radial glia need a specific signal boost to emerge in organoids. Signs hint that truncated radial glia may arise there too: related lining cells grow from radial glia, a marker protein appears in such cultures. Gene tweaks shift gene patterns in the expected direction. Firm proof, needing combined markers and shape checks, is still missing. The authors chart what proof would settle whether it truly forms in organoids.
pmc-13526726:
Qian Wang leads a very large team in a 2026 study showing that a gut germ common in ulcerative colitis worsens bowel inflammation through a product called succinate. An upset gut flora marks this bowel disease, yet the organisms and molecules behind it were unclear. Gene tests on stool from 37 patients and 30 healthy controls singled out Fusobacterium varium.

Germ-free mice given the germ came down with worse chemically induced colitis, and fluid the germ grew in switched on inflammatory signaling in reporter cells. Lab sorting of that fluid found succinate as a leading active product. Succinate worsened colitis and drew in neutrophils, while blocking a neutrophil receptor kept cells from moving in and eased disease. In neutrophil-like cells grown in dishes, it turned on inflammatory pathways through its receptor SUCNR1 and set off release of a chemokine that calls more cells in.
pmc-13527126:
Xiao and colleagues report a 2026 machine learning-guided method that makes single photons of infrared light convert into higher-energy light far more efficiently. This conversion, called upconversion, is usually weak and slow. Their cascade pumping approach stacks photons step by step, treating a middle energy state of lanthanide ions as a fresh starting level.

In a holmium-doped test material, emissions grew stronger by two to three orders of magnitude, meaning hundreds of times brighter. The response reached wavelengths near 2,100 nanometers and sped up from 30 milliseconds to 54 microseconds. The method also worked with three other lanthanide ions and produced near-pure red, green, and blue output. The team showed sensitive, fast carbon dioxide sensing as one use.
pmc-13527926:
Barbara Igriczi and five colleagues report a 2026 survey of rotaviruses in diarrheic piglets on nineteen Hungarian farms, using nanopore sequencing to read viral genomes. Rotaviruses are a leading cause of diarrhea in young pigs, yet species B and C are far less studied than species A.

Among 77 fecal samples, species A and C each appeared in over half, species B in about forty percent, and mixed infections were frequent. The team recovered full genomes for several strains of each species and found wide genetic variety, including the common A combination G9P[23]. Three species B sequences matched no known VP4 type, suggesting a new lineage, and species C showed a possible novel type as well. Continued monitoring is urged.
pmc-13528026:
Clementine Wood and ten colleagues describe building a genetic care pathway for ALS in northern England in a 2026 paper. ALS is a progressive nerve disease, and genes drive a sizable share of cases. The Manchester centers reviewed records for 326 patients. Testing uptake, counseling, and record quality varied a lot. Patient surveys showed fuzzy recall of talks about genes.

Those findings shaped a shared Greater Manchester pathway. It sets clear steps for spotting candidates, pre-test talks, consent, testing, sharing results, and family support. Team roles are spelled out. Scores will track how well it works, and feedback will drive updates. The authors offer the pathway as a model for fair, standard gene care in routine clinics. They note it must keep pace with fast-moving science.
pmc-13530126:
Erfan Shafipour, Zohreh Mirjafary, and Hamid Saeidian use computer models in 2026 to test whether a trick called hyperconjugative aromaticity can spread electrons around two unusual ring molecules. Penguinone and its sulfur cousin start out nonaromatic, meaning their electrons stay localized. Bulky donor groups might push charge into the ring.

Quantum math measured shape, electron flow, and magnetic signs of aromatic character. Silicon and germanium donor groups boosted spreading by forming a near six-electron system, while a fluorine group pulled electrons away and weakened it. Sulfur versions often spread charge further, which the authors link to sulfur size.
pmc-13530226:
Hyemin Hwang and colleagues classify fine dust pollution by chemical makeup in a 2026 machine learning study. The health effects of PM2.5 particles depend on what they contain, so grouping days by chemistry helps target controls. Mapping and clustering methods sorted observations from a national monitoring database into chemical regimes.

City and industrial zones leaned toward traffic and factory patterns, while coastal and island sites leaned toward sea salt and cleaner background patterns. A forest model then predicted regime labels with strong accuracy and held up at three unseen sites. The tool offers a quick first diagnosis where detailed source studies are missing.
pmc-13531826:
Rui Wang and co-authors introduce in 2026 a generative method that fills gaps in spatial gene maps across tissue slices and platforms. Spatial transcriptomics reads gene activity with location attached, yet slices from different tools rarely align neatly. Their framework, GenOT, blends graph learning with optimal transport math, which matches distributions at least cost.

A transport-based center method rebuilds how expression changes across space and time between unlike samples. Benchmarks showed gains in finding tissue regions, interpolating across platforms, and rebuilding developmental paths. The tool targets a core bottleneck in comparing tissue maps from mixed sources.
pmc-13531926:
Deying Huang and colleagues built a chart that predicts cyclophosphamide response in muscle disease with lung disease. Published in 2026, the backward-looking study enrolled 62 patients with muscle disease and interstitial lung disease, split into eighteen responders and forty-four nonresponders to the drug. Responses vary widely and focused trials are scarce, leaving doctors without a picking tool.

Five predictors emerged: two imaging signs of infected lung regions, two autoantibodies called anti-MDA5 and anti-Jo1, and IgA levels. A chart joining them scored well, with strong accuracy on both responders and nonresponders and guesses matching real outcomes. Benefit curves confirmed net clinical gain. The authors present a sound aid for tailoring a first-line therapy, pending checks in larger cohorts.
pmc-13532826:
Ellen Tameeris and colleagues compared nose sprays and antihistamines for quality of life in children with pollen allergy. Published in 2026, the post hoc analysis drew on a single-blind trial of 132 children and adolescents aged six to eighteen with grass pollen allergy, treated for three months of pollen season. Daily nose spray, on-demand nose spray, and on-demand oral antihistamine arms were compared.

Daily nose spray improved overall quality of life most in adolescents, beating the minimal important difference, with nasal and practical gains leading. In younger children, antihistamines improved quality of life more than nose sprays. Baseline scores were already good before pollen exposure, and no arm differed at baseline. The authors present age-specific guidance: daily spray for teens, antihistamines first for younger children.
pmc-13534526:
Manisha, Karunakar A Kotegar, and Shavantrevva Bilakeri present in 2026 CaReS-BiNet, a deep learning framework that classifies heart rhythm faults from ECG traces. Heart signals vary in shape, classes are heavily unbalanced, and models often fail on new datasets. Their design joins multi-scale filters, attention, and two-way sequence modelling in one system.

On a standard arrhythmia database the model reached high accuracy and F1 scores, beating most compared methods on recall. A second database gave even higher scores, and added noise training improved toughness. Step-by-step removal tests confirmed each part of the design helped.
pmc-13536626:
Ángel Ramírez-Fernández and twenty-six colleagues published this 2026 study building a dual T cell therapy against tumours with the KRAS G12V mutation. Such cells fail when tumours vary their targets or lose the HLA marker. The team inserted a targeted receptor for the KRAS mutant, shown on HLA-A*11:01, into gamma-delta T cells. These are a flexible immune cell type, and the cells kept their receptor as a second weapon.

The cells killed matching tumour cells in dishes and animals. To cover tumours that lose the HLA marker, the team added nanoparticles with messenger RNA encoding a bispecific engager, a bridge that drags T cells onto mesothelin-bearing cancer cells. In humanised mice, the cells alone controlled growth, while adding the nanoparticles produced complete responses and prolonged survival. The authors present the pairing as a repeat-dose strategy against an escape route.
pmc-13536726:
Miguel Del-Pino and Emilio J Sanz test whether online training helps family doctors cut needless stomach acid drug use in a 2026 Canary Islands trial. Proton pump inhibitors help acid disorders, yet many long-term prescriptions lack a proper reason. Doctors were grouped by whether they took the training right away, waited, or showed no interest. Prescribing fit and drug spending were tracked over 24 weeks.

Before training, only a small share of open-ended prescriptions met guideline reasons, and training did not raise that share. Spending still diverged, with the trained group showing a median saving per doctor while both comparison groups spent more. The authors argue that even modest prescribing gains matter at scale, and they call for longer follow-up and better recording of reasons for treatment.
pmc-13538526:
Tomasz Berezowski built a checked fine-scale dataset of river depths and widths for Poland. Published in 2026, the dataset draws on field surveys of cross-sections across 246 rivers from 2011 to 2013. River width and depth feed flood models and bridge design, yet dense public sets for checking models were scarce.

The final set holds 20,782 records of width, depth, water level, and center-point spots, all near bankfull flow. Widths run from a third of a meter to 2,384 meters, and depths from five millimeters to just over seventeen and a half meters. Checks found depths below the EU terrain surface, widths closely matching a global river map, and center points within under two meters of a Polish map. The set suits training river-shape models and checking large-scale water products.
pmc-13539926:
Xiao Wang and six colleagues compare, in a 2026 records study, two ways of plating an unstable ankle fracture at the outer bone, classed as Danis-Weber B. Standard side plates can rub soft tissue and often get removed later, so a slimmer double-plate option was tested.

Charts covered 120 patients treated between 2016 and 2020 and followed for three years. Double mini plates took longer in theatre, yet bones united sooner and ankle function scores ran higher from three months onward. Complications were fewer, and far fewer double plates needed removal. The authors present the method as a workable alternative needing prospective confirmation.
pmc-13540226:
Thomas A Owen and eight colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a drug called KMN-159 that switches on the EP4 receptor and may help regrow dental bone. Bone loss around teeth and implants remains a practical problem in dentistry.

Human and rat marrow stem cells treated with the drug matured faster toward bone-forming cells and laid down more mineral in laboratory dishes and in bone scaffolds. In rats, treated tooth sockets and the bone around fresh implants gained volume. A pilot test in minipigs carrying human implants pointed the same way. The authors propose KMN-159 as a candidate for dental, facial, and broader skeletal repair work.
pmc-13540826:
Rui Ma and colleagues trace a tiny RNA message in a 2026 study. Immune cells in fat tissue send this message to fat cells. The message disturbs how fat cells handle sugar and fat. It is called miR-714. It travels in small parcels named exosomes.

The message targets the receptor for a growth factor, IGF1. Database mining first flagged this pairing. Fat mice on a rich diet then confirmed it. Their parcels held more miR-714, and fat held less receptor. Tests in cultured fat cells verified the direct binding. Adding the message cut glucose use, while fat stores climbed. The team proposes this axis as a drug target.
pmc-13540926:
Sisi Chen and colleagues study nursing interns in China in a 2026 survey. They asked why some interns feel like frauds on the ward. That feeling is called the imposter phenomenon. The jolt of moving from classroom to clinic is transition shock. Both states link to poor adjustment in new nurses.

Forms from 384 interns measured shock and imposter feelings. They also measured two ways of handling emotion. One way rethinks a hard situation more kindly. The other suppresses what one feels. Shock and suppression tracked with stronger imposter feelings. Rethinking tracked with weaker ones. Rethinking also softened the shock link, while suppression strengthened it.
pmc-13542226:
Ashis Talukder and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study on how Bangladesh handles the double burden of malnutrition, where undernutrition persists while overweight and obesity climb. Senior nutrition stakeholders from government, aid groups, and research bodies were interviewed between June and August 2025. The authors asked how these leaders understand the problem, whether national policy treats both forms of malnutrition together, and where delivery breaks down.

Twelve interviews, read through reflexive thematic analysis, produced four themes. Recognition of the double burden was strong at senior level yet weak at the front line. Policy still centred on undernutrition, coordination across sectors was largely symbolic, and no specific indicators tracked progress. Stakeholders urged stronger joint governance, food system reform, and programmes that tackle both problems at once, a chance the authors link to the coming revision of the national nutrition plan.
pmc-13542726:
Lee and colleagues improved a laboratory method for making circular RNA. These rings last longer than straight RNA strands and are attractive for vaccines and gene therapies. Their 2026 study refines a self-splicing technique based on a group I intron, a self-cutting RNA segment, which produces clean rings without leftover sequences. The older version worked poorly when the target gene was long.

Lee screened target sites within each gene and found that picking the right site sharply raised the share of RNA that successfully closed into rings. Redesigning one construct segment, including adding a short tail of adenine building blocks and a matching antisense stretch, improved efficiency further. For long genes of roughly eight thousand building blocks, the optimized method circularized up to twice as efficiently as the standard competing approach. That widens the range of therapies this clean production route can serve.
pmc-13543526:
Yi Hua, Hua Wang, and Xu Yang published a 2026 radiological study comparing recurrent kneecap dislocation in patients whose skeletons are still growing with those fully mature. Anatomy decides much of this injury's risk, and children's anatomy differs from adults'. Records covered 85 patients and 106 knees treated between 2016 and 2024, split by whether the growth plates had closed. Scans measured kneecap height, groove shape, kneecap shape, tilt, and leg rotation.

Immature patients, averaging thirteen and a half, had strikingly higher kneecaps: their height index averaged 1.5 against 1.3 in adults, and a high kneecap appeared in about eighty-five percent of young knees. Young patients also showed more kneecap tilt and more inward thigh rotation, yet their kneecap shape was less severely malformed than adults'. Growth stage therefore changes which anatomical faults dominate, with implications for choosing corrective surgery.
pmc-13543626:
In a 2026 study, Shiming He and colleagues compared versions of the triglyceride-glucose index as markers of cardiovascular-liver-metabolic multimorbidity. The index is a blood-based estimate of insulin resistance, and the condition is the clustering of heart, liver, and metabolic diseases in one person. In a national sample of 20,235 adults, the plain index and versions blended with waist and body-shape measures were tested against the combined condition and against long-term death risk.

Every version rose with multimorbidity, and the obesity-blended versions performed best at identifying it, with accuracy scores above 0.83 for the waist-weight and visceral-fat variants. Having the combined condition also amplified the mortality risk carried by high index values. Machine-learning importance analysis echoed the same two leaders. A refined blood-and-body index, the authors suggest, could screen for this dangerous clustering more sharply than metabolic measures alone.
pmc-13543726:
Lorena Martínez-Zamora and colleagues published a 2026 study turning pomegranate peel, a juice-industry waste rich in the antioxidant punicalagin, into an edible coating for fresh-cut celery. Peel extract was freeze-dried inside three carrier materials at two ratios, and the best powders were dipped onto celery sticks whose colour, weight, and chemistry were tracked for thirteen refrigerated days.

Inulin at the lower carrier ratio preserved the most plant chemistry through encapsulation. Coated celery browned far less than uncoated sticks, with colour change near eight units against thirteen, and lost only about half a percent of weight against two percent. The coating also donated its own punicalagin to the celery, peaking around day nine, while the vegetable's native phenolics held up better. Waste peel, the authors argue, can be revalorised as an active, edible preservative.
pmc-13544626:
Laura Foley published a 2026 study of how Malaysia's policy actors talk about women who migrate for work, especially domestic work, and how gender assumptions shape that talk. The research combined document analysis with semi-structured interviews held in 2018 with forty-one policy actors across Malaysia and the wider region. From an actor-centred angle, Foley traced the stories these officials and advocates tell about why women migrate and what should be done about them.

One narrative dominates: the migrant domestic worker as victim of abuse, needing protection, her story often folded into trafficking frames, while her labour itself stays undervalued and almost invisible. The paradox the title names is stark: women are discursively cast as silent, sacrificing, and subordinate, and the protective story flourishes. Yet migrant domestic workers remain largely unprotected in Malaysian law, policy, and practice. Narrative, Foley argues, can substitute for rights.
pmc-13544726:
An Song and colleagues published a 2026 letter reporting a forty-year retrospective study of primary hyperparathyroidism at Peking Union Medical College Hospital. That hospital is a major Chinese referral centre for metabolic bone disease. In this disorder an overactive parathyroid gland floods the body with hormone and calcium, eroding bone and forming kidney stones. Western countries shifted long ago toward mostly symptom-free cases found by routine blood tests, while China's picture over the long term was unclear.

The team assembled 2,367 inpatients treated between 1980 and 2019 with the sporadic form of the disease, excluding inherited and secondary cases. They charted how symptoms, calcium patterns, and gland pathology changed across the decades. Recent reports from other Chinese centres show symptom-free shares already rising toward Western levels. A four-decade single-centre record, the authors argue, is the surest way to see a disease's face change as detection improves.
pmc-13545326:
Koney and co-authors chronicle how the University of Ghana moved histology teaching online during COVID-19, replacing microscope slides with virtual microscopy, digital slides students can pan and zoom on a screen. The 2026 study follows medical and dental students through the pandemic adoption. It asks what helped and what blocked them in a low-resource setting where the obvious barriers, computers and internet, are only part of the story.

Awareness and use of the virtual resources climbed significantly across the pandemic period. Students who used the system praised its advantages yet over ninety percent still wanted it combined with traditional microscopes rather than replacing them. Active users blamed poor internet and weak promotion by their teachers as the obstacles. The authors conclude the technology won student support, and that institutional reluctance and infrastructure, more than student resistance, will decide whether such tools stick in universities.
pmc-13545626:
Yingze Ning, Shuai Tian, and Guangliang Qiang reported in 2026 a rare and dangerous complication during preparation for lung surgery. A 60-year-old man with an 11-millimeter ground-glass nodule had a wire placed beside the nodule under CT guidance so surgeons could find it during the planned operation. The placement itself went smoothly.

On the scan taken right afterward, the patient lost consciousness and his heart stopped, with monitors showing ventricular fibrillation. Images revealed roughly 10 milliliters of air inside the left ventricle of his heart. Resuscitation with chest compressions, shocks, and epinephrine restored his circulation after about 15 minutes, and he was moved to intensive care. The case underlines how quickly air embolism must be recognized during lung puncture procedures.
pmc-13545726:
Ali M. Abdelaziz and co-authors pooled in 2026 the results of 71 studies covering more than 480,000 patients to compare outcomes for women and men after catheter-based aortic valve replacement. Because women present with different anatomy and health profiles, the team rebuilt individual survival data from published curves to track both early hazards and long-term survival.

Women faced higher risks in the first month, including more strokes, serious bleeding, and vessel complications, and slightly higher early mortality. Over follow-up stretching to ten years, the pattern reversed, with women dying less often from all causes and from cardiovascular causes. The authors call for care around the procedure that takes these sex-specific risks into account rather than treating both groups identically.
pmc-13546226:
Hee-Sung Kim and colleagues reported in 2026 on the long-term kidney safety of lobeglitazone, a diabetes drug, in Korean patients with type 2 diabetes. Their review of records from 30 hospitals covered 2,743 patients who had taken the drug for at least a year, with follow-up stretching to six years. Kidney filtration and urine protein, the two measures most watched for diabetes-related kidney damage, were the main outcomes.

Filtration rates stayed essentially flat across all stages of kidney disease, and urine protein categories were unchanged in roughly four fifths of patients. Blood sugar control improved by about a point on the HbA1c scale and held there, while cholesterol measures and insulin resistance also improved. Side effects matched the drug's known profile, and events of special concern were rare.
pmc-13546726:
Ana Karen Frutis-Moto and colleagues combined in 2026 the results of 32 studies to judge whether tannins, bitter plant compounds, reliably cut methane from ruminant digestion, a notable source of greenhouse gas. The pooled data held 213 observations split between foliage feeds and forage feeds, and the team built equations to predict methane from tannin type and feed composition, checking them on held-back data.

Tannins measured in the studies varied enormously. In foliage, condensed tannins were linked with less methane, while in forages total tannins were linked with slightly more, a reversal showing that the feed base matters as much as the compound. Prediction equations worked moderately well, better for forages. The authors offer the equations as a quick screening tool for candidate feeds.
pmc-13547226:
Carmen K Chan and colleagues used engineered mice in 2026 to test whether a form of inflammatory cell death in fat cells drives obesity. Necroptosis, the death mode in question, runs through a protein called RIPK3, which was switched on in the fat of obese mice and tracked with body mass in human fat samples. The team deleted either RIPK3's activation piece or caspase-8, a second death regulator, specifically in fat cells.

Removing caspase-8 from fat cells made mice leaner, yet deleting RIPK3 alongside it erased that protection, and removing only the RIPK3 activation piece changed nothing about weight or blood sugar. Cell experiments suggested caspase-8 supports fat cell formation directly. The authors conclude the caspase matters for building fat, not mainly through the necroptosis route.
pmc-13547326:
Yang Li and co-authors paired two satellite techniques in 2026 to measure how falling groundwater and sinking land relate in Tianjin. The city sits on the North China Plain and has long sunk from over-pumping. Gravity satellite data tracked water storage from January 2023 to February 2025, while radar interferometry mapped ground movement over the same window. A lag-aware correlation method then asked how closely the two series move together and which one leads.

Water storage rose across most of the region yet fell in the northern Binhai area, where sinking also concentrated in funnels reaching about 68 millimeters per year. Sinking followed water changes with delays between about six weeks and nine months, depending on the zone. The authors offer the lag estimates for prevention planning and early warning.
pmc-13547626:
Chong Chen and co-authors measured in 2026 how well young chickens can actually absorb amino acids from wheat shorts, a cheap milling by-product. They also built equations to predict that value from simple chemistry. Nearly a thousand pullets ate diets based on ten wheat shorts samples from different regions, at both the brooding and growing stages, with a marker tracking digestion.

Digestibility swung widely between samples, with cysteine the hardest amino acid to absorb and glutamic acid the easiest at both ages. Fiber measures, starch, and energy content predicted digestibility best, and the top equations explained up to about 98 percent of the variation in one case. The authors give feed makers a way to price and use a variable ingredient without running animal trials each time.
pmc-13548526:
Lauren L. O'Mahoney and colleagues map how researchers measure outcomes for people living with several long-term conditions at once, in a 2026 overview of reviews. Care settings and study populations differ widely, so results rarely line up, and agreed outcome sets cover only part of the field. The team searched five databases and screened thousands of records to chart which outcomes appear and how they are measured.

Ten reviews covering 709 primary studies met their criteria. Quality of life and health care use appeared most often, while treatment burden, patient engagement, and outcomes for children were seldom assessed. Only one existing outcome set included low- and middle-income countries. The authors call for wider stakeholder input, better validation of instruments, and outcome sets that work across countries and care settings.
pmc-13548926:
Miao Zhao and colleagues build lattice materials whose crushing behavior is programmed by geometry alone, in a 2026 materials study inspired by seashell nacre. Mixing soft and hard materials complicates printing, so the team instead printed one material in two lattice styles: bending-dominated cells that act soft and stretching-dominated cells that act hard. Arranging the two styles in coded spatial patterns mimics nacre's layered toughness.

Changing the code changed the whole mechanical story, including how the material stiffens, where it plateaus while crushing, and how it fails step by step in a planned sequence. Coupling between the phases made the blend absorb more energy than either lattice alone, and the plateau stress could be tuned. A data-driven model learned the code-to-behavior map, letting the team design backward from a wanted response to a pattern.
pmc-13550026:
Nanjian Xu and colleagues review biomaterial scaffolds loaded with stem cells as a strategy to calm inflammation after spinal cord injury, in a 2026 article. The inflammatory cascade that follows the injury is a chief obstacle to repair, and nursing these patients is complicated by bladder, skin, breathing, and pain problems. Scaffolds give transplanted cells a supportive home while both parts jointly steer the immune environment.

The review lays out how to choose scaffold materials and cell types. It then covers tactics from structural support and immune tuning to cell-free options. Those options include stem cell vesicles and smart materials that respond to their surroundings. Evidence from animal models is weighed against the hurdles of human translation. The authors close with trends toward materials that adapt over time, integrate several functions, and aim at precise regeneration.
pmc-13550326:
Bo Li, Liying Zhu, and Jiewu Zhang hunt for genes governed by a chemical tag on RNA that matter in thyroid cancer, in a 2026 study mixing computation with bench tests. The tag, called m7G, tunes how RNA messages are used, and its network in thyroid carcinoma was largely blank. Network analysis and three machine learning methods on tumor datasets converged on two feature genes, GPSM3 and ZNF831, with the latter drawing the deepest look.

Staining of patient tissue confirmed ZNF831 differs between tumor and normal thyroid. Forcing extra ZNF831 into thyroid cancer cells slowed their growth and movement, marking it as a likely tumor suppressor. Its levels also tracked with how much immune infiltration a tumor carried. The authors present the gene as a candidate target and call for work on the mechanism linking the RNA tag to it.
pmc-13550426:
Ramesh Kumar Ayyasamy and colleagues combine frequency modulation with machine learning to analyze bandwidth and defend fiber-optic networks, in a 2026 engineering study. Optical links carry the world's data, and both capacity planning and attack detection strain rule-based tools. Their method estimates signal bandwidth with a dynamic frequency-modulated support vector machine, while a blockchain-reinforced adversarial Bayesian neural network models the security side.

In experiments, bandwidth estimation erred by only three percent, throughput reached ninety-seven gigabits per second, and spectral efficiency hit a strong mark. On defense, attack detection scored ninety-eight percent accuracy with false positives held near one and a half percent. The authors present the pairing as a route to optical networks that run fast and guarded at once, though the evaluation stays within their signal-based modeling setup.
pmc-13554226:
Jicheng Cong, Xiaotian Ran, and Chunbin Qin present a learning method that stitches photos into wide views without losing tiny objects in a 2026 study. Classic stitching blurs small items and warps busy scenes. Their system borrows a fast detector's eye for features, then sharpens the low-detail maps where small objects hide. Pooling across scales helps match points between shots of different sharpness.

A deep module computes the warp between views, guided by math that maps points exactly. Training losses reward crisp alignment around small objects most of all. On two test sets, stitched views scored higher on sharpness and likeness measures than rival methods. The model also ran leaner, using less memory and computing power than heavier rivals.
pmc-13556326:
Ji Zhang and six colleagues published this 2026 study building a safer vaccine candidate against tick-borne encephalitis virus, a flavivirus that causes brain inflammation across Europe and Asia. Their trick is deleting the virus's NS1 gene so it cannot replicate, while growing it in cells that supply NS1 from a virus, Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus. The defective virus was passaged to confirm the deletion stayed put and could not regain replication in cells.

Safety and protection were tested in mice. Even a high dose of the virus caused no symptoms. An immunisation gave complete protection against a lethal dose of wild-type virus: every vaccinated mouse survived, while unvaccinated controls all died with weight loss and virus in the blood. Protection tracked with levels of virus-specific antibodies, neutralising antibodies and killer T cells. The authors present the platform as proof of concept for flavivirus vaccines.
pmc-13556926:
Ullah and colleagues published a 2026 study on genes and response to a blood pressure pill pairing. The pairing joins valsartan with a water pill in one fixed dose. A common gene variant in the ACE gene may shift how patients respond. The team followed 645 patients in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, for three months.

After dropping poor pill-takers, 627 patients fed the final analysis overall. Patients with the mixed ID gene type saw the weakest pressure drops. Their top-number falls lagged the II group by a clear margin. The DD group showed the best raw drops, though not firmly proven. Gene-guided first choices may follow if bigger studies agree, they say. The target for success sat below 140 over 90 in pressure terms.
pmc-13557626:
Hui and colleagues report in 2026 a Mendelian randomization study testing whether four dietary patterns actually cause changes in heart and metabolic health. The technique uses inherited gene variants as natural experiments, and the authors also test whether taste-and-smell gene variants make sharper tools for the job.

Using conventional genome-wide variants as instruments, a pescatarian dietary pattern was associated with lower fasting insulin, a result that survived multiple sensitivity checks. Apparent links between an unhealthy pattern and higher blood pressure and blood sugar were flagged as unreliable. One of only two instruments was itself tied to caffeine intake. The taste-and-smell receptor variants produced no significant findings at all, which the authors attribute to insufficient statistical power. Overall they conclude dietary patterns show at most modest direct causal effects in this design.
pmc-13558626:
Fan Zheng and seven colleagues designed in 2026 a light-trapping grating that could let single-photon detectors run faster without losing sensitivity. Superconducting nanowire detectors excel in the near infrared, yet sparse wires absorb poorly while dense wires recover slowly after each detection. Their answer is a silicon dielectric grating that excites a Fano resonance, a sharp optical interference effect, above wires covering only a tenth of the surface.

Simulations at the telecom wavelength of 1550 nanometres, run with a standard time-domain solver, showed absorption above ninety-eight percent under ideal conditions despite the ultralow wire coverage. Sparse wires carry less kinetic inductance, which is what slows detector reset, so the design promises speed and efficiency together. The authors offer the scheme as a blueprint for next-generation photon counting in communications and imaging.
pmc-13559126:
Zhao and co-authors review how rewired metabolism may drive Kawasaki disease, a childhood vessel inflammation that threatens the coronary arteries. Their 2026 narrative review gathers clinical, experimental, and mechanistic studies linking immune overactivation to endothelial dysfunction, the failure of the vessel lining that produces artery lesions.

The evidence shows extensive metabolic remodelling: faster sugar burning through glycolysis, disrupted fat handling and fatty acid oxidation, altered amino acid use, and a disturbed energy cycle in mitochondria. Mouse models mirror several shifts, including changed tryptophan handling and more lactate. One pathway stands out: activation of the kynurenine route, which drains tryptophan, tracks with amplified inflammation and mitochondrial impairment. Gut microbe imbalance adds a further layer. The authors present metabolism as the connective tissue between immune attack and vessel damage, and a possible treatment lever.
pmc-13560126:
Elma Satrovic's team assessed how money growth, nature's capacity, and clean energy shape green outcomes, in a 2026 study. Earlier work looked at finance and green outcomes apart, leaving unclear whether countries rich in natural resources can steer finance toward greener ends. The team studied ten countries with large nature reserves from 1995 to 2020 using a modified STIRPAT framework with panel quantile methods.

Nature's capacity, economic complexity, and clean energy helped green outcomes, while finance growth, economic growth, and population growth dragged against them. Notably, finance hurt less, and in time helped, where nature's capacity was higher, suggesting joint growth of both can pay off. The authors urge policies that protect ecosystems, steer finance toward renewables, and align with the Sustainable Development Goals.
pmc-13560226:
Induja K and colleagues report purple urine bag syndrome in a woman in her forties recovering from a stroke. Their 2026 case report describes a bedbound patient dependent on a long-term urinary catheter whose collection bag turned a striking purple. The odd color arises when gut bacteria break down tryptophan in alkaline urine, tinting the plastic.

Urine testing showed an alkaline pH with significant white cells, and culture grew Klebsiella pneumoniae. Treatment combined a fresh catheter, levofloxacin chosen against the cultured germ, better bowel habits, and more fluids. The purple color and the infection both resolved fully. The authors stress that the strange hue usually signals a hidden urinary infection rather than a crisis in itself. Careful catheter hygiene, microbiological checks, and patient education form the wider lesson for catheter-dependent patients.
pmc-13560626:
Siaa Girotra and colleagues publish the process evaluation protocol for the TReAT trial, which tests an app-based telerehabilitation program after knee replacement surgery in India. The app bundles education, exercise videos, a progress diary, two-way messaging, and remote therapy planning to fix poor adherence to home rehabilitation.

The process study runs alongside, using the RE-AIM framework to weigh reach, fidelity, and adoption. Screening logs, app analytics, interviews, and researcher notes feed a mixed-methods design guided by a logic model. Comparing the two hospital settings should show how context bends implementation, informing scale-up of mobile rehabilitation across India.
pmc-13561726:
Jie Xu, Hongjin Shi, and Jinsong Zhang compare the male infertility burden across five East Asian countries using Global Burden of Disease 2023 data. Their 2026 analysis extracts case counts, prevalence, and disability years for China, Japan, both Koreas, and Mongolia, then models trends since 1990 and forecasts China's path to 2051. Cultural pressure around childbearing sharpens the issue regionally.

East Asia carried about 12.827 million male infertility cases in 2023, with China holding 92.8 percent of them in the reported estimates. China also posted the highest standardized prevalence and disability rates, while South Korea posted the lowest. Mongolia's burden rose fastest over the three decades, while Japan and South Korea declined. Secondary infertility dominated in China and Japan. Forecasts keep China's caseload near 10.759 million by 2051, mostly secondary. The authors urge country-specific prevention strategies.
pmc-13562126:
Gabriele Leonie Schwarz and colleagues explore how very old patients and their relatives wish to take part in intensive care decisions. Their 2026 qualitative study analyzes free-text answers from a Norwegian survey run between November 2021 and March 2023 among outpatients aged eighty and over and their next of kin. Hypothetical scenarios of life-threatening illness framed the questions.

Of the respondents, 210 people supplied 339 relevant comments. Five wishes emerged: to seek scientific knowledge, to contribute personal knowledge of the patient, to have care tailored to how differently old people age, to improve the decision process itself. A fifth wish was to strengthen feelings of security. Read through an uncertainty framework, each wish became a way of coping with the deep uncertainty of critical illness decisions. The authors urge teams to admit family knowledge into decisions and to keep relatives present when very old patients need critical care.
pmc-13562326:
Mengqi Xie and four colleagues review healing medicine for the injured endometrium, the uterine lining whose damage brings adhesions, thin lining, and chronic inflammation that cause infertility. Their 2026 review screens writings from 2000 to August 2025 across four databases and keeps 102 studies for close reading. Hormones and surgery, the standard tools, fail patients with moderate to severe damage.

Cell therapies using mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow, cord blood, or the endometrium itself are weighed source by source. Cell-free options, platelet-rich plasma and extracellular vesicles, get the same graded treatment, then come lab-built strategies on hydrogels and scaffolds. The authors grade evidence by tiers rather than lumping promise as one. Their arc runs from broad regeneration toward precise fixes matched to the injury. The review gives doctors and researchers a clear map of a fast-moving fertility frontier.
pmc-13562526:
Roy Ramati and two colleagues test an idea that autistic and psychosis-like traits pull perception in opposite directions and can cancel out. The 2026 study ran two experiments, with 81 and 93 healthy volunteers. Each person judged the tilt of the middle item in fast three-item sequences, then filled in questionnaires on both trait families.

Statistical mapping of the trait pairs found that people with both traits raised together made fewer errors about which item came when. One trait alone gave no such benefit. The pattern fits the diametric model, where opposing tendencies compensate. The authors say the balance idea now reaches mid-level perception, and it may help explain why symptoms vary so much between people who carry both trait sets.
pmc-13562726:
Michalis Piponidis and Theocharis Theocharides argue that a drone's object detector should reshape itself to match the height it is flying at. Objects shrink and spread as altitude changes, yet one fixed network wastes scarce onboard power by treating every view the same. Their 2026 work trains several lean network settings, each tuned for a band of altitudes, varying image size, network width, and filter size. A threshold rule then swaps settings in flight as the drone climbs or descends.

Two datasets rich in altitude variety confirmed that the best settings differ sharply between low and high flight. With well-chosen thresholds, the switching system lost almost no accuracy against a single heavyweight network, while saving large amounts of computation and memory. Poorly placed thresholds, the analysis shows, erode that bargain. The authors pitch altitude-aware switching for surveillance, rescue, and environmental patrol drones that must think fast on small batteries.
pmc-13563726:
Xiaodong Sun and fifteen colleagues report how a stronger eye injection performed in Chinese patients within the global PULSAR trial for wet age-related macular degeneration. The disease leaks fluid into the retina and steals central vision. The trial compared aflibercept at 8 milligrams, given every 12 or 16 weeks after starter doses, against the standard 2 milligrams every 8 weeks. This 2026 analysis covers the China subgroup through week 48, describing vision change, retinal thickness, staying power, and safety.

Vision gains were healthy in all arms: 13.2 letters on the eye chart for the 12-week group, 9.7 for the 16-week group, and 10.0 for standard care, with group sizes of 31, 31, and 39. Retinal swelling fell by similar amounts everywhere. Most patients held their long intervals, 88.5 percent at 12 weeks and 73.1 percent at 16. Eye side effects matched across arms, echoing the full trial's verdict.
pmc-13563826:
Xingjian Li and seven colleagues describe a salvage operation for dialysis fistulas whose outflow vein has blocked at the elbow. A working fistula is a lifeline for kidney patients, and re-routing its drainage into the basilic vein can save the access without material. Their 2026 technical note reviews nine patients treated at one centre between December 2023 and March 2026. Warning signs included vein pressure alarms during dialysis, clotting of the outflow, and weak blood flow. Every patient had high blood pressure; two had diabetes.

After the rerouting, each fistula regained its normal thrill and lost its pulsing. All nine accesses served dialysis within 48 hours. Two wound bleeds settled with bedside care, and no early clotting, nerve injury, infection, or access loss occurred. Five patients later needed touch-up procedures for renewed narrowing. The authors offer the method as an own-tissue rescue for chosen arms, labelled as early experience.
pmc-13570426:
Liam P. Fawcett and Nicholas M. Levinson dissect, in a 2026 study, how an unusual activator protein called SPY1 switches on CDK2, a key engine of cell division, without the phosphate tag that the normal activator requires. Fluorescence experiments tracked shape changes in the engine as each activator bound, in both tagged and untagged states.

SPY1 activated both forms as strongly as the standard activator and shifted the engine's shape just as far. A mutant version long thought to mimic the phosphate tag failed on untagged CDK2 yet worked fully on tagged CDK2, proving the activator uses two separate tricks. The distinction matters for designing drugs that block this division engine in cancer.
pmc-13572326:
Eva A. S. Koster and colleagues modelled infection, vaccination, and excess death together across the Dutch population over age 63 during the pandemic. Earlier work had not captured all three dynamics in one comprehensive model. Their 2026 study used nationwide records for 3,826,770 people, with no selection. It compared deaths in 2020 and 2021 with background death rates from 2015 to 2019, tracking infections, repeat infections, vaccinations, and deaths in a multi-state model.

Excess deaths reached 0.34 percent of the cohort, about 4.4 percent of all deaths seen, higher in men and in older groups. Excess death clustered in the first four weeks after a positive test but lingered beyond it. Vaccination cut excess deaths sharply even when infection still occurred. The authors present the model as a fuller picture of how COVID-19 raised deaths in older adults, during and after acute infection.
pmc-13572426:
Ramesh N S V S C Sripada, with six colleagues, presents a 2026 computer framework for spotting silicosis on chest X-rays. Silicosis is lung scarring from fine silica dust, a risk in mining and stone work. Chest X-rays are cheap and common for screening, yet early signs can be easy to miss by eye.

The framework, called MDLF-EISD, joins several kinds of input in a deep learning model built to flag the disease early. Neural networks that learn from images sort the X-ray patterns linked to dust damage. The authors frame the tool as a way to speed up routine checks and prompt care sooner. In their account, the design draws on past gains in image-based diagnosis of lung disease. The aim is sharper first calls in busy screening programs.
pmc-13572526:
Ran Zuo and colleagues found an enzyme that helps lung adenocarcinoma hide from immunotherapy, and a way to unmask it. Checkpoint drugs against PD-1 transformed lung cancer care, yet only a minority of patients respond, and resistance is common. Their 2026 study examined cytoplasmic phospholipase A2 alpha, an inflammation-linked enzyme overexpressed in tumours with poor prognosis.

Silencing the enzyme slowed cancer growth, but in immune-competent animals it also raised PD-L1, a shield against immune attack. Pairing silencing with anti-PD-1 therapy, however, drove killer T cells into tumours and suppressed growth synergistically. The authors propose the enzyme as a target to overcome PD-1 resistance, especially in patients with high enzyme levels and low baseline PD-L1.
pmc-13573326:
Salima Meherali, with 16 colleagues, sets out a 2026 protocol for a scoping review on sexual and reproductive health information for young people with chronic illness. The focus falls on youth aged 15 to 24 who live with epilepsy, a heart defect from birth, or lupus. Each condition adds its own risks around pregnancy and birth control.

The review will map what these young adults need to know, what they can get, and what blocks or aids access in the United States and Canada. In epilepsy, seizures, drugs, and hormones interact in ways that raise the chance of unplanned pregnancy. In heart disease, many pregnancies carry cardiac risk, and birth control advice often comes late. The team will gather and sort the published and grey sources by set rules. The map aims to guide services that reach these youth sooner.
pmc-13574826:
Yang Zhang, with ten colleagues, presents a 2026 attention scheme for sorting pathology images, the microscope slides used to spot cancer early. Such slides mix tangled textures and wide variety, and most tools lean on local detail alone. Frequency views, which split an image into wave bands, rarely let those bands talk to each other.

The scheme, called MFHA, blends attention across scales in the frequency view. Coarse bands carry the broad layout of tissue, while fine bands hold cell-level clues. Letting the bands interact aims to fuse both into one read. The authors pitch the fusion as a fix for missed detail in hard cases. Finer sorting of slide types guides treatment choice, so gains here feed straight into care. The work targets labs where expert slide readers are scarce.
pmc-13576126:
Connor D Drake leads a 2026 study of what helps or hinders a full virtual care programme for poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. This stubborn form of diabetes affects roughly one in ten patients and drives much harm and cost. The programme had beaten standard telehealth in a trial, so the team asked how it would fit routine care.

Interviews covered 19 patients and eight staff. The programme matched primary care goals for self-management, yet it demanded new communication patterns with existing teams. Its intensity made keeping patients engaged a challenge. Suggested fixes included standard training for providers and tighter links to local resources. Staffing may need new roles or shifted duties. The authors say existing clinic structures give the model a workable base.
pmc-13576226:
Pikka Jokelainen and four colleagues report antibody findings for two parasites in semi-domesticated reindeer across Finland and northern Norway in a 2026 study. The parasites are Toxoplasma gondii, which can infect people, and Neospora caninum. Both spread widely in other animals, yet reindeer data were thin.

Blood from 635 reindeer gathered in 2015 was tested with commercial assays. Just 35 animals, 5.5 percent, carried Toxoplasma antibodies, and none carried Neospora antibodies. Adults showed higher rates than calves. Rates climbed steadily from north to south, a gradient the authors link to heavier contamination of the environment with parasite eggs in the south. The authors present the survey as a baseline for a food and culture species of high value to Sámi herders.
pmc-13578826:
Mark Pawson, Mike Vuolo, and Brian C Kelly ask cannabis users what they think of a standard dose unit for THC, the plant's main active compound, in a 2026 interview study. Fifty adult users took part, from states with and without legal sales. Each was told how a standard drink works for alcohol. Each was then asked if a matching unit for cannabis would help as products grow stronger and more varied.

Most welcomed the idea, though a few doubted how it would run in practice. Users saw the unit as most useful for beginners and light users, for pacing intake, and for judging when driving stays unsafe. Seasoned users said such a unit would have helped them at the start. Clear teaching is needed, the authors warn, so the unit is not misread as a safety promise.
pmc-13579726:
Bruno F A Ferreira and colleagues pair vessel scans with spot vision tests in Behçet's disease of the retina, in a 2026 study. The illness inflames eye vessels in flares, and quiet phases can still hide damage. Fourteen patients, twenty three eyes in all, were followed every four months for a year while the disease stayed inactive. Average age sat near forty.
