Men and patients under forty five showed the strongest shifts on thickness and vessel measures. Vessel density swung opposite to the size of the center spot that lacks vessels, and tracked with layer thickness. One upper sector vessel measure matched center vision sensitivity closely. Every marker held steady across the year in patients kept in remission. The authors urge caution, since the group was small and the cuts were exploratory.
pmc-13579826:
Betül Zehra Karip and colleagues test a rosemary compound against radiation skin damage in rats, in a 2026 study. Radiation care burns skin in most patients, driving stress damage, inflammation, and scarring. Forty two male rats were split into seven groups: plain controls, radiated groups checked at two or four weeks, saline treated radiated groups, and groups given the compound by injection.

Untreated radiated skin broke down, lost layers, and filled with inflammatory mast cells, while blood flow shrank. Two stress markers tied to scarring and DNA damage climbed in those groups, as did chemical signs of oxidative strain. Compound treated rats kept far better skin form, lower marker levels, and calmer tissue chemistry at both checks. The authors read the compound as a shield worth testing further.
pmc-13582026:
Pau Llàcer and colleagues asked whether multidisciplinary heart-failure follow-up helps patients of every age, using the Spanish RICA registry. The prospective cohort included 5,644 patients hospitalized for acute heart failure, with a mean age near 80 years, followed for one year. Half received care in UMIPIC comprehensive management units, and the rest received conventional care.

About a quarter of patients died and nearly as many were readmitted for heart failure during follow-up. UMIPIC follow-up was tied to lower mortality and readmission overall, and the survival gain appeared most pronounced among patients aged ninety and older. Very old patients should therefore not be excluded from multidisciplinary heart-failure programs, the authors argue.
pmc-13587426:
Alessandra Masullo and colleagues find that losing one form of a repair protein can help DNA fix itself more cleanly. The setting is Fanconi anemia, a rare inherited disorder where broken DNA repair leaves the genome unstable and raises cancer risk. Working in the worm C. elegans, a stand-in where the same repair pathway is conserved, the team focused on RAD-51, a protein that runs the accurate repair route called homologous recombination.

Worms make three forms of RAD-51, and removing just the long form, isoform A, made the accurate route work better rather than worse. In worms already lacking the Fanconi protein fcd-2, losing that form eased development and fertility faults and cut the clumping of chromosomes in germ cells. The balance between the tidy and the sloppy repair routes, the authors argue, can be tipped by which forms of one protein a cell chooses to make.
pmc-13589926:
Bei Li leads a 2026 study linking gut microbes to autism, a condition marked by hardships in social contact and by repeated acts. Working with mice bred to model autism and with human data, the team looked at how gut bacteria break down tryptophan, a building block from food. One product stood out: 5-HTP, a close chemical kin of serotonin.

Mice given 5-HTP from gut bacteria showed less anxiety, fewer repeated acts, and better social acts. Li and the team traced the effect to the brain, which the compound can reach from the blood. There it eased overactive growth signals and steadied the fine branches of nerve cells. The work hints at a gut based route to new autism care.
pmc-13591726:
Lana M Agraib and three colleagues chart, in 2026, how much of the Jordanian adult diet comes from ultra processed foods. The NOVA system sorts foods by how heavily they are made in factories. Their survey used a checked food questionnaire with 537 adults aged 19 to 64. Energy from each NOVA group was tallied and compared by sex, age, and body size.

Ultra processed items supplied over half of all daily energy, ahead of barely processed foods at about a third. Men ate more in total and leaned harder on factory foods, while women ate more lightly processed items. Younger adults also leaned toward ultra processed choices. Agraib and the team call for focused public health steps to shift habits.
pmc-13593626:
Fabio Bazzarelli and colleagues present a membrane-based method for making solid lipid nanoparticles loaded with diclofenac sodium, a common anti-inflammatory drug that breaks down in light. Their 2026 study compares the new membrane nanoprecipitation process with the usual batch approach, using cocoa butter as the solid fat.

With an acetate buffer at pH 4.1 as the non-solvent, the membrane route gave particles averaging about 421 nanometers across, trapping roughly 95 percent of the drug inside. Under simulated sunlight the protected drug held up far longer than the drug dissolved in water, keeping the same remaining level for minutes instead of seconds. The authors describe membrane nanoprecipitation as a sustainable way to produce light-stable drug carriers continuously rather than batch by batch.
pmc-13595526:
Jinxuan Su and Hongzhong Jin review skin aging as a connected system rather than a list of separate faults, organizing the mechanisms at three levels. Their 2026 synthesis begins with chemical marks on DNA that drift with age and lock in worn-out gene programs, then moves to exhausted cells and their remodeled energy factories.

At the tissue level, the cleanup of those exhausted cells falters as the immune system itself ages. The stranded cells pump out inflammatory signals. Those signals keep the skin in a state of low-grade irritation. They also break down its supporting matrix. Each level feeds the next, the authors argue. Against that map they set the emerging toolkit. It includes drugs that clear or quiet senescent cells, epigenetic and mitochondrial modulators, biologics, and immune therapies. Regenerative and device-based approaches complete the list. Together they sketch where targeted treatment of aging skin might go.
pmc-13596826:
Chunye Yang, Xuedong Yu, Hongshun Li, and Dawit Dibekulu modeled how motivation, study strategies, and word knowledge connect for Chinese students learning English. Their survey and word-test data covered 230 students in Wuhan, mostly in their first two years, analyzed with structural equation modeling.

Motivation sat slightly below the midpoint, and students favored thinking strategies, the direct tactics for working with words, over memory and self-management methods. Motivation strongly predicted strategy use and somewhat predicted word breadth. Strategy use did not predict word knowledge at all once motivation was counted for. No indirect path through strategies appeared either. The authors draw a practical moral: teachers may gain more from feeding students' drive to learn. Drilling strategy sets helps less, since driven students may not turn them into words known.
pmc-13598126:
Ankita J Sachla, Miguel Piñeros, and John D Helmann pinned down why manganese helps the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis build biofilms on plant roots. The work underpins its use as a crop-friendly microbe. Two membrane proteins switched on by manganese-sensing genetic riboswitches, MeeY and YybP, turned out to be required for the films in their 2026 study.

Knocking out either gene cut production of the biofilm's sugary matrix and drained the matrix of its divalent metal ions. Removing a master repressor restored the sugar but not the metal loading, proving the proteins do two separable jobs: enabling matrix production and stocking it with metals. One of the pair is a suspected manganese exporter and the other was functionally unknown until now. The authors present both as previously unappreciated regulators linking metal sensing to the physical construction of the biofilm.
pmc-13602526:
Anna Swenson and colleagues report real-world results in 2026 for mepolizumab in patients with chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. This stubborn sinus condition involves polyps, blocked noses, and lost smell, and trials had shown the antibody drug helps. What routine practice added was unclear. Using linked records and insurance claims from United States clinician networks, the team compared each patient's care use and symptoms before and after starting the drug.

Within six months, visits fell across the board, including ear, nose and throat and allergy appointments. Fewer patients needed oral corticosteroid prescriptions, dropping from 36 to 27 percent, and oral antibiotics fell from 38 to 23 percent. Charted symptoms improved too: loss of smell was reported by 53 percent fewer patients, with facial pain, discharge, and obstruction also down. In everyday care, the authors conclude, the drug trims healthcare use and medication burden early.
pmc-13612326:
Zhifu Yang leads a nine-author team comparing two ways to guide heart ablation for atrial fibrillation. Standard practice steers catheters with X-ray fluoroscopy, which means heavy lead aprons and radiation for staff. Their alternative uses ultrasound imaging from inside the heart itself, aiming for zero X-rays. The retrospective study covered 177 ablation patients at Ningbo No. 2 Hospital between December 2023 and June 2026. Operators rated their fatigue right after each case.

Procedure time, puncture duration, and success rates were indistinguishable between workflows. Complications were rare in both: one tamponade in the fluoroscopy group, none in the zero-fluoroscopy group. The striking gap was human. Operators scored their physical fatigue at 1.1 against 6.8 on a ten-point scale, and procedural discomfort at 1.3 against 7.2, favoring the apron-free method. The authors attribute the relief mostly to ditching lead. They recommend prospective trials to confirm patient outcomes hold while staff bodies are spared.
pmc-13613726:
Daqian Zhou and colleagues report a 2026 study of nodakenin, a compound from traditional Chinese medicine, and its power to slow ageing in the cells of spinal discs. Disc wear is a common, stubborn cause of back pain, and it is driven by ageing of the soft centre cells of the disc. Those ageing cells suffer damage to their mitochondria, the cell's energy makers, and pile up harmful oxygen by-products.

The team focused on two control systems: a protein called SIRT6 and a cleanup route named PINK1/Parkin that removes worn-out mitochondria. Clearing bad mitochondria keeps oxygen waste down and slows cell ageing. Testing nodakenin against these pathways shows whether a plant compound could protect disc cells, a route that current treatment for disc wear barely touches. Readers get a clear view of a lab path toward gentler back pain care.
pmc-13614126:
Yukun Liu and colleagues present a 2026 deep learning system for predicting which pairs of molecules will form cocrystals, solid materials built from two compounds in one crystal. Drug makers use cocrystals to improve how medicines dissolve and last, yet hunting for good pairs by trial and error is slow and often blind. Earlier computer models gave weak detail and could not explain their own answers.

The new system reads molecules as Morgan fingerprints, a numeric sketch of their structure, and uses a cross-attention method to weigh how the two partners interact. It reached an accuracy score of 0.9878 on the main test measure. Extra checks compared rival models, varied settings, and used SHAP analysis to show which features drove each call. Chemists get both a fast screen and a look at the reasoning behind it.
pmc-13614826:
Kumar and co-authors read Google searches as a public health instrument, in this 2026 infodemiology study. The study covers four common childhood urological conditions. These are a blocked kidney drainage junction, urine reflux toward the kidneys, hypospadias, and undescended testis. Using two decades of Google Trends data, 2004 to 2024, they sorted caregiver queries into symptom-seeking and treatment-seeking and computed the ratio between them.

Patterns diverged sharply by condition. Hypospadias searching was overwhelmingly treatment-focused throughout, with a symptom-to-treatment ratio of just 0.003 in their normalized measure, while the kidney blockage condition showed the highest symptom orientation, peaking at a ratio of 1.75 in 2016. Undescended testis searches drifted steadily toward symptom interest over time, and the pandemic suppressed kidney-condition searches while hypospadias held stable. The authors offer the gaps as targets for caregiver education.
pmc-13619126:
Poliana Fialho de Carvalho and five colleagues studied whether neighborhood deprivation shapes preventive care for older Brazilian women. Using baseline data from a national aging survey from 2015 and 2016, they looked at 5,314 women aged fifty and older. Outcomes included mammograms, Pap smears, and checks of cholesterol, blood sugar, and blood pressure, split by public system use or private insurance.

Women in more deprived areas had lower odds of blood sugar and cholesterol testing, and the pattern held for both public and private patients. The gap was wider among women relying on the public system. No equally clear gradient appeared for every service checked. The authors argue that policy should target these local inequalities directly, since a test missed early can mean a chronic disease found late.
pmc-13619326:
Ruben Raj Ellan Govan and four colleagues present four patients treated at one center for amyloidosis of the larynx, a rare buildup of abnormal protein in the voice box. All four cases were confirmed by tissue testing. The illness can look like a benign lump, cancer, inflammation, or a voice problem, which makes diagnosis tricky.

Two patients had localized disease of the AL type, the form linked to antibody proteins. One had airway deposits alongside known multiple myeloma, a bone marrow cancer. The fourth had untyped deposits across both sides of the larynx and the vocal cords. Care ranged from watchful airway checks to scope-based removal, chosen by symptoms, spread, and overall risk. The authors stress comparing such cases side by side, because shared diagnostic steps lead to very different treatment paths.
pmc-13619726:
Konishi and colleagues test a water soluble iodine contrast agent for videofluoroscopic swallowing studies, the moving X-ray exams that show how a person swallows. The standard agent, barium sulfate, can harm the lungs if it is inhaled into the airway, a risk in patients with swallowing disorders. Their 2026 study examines twenty patients at Hiroshima University Hospital who had the exam with iodixanol, sold as Visipaque 270. It compares the images with barium images from the same patients.

No adverse events followed the iodine agent, in the gut or elsewhere. Two radiologists' evaluations of the iodine studies proved equivalent to the barium studies under a formal test. The new agent matched the old on clarity within a preset margin. An agent that washes out of the airway and still shows the swallow could lower the stakes of testing the frailest patients, the authors suggest, pending confirmation.
pmc-13620126:
Marianne H Hannisdal and nine colleagues asked whether the way a grade 4 glioma looks at diagnosis can forecast where and when it will return, in a 2026 study. These brain tumors always recur, yet radiation planning still uses uniform margins around the tumor for everyone. The team analyzed 390 paired MRI scans from Norwegian centers and a public archive, using deep learning to outline the tumor's enhancing core and its non-enhancing parts.

The balance between those two parts predicted survival on its own: tumors with a low core share lived longer, even after accounting for age and two key gene markers. In the toughest genetic subgroup, a low ratio meant several extra months of median survival. Tumors starting in the back of the brain wandered to new sites most often and returned fastest. The authors propose risk-based, personalized radiation margins instead of one-size margins.
pmc-13620826:
Muhammad Nauman-ul-Haq and ten colleagues examined whether liver transplant patients can safely have their breathing tube removed right in the operating room. Early removal is a goal of modern recovery pathways, yet many centers still keep living donor recipients on ventilators in intensive care out of caution. Their single-center review covered 158 consecutive adults who met set physiological criteria during surgery.

Forty-seven patients were extubated immediately, and only one needed the tube put back. The immediate group left intensive care about a day sooner on median, with a similar hospital stay overall. One-year survival ran higher in the immediate group, with the clearest advantage in patients with middling liver disease scores. The authors call the practice feasible and safe in carefully chosen patients, while asking for matched comparisons before calling the survival gap real.
pmc-13621226:
Hiroya Morita, Shunichiro Orihara, Fumitaka Shimizu, and Masataka Taguri examine a shortcut in causal statistics that may not be as safe as researchers assume. Observational studies often weight patients by their chance of receiving a treatment, then fit a survival model. Most software estimates the uncertainty while ignoring that the weights were themselves estimated, a shortcut known to play safe when the target is the average effect across everyone.

The team asked whether that safety survives when the target changes to the effect in treated patients, or in patients where the groups overlap. Math, simulations, and a real dataset all gave the same answer: the uncorrected estimate can run too tight rather than too wide under those other weights. Confidence intervals built on it could claim more certainty than the data hold. The authors recommend variance methods that account for weight estimation whenever such models leave the standard target.
pmc-13623126:
João Vitor Barrio and colleagues chart deaths from cardiovascular disease in Campo Grande, capital of a Central-West Brazilian state, across a full decade. Heart and vessel diseases lead mortality in Brazil, yet no city-level study existed for this region. Their ecological study draws on the national mortality register for 2013 to 2022.

Of nearly sixty thousand deaths, about fourteen percent came from cardiovascular causes, and ischaemic heart disease, where narrowed arteries starve the heart, dominated. Men and people over sixty carried most of the burden. Overall rates rose by about a quarter across the decade, speeding up after 2019. Two findings stand out: wealthy neighbourhoods often showed higher mortality, against the usual pattern, and most heart disease deaths happened outside hospital, many at home. Maps showed tight clusters of high and low mortality. The authors offer the maps as a guide for placing prevention efforts.
pmc-13624226:
Panayiota Neophytou and colleagues published this 2026 case-based review on nerve pain in CANVAS, a rare inherited disorder that affects balance, sensation, and reflexes. The condition stems from repeat expansions in the RFC1 gene, and pain has been poorly measured in it until now.

The authors present a fifty-eight year old woman with confirmed CANVAS whose main symptom was one-sided nerve pain, followed over three years. They then pooled fourteen studies covering four hundred forty-five patients. Nerve pain appeared in about forty-three percent of patients and may start early in the illness. The review argues that painful sensory nerve damage should prompt doctors to consider CANVAS and order genetic testing sooner.
pmc-13624326:
Yu Fang and colleagues slow down the split-second chemistry that makes water-filter membranes, so they can watch it happen. These polyamide skins form where two liquids meet and react instantly, tangling the supply of ingredients with the reaction. The team built a rig feeding one ingredient, an amine, from a solid source at a steady rate, separating supply from reaction.

A vibrating quartz sensor weighed and felt the growing film in real time. The trace split into three acts: loose chains forming before the gel point, clumps gathering into a network, then slower thickening as the film blocked ingredients, ending in a stiffer skin. Adjusting the starting ratio of ingredients shifted each act's timing and the young network's looseness, which in turn set the finished membrane's pore cutoff, surface charge, and salt rejection. The authors offer the kinetic map as a design tool for membrane makers.
pmc-13625026:
Cassandra Phoenix, Meridith Griffin, and Erica V Bennett study how menopause symptoms bend the daily rhythms of exercise. They borrow rhythmanalysis, a lens from the French thinker Henri Lefebvre that reads life through repeating cycles, and apply it to survey answers from 249 women. Symptoms meet seasons, hormone swings, and body clocks, and the mix resets each woman's sense of when movement feels possible.

Women described energy, rest, and the wish to move rising and falling in patterns that blocked activity at some hours yet opened it at others. Many answered with new pacing, shifted routines, and closer listening to their bodies. The authors urge activity advice that flexes with these rhythms instead of treating menopause as a simple barrier or aid.
pmc-13625426:
Outi Linnaranta leads a Finnish team, publishing in 2026, that sets out to judge a national rollout of brief counseling for depressed teenagers. Interpersonal counseling, a short form of a proven talk therapy, was placed in primary care because the full therapy was hard to staff. Their protocol follows some nine thousand pupils in grades seven to nine, aged thirteen to seventeen, in selected schools.

At six months the pupils sort into three paths: the new counseling, other psychosocial care, or no care. The chief test is how many reach specialist psychiatric services within two years, with mood scores, well-being, and social inclusion tracked along the way. Cost checks use surveys and national registers reaching ten years back and forward, so value for money can be weighed beside health gains.
pmc-13625826:
Shuning Wang and colleagues mine blood gene data from people with Parkinson's disease and land on a surprise: the alarm protein HMGB1 is turned down, not up. Earlier reports had claimed the opposite in blood, so the team pooled several data sets of white blood cells and applied machine learning, single-cell reads, and computer perturbation tests. HMGB1 alone marked patients with modest accuracy, and two T-cell types sat at the hub of cell chatter.

Turning HMGB1 down in the computer tugged two partner genes, S100A8 and S100A9, upward, and those genes feed an inflammation path called IL-17 signaling. The authors propose an axis in which quiet HMGB1 rides with louder S100 genes and a lit IL-17 path, apart from the usual inflammation story. Drug databases even offered candidate compounds that touch the network.
pmc-13626026:
Oliver Razum, Joseph Kuhn, and Dagmar Starke mark ten years of the Journal of Health Monitoring in this editorial. The journal, published by Germany's Robert Koch Institute, appears in German and English, and it carries the country's federal health reporting to both domestic and world readers. Its pages track health status, behavior, and care structures, with a steady focus on how health divides across social groups and why.

Milestones line the decade: listing in the Directory of Open Access Journals in 2023, full texts archived in PubMed Central, and indexing in Scopus from 2025. The editors frame familiarity as a strength and openness as a duty, arguing a trusted house journal must still earn its place beside thousands of rivals. Their audience spans care, policy, and research alike.
pmc-13627226:
Amalia Gastaldelli, Egeria Scoditti, and Maria Paula Macedo, publishing in 2026, review the metabolic engines that push fatty liver disease from simple fat storage toward inflammation and scarring. Their account starts with insulin resistance and broken fat tissue, which flood the liver with fuel, while the liver makes still more fat of its own. The hormone pair insulin and glucagon falls out of balance, bending both sugar and fat traffic and draining the liver's flexibility.

Injury follows as toxic fat and sugar stress hepatocytes, fat tissue and liver trade inflammatory signals, and scar-forming cells wake, settling into a chronic low-grade inflammation the field calls metaflammation. Sex hormones and the gut-liver-fat triangle explain why the disease wears different faces in different people. The synthesis maps where future drugs might cut the circuit.
pmc-13627726:
Emma Wagner and colleagues map not just where two immune checkpoint proteins sit in melanoma, but where they actually touch. Drugs that block the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair work by breaking that contact, yet clinics still dose by protein counts alone. Their method, FuncO:TiME, layers functional interaction mapping with tissue profiling on melanoma samples taken before and after checkpoint therapy, counting millions of pixel-level contacts.

The contact maps varied wildly across each tumor, in patterns the protein counts never hinted at. After treatment, contacts rose even where protein levels stood still, proof that the two measures can walk apart. Reading the handshake rather than the headcount, the authors argue, could one day guide who gets these drugs and how they are combined.
pmc-13628526:
Darren Holmes and five colleagues describe a new route to a family of twisted salts whose shape is locked by hindered rotation, published in 2026. The products are atropisomeric quinolinium salts, molecules whose parts cannot rotate past each other, so the molecule keeps a fixed handedness much like a left or right glove.

Their method swaps a group on the ring while preserving that handedness, passing through a short-lived chlorine-bearing intermediate. Measurements by crystallography, electrochemistry, and light absorption showed the salts rotate so slowly that their shapes would persist for millennia, and they display unusual light-related behaviour and easy oxidation. A simple deprotonation step also gave a neutral chiral relative, widening the family available for study.
pmc-13628726:
Hongfeng Ao and Qian Liu revisited how well standard tissue markers support prostate cancer diagnosis alongside Gleason grading, published in 2026. Their retrospective study covered 147 men treated at two Chinese institutions between 2020 and 2024, eighty-eight with prostate cancer and fifty-nine with benign prostate enlargement.

Cancer tissue stained positive for the androgen receptor and prostate-specific antigen markers significantly more often than benign tissue, though rates were modest. A third marker, P504S, was positive in every cancer case tested but also appeared in about a quarter of benign samples. Staining patterns shifted with tumour grade, while a fourth candidate marker was negative throughout. The authors support the first three markers as useful helpers beside Gleason scoring, especially in ambiguous cases.
pmc-13637126:
Sara khaleghi and five colleagues published this 2026 analysis of cardiovascular death trends in northern Iran from 2011 to 2023. The team pulled every cardiovascular death recorded in Mazandaran province from health and civil registration sources, more than seventy-three thousand deaths in all. Rates were standardized by age so years could be compared fairly. A trend method that hunts for turning points traced how the death rate moved across the thirteen years.

The overall rate eased downward across the period. A clear decline ran to 2018, then the line wobbled upward through the pandemic years without firm statistical support, then fell sharply again after 2021. Men died at higher rates than women throughout. Ischemic heart disease stayed the leading specific killer, with hypertensive disease second. The authors aim prevention at those two causes, and at older adults and men in particular, to keep the decline going.
pmc-13642526:
Seo and colleagues present in 2026 a physics-guided neural operator. This machine learning model predicts how electromagnetic fields spread through tiny optical devices at any wavelength in the visible band, even wavelengths it never saw in training. Slow full-wave simulations are a bottleneck in designing such devices.

Two ideas drive the model. Spectral consistency ties how fields change with wavelength to spatial frequency, and a conditional embedding feeds the model a refined wave prior for the requested wavelength. Tested on three platforms, a single-layer metalens, a five-layer spectrum splitter, and a freeform waveguide, the solver cut field prediction error sharply. Against earlier operator-learning methods the cut reached up to about four fifths on the simplest platform. It runs about forty-two times faster than a standard numerical solver with far fewer parameters.
pmc-13642926:
Fadillah Maani and ten colleagues present FetalCLIP, a 2026 vision-language foundation model for fetal ultrasound. Reading these scans is subjective and skill-dependent, and paired image-text data for training such models have been scarce.

The model learned from 210,035 ultrasound images matched with text, the largest paired set of its kind reported. Across tasks it beat comparison systems: sorting scan types, estimating gestational age, detecting heart defects, and outlining fetal structures. It also stayed strong when only few labeled examples were available for a new task. The team released the model publicly so other groups can build on it.
pmc-13643926:
Katherine D Chau and four colleagues present a study of the germs and plants tied to wild bees across bee families and city settings. Bees carry bacteria and fungi. They also gather pollen and nest scraps, and those ties may shift with city life.

The team read gene markers from thirty-two species in five families. Bacterial and fungal mixes stayed much the same across bee lines, body traits, and city levels. Plant ties told a split tale. They shifted with bee traits and with how built-up a place was. In city areas, plant ties were the main thing that set bee species apart. Some families carried richer germ and plant mixes than others.
pmc-13645526:
Shadi Boqaaiya and seven colleagues present a retrospective comparison of cataract surgery outcomes in older Jewish and Arab patients in northern Israel, treated inside one shared hospital system. Records covered 251 patients aged sixty and over operated during 2023 at Ziv Medical Center in Safed.

Baseline age, sex, and vision were similar, but Arab patients carried more diabetes and hypertension. At thirty days their corrected vision lagged the Jewish group's, and complications such as corneal swelling and capsule rupture were more frequent. The authors attribute the gap to structural, economic, and comorbidity factors rather than ethnicity itself, and call for prospective multicenter work.
pmc-13646726:
Jiawang Zhao and Ping Yin audit how studies of stomach acid drugs and a severe gut infection define what they measure. The drugs are proton pump inhibitors, widely used for reflux, and the infection is Clostridioides difficile, a cause of dangerous diarrhea. Rather than asking whether the drugs raise risk, the pair ask whether each published result could even observe its claimed outcome cleanly. Eleven evidence sources passed their screening.

The sources turned out to target different things: most measured new infections, while others measured detection, severity, or death among the already infected. Effect measures, time windows, and case-finding methods varied widely, and three reviews mixed definitions from their source studies. Two registry reports overlapped and were counted as one cluster. The authors conclude the estimates do not answer one shared question, and they offer their observability profile as a tool for readers of tangled literatures.
pmc-13647126:
Mya G. Flannery, Mona A. Hamad, and Spencer S. Gang test whether two enzymes of purine salvage, a recycling pathway for DNA building blocks, also guard worms against infection. In the standard lab worm, breaking these enzymes switches on an internal defense program against intracellular pathogens. The trio asked whether the same holds in two cousin species, Caenorhabditis briggsae and Caenorhabditis remanei. They silenced the matching genes in each species with a feeding method.

Silencing either enzyme switched on the worm versions of the defense marker genes in both species, just as in the lab worm. The result shows the immune role of these recycling enzymes is conserved across the genus, not a quirk of one species. That conservation suggests an old, shared link between basic metabolism and innate defense. The work gives evolution researchers a firm comparative foothold for tracing how the pathway was recruited into immunity.
pmc-13648226:
Ahmed I. Yunus and three colleagues test a reinforcement-learning controller, software that learns actions from rewards, for a full-scale anaerobic digestion plant that turns wastewater solids into biogas. Digesters are usually run cautiously because feedback is slow and upsets can destabilise the biology.

A calibrated digital twin model of the plant was built first, then a learning policy was trained on simulated years of operation to raise gas output while penalising acidity and instability signals. Tested against historical and rule-based control, the policy matched output in simulation and suggested a modest possible gain on real plant data. The authors stress that the benefit carries substantial uncertainty and needs careful interpretation.
pmc-13648826:
Maphe Mthembu and eleven colleagues survey human papillomavirus infection among teenage girls and young women living in a rural South African district with a heavy HIV burden. The virus causes cervical cancer, and women living with HIV face higher risk, yet local data on which viral types circulate in this age group were limited.

Nested in a larger population trial, the study tested vaginal swabs from 187 participants, about half living with HIV. Roughly seven in ten carried the virus, and high-risk types were more common among those with HIV, with different dominant types by HIV status. No infections with the two types targeted by the national vaccine appeared among vaccine-eligible participants. Condomless sex and other infections raised the odds.
pmc-13649726:
Shige Li and colleagues pooled trials on whether more protein helps adults in intensive care. The best dose has long been in doubt, and fresh hints said effects might split by patient type. Their search found 33 trials with 11,622 patients in all.

More protein did not cut deaths, time on breathing machines, or time in the unit, and strict checks backed those flat results. Some muscle measures did favour the high group, yet life quality trended a bit worse. Blood waste rose on high protein, as expected. One split stood out: patients with sharp kidney injury died more on high protein, while those who also got rehab care fared better. The authors urge care in dosing by patient type.
pmc-13650426:
Kateryna Riabchenko and one co-author assess the future of voluntary hospitalization insurance in Switzerland. That private top-up cover pays for perks such as a private room and free choice of doctor during hospital stays. Mandatory insurance has widened over time, and hospital financing reforms now share more inpatient costs from public funds, shrinking the private product's old role.

Drawing on papers, policy documents, market data, and ten interviews with stakeholders, the brief names four pressures. They are growing dependence on the mandatory system, changing patterns of hospital use, uneven gains between insurers and hospitals, and fragmented price arrangements. Three responses follow: modernize the products through innovation, speak more clearly with policyholders and patients, and publish better public reporting on coverage, pricing, and use. The authors argue that openness plus fresh ideas will decide whether this insurance stays a credible part of the Swiss system.
pmc-13650726:
Zhao Feng Liu and seven colleagues, publishing in 2026, weigh two strategies against brain spread of small cell lung cancer. One option irradiates the brain in advance to kill invisible deposits. The other watches the brain with regular magnetic resonance scans and treats only what appears. The preventive approach is traditional, yet it carries cognitive costs.

Fourteen studies covering 2,881 patients were pooled. In limited-stage disease, preventive irradiation improved survival and time without progression while cutting brain metastases, a clear win. In extensive-stage disease it still halved the brain metastasis risk, yet survival and progression outcomes matched the surveillance group. The authors conclude that preventive treatment keeps its place when disease is limited, while active scanning may serve extensive-stage patients just as well with less toxicity. Searches ran through April 2025 across five databases.
pmc-13651526:
Suzanne E Davison and five co-authors turn sulfurdiimides, the nitrogen cousins of sulfur dioxide, into traps for carbon radicals, unlocking a new family of sulfur-nitrogen drug motifs. Such aza-sulfur groups are prized in medicine and crop protection for their tunable traits, yet they are hard to make, and sulfurdiimides had never been used this way.

The team synthesized a series of stable, unsymmetrical sulfurdiimide reagents whose appetite for radicals can be dialed by choosing the right nitrogen substituent. A paired acridine and copper catalyst system then stripped carbon dioxide from plain carboxylic acids, abundant commercial starting materials, and steered the resulting radicals into the waiting sulfurdiimides. The products, sulfinamidines, arrived in wide variety with good tolerance for other chemical groups, and the process scaled cleanly. The authors present the platform as a swift doorway into complex sulfur(VI) groups.
pmc-13651826:
Zhi Feng Sherman Lim and twelve colleagues engineer regulatory T cells, the immune system's peacekeepers, to carry a custom receptor aimed at one target in Sjögren's disease. The disease is an autoimmune attack on moisture glands. Patients often lack effective regulation, and today's treatments only soothe symptoms or suppress immunity broadly.

The receptor recognizes a dominant fragment of the Ro60 protein, a hallmark autoantigen, displayed by the risk gene variant strongly tied to the disease. In laboratory tests the engineered cells suppressed the autoreactive T cells that drive the disease more effectively than ordinary unmodified regulatory cells drawn from many donors. The work is preclinical proof of concept, not a patient result. The authors argue the Ro60 axis is genuinely pathogenic and that antigen-specific regulatory therapy could restore tolerance for the genetically defined slice of patients who carry that display molecule.
pmc-2803126:
Chen, Arendall, Headd, and co-authors present MolProbity, a web service for validating macromolecular structures. Crystallographers publish atomic models whose quality varies, and errors can hide in fine detail. MolProbity evaluates model quality broadly, at both whole-structure and local levels, for proteins and nucleic acids alike.

A key strength comes from carefully placing hydrogen atoms, which sharpens detection of clashes and bad geometry. Users get a clear report of where a model is sound and where it needs rebuilding. Routine validation with such tools raised the trustworthiness of the public structure archive.
pmc-5331226:
Schafer, White, Iijima, and their team asked in 2017 if senescent cells drive a fatal lung disease. The disease, called IPF, scars the lungs from the inside. Breath grows harder year by year, and no cure exists. Its cause is not known.

Senescent cells are old cells that have stopped dividing. Marks of such cells show up in diseased lung tissue. In old mice, clearing these cells made lungs work better. The team tested whether the same cells help drive the disease itself. If they do, drugs that clear senescent cells could be a new path to treat a disease that now has few options.
pmc-5702726:
Benjamin Callahan, Paul McMurdie, and Susan Holmes argued for a change in marker-gene analysis in 2017. Studies of microbes often group DNA reads into clusters that differ by less than a set cutoff. Those clusters, called operational taxonomic units, blur real differences between strains.

New methods can instead recover the exact DNA sequences present in a sample. Exact variants give finer detail, can be compared across studies, and carry stable labels. The authors show the older clustering step is no longer needed. Their case helped shift the field toward exact sequence methods, which are now standard in microbiome work.
pmc-6602426:
Konrad Labun, Tessa Montague, Maximilian Krause, and coauthors presented CHOPCHOP version 3 in 2019. CHOPCHOP is a web toolbox for designing CRISPR experiments. The CRISPR system began as a way to cut DNA at chosen spots.

The toolbox has grown beyond simple editing to target RNA and to switch genes on or off without cutting. Users pick a genome, name a target, and get ranked guide designs with predicted off-targets. Visual displays show where guides land. Bench scientists lean on it to plan screens and edits before ordering any reagents in the laboratory.
pmc-7338126:
Nader Salari and colleagues pooled the world's early evidence in 2020 on how the COVID-19 pandemic weighed on the minds of ordinary people. Their systematic review and meta-analysis gathered studies that measured stress, anxiety, and depression in general populations during the crisis. They argued that watching population mental health during such an emergency should be an immediate priority for health systems.

Combining the studies, the authors estimate how widespread each of these problems was while the pandemic unfolded. Their figures gave officials an early sense of the scale of distress beyond hospital walls. The review is also a record of how quickly mental health research mobilized, and of the uneven quality of those first rapid surveys.
pmc-7567026:
The Global Burden of Disease 2019 Diseases and Injuries Collaborators published in 2020 the flagship accounting of what makes people sick and injured around the world. Their systematic analysis covers three hundred sixty-nine diseases and injuries. It spans more than two hundred countries and territories across the years 1990 to 2019.

For each condition, the study estimates how many people live with it, how many die from it, and how much healthy life it costs. One shared method is applied everywhere, so a stroke in one country and malaria in another enter the same ledger. Health leaders use this ledger to spot neglected conditions, track progress against major killers, and argue for funding with numbers that critics can check.
pmc-9849126:
Mitja Kurki and a large team of collaborators described FinnGen in 2023, a project drawing genetic insight from Finland's well documented population. Finland is a population isolate, shaped by a founding bottleneck long ago. Harmful variants that are rare elsewhere often survive there concentrated in a smaller number of low frequency variants, which makes them easier to find and study.

FinnGen links genetic data from hundreds of thousands of Finns with detailed health records. The article explains the resource and the discoveries that structure makes possible, including variants that point to disease mechanisms and drug targets. Findings from isolates have repeatedly taught lessons that apply to everyone, which is why the world's geneticists watch this project.
queste-holy-grail-comfort-1926:
The Quest of the Holy Grail is W. W. Comfort's 1926 English version of the Queste del Saint Graal. That French text formed part of the vast Vulgate cycle of Arthurian romance. Its mood is stern and monastic, quite unlike the lighter tales of Arthur's court.

Only the pure may achieve the Grail in this telling. Galahad, Perceval, and Bors ride out and, by grace, they succeed. Lancelot, the greatest knight of the world, is shut out by his sin with the queen. The quest becomes a lesson in repentance, and it changed how all later writers told the Grail story.
radin-crashing-thunder-1926:
Crashing Thunder was a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) man who told his life story to Paul Radin, who published it in 1926. Few books of the era let a Native American speak at such length in the first person about his own life.

He tells of his upbringing, his visions, his years of drinking and violence, and his turn to the peyote religion. His story moves through the Thunderbird clan's world of spirits, feasts, and obligations. Radin kept the telling close to the man's own voice and order. The result reads like a novel but is a real life, and it opened a new kind of native autobiography.
rasa-jala-nidhi-or-ocean-of-indian-chemi: Rasa-Jala-Nidhi, or Ocean of Indian Chemistry and Alchemy, volume one, was compiled in Sanskrit by Rasacharya Kaviraj Bhudeb Mookerji, M.A., principal of the Bengal College of Ayurveda, with an English translation by the author himself; the title page prices it at six rupees, ten abroad. The contents shown open with an introduction, then chapter one on the requisites for metallurgical operations, the qualifications of teacher and disciple, and the construction of a laboratory.
schleiermacher-soliloquies-1926:
Schleiermacher's Soliloquies, his Monologen of 1800, are a New Year gift the young thinker wrote for himself and his friends. Horace Leland Friess translated them for the Open Court edition of 1926. Friedrich Schleiermacher had just published his famous Speeches on Religion, and the Soliloquies turn the same searching mind inward.

The romantic self holds dialogue with itself on freedom, youth, aging, and the shape of a worthy life. Schleiermacher vows to stay true to his inner law against the world's pressure to conform. The prose glows with the ideals of his circle: friendship, love, and self-culture. Readers meet here the private voice of liberal theology's founder, thinking aloud.
scott-hermetica-vol-3-1926:
Walter Scott closed his Hermetica project with a third volume of notes in 1926. Commentary here covers the Latin Asclepius and the Hermetic excerpts in Stobaeus. The volume completes one of the fullest commentaries on ancient mystical writing.

The Asclepius is the famed dialogue on God, man, and Egypt's coming ruin. Stobaeus, a later collector, preserved Hermetic scraps found nowhere else. Scott walks through every hard line and links pieces to the wider tradition. His notes connect philosophy, religion, and magic in late antiquity. Together the three volumes gave English readers a complete Hermetic library with guidance.
smuts-holism-evolution-1926:
Holism and Evolution, published in 1926, is Jan Christiaan Smuts's philosophy of wholes. Smuts, the South African soldier-statesman, coined the word holism here for his claim that nature builds ever richer wholes, and that this building is evolution's deepest fact.

From matter to life to mind to personality, each level is a whole more than the sum of its parts, and mechanism cannot exhaust it. Smuts writes as a field naturalist and a statesman, not a laboratory man. The book influenced ecology and systems thought far beyond philosophy. Its vision of wholes remains its author's most original legacy.
spengler-decline-west-vol-1-1926:
Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 1, appears in Charles Francis Atkinson's translation of 1926. Subtitled Form and Actuality, the volume states Spengler's bold scheme. Cultures, he argues, are organisms that pass through birth, growth, maturity, and decay. Each has its own soul and its own mathematics, art, and science.

The West, in his reading, has entered its late, hard phase of civilization. Spengler compares cultures side by side in vast tables of parallel ages. Critics call the method prophetic rather than scientific. The book was the most debated philosophy of history of its century. Atkinson's version carried the debate into English.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5026:
Ulysses S. Grant gives eight yearly addresses, from December 6, 1869, to December 5, 1876, parted by three stars. Coming before Congress for the first time as chief magistrate, Grant voices thanks for the many gains the nation holds. Peace reigns at home, no binding pacts abroad bode trouble, and the land, of a size to feed five hundred million people, teems with crops and useful minerals.

Forty million free people speak one tongue, he notes, with schooling open to all and no road to fame barred. The press, the pulpit, and the school stand free, and income flows into the national chest past the government's needs. Concord is fast coming back within the home borders, Grant adds, and crafts new to the country are taking root as the wounds of war close.
summers-history-witchcraft-1926:
Montague Summers was a Catholic priest and a firm foe of witchcraft. His History of Witchcraft and Demonology came out in 1926. Summers held, as few of his day did, that the witch cult was real. His book tells the tale with vast stores of fact.

Pacts with the Devil, sabbats, and spells fill the early parts. The great trials of Europe and the New World take up the rest. Summers cites trial rolls, old tracts, and church law in bulk. The book is a mine of tales, read best with a keen eye on its slant.
swift-gullivers-travels-1726:
Jonathan Swift published Gulliver's Travels in 1726, in the first edition text used here. The full title sends Gulliver into several remote nations of the world. Readers took it first as a true travel tale, then as fierce satire.

Gulliver visits Lilliput, where men are six inches tall and wars turn on eggs. In Brobdingnag he is tiny, and a huge king scorns England's pride and guns. Later trips reach a flying island and the wise horse Houyhnhnms and brutish Yahoos. Man looks worse at each stop, and pride takes the hardest knocks of all. Swift's prose stays cool while the charges grow more and more savage.
tawney-religion-capitalism-1926:
R. H. Tawney published Religion and the Rise of Capitalism in 1926, a classic of economic history. Tawney, an English historian and socialist, studies how Christian teaching met the new market world. Medieval bans on usury gave way as commerce grew. Puritan teaching, he argues, could both discipline greed and bless success.

The book is often called the English answer to Weber's Protestant ethic. Tawney writes with moral force and fine irony. He mourns a lost age when faith set limits on acquisition. His closing plea joins economics to ethics. The work remains a humane, learned critique of acquisitive society. It shaped British social thought for decades.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 26 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated May 6, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a special inducement. A subscriber who pays $2.50 for a year's subscription in a new name receives a book. The book is Rand, McNally and Company's 1897 Atlas of the World. It holds 160 pages of colored maps, printed from new plates. Its regular price is $2.50.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Don Quixote, by Miguel de Cervantes, reaches Volume 2, Part 26 here, in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter twenty-three tells of the wonderful things the incomparable Don Quixote said he saw in the profound cave of Montesinos. The chapter title warns that the size and strangeness of the claims cause the adventure to be deemed apocryphal.

At about four in the afternoon, with the sun veiled in clouds, Don Quixote begins his account for two hearers. He starts by measuring the depth at some twelve or fourteen times a man's height. Cervantes frames the tale as a report twice-told, leaving the reader to judge a vision no witness can check.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
A supplementary number of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, numbered 288, leads with a feature called Spirit of the Annuals for 1828. The annuals were gift books, and the magazine calls their new crop a splendid intellectual banquet served by master spirits of the age. A footnote hopes the word master will not seem ungallant, since the ladies contributed the best poetical portion of the feast. This display of female talent, the editor warns the lords, grows in brilliancy yearly.

The editor then sorts contributors by a wine list joke. L.E.L. and Hood count as hock and champagne, still and sparkling. Miss Mitford and Bernard Barton rank as bucellas, a lighter white wine. Mrs. Hemans alone supplies the lacrymae Christi. Above the feature sits an engraving of a victorious armament returning to a Greek city.
the-two-guardians-or-home-in-this-world-:
Charlotte Mary Yonge's Two Guardians appears in a second record whose preface matches, word for word in substance, the one heading its sibling copy in this library. Yonge explains that her tales convey their moral rather than inculcating it directly, picturing ordinary life with its small daily events turned to the best account. Great events are excluded, excitement sacrificed to character painting, and each story built on a key-note principle, as Abbeychurch teaches self-control against conceit.

The preface then turns to The Castle Builders. That tale shows the instability of mind that follows a neglected daily course. Its characters want a practical, obedient life, yet do not seek strength in the appointed means of grace. Readers holding either record get the same authorial map. The novel itself, of Marian and her guardian, begins after this shared doorway.
tilden-toxemia-explained-1926:
John Henry Tilden blamed nearly all illness on one cause, and Toxemia Explained of 1926 states his case in full. Tilden, a Denver doctor who had turned against drug prescribing, taught that waste the body fails to clear poisons the blood. That state, toxemia, then shows itself as many different diseases.

Rest, fasting, and right living form his cure, since drugs only mask the warning signs. Tilden walks readers through digestion, habits, and the slow build-up of enervation, his word for drained nerve energy. The book became a classic of natural hygiene, and its plain, stern advice still finds readers.
tob-0144-61626:
Volume four completes the Gutenberg set of The Secret Doctrine with further theosophical pieces. Blavatsky's scheme of cosmic cycles, root races, and hidden masters fills out its last corners here. Readers who have come this far meet the system at its most detailed and most demanding.

The extra writings answer objections, expand on symbols, and tie loose threads from the earlier volumes. Little in them makes sense alone; together they crown the largest occult system of the nineteenth century. Whether one accepts a word of it or not, the work's scale and influence are hard to deny. The full set rewards slow, patient reading.
tob-10626:
Unknown authors in the early centuries told the story of Adam and Eve after Eden in the Life of Adam and Eve. Versions survive in Latin, Greek, and other tongues. The work belongs to the pseudepigrapha, Jewish and Christian writings outside the Bible's canon.

After their expulsion, Adam and Eve repent in hunger and grief, with Adam standing forty days in the Jordan River. Satan tells his own fall, Eve laments her fault, and the book ends with Adam's death and burial. Tender and sad, it fills gaps Genesis leaves open and shaped later tales of the first parents.
tob-10826:
Henry Ridgely Evans spent his hours with ghosts professionally: he was a stage magician and a debunker of fraudulent mediums. Hours with the Ghosts visits haunted houses, spirit photographs, and slate-writing mediums, then looks for the tricks behind them. Entertainment and exposure proceed together, with one skeptical eyebrow raised.

Evans retells famous hauntings and séances in detail before explaining wires, confederates, and sleight of hand. He loves a good ghost story too much to be dull, and knows stagecraft too well to be fooled. Readers who like their spooks investigated, by a man who could perform the tricks himself, will enjoy his company.
tob-13326:
Edwin Arnold published The Light of Asia in 1879, an epic poem telling the Buddha's life in Miltonic blank verse. The sheltered prince Siddhartha, raised behind palace walls, encounters age, sickness, death, and a wandering ascetic: the four sights that drive his search. Enlightenment under the bodhi tree forms the climax.

Arnold's poem sold hundreds of thousands of copies and introduced the Victorian world to Buddhism more effectively than any scholarly treatise of its day. He presents the Buddha with Christian-era reverence, a framing modern readers will notice. As a cultural event, The Light of Asia genuinely lit a path for Western interest in Asia's religions.
tob-4026:
Benedictus de Spinoza wrote his Ethics in geometric form: definitions, axioms, propositions, and proofs, as if philosophy were Euclid. Its claim is the most radical of the seventeenth century. God and Nature are one substance, everything follows from that substance's nature by necessity, and human freedom lies in understanding necessity rather than escaping it.

Spinoza had been excommunicated from Amsterdam's Jewish community and published nothing under his name during his life; the Ethics appeared after his death. Emotions, bondage, and the intellectual love of God occupy its later parts. Patient readers find a serene, demanding system that modern philosophy keeps rediscovering.
tob-4126:
Reynold A. Nicholson's first book, in 1898, selected poems from the Divan of Shams-i Tabriz. The poems are Rumi's, named for Shams, the wandering friend whose love and loss remade Rumi into a poet. Nicholson, then a young scholar, chose lyrics of love-madness as the road to God.

English readers met Rumi the lyric poet here, decades before Nicholson's great Mathnawi translation. The versions are free but fervent, drunk on their subject in the right way. Checked from the 1919 printing, the selection still glows. It shows both poets at once: Rumi in Persian fire, Nicholson in English devotion.
tob-4226:
A. E. Waite played detective in The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts, published in 1898. He surveys the grimoires one by one: the Key of Solomon, the Grimorium Verum, the Grand Grimoire, and their kin. For each he asks what the rituals actually say, apart from the legends around them.

Waite prints rites of evocation and pact in detail, then judges them with a scholar-magician's dry scorn. His critical sorting shaped how the next century read the whole grimoire shelf. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book remains a sharp, skeptical guide through magic's darkest library.
toland-celtic-religion-druids-1726:
John Toland was an Irish free thinker. He wrote this study of Celtic faith and learning late in life, and it came out in 1726, after his death. The text here is from the 1815 printing. Toland was known for bold views on faith and church power.

He treated the druids as men of their time, not as priests of dark rites. With a cool eye he sifted old Greek and Roman reports from Welsh and Irish lore. His book was the first clear, sharp account of the druids in the age of reason.
tombazi-photographic-expedition-kangchen:
Nicholas Tombazi took a camera to the glaciers of Kangchenjunga and came back with a tale for the ages. His Account of a Photographic Expedition to the Southern Glaciers appeared in 1926. In it he tells what he saw on the Sikkim side in 1925.

At 15,500 feet he watched a wild man, as he took it, moving on the slope below him. He tells of the form, the gait, and the measured footprints left in the snow. His is the most detailed early yeti report from a trained observer. The book anchors the whole shelf of yeti lore.
twelfth-night-pg1526: A contents list and cast list open this Twelfth Night record, credited to William Shakespeare. The scenes move between the Duke's palace, the sea-coast, and Olivia's house and garden across five acts. The persons include Orsino, the twins Viola and Sebastian, and the countess Olivia. Sir Toby Belch, Sir Andrew Aguecheek, and the steward Malvolio promise the comedy's mischief. Only the contents and cast are present here, so the play itself does not appear.
un-ga-res-26: Two working groups owe their start to Resolution 26, passed by the UN General Assembly in its first session in 1946. One group was to weigh the transfer of some tasks, work, and assets of the dying League of Nations to the new UN. The other was to study where the UN should build its lasting home. Every member state could sit on both groups.
un-ga-res-a-69-26:
Africa's ban on nuclear arms is backed in Resolution A/69/26, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Treaty of Pelindaba, signed in Cairo on 11 April 1996, made the whole African continent a zone free of nuclear weapons. The Security Council had hailed the signing the next day as a real gain for world peace and safety.

The text recalls Assembly votes of 1996 and 2001 on the treaty, and the stands of the African Union. Zones free of nuclear arms, it argues, raise safety most where strains run high, and it names the Middle East as such a place. The vote urges the treaty's full force and reach across Africa.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 26, from the first session in 1946, is a brief founding order. The Assembly set up two temporary committees open to every member state. One was a League of Nations Committee, to weigh the transfer of certain League duties, work, and assets. The other was a Permanent Headquarters Committee, to weigh the site of the United Nations' lasting home.

Resolution 69/26 of the General Assembly welcomes the African Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone Treaty, the Treaty of Pelindaba, signed in Cairo in 1996 and in force since 15 July 2009. The Assembly calls on African states that have not yet signed or ratified to do so quickly. It thanks the nuclear-weapon states that have signed the treaty's protocols and urges them to ratify. It asks states parties to complete safeguards agreements with the International Atomic Energy Agency. Three conferences of states parties had met in Addis Ababa by 2014.
un-sc-res-1026:
Bosnia's peace deal had just been initialed when the Council met in November 1995. On 30 November 1995 it extended UNPROFOR until 31 January 1996. The force would hold the line pending the peace agreement's use. The Dayton deal had been initialed on 21 November. Bosnia, Croatia, and Yugoslavia were among its signers. The Council welcomed the Secretary-General's report on the next steps.

The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed on the peace process. His reports would carry facts and advice on carrying out the deal. The short extension bridged an awkward gap. A NATO-led force was about to take over the military task. UNPROFOR's troubled three years were nearly over.
un-sc-res-126:
Kashmir's stalled settlement was reviewed by the Security Council on 2 December 1957. Gunnar Jarring, Sweden's representative, had traveled to the region under resolution 123 (1957) and reported on what blocked progress. Both India and Pakistan still accepted the plan for a free and impartial plebiscite on the future of Jammu and Kashmir. The Council thanked Jarring and voiced concern at the lack of movement.

The Council asked both governments to make no statements and take no steps that could worsen the situation. Each was to urge calm on its own people so that talks could go forward. The United Nations Representative for India and Pakistan was asked to propose further action to the parties. He was authorized to visit the subcontinent for that purpose. He had to report on his efforts as soon as possible. Demilitarization remained a key step toward any settlement.
un-sc-res-1526:
Terrorism financing is the battleground of Resolution 1526, adopted in January 2004. It tightened the sanctions system aimed at Al-Qaida and the Taliban, which listed people and groups whose money had to be frozen. A new team of experts was created to watch how states complied.

The text sharpens the list's rules, presses states to act against listed names at home, and gives the monitoring team a wider reach. Sanctions texts like this one run quietly in the background of counterterrorism for years. This one shows the machinery being rebuilt after early lists proved patchy and uneven.
un-sc-res-1626:
UNMIL was extended with an election surge on 19 September 2005. Liberia's presidential and legislative elections were set for October. State authority was spreading, with a new police service and fresh judges. The transitional government had just signed the GEMAP program on honest economic management. UNAMSIL in Sierra Leone was set to close on 31 December 2005.

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate for six months. Liberian parties were called to show full commitment to a democratic process free of violence. With troop contributors' consent, UNMIL could help guard the Special Court for Sierra Leone's premises once UNAMSIL left. A temporary rise in the mission's personnel ceiling was authorized to cover the elections. Extra staff would secure the vote and the weeks around it. The world was called to answer Liberia's continuing needs generously. GEMAP's swift start was welcomed as the path to lifting the sanctions of resolution 1521 (2003).
un-sc-res-1726:
Côte d'Ivoire's mission received a short extension at the end of 2006. On 15 December 2006 the Security Council kept UNOCI and its French support force until 10 January 2007. The Secretary-General had reported on the country that month. The Council restated its support for the impartial forces on the ground. It voiced serious concern at the stalled peace process. Elections had been delayed again that autumn.

The brief term covered the year-end while a new plan was weighed. An African Union backed roadmap had set fresh deadlines weeks earlier. The mission's troops held the zone between government and rebel areas. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. A longer renewal with a revised mandate followed in January.
un-sc-res-1826:
Côte d'Ivoire returns in United Nations Security Council Resolution 1826, adopted on 29 July 2008. The Ouagadougou peace deal was slowly taking hold. A first round of presidential elections was set for 30 November 2008. Rights abuses, including sexual violence, still scarred daily life.

The text renews the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire and its French support force until 31 January 2009. The mission must give the election commission transport and other practical help. Ivorian forces and former rebels are urged to draw up one shared security plan for the vote. The Council also presses for faster voter listing, disarmament, and the return of state services.
un-sc-res-1926: Judge Thomas Buergenthal resigned from the International Court of Justice in 2010. His departure would take effect on 6 September that year. On 2 June 2010 the Security Council fixed the date to fill the vacancy. The election would be held on 9 September 2010. It would take place at a Council meeting and at a General Assembly meeting. The Assembly was then in its sixty-fourth session. The short text performs only that scheduling act.
un-sc-res-2026: Resolution 2026 stands in the Security Council's numbered output, preserved here as an official-record transcription from English Wikisource. The Council's decisions are the primary documents of its work, outliving the debates around them. This decision is kept whole: the facts as the members stated them and the steps they voted to take in response.
un-sc-res-226:
The Congo accused Portugal of hosting its enemies in 1966. Congolese leaders said Angola, under Portuguese rule, served as a mercenary base. Portugal replied that no mercenaries or camps existed there. On 14 October 1966 the Council took note of both statements. It then urged Portugal to match its own denial with action. Foreign mercenaries must not use Angola to meddle in the Congo's affairs.

All states had to keep out of the Congo's domestic business. The Secretary-General was told to watch how the resolution was used. The vote was unanimous. The text reflects the Congo's early years of coups and foreign plots. Mercenary bands based across its borders were a constant threat to the young state.
un-sc-res-26: How judges of the world court are picked gained a shared rule in Security Council Resolution 26, of 4 June 1947. The Assembly had adopted a stopgap rule in November 1946, if the Council would agree. Under it, a meeting held to elect court judges must sit on till each open seat is filled, by a full majority of votes in one or more rounds. The Council agrees to the rule and adopts it for its own such meetings too.
un-sc-res-326: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 326, catalogued here for 1970. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-426:
One day after the Council created UNIFIL on paper, it gave the new force its legal shape. Resolution 425 had ordered Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon and called for a United Nations force there. The Secretary-General reported on 19 March 1978 on how to carry that order out. Resolution 426 was adopted the same day.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report in full. It decided that the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon would be established on the terms set out in that report. The force was set up for an initial period of six months. After that, it would continue in operation if required, provided the Council so decided. The short text is the founding decision for UNIFIL. The force it created in March 1978 is still the basis of the United Nations presence in southern Lebanon.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Peace came to Bosnia on paper in November 1995. The Dayton talks had birthed a pact. The sides first signed their names to it on 21 November in Ohio. A formal rite would come later. UNPROFOR, the much-tried force in Bosnia, still held the field. Resolution 1026 passed with no dissent on 30 November 1995.

The force's term stretched to 31 January 1996, and no more by this grant. The pause let the Council plan the handover. The chief had to send word fast on how the pact would shift tasks. His report of 23 November fed the choice. The goal was a clean pass of the baton, as the pact set out. The force won warm praise for its hard years of work.

Kashmir's stalled settlement is the subject of Resolution 126, adopted on 2 December 1957 by ten votes to none with one Soviet abstention. A Swedish envoy, Gunnar Jarring, had traveled to India and Pakistan for the Council that spring and reported on his mission. Both governments still accepted the older UN plan: Kashmir's future decided by a free and impartial vote of its people.

The Council thanked Jarring for his careful work. It noted with concern that his report showed no real progress toward a settlement. Demilitarization of the state featured in the text as one of the steps on the way. The resolution kept the plebiscite framework formally alive even as the two countries' positions hardened into the pattern that still defines the dispute.

Belgrade's fresh start at the UN ran through this line of 2000. On 31 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1326 without a vote. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was now just Serbia and Montenegro. A decade of wars had shrunk it. Its president had fallen that same month. The state applied as a new member, not as heir to the old seat.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit it. The Assembly seated it the next day. The step settled a long legal fight in quiet fashion. The old federation's membership had passed to no heir on its own. Belgrade accepted a clean slate, and the world body moved on.

Switzerland, the great holdout, joined the UN by way of this line. On 24 July 2002, the Council adopted Resolution 1426 without dissent. It met twice in one day to do so. Swiss voters had backed joining in a national vote that March. Decades of strict neutrality had kept the country out until then.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Swiss Confederation. The Assembly seated it that September. The arrival closed the largest gap in the UN's claim to speak for all states. Switzerland kept its lasting neutrality all the same. It also kept its role as host of the UN's Geneva hub.

Sanctions on Al-Qaida and the Taliban are strengthened on 30 January 2004. The measures — asset freezes, travel bans, and an arms embargo on listed people and groups — dated from earlier resolutions. States, the Council found, needed clearer duties and better help in applying them.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sharpened how the measures should be carried out and widened the sanctions committee's role in watching over them. A stronger monitoring arrangement is set up to help the committee track compliance and breaches. States are pressed to enforce the freeze and bans fully against everyone on the committee's list, and to report on the steps they have taken.

Resolution 1626, adopted on 19 September 2005, links Liberia's elections to safety for the Special Court for Sierra Leone. Liberia was preparing for October presidential and legislative votes, state authority was spreading, and a new economic management program had been signed. Next door, the UN Mission in Sierra Leone was due to end on 31 December 2005, leaving the court without its guard force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, until 31 March 2006. It lets UNMIL send up to 250 soldiers to Sierra Leone from November 2005 to guard the Special Court, with a matching short-term rise in UNMIL's ceiling. It also lets UNMIL rush more troops in to pull those guards and court staff out if a grave safety crisis hits. A drawdown plan for UNMIL is requested for March 2006.

A short extension for a peacekeeping operation in crisis is what Resolution 1726 delivers. Adopted on 15 December 2006, it concerns Côte d'Ivoire, where a civil conflict had split the country and stalled elections. The Council voiced serious worry about worsening conditions and the suffering and displacement of civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council extended the mandates of UNOCI, the UN operation there, and of the French forces backing it, but only until 10 January 2007. That brief window, less than a month, shows the Council buying time while a political deal remained out of reach. It also kept the matter under active review.

Côte d'Ivoire's long-delayed presidential election anchors Resolution 1826, adopted on 29 July 2008. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement of March 2007 had set a peace path, and the first round of voting was set for 30 November 2008. Voter identification and registration still lagged, militias had not fully disarmed, and rights abuses, including sexual violence, continued despite general improvement.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, and the French forces supporting it until 31 January 2009, above all to back free and fair elections. UNOCI must help deliver security for the vote and logistics for the electoral commission. The Council urges faster progress on identification, disarmament, and restoring state authority nationwide. It will review the mandate and troop levels by January 2009, with a report three weeks before that includes benchmarks for a possible phased drawdown.

A judge from the United States chose to step down in 2010. Thomas Buergenthal had sat on the world court for a decade. His term still had time to run. Word of his choice reached the Council that spring. He would leave on 6 September 2010. Resolution 1926 passed on 2 June 2010.

The poll to fill his seat was set for 9 September 2010. Voters in the Council and the Assembly's sixty-fourth session would cast at the same hour. That joint poll is how court judges are always picked. The new judge would serve just the rest of the old term. Buergenthal had fled Nazi camps as a boy. He grew to shape world human rights law. The text marks his exit with the court's plain, set form.

Talks on reuniting Cyprus were moving into a more intensive phase at the end of 2011. Resolution 2026, adopted on 14 December 2011, concerns UNFICYP, the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were negotiating a settlement. The aim was a federation with two zones and two communities. Cyprus's government had agreed that the force should stay.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate until 19 July 2012. It urged both leaders to speed up the talks. The core issues had to be settled before a planned meeting in January 2012. The text also pressed for steps that build trust. More crossing points on the Green Line were one example. Renewed mine clearing in the buffer zone was another.

Mercenaries in Congo drew the Council's fire in the fall of 1966. Congo's envoy said Angola was their base. Angola was then ruled by Portugal. Lisbon's man swore no such camps stood there. Both tales were heard at the 1306th meeting. Resolution 226 passed with no dissent on 14 October 1966. The same day, Botswana won its seat vote.

Portugal was urged, on its own sworn word, to bar the use of Angola. No armed bands could train there to meddle in Congo's affairs. All states were told to keep out of Congo's home fights. The chief had to watch how the call was heeded. Congo's tale had a long tail: this text fed the chain of bans that the 1967 mercenary text would build on.

How judges of the International Court of Justice are elected is the only subject of Resolution 26, adopted unanimously on 4 June 1947. The General Assembly had adopted a rule for its election meetings the year before. Under that rule, a meeting continues until candidates win an absolute majority of votes for all the seats to be filled. The Council agreed to the Assembly's rule. It then adopted the same rule for its own election meetings. The resolution was sent to the General Assembly for its information.

Zambia complained in early 1973 about attacks by the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia. Zambia said the Rhodesian actions included an economic blockade and military threats. South African forces were working with the regime, Zambia charged. The actions were hurting Zambia's security and its economy. Resolution 326 was adopted on 2 February 1973.

The Council condemned every act of provocation and harassment against Zambia. It also condemned repression inside Rhodesia, including recent collective punishments. South Africa's military and armed forces had to withdraw at once and in full. They were to leave Southern Rhodesia and the border with Zambia. Britain, as the ruling power, was told to make sure that happened. Britain also had to bring the illegal regime's actions to an end.

Southern Lebanon gained a UN force in the spring of 1978. On 19 March, the Council adopted Resolution 426. Twelve members voted yes, none voted no, and two held back. China took no part in the vote. Days before, Resolution 425 had demanded that Israel pull out of the south.

The text backs the Secretary-General's report on how the force would work. It sets up the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon for six months at first. The Council could renew it later if need be. The force, known as UNIFIL, had three tasks. It would confirm the Israeli pull-out, restore peace, and help Beirut regain control of the south.
whitehead-religion-making-1926:
Alfred North Whitehead published Religion in the Making in 1926, based on his Lowell Lectures. Whitehead treats religion as a human response to a vision of truth. He traces religion from tribal rites and ritual to more rational, universal forms. Solitude, he argues, stands at the heart of mature faith.

He asks how religion can stay honest in an age of science. Dogmas, he says, are formulas that point beyond themselves and must not harden. The book became a source text for process theology. Whitehead links God to the lure toward value in the world. It is a brief, humane work of religious philosophy.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: Only the Project Gutenberg header is present for Widger's Lincoln set, so no quotations from Lincoln appear. The header gives the full title: quotations from Abraham Lincoln's writings. David Widger's set is number 10 in his series. Release is dated January 2003, as etext number 3626. First posting was June 25, 2001, and the edition is number 10. His contact line begins at the foot of the part shown. Standard license and donation text fills the rest.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol26:
The Journal of Discourses closes with Volume XXVI, printed at Liverpool in 1886 after more than thirty years. Twenty-six volumes hold sermons from 1854 onward, the longest such record of the Latter-day Saint movement ever made. Brigham Young's generation and its heirs speak across the whole run, caught in shorthand and fixed in print.

The final volume keeps the familiar form: doctrine, counsel, and defense from the senior elders of the church. With it, an archive ends that historians of American religion use daily, since nothing else preserves a faith's pulpit so fully. The set stands complete, a church's own voice across three decades.
